## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Commentary on the Theragāthā
## (Volume II)
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-awakened One
## 4. Catukkanipāta (Book of Fours)
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nāgasamāla

The verses beginning with "Alankatā" are those of the Venerable Elder Nāgasamāla. What is their origin? This elder was also born into a respectable family during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. Upon reaching the age of discretion, he saw the Teacher walking on the ground which was intensely hot due to the summer sun's heat. With a heart full of faith, he offered a parasol. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, he was born into the Sakyan royal family and was named Nāgasamāla. When he came of age, he gained faith during a gathering of his relatives, ordained, and served as the Buddha's attendant for some time.

One day, while entering the city for alms, he saw a certain dancing girl, beautifully adorned and decorated, dancing on the main road to the accompaniment of musical instruments. He reflected: "This is merely the movement and transformation of the physical body through the diffusion of the wind element produced by the activity of the mind. Alas! Conditioned things are indeed impermanent." Establishing his insight based on the nature of rise and fall, and intensifying his vipassanā, he attained Arahantship. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The earth was like glowing embers, the ground was covered in hot ashes;
The Buddha Padumuttara was walking in the open air."
2:
"Taking a white parasol while traveling, I saw the Buddha there, and joy arose within me.

'The ground is covered with mirages, this earth is like glowing embers, and fierce winds are blowing, causing discomfort to the body.

'Please accept this parasol, which dispels cold and heat and wards off wind and sun; I wish to experience the peace of Nibbāna.'

Knowing my intention, the Buddha Padumuttara, the Compassionate One, the Merciful One, the Renowned One, the Victorious One of that time, accepted it.

For thirty aeons, I exercised the sovereignty of the king of devas, and five hundred times I was a Cakkavatti king.

I also obtained countless instances of regional kingship; this is the result of my own good deeds previously performed.

This is my final birth; my last existence is proceeding. Even now, a white parasol is held over me at all times.

In the aeon one hundred thousand years ago, I gave that parasol; since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of the gift of a parasol.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

However, after reaching Arahantship, he said:

"Adorned, well-dressed, wearing garlands and anointed with sandalwood, a woman, a dancer, was dancing in the middle of the main road to the sound of music.

Having entered for alms, as I was walking, I gazed at her; adorned and well-dressed, she was like a snare of Death laid out.

Then, wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) arose within me; the danger (ādīnava) became manifest, and disenchantment (nibbidā) was well-established."
3:
"Then my mind was liberated; see the excellent nature of the Dhamma! The three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

With these four verses, he declared his attainment of Arahantship by way of praising his own practice.

In those verses, 'Alankatā' means her body was adorned with ornaments such as bracelets and anklets. 'Suvasanā' means wearing beautiful garments, dressed in splendid clothes. 'Mālinī' means wearing garlands, adorned with flower wreaths. 'Candanussadā' means having a body anointed with sandalwood paste. 'Mazzhe mahāpathe nāri, tūriye naccati naṭṭakī' means in the aforementioned place, a woman, a dancer, an actress, was dancing in the middle of the city street while five-fold musical instruments were being played, performing the dance as it had been arranged.

'Piṇḍikāya' means for the sake of alms. 'Paviṭṭhohaṃ' means I, having entered the city. 'Gacchanto naṃ udikkhisaṃ' means while walking on the city street, looking at the road to avoid dangers, I saw that dancer. How was she? 'Maccupāsaṃva oḍḍitaṃ' means like a set snare of Death. Just as forms and so on, which are like the snares of Death, the King of Death, are spread out and exist in the world, bringing certain harm to beings, so too this dancer, for those blind worldlings who remain without wise reflection, brings certain harm; thus she is said to be like the snare of Death.

'Tato' means because of being like the snare of Death. 'Me' means to me. 'Manasikāro yoniso udapazzatha' means wise reflection arose thus: "This heap of bones, bound by sinews, plastered with flesh, covered by skin, impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive, subject to the nature of impermanence, rubbing, massaging, breaking, and dissolution, is displaying such transformations."

'Ādīnavo pāturahosi' means thus, by way of contemplating the nature of the body, when reflecting on the rise and fall and the inherent fragility of that body and the mental states (citta and cetasika) dependent on it, they appeared as fearful as ogres or demons, and the fault of manifold dangers became manifest to me. And in contrast to that, the benefit of Nibbāna was seen. 'Nibbidā samatiṭṭhatha' means disenchantment (nibbidā-ñāṇa), accomplished through the power of the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā), became well-established in my heart; not even for a moment did the mind cling to those material and immaterial phenomena; rather, through the desire for liberation, a state of equanimity (udāsīna) toward those formations arose.

'Tato' means after the arising of insight. 'Cittaṃ vimucci me' means my mind was liberated from all defilements by the sequence of the Path (magga) produced by supramundane cultivation. By this statement, the arising of the Fruit (phala) is shown. Indeed, at the moment of the Path, one is being liberated from defilements, and at the moment of the Fruit, one is liberated. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nāgasamāla is finished.
4:
'Tato' means after the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). 'Cittaṃ vimucci me' means that through the sequence of the path (magga) occurring due to supramundane cultivation (lokuttara-bhāvanā), my mind has been liberated from all defilements (kilesas). By this, he shows the attainment of the fruit (phala). For at the moment of the path, defilements are being liberated, and at the moment of the fruit, they are liberated. The rest is as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Nāgasamāla is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Bhagu

The verse beginning with 'Ahaṃ middhena' is that of the Venerable Bhagu. The story of his origin is as follows: In the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born into a noble family. Upon reaching maturity, when the Buddha attained Parinibbāna, he honored the relics of that Buddha with flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Nimmānarati heaven and wandered through the realms of gods and humans repeatedly. In this Buddha-era, he was born into the Sakyan royal family and received the name 'Bhagu'. When he reached maturity, he went forth and ordained together with Anuruddha and Kimala. While residing in the village of Bālakaloṇaka, one day, to dispel the overcome of sloth and torpor (thina-middha), he left the monastery and, while ascending the walking path (caṅkama), he fell down. Taking that very fall as a goad (aṅkusa), he dispelled sloth and torpor, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"When the Buddha Padumuttara of great fame attained Parinibbāna,
I made flower garlands and placed them upon his body (relics).

Having gained confidence in that Buddha, I went to the Nimmāna realm;
While in the world of gods, I remembered that meritorious deed.

A rain of flowers falls on me from the sky at all times;
If I wander in the human world, I become a king of great fame.

There, a rain of blossoms falls on me always;
By the power of that flower offering to the All-Seeing One.

This is my last existence, my final birth;
Even today, a rain of flowers falls on me always."
5: "One hundred thousand aeons ago, I offered a flower. Due to the merit of that offering to the Exalted One, I have never known a miserable rebirth. My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out." The Teacher, approaching the Elder who had attained Arahantship and was spending his time in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna, in order to express appreciation for his solitary dwelling, asked: "Dear monk, are you living diligently?" Desiring to make known his diligent dwelling, the Elder recited these four verses: "Overcome by drowsiness, I left the dwelling. As I was ascending the walkway, I fell right there on the ground at the stairs of the walkway. Having wiped my limbs and ascended the walkway again, I paced on the walkway with a well-concentrated mind within. Then, wise attention arose in me; the danger became manifest, and revulsion was established. Then my mind was liberated. Behold the excellence of the Dhamma! The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out." In those verses, "middhena pakato" means overcome by drowsiness, which is characterized by mental sluggishness and the nature of destroying energy. "Vihārā" means from the dwelling. "Upanikkhamiṃ" means went out to walk. "Tattheva papatiṃ chamā" means fell on the ground right there at the stairs of the walkway due to being overcome by sleep. "Gattāni parimajjitvā" means wiping one's limbs that were covered in dust from falling on the ground. "Punapāruyha caṅkamaṃ" means ascending the walkway again without shrinking back with the thought, "Now I have fallen." "Ajjhattaṃ susamāhito" means walking with a well-concentrated and one-pointed mind by removing the hindrances in the meditation object within. The rest is as previously explained. This very verse was the Elder's declaration of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa). ## The Commentary on the Verses of Bhagu Thera is finished.

## 3. Sabhiyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Pare ca" is the verse of the Venerable Sabhiya. What is the account of this Elder’s origin? This Sabhiya, having performed special merits under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome deeds in various existences, was reborn in a good family during the time of Kakusandha Buddha. Upon reaching the age of discretion, he saw the Blessed One going for his day-rest and, with a heart full of faith, offered him a pair of sandals. Due to that wholesome kamma of offering sandals, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. After the Parinibbāna of Kassapa Buddha and the establishment of the golden stupa, he ordained in the Dispensation along with six other young men of good family, being the seventh member of the group. While residing in the forest after taking a meditation subject, they were unable to attain any special distinction. He then said to the remaining six: "When we go for alms, we still have concern for life. One who has concern for life is unable to attain the supramundane Dhamma. To die as a worldling (puthujjana) is also very painful. Come, let us build a ladder, climb to the mountain top, and practice the Dhamma of a recluse without concern for body or life." They did exactly as he suggested.

At that time, among them, the Great Elder, being possessed of the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā) on that very day and brought alms-food from Uttarakuru. The others said: "Venerable sir, you have completed your task. Even mere conversation with you is a proliferation (papañca) for us. We shall only practice the Dhamma of a recluse. You should enjoy the happiness of the Dhamma in this very life by yourself," and they refused the alms-food. The Elder, unable to make them accept, departed.

After two or three days had passed, one among them realized the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala) along with the supernormal powers. When he spoke in the same manner, he was also refused and departed. Among them, the Arahant Elder attained Parinibbāna, and the Non-returner Elder was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes). The remaining five monks died as worldlings and, after enjoying divine bliss in the six heavens of the sensual sphere in both direct and reverse order, passed away from the deva realm during the time of our Buddha. One took rebirth in the Malla royal family, one in the Gandhāra royal family, one in a foreign land (Bāhira), and one in the womb of a woman of good family in Rājagaha.

The remaining one took rebirth in the womb of a female wanderer (paribbājikā). That female wanderer was the daughter of a certain khattiya. Her parents, saying "Let our daughter learn various doctrines," entrusted her to a certain wanderer. Then, that wanderer committed misconduct with her, and she became pregnant. Seeing her pregnant, the wanderers expelled her. While she...
7:
(That woman), while traveling to another place, gave birth in a public hall (sabhā) along the way. For that reason, the boy was given the name Sabhiya. When Sabhiya grew up, he ordained as a wanderer, learned various sciences, and became a great debater. While wandering about engaged in debates, he found no one equal to himself. He built a hermitage at the city gate and lived there teaching sciences to princes and others. A Brahma (a former companion) who had been reborn in the Brahma realm—having attained jhāna after loathing the female state of one who had been his mother—prepared twenty questions and gave them to him, and he went about asking various recluses and brahmins. They were unable to explain the meaning of those questions. In the Commentary on the Sabhiya Sutta, however, it is stated: "A Suddhāvāsa Brahma prepared those questions and gave them."

When the Blessed One, having set in motion the Noble Wheel of Dhamma, arrived at Rājagaha in due course and resided at Veluvana Monastery, Sabhiya went there, approached the Teacher, and asked those questions. The Teacher answered those questions for him; all this should be understood according to the method found in the Sabhiya Sutta. When the questions were answered by the Blessed One, Sabhiya gained faith, ordained, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"To the Sage Kakusandha, the Brahmin who had attained mastery,
As he was going to his day-rest, I offered a foot-rest (sandals).
In this very aeon, because of the gift I gave then,
I do not know of any unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of the foot-rest.
My defilements are burnt up... (pe)... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

After becoming an Arahant, while Devadatta was striving to cause a schism in the Sangha, Sabhiya, wishing to give advice to the monks who were followers of Devadatta, said:

"Others do not realize that we here must die;
But those who do realize this, their quarrels are settled.
When those who do not understand live as if they were immortal,
Those who understand the Dhamma live without affliction among the afflicted."
8:
“Whatever wholesome action is performed laxly, whatever practice is undertaken in a defiled manner (such as seeking alms in improper places), and whatever practice of the holy life is performed with suspicion—these do not yield great fruit. Such a carelessly performed wholesome deed does not bring great benefit to the person who performs it, nor to the donors of the requisites. For one who has no respect for their fellow practitioners in the Saṅgha, they are far from the True Dhamma, which is the path, fruition, and realization. It is as the sky is far from the earth.” Thus, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma with four verses.

In those verses, “pare” (others) refers to those, excluding the wise, who are preoccupied with disputes by demonstrating the eighteen grounds of schism, such as taking non-Dhamma as Dhamma and Dhamma as non-Dhamma. While they are disputing, they do not realize, “We are constantly and continuously moving toward the presence of the King of Death.” However, the wise ones in that situation realize, “We are moving toward the proximity of death.” Because of this realization, their quarrels and disputes are settled. These wise ones, knowing this, give rise to wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and practice for the settling of quarrels and disputes. Then, through their practice, those quarrels are settled.

Alternatively, “pare” refers to those who are outside the Dispensation (Sāsana) because they do not accept the instructions and advice of the Teacher. As long as they do not realize, “By holding wrong views, we are striving in this world in opposition to the Dispensation,” the disputes will not be settled. But when, by abandoning those views, they realize non-Dhamma as non-Dhamma and Dhamma as Dhamma as they truly are among those engaged in disputes, then, depending on those wise persons, the quarrels known as disputes are settled. Thus should the meaning be understood here.

“Yadā” means at which time. “Avijānantā” means not knowing the means to settle disputes, or not knowing Dhamma and non-Dhamma as they truly are. When they live and wander about like immortals—as if they have transcended old age and death—being agitated, arrogant, restless, talkative, and of scattered speech, then the dispute is not settled. “And those who know the Dhamma” (vijānanti ca ye dhammaṃ): those who know the Dhamma of the Teacher’s Dispensation as it truly is, live without defilements and without suffering among beings who are afflicted by the disease of defilements. Through them, the dispute is completely settled. This is the meaning.

“Yaṃ kiñci sithilaṃ kammaṃ” refers to any wholesome action performed poorly with a loose grasp because of shrinking from the task. “Saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ” refers to undertaking a practice that is defiled by wrong livelihood, such as wandering in improper places like the dwellings of courtesans, or by deception and so on. “Saṅkassaraṃ” refers to an action that is remembered with suspicion. Having heard of some improper behavior in the monastery, [thinking] “This was surely done by the monk named so-and-so”...
9:
Any wholesome action performed with a loose grasp and in a poor manner due to shrinking from the task is called a lax action.

Undertaking a practice that is defiled by wandering in improper places, such as the dwellings of courtesans, or by wrong livelihood such as deception, is called a defiled action.

An action that is remembered with suspicion is called “saṅkassara.” Having heard of some improper behavior in the monastery, others suspect, “This was done by the monk named so-and-so; was it not indeed done by this person?” Or, seeing the Saṅgha assembled for a certain task like the Uposatha, one suspects within oneself, “Surely these monks have assembled because they know my conduct and wish to expel me.” Such an action that is remembered, suspected, or repeatedly suspected with one's own doubts is called “saṅkassara.”

The practice of the monastic life, called the holy life, of such a nature does not bring great fruit to that person. Only because it does not bring great fruit to that person, it also does not bring great fruit to the donors of the requisites for that person. Therefore, one should be of a practice of effacement (sallekha). For one who practices effacement, there is no opportunity for dispute. This is the meaning.

“Respect is not found” (gāravo nūpalabbhati) means that for a person who does not respectfully accept instructions, there is no respect or reverence for fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī) who are worthy of respect. Such a person is far from the True Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti) and the True Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha). For the teachers do not train such a person; and not being trained and not being attentive, they do not practice. For one who does not practice, how can they penetrate the Four Noble Truths? Therefore, it is said, “They are far from the True Dhamma.”

As for the example: “Just as the sky is far from the earth.” The sky is naturally far from the earth element. There is never any mixing. For that very reason, it is said:

“The sky is far and the earth is far,
The other shore of the ocean is said to be far.
O King, they say that even further than that
Is the Dhamma of the virtuous and the Dhamma of the non-virtuous.”

## The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Sabhiya is finished.
10:
If one does not listen (to the Dhamma) and does not practice, how can such a person penetrate and realize the Four Noble Truths? This is the meaning to be noted. Therefore, it was said, "He is far from the True Dhamma (Saddhamma)." For example, just as the sky is far from the earth. The sky is naturally very far from the earth and the element of extension (pathavī-dhātu). There is never any mixing between them. For that very reason, it was said:

"They say the sky is far, and the earth is far; they say the far shore of the ocean is also far.
O Great King, they say that even further than the earth, the sky, and the ocean is the distance between the Dhamma of the virtuous and the Dhamma of the wicked."

The commentary on the verses of Elder Sabhiya ends.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nandaka

The verse beginning with "Dhiratthu" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Nandaka. The background of this Elder is as follows: In the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was a wealthy merchant of great fortune in the city of Haṃsavatī. While listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who exhort the bhikkhunīs. Aspiring for that position, he made an offering of cloth worth one hundred thousand to the Buddha and made a resolution. He also performed an offering of lamps at the Buddha's Bodhi tree.

From that life onwards, while wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was reborn as a Karavīka bird during the time of the Buddha Kakusandha. Singing sweetly, he performed a clockwise circumambulation (padakkhiṇa) of the Buddha. Later, he was reborn as a peacock and, with a mind full of faith, sang sweetly three times every day at the entrance of a cave where a certain Paccekabuddha resided.

Having performed meritorious deeds in various lives in this manner, he was reborn into a noble family in the city of Sāvatthī during the time of our Buddha. He was given the name Nandaka. Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Dhamma from the Buddha, gained faith, and ordained. Developing insight (vipassanā), he attained the fruit of Arahatship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"With a mind of faith and joy, I offered three torches at the supreme place near the Bodhi tree of the Buddha Padumuttara.
One hundred thousand aeons ago, I offered those torches. I have never known a woeful rebirth. This is the fruit of offering lamps.
My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

While spending his time in the bliss of liberation (vimutti-sukha) as an Arahat, he was instructed by the Buddha to exhort the bhikkhunīs. On one Uposatha day, through a single exhortation, he caused five hundred bhikkhunīs to attain the fruit of Arahatship. For that reason, the Buddha appointed the Elder Nandaka to the foremost position among those who exhort the bhikkhunīs.

Then one day, while the Elder was wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, a woman who had been his former wife looked at him with lust and laughed. The Elder, seeing her behavior and wishing to preach the Dhamma by revealing the loathsomeness of the body, said:

"Woe to you, full of impurity, foul-smelling, belonging to the side of Māra, and oozing with defilements. In your body, there are nine openings that flow at all times."
11:
"Do not think of the laughter and actions of the past; do not think that I will act in the same way now. Do not approach such Tathāgatas (noble disciples). They do not even delight in the heavenly realms, let alone in the human world.

Only those fools who lack wisdom, who have evil thoughts, and are shrouded in delusion, delight in that snare which is the bond cast by Māra.

For those Arahats in whom lust, hatred, and ignorance have been extinguished, such noble ones do not delight in those sensual pleasures, having cut the cord of craving and being free from bonds."

Thus he recited the verses. In those verses, 'dhī' is a particle (nipāta) used in the sense of disgust. The letter 'ra' is a euphonic junction (sandhi). The meaning is: 'I loathe you; may you be loathsome.' The words beginning with 'pūre' are vocative terms showing the loathsomeness of that woman. 'Pūre' means being filled with various extremely disgusting corpses and various kinds of impurities. 'Duggandhe' means naturally foul-smelling because of being filled with corpses. 'Mārapakkhe' means that because dissimilar objects (visabhāga-vatthu) such as women are the cause of improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) for blind worldlings, they increase the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra) and give an opportunity to the Māra of the devas (devaputta-māra). Therefore, they belong to the side of Māra. Thus it is said, 'mārapakkhe'. 'Avassute' means 'oozing' because of the constant flowing of defilements and the leaking of impurities in various places. Now, regarding the nine openings in her body that flow at all times, he showed the places where impurities leak out, such as 'eye-wax from the eyes,' etc.

Thus, knowing the body as it truly is—having nine openings, constantly leaking, and filled with impurities—he said, 'mā purāṇaṃ amaññittho,' meaning: do not dwell on the laughter, smiles, and play that occurred in the past before you knew the truth; do not think, 'he will act like this now too.' In saying 'māsādesi tathāgate,' he meant: just as the former disciples of the Buddha came (āgata) with the fulfillment of supporting conditions (upanissaya-sampatti), or as they went (gata) or practiced with right practice, and as they arrived at, attained, and realized the true characteristics of material and mental phenomena and the Four Noble Truths, so too have these disciples of the Buddha come. Because of this sense of coming, practicing, and realizing without distortion, they are called 'Tathāgatas.' He spoke of the manner in which they should not be approached, saying: do not approach these noble disciples with lust or by looking down on them as if they were ordinary beings.
12:
When that woman approached, the Elder said, "Do not offend [the disciples of the Buddha]." He stated the reason why they should not be offended: "Those disciples of the Buddha do not delight even in heaven, which possesses happiness that even an Omniscient Buddha cannot fully describe in this life; how much less would they delight in human sensual pleasures?" Indeed, those disciples of the Buddha do not delight even in heaven, which has happiness that even an Omniscient Buddha cannot fully describe in this life. Because they have clearly seen the danger in conditioned things, they do not give rise to lust. There is no need to even mention that they do not delight in human sensual pleasures, which are like a heap of dung.

Regarding the phrase "Ye ca kho": those who are fools because of their foolish efforts, who are unwise because they lack the wisdom of the essence of Dhamma (dhammojapññā), who think bad thoughts by perceiving beauty in the foul (asubha), and whose minds are entirely shrouded by the delusion of ignorance—such blind worldlings (andhaputhujjana) remain attached to, infatuated with, and deeply immersed in the snare of Māra, which is the bond laid by Māra and designated as "woman."

Regarding the word "Virājitā": for those Arahants, lust (rāga)—which is difficult to remove like oil on a cloth soaked in oil—hatred (dosa)—which like an enemy destroys whenever it gets a chance—and ignorance (avijjā)—which is the nature of not knowing—have been entirely abandoned and cut off by the passionlessness (virāga) of the Noble Path. Such persons have cut the cord of craving for existence with the sword of the Path of Arahantship. Because they have no bondage to any object, they are called "unbound" (abandhanā) and do not delight in the aforementioned snare of Māra. Thus, the Elder Nandaka preached the Dhamma to that woman and departed.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nandaka is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Jambuka

The verses beginning with "Pañcapaññāsa" are those of the Venerable Jambuka. What is their origin? This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various lives. In the time of Tissa Buddha, he was born into a respectable family. Upon reaching maturity, he had faith in the Supreme Enlightenment of the Teacher and worshipped the Bodhi tree by fanning it. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was born into a respectable family. Upon reaching maturity, he went forth in the Dispensation and lived as a resident monk (āvāsika) in a monastery built and donated by a certain lay follower.
13:
That lay follower was attending to the resident monk. Then one day, an Arahant Elder wearing coarse robes came from the forest toward the village to have his hair shaved. Seeing that Elder, the lay follower was inspired by his deportment. He had a barber shave the Elder's hair and beard, offered him excellent food, donated beautiful robes, and invited him to stay, saying, "Venerable Sir, please reside right here."

Seeing this, the resident monk, being of a jealous and stingy nature, said to the Arahant Elder, "O monk, it would be better for you to pluck out your hair with your fingers, go naked, and live by eating dung and urine as food than to live here being attended to by this wicked lay follower."

Having said this, he immediately entered the latrine and, as if serving thick milk-porridge, he scooped up dung with his hand and ate as much as he desired, and also drank urine. Having lived his whole life in this manner, he died and was boiled in hell. Later, because of the remaining result of that kamma, even when born among humans, he became a naked Nigaṇṭha for five hundred lives and was a dung-eater.

Again, in this Buddha-era, although he was born into a human womb, due to the power of the kamma of insulting a Noble One (ariya), he was born into a poor family. Even when fed milk or cream or ghee, he would reject them and drink only urine. When fed rice, he would reject it and eat only dung. Thus growing up by consuming dung and urine, he continued to consume them even when he reached maturity. People, being unable to stop him from such consumption, abandoned him. Being abandoned by his relatives, he went forth as a naked ascetic. He did not bathe, bore the coating of dust and dirt, plucked out his hair and beard, and rejecting other postures, stood on only one leg. He would not accept invitations for meals but undertook a month-long fast. Every month, he would take only as much food as could be held on the tip of a blade of kusa grass and lick it with the tip of his tongue during the day. At night, however, thinking, "Wet dung contains living beings," he would not eat it but ate only dry dung. Fifty-five years passed while he acted in this way. The multitude of people, thinking, "He is one of great austerity and few desires," were devoted and inclined toward him.

Then the Blessed One, seeing the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Fruit of Arahantship shining like a lamp inside his heart, went there himself. By preaching the Dhamma, the Buddha established him in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). He granted him ordination as an "Ehi Bhikkhu," encouraged him in insight meditation (vipassanā), and established him in Arahantship. This is the summary here. As for the details...
14:
It should be understood in the manner stated in the commentary on the verse beginning with 'Māse māse kusaggena' (Jambukattheravatthu) in the Dhammapada. That elder, having established himself in the fruit of Arahantship, at the time of his Parinibbāna, wishing to show that 'Even though I practiced wrongly at first, by relying on the Blessed One, I have attained the extraordinary Dhamma that should be attained by disciples,' recited these four verses:

'For fifty-five years, I bore dust and dirt;
Eating food only once a month, I plucked out my hair and beard.
I stood on one leg and avoided sitting;
I ate dry excrement and did not accept invited alms.
Having done such many evil deeds that lead to woeful states,
While being swept away by the fourfold flood, I went to the Buddha for refuge.
Behold my taking of refuge! Behold the excellent nature of the Dhamma!
The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

In those verses, 'For fifty-five years, I bore dust and dirt' means that by practicing naked asceticism and rejecting bathing, for fifty-five years he bore the external dust (rajo) and the dirt of the body (jalla) that adhered to his person. 'Eating food only once a month' means that while eating excrement at night, for the sake of deceiving the people, he assumed the name of a 'month-faster' (māsopavāsika) and ate the food given by those seeking merit only once a month, placing it on the tip of his tongue. 'Plucked out' means that he applied ashes to loosen the roots and then plucked out his hair and beard with his fingers. 'I stood on one leg and avoided sitting' means that he completely avoided sitting and, while standing, he would raise both hands and stand on only one leg. 'Uddesa' refers to invited alms. Some say it means food prepared specifically for someone. 'Did not accept' means he rejected it without receiving it. 'Having done such many evil deeds that lead to woeful states' means that he performed and produced many evil deeds in past lives and in this life which produce such results and lead to woeful states.
15:
'While being swept away by the great flood' means while being repeatedly dragged toward the ocean of the round of rebirths in woeful states by the great flood such as the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), and especially by the flood of views (diṭṭhogha). 'I went to the Buddha for refuge' means that having obtained this human existence with difficulty through such an opportunity of meritorious deeds, now, by the power of merit, I have approached the Buddha as my 'refuge'; with unwavering faith that 'The Blessed One is the Sammāsambuddha,' I gained confidence in the Teacher. 'Behold my taking of refuge! Behold the excellent nature of the Dhamma!' means behold my taking of refuge in the Triple Gem, and behold the excellent nature of the Dhamma of the Dispensation, whereby even I, who had practiced such wrong views, was brought to such an extraordinary attainment by the Teacher with just a single word of advice. He shows that attainment with the words 'The three knowledges' and so on. Therefore, it is said (in the Apadāna):

'I paid homage to the Bodhi tree of the Blessed One Tissa;
Raising a fan there, I fanned the lion-throne (Sīhāsana).
Ninety-two aeons ago from now, I fanned the lion-throne;
I do not know of any rebirth in a woeful state; this is the result of fanning.
My defilements have been burnt away... (pe)... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.'

## The Commentary on the Verses of Jambuka Thera is finished.

## 6. Senakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with 'Svāgataṃ vata' is the verse of the Venerable Senaka Thera. What is its origin? This elder also had performed extraordinary merit under previous Buddhas and, while accumulating merits in various births, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. When he reached maturity, one day he saw the Teacher and, with a confident mind, honored the Blessed One with a peacock-feather fan. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans, and in this Buddha-arising, he was reborn in a Brahmin family, being conceived in the womb of the sister of the Elder Uruvela Kassapa; his name was Senaka. When he reached maturity, he attained proficiency in the sciences and arts of the Brahmins and lived as a householder. At that time, every year in the month of Phagguna, during the festival of the Uttara-phagguṇီ constellation, the great multitude would perform ceremonial bathing at the landing place of Gayā. For that reason, that festival was called Gayāphaggū. At that time, on the day of such a festival, the Blessed One was staying near the landing place of Gayā out of compassion for veneya beings. The multitude also came to that place from various directions, wishing to perform the ceremonial bathing in the Gayā River. At that moment, Senaka also arrived at that place for the purpose of the ceremonial bathing.
16:
## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Senaka (Senakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā)

That festival is called "Gayāphaggū." At that time, on the day of such a festival, the Blessed One was staying near the Gaya riverbank out of compassion for beings who were to be led (veneyya). The multitude of people also came to that place from various directions with the intention of performing ritual bathing at the riverbank. At that moment, Senaka also arrived at that place for the purpose of ritual bathing. Seeing the Teacher preaching the Dhamma, he approached, listened to the Dhamma, and having gained faith, he went forth as a monk. While applying himself to the practice of insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"Taking a peacock-feather fan, I approached the Leader of the World.
With a confident and joyful mind, I offered the peacock-feather fan.
By this offering of the peacock-feather fan, and by my intentions and aspirations,
The three fires—lust, hatred, and delusion—have been extinguished; I obtain vast happiness.
How wonderful is the Buddha! How wonderful is the Dhamma! How wonderful is the perfection of our Teacher!
Having given the peacock-feather fan, I obtain vast happiness.
My three fires are extinguished; all existences are uprooted.
All taints (āsavas) are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.
In the thirty-first aeon from now, I gave that gift at that time.
Due to the merit of that peacock-feather fan offering, I have never known a miserable rebirth.
My defilements have been burnt away... (and so forth) ... I have followed the Buddha's teaching."

After reaching Arahatship, reflecting on his own practice and with a sense of joy that had arisen, he uttered these inspired verses (udāna):

"At the Gaya river, during the Gayāphaggū festival,
It was indeed a good coming for me, that I saw the Fully Enlightened One,
Preaching the supreme Dhamma.

The one of great radiance, the teacher of the group, the one who has reached the summit, the leader,
The conqueror of the world with its devas, the one of incomparable vision,

The Great Naga, the Great Hero, the one of great splendor and free from taints,
The one whose taints are all exhausted, the Teacher who is fearless from any direction."
17:
Elder Senaka, after reaching Arahatship, reflected on his practice and with joy, uttered these inspired verses: "Long defiled indeed was I, bound by the fetters of views; the Blessed One freed me, Senaka, from all ties," and so forth, reciting these four verses.

In those verses, "Svāgataṃ vata me āsi" means "My coming was indeed well-come" or "My arrival was truly auspicious." "Gayāyaṃ" means near the Gaya riverbank. "Gayaphagguyā" means during the Gayāphaggū festival, held under the Uttaraphaggunī constellation in the month of Phagguna. The word "Yaṃ" and what follows shows the reason for it being a good coming. In that context, "Yaṃ" means "because." "Addasāsiṃ" means I saw. "Sambuddhaṃ" refers to the Blessed One who is called 'Sambuddha' because he rightly and by himself understood all phenomena. "Desentaṃ dhammamuttamaṃ" means preaching the Dhamma which is supreme among all things and is the certain means of deliverance from Saṃsāra, in accordance with the inclinations of the beings to be led.

"Mahappabhaṃ" means endowed with great physical radiance and the radiance of wisdom. "Gaṇācariyaṃ" means the teacher of groups, such as the assembly of monks, because he disciplines them with the highest restraint and teaches them conduct and training. He is called "Aggapattaṃ" because he has attained the summit of virtues such as morality (sīla). He is called "Vināyakaṃ" because he disciplines beings like devas and humans with the highest discipline, and because he himself is without a leader. He is called "Jina" (Conqueror) in the world with its devas because he remains unconquered by anyone while overwhelming the entire world, and because he has conquered the five Maras. He is called "Aggajina" because he has the supreme victory in the world with its devas. He is called "Atuladassanaṃ" (one of incomparable vision) because his physical body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks, and his Dhamma-body is adorned with attributes such as the ten powers (bala) and the four intrepidities (vesārajja), and because he is seen as immeasurable and peerless by the world including the devas.

He is called "Mahānāga" because he is like a great elephant in his gait, strength, and effort, and because he possesses great majesty among the 'Nagas' (those whose taints are exhausted). He is called "Mahāvīra" because he crushes the army of Mara and possesses great heroism. "Mahājutiṃ" means having great majesty and great splendor. He is called "Anāsava" because he does not have the four taints. He is called "Sabbāsavaparikkhīṇa" because he has exhausted all taints along with their habitual tendencies (vāsana). Although disciple-buddhas and silent-buddhas are also those with taints exhausted, only the Fully Enlightened Buddhas abandon the taints along with habitual tendencies; to show this, after saying "Anāsava," he said again "Sabbāsavaparikkhīṇa."

He is called "Satthāra" (Teacher) because he repeatedly admonishes beings according to their needs regarding the benefits of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (Nibbāna). He is called "Akutobhaya" (fearless from any direction) because of his courage through the four intrepidities and his lack of fear from any danger. Because I saw such a Fully Enlightened One, my coming was indeed a good coming. He spoke these four verses to express the virtues he attained through seeing the Buddha. In those verses, "Cirasaṅkiliṭṭhaṃ" means defiled for a long time in the beginningless Saṃsāra by the objects of defilement, which cause one to be soiled like a pot full of vinegar, a pot full of thick gruel, or a worn cloth smeared with grease.
18:
Because he is free from any danger, he is "one who has nothing to fear from any side" (akutobhaya). Because I have seen such a Fully Enlightened One, the connection of the meaning is: "Indeed, his coming was a blessing to me."

Now, wishing to show the benefit he obtained by seeing the Blessed One, he spoke the fourth verse. Its meaning is: Like a pot filled with vinegar, like a pot filled with gruel, or like a worn cloth soaked in fat, I have been defiled for a long time in the beginningless Saṃsāra by the objects of defilement (saṃkilesavatthu). Like a dog tied to a post with a leash, I was bound to the post of "identity" (sakkāya) by the cord of "wrong view" (diṭṭhi). While releasing me from that identity, the Blessed One, my Teacher, has indeed released me, named Senaka, from all bonds such as covetousness (abhijjhā) with the hand of the Noble Path. Thus, he expresses his great devotion to the Blessed One.

## The commentary on the verses of Elder Senaka is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sambhūta

The verse beginning with "Yo dandhakāle" is that of the Venerable Elder Sambhūta. What is its origin? He too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various lives, was reborn as a Kinnara on the banks of the Candabhāgā River in a world empty of Buddhas. One day, seeing a certain Paccekabuddha, with a confident mind, he paid homage and worshipped him with Arjuna flowers while holding his hands in salutation. Due to that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn into a noble family in this Buddha's era and was named Sambhūta. When he came of age, after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Treasurer of the Dhamma, Elder Ānanda. Having gained faith, he ordained, practiced the ascetic life, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"On the bank of the Candabhāgā River, I was then a Kinnara;
I saw the stainless Buddha, the Self-Enlightened, the Unconquered.

With a confident and joyful heart, filled with awe and hands in salutation,
I took an Arjuna flower and worshipped the Self-Enlightened One.

By that well-performed deed and by my intention and aspiration,
Having abandoned the Kinnara body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven."
19:
"Thirty-six times I was the King of Gods, ruling as the lord of devas. Ten times I was a Wheel-Turning Monarch, ruling as a great king.

As for being a regional king, it was many times, beyond counting. How wonderful! I have sown the seed of merit in the Paccekabuddha, who is like a fertile field.

My merit exists; I have reached the homeless state of a monk. Today, in the dispensation of the Buddha, the son of the Sakyans, I am worthy of offerings.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Having attained Arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of liberation, one hundred years after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, when the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī were upholding the ten (unlawful) points, seven hundred Arahants, urged by Elder Yasa, the son of Kākanda, destroyed that wrong view, upheld the True Dhamma, and performed the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya. At that time, while pointing out what was not Dhamma and not Vinaya of those Vajjiputtaka monks, the Elder, with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), said:

## He who hastens when he should be slow, and is slow when he should hasten—that fool, through improper arrangement, meets with suffering.

## His interests decline like the moon in the dark fortnight. He reaches ill-repute and falls out with his friends.

## He who is slow when he should be slow, and hastens when he should hasten—that wise man, through proper arrangement, attains happiness.

## His interests are fulfilled like the moon in the bright fortnight. He reaches fame and glory and does not fall out with his friends.

Reciting these verses, he declared his attainment of Arahantship.

In those verses, "Yo dandhakāle tarati" means: when a Vinaya-related doubt (kukkucca) arises regarding something to be done, such as "Is it allowable or not?", as long as one has not yet removed that doubt by asking a learned expert in Vinaya, to suppress and transgress during that time when one should be slow in that matter. "Taraṇīye ca dandhaye" means: in the case of a layperson, in taking refuge and undertaking the precepts, etc.; in the case of a monk, in performing major and minor duties, etc...
20:
Even when the time has arrived to swiftly perform major and minor duties, or to engage in the practice of Samatha (tranquillity) and Vipassanā (insight), if one does not strive quickly in those matters but procrastinates, thinking, 'I will do it in the coming month or the coming fortnight,' one spends time without performing those duties. By such improper arrangement—acting quickly when one should act slowly, and acting slowly when one should act quickly—and by the lack of proper arrangement through a lack of skillful means, a person of dull wisdom or weak intellect encounters misfortune and suffering both in the present and in the future.

'Tassatthā parihāyanti' means that for such a person, their welfare, including benefits in the present life, declines, perishing and coming to an end day by day, like the moon in the dark fortnight. They reach a state of ill-repute, being censured by the wise with words such as, 'This person has no faith, no devotion, is lazy, and lacks energy.' 'Mittehi ca virujjhati' means that by not accepting the advice of noble friends (kalyāṇamitta) who give counsel saying, 'Practice in this way, do not practice in that way,' and by saying, 'We are not those who should be given advice,' one becomes an adversary to those friends.

The meaning of the remaining two verses should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated. In this context, some teachers present the meaning of the words 'tarati dandhaye' in terms of the uplifting and restraining of the meditative mind. That meaning is suitable for the later verses. As for the first two verses, they were spoken by the Elder with reference to the Vajjiputtaka monks who were expelled by the Saṅgha after showing the ten points of dispute, because they were remorseful for not having practiced the recluse's Dhamma (samaṇadhamma) that should have been practiced since the time of their ordination. The later verses, however, were spoken with reference to those who, like himself, have practiced well and remain having attained the fruit of Arahatship, which is their own benefit.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sambhūta Thera is Finished.

## 8. The Commentary on the Verses of Rāhula Thera

The verses beginning with 'Ubhayena' are those of the Venerable Rāhula Thera. What is the background story? This Elder also had performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a noble family. When he reached the age of wisdom, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position among those who desire training (sikkhākāma)...
21:
Seeing that position, he too aspired for it and performed noble merit, such as cleaning and purifying the lodgings and lighting lamps, and made a resolution.

After passing away from that life, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of the appearance of this Buddha, he was conceived in the womb of Queen Yasodharā, depending on our Bodhisatta. He received the name Rāhula and grew up surrounded by a great retinue of princes. The procedure of his ordination is exactly as it appears in the Khandhaka (Mahāvagga).

Having ordained, he received well-given advice through many Sutta discourses in the presence of the Teacher. Being of mature wisdom, he exerted himself in Vipassanā and attained Arahatship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

'In the seven-storied palace of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Chief of the World, the One of Such-like quality (Tādi),
I spread a silk canopy as an offering.

Surrounded by a thousand stainless ones (arahants), the Great Sage, the Lord of bipeds, the Bull among men,
Approached the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī).

Illuminating the Fragrant Chamber, the God of gods, the Bull among men,
The Teacher, standing in the midst of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, spoke these verses:

"Whoever has illuminated this sleeping place, which is well-spread like a mirror-surface,
I shall praise him; listen to my words.

Palaces made of gold, made of silver, and also made of beryl,
Whatever is pleasing to the heart, shall arise for him.

Sixty-four times he will be the Lord of Devas, Sakka, and rule the celestial realm;
A thousand times he will subsequently be a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).

In the twenty-first kappa from now, he will be a khattiya named Vimala,
A conqueror of the four quarters, a Universal Monarch.

The city named Reṇuvatī, well-constructed with bricks,
Will be three hundred (units) in length and endowed with a square shape.

The palace named Sudassana, created by Vissakamma,
Endowed with noble gables and adorned with the seven gems, will exist."'
22:
'That city of Reṇuvatī will not be silent, resounding with the ten sounds, crowded with wizards (vidyādharas), like the city of Sudassana of the devas.
When the sun rises, its light goes forth; so too, the radiance of that palace will always beautify that city for eight yojanas all around.
In a hundred thousand kappas from now, the Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka dynasty, will appear in the world.
Passing away from the Tusita heaven, urged by his former wholesome roots, he will be the biological son of the Blessed One Gotama.
If he were to live in the home, he would be a Universal Monarch. However, it is impossible for such a one to find delight in the home life.
Having gone forth from the home, he will ordain as one of good vows. By the name of Rāhula, he will become an Arahant.
As a jungle fowl would protect its egg, or as a yak protects its tail, I, being wise and endowed with virtue, protected myself (my virtue).
Having understood the Dhamma of that Blessed One, I lived delighting in the Dispensation. Having fully understood all taints (āsavas), I dwell without taints.
My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's bidding has been done.'

Having reached Arahatship, reflecting on his own practice and wishing to declare his attainment of Arahatship, he said:

'Endowed with both (birth and practice), they know me as Rāhula the Blessed (Rāhulabhadda). I am the son of the Buddha, and I am one with the eye of wisdom regarding the Dhammas.
My taints are exhausted, and there is no more renewed existence. I am an Arahant worthy of offerings, possessor of the threefold knowledge, a seer of the Deathless.
Blinded by sensual pleasures, covered by the net of craving, overshadowed by the roof of craving, they are bound by the Kinsman of the Heedless (Māra), like fish at the mouth of a trap.'
23:
"I, having abandoned sensual pleasures, having cut the bond of Māra, having uprooted craving along with its root, have become cool and extinguished." He uttered these four verses.

In those verses, "endowed with both" (ubhayeneva sampanno) means being endowed with the two types of fulfillment: fulfillment of birth and fulfillment of practice. "They know me as Rāhula the Blessed" (Rāhulabhaddoti maṃ vidū) means his fellow practitioners recognize him as "Rāhulabhadda." Indeed, upon hearing the news of the birth of Prince Rāhula, the Bodhisatta said, "A Rāhu (an obstacle) is born, a bond is born." Based on these words, King Suddhodana gave him the name "Rāhula." Here, the Elder uses the same designation given by his father, saying, "They know me as Rāhula the Blessed." The word "Bhadda" is a term of praise.

Now, to show that double fulfillment, he spoke the words beginning with "And because I am" (yañcamhi). In that context, "yaṃ" means "because." The word "ca" has a conjunctive sense. "I am the son of the Buddha" (amhi putto Buddhassa) means he is the legitimate breast-born son of the Fully Enlightened One. "In the teachings" (dhammaesu) means in mundane and supramundane teachings, specifically the Four Noble Truths. "Possessing vision" (cakkhumā) should be understood as being one who possesses the eye of wisdom through the Path.

Again, to show his double fulfillment through other means, he spoke the verse beginning with "And because my taints are destroyed" (yañca me āsavā khīṇā). There, "worthy of offerings" (dakkhiṇeyyo) means one deserving of noble gifts. "One who sees the Deathless" (amataddaso) means one who habitually beholds Nibbāna. The remaining words are easy to understand.

Now, to show how the multitude of beings, lacking the fulfillment of knowledge and the fulfillment of liberation, wander in saṃsāra like fish in a trap, and to show his own possession of that double fulfillment, he spoke the two verses beginning with "Blinded by sensual pleasures" (kāmandhā). There, "blinded by sensual pleasures" means those who are blind regarding sensual pleasures. Due to the sensual defilements (kilesa-kāma) classified as desire and lust, etc., they are as if blinded by their inability to see the danger in the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma) such as visible forms. "Ensnared in the net" (jālapacchannā) means they are particularly covered and entangled by the net of craving (taṇhā) which overspreads all three realms of existence. "Covered by the roof of craving" (taṇhāchadanachāditā) means they are obstructed and covered without remainder by that roof called craving. "Bound by the kinsman of the negligent, like fish in the mouth of a trap" (pamattabandhunā baddhā, macchāva kuminamukhe) means that just as fish are caught in the mouth of a fisherman's net-bag at the mouth of a trap, Māra has bound these beings with the fetter of sensual pleasure, from which they cannot escape and remain trapped within. Having abandoned that fetter of sensual pleasure through the preliminary practice, having completely cut the bond of the Māra of defilements with the weapon of the Noble Path, and having uprooted craving such as sensual craving along with its root of ignorance, and because all the fevers of defilements have been stilled...
24:
...these beings, being bound by that fetter of sensual pleasure, cannot escape from it and remain within the bond.

Having abandoned such sensual pleasure which has become a bond through preliminary practice, having cut the bond of the Māra of defilements, and then having uprooted it without remainder with the weapon of the Noble Path, and by that very cutting, having uprooted craving such as sensual craving along with its root known as ignorance, and because of the absence of all distress and fever of defilements, I have become cool and extinguished through the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu). This is the meaning.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Rāhula is Finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Candana

The verse beginning with "With gold" (jātarūpena) is that of the Venerable Elder Candana. What is the background story? This Elder also had performed meritorious services (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. Thirty-one aeons ago, in a world empty of a Buddha, he was reborn as a tree-deity. Seeing a Paccekabuddha named Sudassana living in a mountain cleft, he was inspired with a confident mind and made an offering of kuṭaja flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha's era, he was reborn in a wealthy family in Sāvatthī and received the name Candana. When he reached the proper age, while living the household life, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One and became a Stream-enterer.

After obtaining a son, he abandoned the household life, ordained as a monk, took a meditation subject for insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna), and lived in the forest. When he came to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Blessed One, he stayed in a cemetery. Hearing of his arrival, his former wife, having adorned herself and taking their young son, went to the Elder's presence with a large retinue. She went with the intention, "I will entice him with feminine wiles and cause him to disrobe." The Elder saw that woman coming from afar and thought, "Now I shall be beyond her reach." He intensified the insight he was already practicing and became an Arahant with the six higher powers. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

Not far from the Himālayas, there is a mountain named Vasabha. In a cleft of that mountain, a Paccekabuddha named Sudassana resided. I took a flower that bloomed in the Himālayan forest and traveled through the air. Right there in the air, I beheld the Paccekabuddha who had crossed the four floods and was free from taints. Then, placing the kuṭaja flower on my head, to that Paccekabuddha...
25: After obtaining an only son, the young man renounced the household life, became a monk, took up Vipassanā meditation, and lived in the forest. When he arrived at Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Blessed One, he stayed in a charnel ground. Hearing that Elder Candana had arrived, his former wife, adorned with ornaments and carrying their young son, went to the Elder accompanied by a large retinue. She went with the intention of enticing the Elder with feminine charms to make him return to the lay life. The Elder, seeing that woman approaching from afar, reflected, "Now, let this not be an opportunity for this woman," and by practicing Vipassanā, he became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: "Not far from the Himālayas, there is a mountain named Vasabha. In the midst of that mountain, a Paccekabuddha named Sudassana resided. I took a flower from the Himālayas and traveled through the air. There, I saw the Sambuddha (Paccekabuddha) who had crossed the four floods and was free from taints. Taking a Kutaja flower and placing it on my head with palms joined, I offered it to the Buddha, the Self-become, the Great Seeker. In the thirty-first aeon from this, I offered that flower. Due to the merit of that Buddha-pūjā, I have never known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of Buddha-pūjā. My defilements are burnt away... (and so on) ...I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching." Having become one with the six supernormal powers, he stood in the air, preached the Dhamma to that woman, established her in the refuges and the precepts, and then returned to his former dwelling place. When asked by his companion monks, "Friend, your faculties are very clear; have you perhaps penetrated the Four Noble Truths?"— "Adorned and covered with golden ornaments, surrounded by a group of female servants, and carrying the young son on her hip, my former wife approached me. Seeing her coming, the mother of my own son, well-dressed and adorned like a snare of death set out— Then, wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) arose in me. The danger (of sensual pleasures) became manifest, and disenchantment (nibbidā) was well-established. Then my mind was liberated. Behold the excellence of the Dhamma! The three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled." By these verses, describing his own practice, he declared his attainment of Arahantship. In those verses, "jātarūpena sañchannā" means her body was covered by ornaments such as head-dresses made of gold; the meaning is she was adorned with all kinds of jewelry. "Dāsīgaṇapurakkhatā" means surrounded by her group of female servants who were appropriately adorned and prepared. "Aṅkena puttamādāya" means she came carrying the young son on her hip, thinking that seeing the son might arouse household-based pleasure. "Āyantiṃ" means coming. "Sakaputtassa mātaraṃ" means the mother of the son born of my breast, my former wife (seeing her).
26:
It means she was surrounded by a group of maidservants walking in front. Thinking, 'Perhaps upon seeing the son, there might arise delight based on the household life,' she came holding the son in her arms.

'Āyantiṃ' means the one who is coming. 'The mother of my son' means the mother of the son born of my breast, meaning my former wife. The Elder said all this, highly esteeming his own total eradication of sensual lust. 'Wise attention arose' means such wise attention arose as: 'Even such prosperity as this is overcome by old age, sickness, and death; alas, formations are impermanent, unstable, and yield no satisfaction.' The remaining words are as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Candana is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Dhammika

The verses beginning with 'Dhammo have' are those of the Venerable Elder Dhammika. What is the story of his origin? This Elder also had performed special merit under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various births. In the time of the Buddha Sikhī, he was a hunter. One day, while the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma to a gathering of devas in a forest grove, he took the sign of the Dhamma teaching, thinking, 'This sound is called the Dhamma.' Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the worlds of devas and humans. When our Buddha appeared, he was born into a Brahmin family in the Kosala country and was named Dhammika. When he came of age, he gained faith on the day the Jetavana monastery was accepted and was ordained. While residing as a resident monk (āvāsika) in a certain village monastery, he was frequently critical and intolerant regarding the minor and major duties of visiting monks. Because of that, the monks abandoned that monastery and left. He remained alone. A lay follower, the owner of the monastery, heard about that matter and reported the situation to the Blessed One. The Teacher summoned that monk and questioned him about the matter. When he replied, 'It is so, Bhante,' the Teacher said, 'Not only now is he intolerant; in the past too, he was intolerant.' Being requested by the monks, the Teacher told the Rukkha-dhamma Jātaka, and wishing to give him further instruction, he recited these verses:

'The Dhamma indeed protects him who practices the Dhamma, just as a great moon...' and so forth.
27:
While wandering in saṃsāra, during the time of our Gautama Buddha, a man named Dhammika was born into a Brahmin family in the Kosala kingdom. Upon reaching adulthood, he gained faith on the day the Jetavana Monastery was accepted as a donation and became a monk. While residing as a local monk in a village monastery, he became frequently critical and intolerant regarding the major and minor duties of visiting monks. Consequently, the visiting monks abandoned the monastery and left, leaving the monk Dhammika alone. A lay supporter (upāsaka) of the monastery, upon hearing of this, reported the matter to the Blessed One. When the Blessed One summoned and questioned the monk, he replied, "It is true, Bhante." The Blessed One then remarked, "This monk is not intolerant only now; he was also intolerant in the past." At the request of the monks, the Buddha preached the Rukkha-dhamma Jātaka and, wishing to give further instruction to that monk, recited these verses:

"Truly, the Dhamma protects the one who practices the Dhamma; Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness. This is the benefit of Dhamma well-practiced: the Dhamma-practitioner does not go to a woeful state.

Indeed, Dhamma and non-Dhamma (adhamma) do not have equal results. Non-Dhamma leads to hell; Dhamma leads to a happy destination.

Therefore, one should have desire for wholesome Dhammas, thus rejoicing because of the Sugata, the Steadfast One (Tādī). Established in the Dhamma, the disciples of the Excellent Sugata, the wise ones who have reached the supreme refuge, are led out (from saṃsāra).

The root of the boil (defilements) is burst; the net of craving is uprooted. For him whose wandering in saṃsāra is exhausted, there is no more anxiety (kiñcana); he is pure like the moon on a stainless full-moon night."

Thus, he preached these four verses.

In those verses, 'Dhamma' refers to the mundane and supramundane Dhamma of good conduct. 'Protects' means protecting from the suffering of the four woeful states and from the suffering of saṃsāra by being a strong support for the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭūpanissaya). 'Dhamma-practitioner' (dhammacārī) refers to the person who practices and develops that Dhamma. 'Well-practiced' (suciṇṇa) means Dhamma that is accumulated with respect and attention, having faith in kamma and its results. 'Happiness' (sukha) refers to both mundane and supramundane happiness.

Between these two, mundane happiness is produced by Dhammas such as those of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) according to their nature, in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives. As for the other, supramundane happiness, it should be said that it is brought about in succession by the wholesome Dhamma practiced while established in the strong support for the cessation of the round; for without that strong support (upanissaya), that supramundane happiness cannot be attained. 'This is the benefit of Dhamma well-practiced: the Dhamma-practitioner does not go to a woeful state' means that for the person who practices Dhamma, not reaching the four woeful states due to such good practice is the benefit and result of the Dhamma well-practiced.

Because it is only through wholesome Dhamma that one reaches a happy destination, and only through unwholesome Dhamma that one reaches a woeful state, the Blessed One spoke the second verse beginning with "Na hi dhammo adhammo ca" to show that these two, Dhamma and Adhamma, have distinct and unmixed results. In that verse, 'Adhamma' refers to unwholesome misconduct (duccarita), which is the opposite of Dhamma. 'Samavipākino' means having equal results. 'Ubho' refers to the distinct and different results of both Dhamma and Adhamma. Therefore, one should have a desire for wholesome Dhammas. 'Iti modamāno sugatena tādinā' means rejoicing because of the Blessed One, who is the Sugata (Well-gone) and who is endowed with the quality of Tādī (steadfastness), being unshaken by the desirable and the undesirable.
28:
Because only through wholesome Dhamma is there a going to a happy destination, and only through unwholesome Dhamma is there a going to a woeful state, the Blessed One spoke the second verse beginning with "Na hi dhammo" to show that these two, "Dhamma and Adhamma," have results that are not mixed with each other. In that verse, 'Adhamma' is misconduct (duccarita) which is the opposite of Dhamma. 'Samavipākino' means those having similar results or equal fruits.

'Tasmā' means because of this aforementioned difference in the results of Dhamma and Adhamma. 'Chanda' is the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda). The connection is: one should have desire for Dhammas, rejoicing and reaching satisfaction because of the Blessed One named Tādī, who is the Sugata, the one who has gone well, the one who has practiced rightly, and who has attained the state of Tādī (steadfastness) amidst desirable and undesirable objects by giving such instructions. Having shown the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) to this extent, the Buddha now spoke the verse beginning with "Dhamme ṭhitā" to show the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). The meaning of that verse is: the disciples of the Blessed One—who is more excellent than those who speak good words and more excellent than those who go to the excellent Nibbāna—being established in the Dhamma of that Buddha, being wise, and having reached the most excellent refuge, escape from all the suffering of the round by virtue of being established in that Dhamma called the taking of refuge; therefore, one should have desire for wholesome Dhammas.

When the Blessed One had preached the Dhamma with these three verses, the monk, while still sitting there, developed insight according to the teaching and attained Arahantship. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the past, I was a hunter in a secluded forest; I saw the Buddha, free from the dust of defilements, preceded by a host of devas.

I heard the sweet Dhamma of Buddha Sikhī, the kinsman of the world, who was revealing the Four Noble Truths and preaching the state of the Deathless.

I gained faith in the voice of the Peerless One; having gained faith in that voice, I crossed over the existence that is difficult to cross.

Thirty-one aeons ago from this auspicious aeon, because of the perception (saññā) of that voice which I obtained then, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of the perception of the voice.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Thus, he was established in Arahantship. Having reached Arahantship, wishing to inform the Teacher of the special attainment he had realized, he declared his Arahantship with the final verse.
29:
In those verses, 'vipphoṭito' means that which has been abandoned by the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa). 'Gaṇḍamūla' (the root of the boil) refers to ignorance (avijjā). This is because ignorance indeed flows or oozes. Just as the Teacher said, "Monks, 'boil' (gaṇḍa) is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā)," the net of craving (taṇhā-jāla), which is the root cause of the five aggregates of clinging called 'boil', has been uprooted by the path. This is due to its association with the source of suffering, the oozing of the impurities of defilements, and its swelling, ripening, and bursting through birth, aging, and dissolution.

'So khīṇasaṃsāro na catthi kiñcanaṃ' means: I, having thus abandoned craving and ignorance, have exhausted the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra); because the root of existence has been abandoned, the impediments (kiñcana) such as lust (rāga) no longer exist, nor can they be found. 'Cando yathā dosinā puṇṇamāsiyaṃ' means: Just as the moon on a full moon night is bright and clear, free from defects such as clouds and mist, so too have I, through the attainment of Arahantship, become one whose defilements like lust are gone and whose portion of the Dhamma is complete.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Dhammika is Finished.

## 11. Sappakattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

'Yadā balākā' and so forth are the verses of the Venerable Elder Sappaka. What is their origin? This Elder Sappaka had also performed meritorious services (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merits in various existences. Thirty-one aeons (kappas) ago from this present Bhadda-kappa, he was reborn as a powerful Naga king. While a Paccekabuddha named Sambhava was seated in an attainment (samāpatti) in the open air, the Naga king took a large lotus and held it over the Paccekabuddha's head as an offering. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named Sappaka. When he reached the age of discretion and gained wisdom, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, gained faith, ordained, and took up a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna)...
30:
Living in the Leṇagiri Monastery on the banks of the river named Ajakaraṇī, that Elder attained Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"Not far from the Himavantā, there is a mountain named Romasa; at that time, the Buddha named Sambhava lived in the open air.

Leaving my own abode, I carried a lotus; having carried it for a whole day, I returned to my palace.

In the thirty-first aeon from now, I worshipped that Buddha; due to the fruit of that worship of the Buddha, I have never known a miserable rebirth (duggati).

My defilements are burnt up... the instruction of the Buddha has been carried out."

Having attained Arahantship, the Elder went to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Teacher. While being attended to by his relatives, he stayed there for a few days, preached the Dhamma, and established his relatives in the refuges and the precepts. He then desired to return to the aforementioned place. His relatives pleaded, "Venerable Sir, please reside here in Sāvatthī; we will attend to you." The Elder, showing his intention to leave, expressed his delight in solitude (vivekābhirati) by praising the place where he resided:

"When the cranes with clean white wings, terrified by the fear of the black cloud, fly seeking their nests, then the Ajakaraṇī River delights me.

When the very pure white cranes, terrified by the fear of the black cloud, search for shelter as they see no shelter, then the Ajakaraṇī River delights me.

Who would not be delighted there, where the rose-apple (jambu) trees on both sides of the river bank, behind my cave, beautify the place?" Thus he recited.
31:
"The frogs, well-freed from the company of pythons, croak with pleasant sounds.
Now is not the time to be away from the mountain rivers;
The Ajakaraṇī is safe, blissful, and very delightful."
Thus he spoke these four verses.

In those verses, "yadā" means at which time. "Balākā" refers to the crane birds. "Sucipaṇḍaracchadā" means having clean, pure, white wings. "Kāḷassa meghassa bhayena tazzitā" means weary and terrified by the danger of rain from the thundering monsoon cloud, which is black like a mountain of collyrium (añjana) because it is heavy with water. "Palehiti" means they will fly up and go from their feeding grounds. "Ālayaṃ" means to their own nest or dwelling. "Ālayesinī" means desiring only to hide in that nest. At that time, "nadī ajakaraṇī rameti maṃ" means the river named Ajakaraṇī, which is full of fresh water, carries away debris, and erodes the banks during the monsoon, delights me; it pleases my mind. Thus, he expressed his delight in solitude by praising the specific season.

"Suvisuddhappandarā" means having a very pure white color, unmixed with other colors, entirely white. "Pariyesati" means searches for. "Leṇaṃ" means a place to live. "Aleṇadassinī" means not seeing a place to live; because there was no permanent dwelling place before, she is called 'one who sees no shelter'. Now, in the monsoon season, being pregnant due to the thunder of the clouds, she searches for a shelter; this means she builds a nest as a permanent dwelling.

"Kaṃ nu tattha... pacchato" means: Behind the great cave where I live, on both sides of the banks of the Ajakaraṇī River, here and there, the rose-apple (jambu) trees beautify the place. They have branches always bent by the weight of fruit and provide a canopy of glossy, smooth leaves. In that place, what being would they not delight? They indeed delight all beings.
32:
"Amatamadasaṅghasuppahīnā" means: 'Amata' refers to the antidote for snake venom. Snakes are called 'amatamada' because they are intoxicated by that venom; the group of those snakes is 'amatamadasaṅgha,' and they have been thoroughly removed or have departed. Small frogs and frogs with pleasant voices croak with a sweet sound in that place. In saying, "Now is not the time to be away from the mountain rivers," it means that just as it is not the time to be away from other mountain rivers at this time, the Ajakaraṇī River is particularly safe because it is free from fierce fish, crocodiles, and so on. It is peaceful and pleasant because it is endowed with beautiful ground, landing places, and sandbanks. It is exceedingly delightful; therefore, the meaning is that my mind delights only in that place.

After speaking thus, he left his relatives and returned only to his own dwelling place. By demonstrating his delight in solitary dwellings, this verse itself served as the Elder's declaration of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sappaka is Finished.
## 12. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mudita

The verse beginning with "Pabbajiṃ" belongs to the Venerable Elder Mudita. As for its origin: This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds of service under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. In the time of Vipassī Buddha, he was reborn in a respectable family, and upon reaching the age of discretion, he saw the Teacher one day and, with a devoted mind, offered a couch (mañca). Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was reborn into a householder's family in the Kosala country and was named Mudita. When he reached the age of discretion, that family was obstructed by the King for some business or other.
