Fearing the King's danger, Mudita fled, entered the forest, and approached the dwelling place of a certain Arahant Elder. The Elder, knowing his state of fear, consoled him, saying, "Do not fear."

When he asked, "Venerable Sir, in how much time will this danger of mine subside?" and was told, "After seven or eight months have passed," he requested ordination to save his life, saying, "I cannot wait for such a long time; I will ordain, Venerable Sir, please ordain me." The Elder ordained him. After ordaining, he gained faith in the Dispensation, and even when the dangers had subsided...
33:
...delighting only in the Dhamma of a recluse, he took a meditation subject and practiced Vipassana. He made a vow, saying, "I will not go out from this dwelling chamber without attaining Arahantship," and by exerting himself in Vipassana, he attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"To the Blessed One Vipassī, the Foremost of the World, the Possessor of Tādī-virtue,
I offered a couch with a devoted mind and with my own hands.
I obtained elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and divine vehicles;
By that gift of a couch, I have reached the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya).
In the ninety-one aeons since I gave that couch,
I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the gift of a couch.
My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

While experiencing the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha) after attaining Arahantship, he was questioned by his fellow monks about his attainment. Desiring to explain the manner of his practice, he recited these four verses:

"I ordained seeking a livelihood, and having obtained the higher ordination,
Thereafter I regained faith and strove with firm energy.
Let this body be broken as it will, let the pieces of flesh be scattered,
Let my two shanks fall away from the knee-joints.
I will not eat, I will not drink, nor will I go out from the monastery,
Nor will I lie down to sleep, as long as the dart of craving is not pulled out.
Behold the energy and exertion of me who dwells in this way;
The three knowledges (tevijjā) have been attained, the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

In those verses, "jīvikattho" means one who desires a livelihood, or one whose purpose is a livelihood. The meaning is that he ordained for the sake of livelihood, thinking, "By ordaining here, I shall live without fear, happily and without exhaustion." "Laddhāna upasampadaṃ" refers to obtaining the status of a monk through the formal act of the fourth motion (ñatticatutthakamma) after first established in the novice-ordination (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā). "Tato saddhaṃ paṭilabhiṃ" means that from the time he became a monk, by associating with good friends and studying the two Mātikās, the three types of Paritta (or Anumodanā), the Dhamma found in the three Pitakas, certain Suttas, and the methods of Samatha and Vipassana, he saw the great majesty of the Buddha and others, and gained faith in the Triple Gem, thinking, "The Blessed One is indeed the Fully Enlightened One..."
34:
...standing firm, having obtained the higher ordination through the formal act of the fourth motion. "Tato saddhaṃ paṭilabhiṃ" means that from the time of his higher ordination, while associating with and serving good friends, and learning the two Mātikās, the three types of Anumodanā, certain Suttas, Samatha meditation, and the method of Vipassana, he saw the great majesty of the Buddha and others and regained faith in the Triple Gem, thinking: "The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha has practiced well." "Strove with firm energy" means that having thus regained faith, while performing the work of Vipassana, he strove with firm and steady energy for the sake of penetrating the Four Noble Truths before long; he exerted himself rightly for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the fulfillment of wholesome states.

To show the manner in which he strove, the verse beginning with "Kāmaṃ" was spoken. In that verse, "kāmaṃ" has the sense of 'at will' or 'certainly let it be destroyed.' "This body" refers to this foul body (pūtikāya) of mine; if it breaks due to the heat of this energy, let it break, let it be cut and broken. "Let the pieces of flesh be scattered" means if, due to this firm exertion, the pieces of flesh are scattered from this body, let them be scattered, let them be destroyed here and there. "Let my two shanks fall away from the knee-joints" means let both my shanks along with the knee-joints, as well as the thighs, break from the hip-joints and fall to the ground. There is also a reading "maṃ," which has the same meaning. The rest is exactly as explained in the method mentioned below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mudita is Finished.
## The Commentary on the Section of Fours (Catukkanipāta) is Finished.
35:
## 5. Pañcakanipāta

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Rājadatta

In the Pañcakanipāta, the verse beginning with "Bhikkhu sivathikaṃ gantvā" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Rājadatta. What is its origin? This elder also had performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a powerful support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences. Fourteen aeons ago, in a world empty of Buddhas, he was born into a respectable family. When he reached the age of discretion, he went into the forest one day on some business. In that forest, seeing a Paccekabuddha sitting at the foot of a tree, he was inspired with a clear mind and offered a very pure ambāṭaka (hog plum) fruit. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was born into a merchant family in the city of Sāvatthī. Because his parents obtained him after propitiating the great King Vessavaṇa, they named him Rājadatta. When he came of age, he took goods on five hundred carts and went to the city of Rājagaha for trade.

At that time, there was a courtesan in Rājagaha who was extremely beautiful, lovely to behold, and endowed with supreme charm, earning a thousand pieces of money daily. Then, the merchant's son, by giving a thousand pieces daily to that courtesan and consorting with her, soon exhausted all his wealth. Becoming poor and unable to obtain even basic food and clothing, he wandered here and there and was struck with a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). One day, he went to the Veḷuvana Monastery together with some lay devotees.

At that time, the Blessed One was sitting surrounded by a large assembly, preaching the Dhamma. He sat at the edge of the assembly, and upon hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One, he gained faith, ordained, undertook the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and lived in a cemetery. At that time, another merchant's son was living with that same courtesan, having paid a thousand pieces. The courtesan, seeing a highly valuable jewel in the hand of that merchant's son, became greedy and had him killed by other thugs to take the jewel. Then, the men of that merchant's son, hearing of the incident, sent out spies. They entered the courtesan's house at night and, without damaging her skin or other parts, killed her and discarded her body in the cemetery. While the Elder Rājadatta was wandering in the cemetery to take up the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta), he approached the corpse of that courtesan to contemplate it as a repulsive object. Although he practiced wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) two or three times, because she had not been dead long, because her skin had not yet been destroyed by jackals and such, and because she was an object of the opposite sex (visabhāga), unwise reflection arose, and he felt sensual lust (kāmarāga) for that corpse.
36:
The elder approached to contemplate the corpse as a repulsive object, and after reflecting wisely two or three times, because she had not been dead long, because her skin had not yet been destroyed by jackals and such, and because she was an object of the opposite sex, unwise reflection occurred, and sensual lust arose for that corpse. Then, with a mind full of dismay, he rebuked and disciplined his own mind. Moving away to a suitable place for a moment, he took up only the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta) that had appeared from the beginning. Reflecting wisely, he attained Jhana, and using that Jhana as a basis, he developed insight (vipassanā) and reached the fruit of Arahantship at that very moment. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Seeing the Buddha, the Self-Become, the Unconquered, in the forest, I took an ambāṭaka fruit and offered it to the Self-Become.

Thirty-one aeons ago from now, I gave that fruit; because of the merit of that fruit offering, I have never known a woeful state. This is the fruit of the offering of fruit.

My defilements have been burned away... (and so on) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.”

Upon reaching Arahantship, as he reviewed his own practice, he was filled with joy and appreciation and recited these five verses:

“The monk went to the charnel ground and saw a woman's body cast away, discarded in the cemetery, full of worms and being eaten.

While some, seeing that vile dead body, feel revulsion, in me, sensual lust appeared; I was like a blind man with a body flowing (with defilements).

Faster than the time it takes to cook rice, I departed from that spot. Mindful and clearly comprehending, I sat down to one side.

Then, wise reflection arose in me; the danger became manifest, and revulsion was well-established.

Then my mind was liberated. See the excellence of the Dhamma! The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.”
37:
In those verses, 'bhikkhu sivathikaṃ gantvā' means that the Elder, called a monk (bhikkhu) because he sees danger in saṃsāra, approached a charnel ground (āmakasusāna) for the purpose of meditating on foulness (asubhakammaṭṭhāna). The Elder spoke this word 'bhikkhu' himself, referring to himself.

'Itthiṃ' refers to a woman (mātugāma), called 'thī' because in this (body), semen, blood, and physical essence (utu) are combined and exist as the continuity of a being. Thus, she is also called 'itthi' by way of natural etymology (sabhāvanirutti). In the case of barren women and others, they are so called because of their similarity to such a woman and because they do not transcend that nature. By the word 'itthi', the corpse of a woman is meant. 'Ujjhitaṃ' means discarded, thrown away without regard simply because it is fit to be discarded. 'Khajjantiṃ' refers to (a corpse) being eaten, being filled with worms.

'Yañhi eke jigucchanti, mataṃ disvāna pāpakaṃ' means that some people of pure nature loathe that evil, low, and base corpse, which is dead because life, heat, and consciousness have departed; they do not even wish to look at it. 'Kāmarāgo pāturahu' means that because of the strength of unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) toward that corpse, sensual lust (kāmarāga) clearly arose in me. 'Andhova savatī ahu' means that although impure things were flowing and trickling from the nine openings of that corpse, I was like a blind man because of not being able to see that impurity. Therefore, it is said:
'One who is lustful does not know the benefit; one who is lustful does not see the Dhamma.
When lust overcomes a man, there is then utter darkness.'
And also: 'Brahmin, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) causes blindness, it causes lack of vision,' and so forth.

In this context, some teachers insert the letter 'ta' in the middle and interpret it as 'not following one's own will due to the eruption of defilements' or 'following the will of defilements.' Other teachers, reading the Pāḷi as 'andhova asati ahu', interpret it as 'becoming one who lacks mindfulness, being like one blinded by sensual lust.' However, neither of these is found in the original Pāḷi.

'Oraṃ odanapākamhā' means in a period of time less than that required for cooking rice. In a time even faster than it takes to cook a measure of rice that has been well washed and soaked, I dispelled lust and departed from that place where lust had arisen in me. Having departed, I was mindful and possessed of clear comprehension, establishing the perception of being a recluse; I was mindful by way of attention to the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and possessed of clear comprehension by way of knowing the nature of things (dhamma) correctly...
38:
...and being possessed of clear comprehension, I approached a suitable place and sat down, having folded my legs crosswise. To me, thus seated, wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) arose, and so forth—the entire sequence of events is just as described below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Rājadatta is Finished.

## 2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Subhūta

The verse beginning with "Ayoga" is that of the Venerable Subhūta Thera. As for the background—this Venerable Subhūta also had performed meritorious service (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. In the time of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, he was reborn in a wealthy householder family (gahapati-mahāsāla) in Bārāṇasī. When he reached maturity, one day he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and, with a devoted mind, established himself in the Refuges and the Precepts. Eight times every month, he offered four kinds of perfumes, piling them up at the Teacher’s Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi). Due to that meritorious deed, he possessed a fragrant body in every place he was reborn.

In this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a householder family in the kingdom of Magadha and received the name Subhūta. When he reached maturity, having the desire for liberation, he left the household life and went forth as an ascetic among the followers of other sects (titthiya). Finding no essence among those other sects, he saw many recluses and brahmins, such as Upatissa, Kolita, and Sela, going forth in the presence of the Teacher and enjoying the happiness of recluseship. He then gained faith in the Dispensation and went forth. Having pleased his teachers and preceptors, he took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and, living in seclusion, developed insight (vipassanā) and attained the fruit of Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"In this auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa), the Great Famous One of the Brahmin lineage,
Named Kassapa by clan, the best of speakers, arose.
He was endowed with the minor characteristics and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
Surrounded by a fathom-wide aura, and covered with a net of rays.
Giving comfort like the moon, making light like the sun,
Bringing coolness like a great cloud, and being the source of virtues like the ocean."
39:
In virtue, he is like the earth; in concentration, he is like the Himavanta mountains. In wisdom, he is as vast as the sky; like the wind, he is unattached to all things.

At that time, I was born into a noble family in the city of Bārāṇasī, which was abundant in wealth and grain and was a collection of various jewels.

Approaching the Lord of the World (the Buddha), who sat surrounded by a great following, I heard the Dhamma, which is like the Deathless medicine and captivates the heart.

Endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, he is like the moon accompanied by the stars. Endowed with the eighty minor marks, he is like a king of Sāla trees in full bloom.

Surrounded by a net of rays, he is like a blazing golden mountain. Encircled by a fathom-wide radiance, he is like the hundred-rayed sun.

The Excellent Buddha, with a golden-hued face, is like the noble king of mountains. He has a heart full of compassion and is like the ocean in terms of his virtues.

The heroic Sage, whose fame is renowned in the world and who is like Mount Sineru, the most excellent of all mountains, is as vast as the sky with his followers.

The Leader of the World, whose mind is unattached to all things, is like the wind. The most excellent Sage, who is the support of all beings, is like the earth.

Like a lotus flower unsullied by water, he is unsullied by the world. He is as magnificent as a great mass of fire that burns away the thicket of wrong views.

He is like a medicine that destroys the poison of defilements in all things. He is like Mount Gandhamādana, beautiful with the fragrance of his virtues.

The heroic Sage, who is a repository of virtues, is like the ocean, a repository of jewels. Like the ocean (or river) that removes the impurities of forest ranges, he removes the impurities of defilements.

He is like a victorious general who subdues the army of Māra. He is like a Universal Monarch who rules over the jewels of the Factors of Enlightenment.

He is like a great physician who cures the disease of faults. Like a surgeon who lances a boil, he is a physician who lances the boil of wrong views and extracts the thorn of defilements.
40:
At that time, the Victorious Buddha, who is the lamp of the world, honored by gods and men, and like a sun among men in the midst of the assembly, preached the Dhamma.

"Through giving, there is great wealth; through virtue, one reaches a good destination; and through meditation, defilements are extinguished." Thus he exhorted.

The entire assembly listened to that extremely pleasant discourse, which is beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end, as if it were the flavor of the Deathless.

Having heard the extremely sweet Dhamma and being inspired with faith in the Buddha's Dispensation, I took refuge in the Buddha and paid homage to him for the rest of my life.

At that time, on the eighth day of every month, I anointed the ground of the Buddha's Fragrant Chamber with the four kinds of perfumes as an offering.

I, who had a foul-smelling body, made an aspiration to have a fragrant body. At that time, the Buddha gave a prophecy that I would obtain a fragrant body.

"Whoever anoints the ground of the Fragrant Chamber even once with perfume, by the result of that kamma, wherever he is born in various lives,

This person will have a fragrant body everywhere; being endowed with the fragrance of virtue, he will be free from taints and attain Nibbāna," he said.

Due to that meritorious deed, intention, and aspiration, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

In this, my final birth, I was born into a Brahmin family. While I was dwelling in my mother's womb, my mother's body was filled with the scent of perfumes.

When I was born from my mother's womb, the city of Sāvatthī became fragrant as if suffused with all kinds of perfumes.

At that very moment, a rain of fragrant flowers fell, and delightful divine scents and precious incense also wafted through the air.

The gods also made the house where I was born fragrant with all kinds of perfumes, incense, and flowers.
41:
When I was young and in the prime of my youth, the Buddha, the trainer of men, tamed Sela the Brahmin along with his followers.

When he arrived at the city of Sāvatthī surrounded by all those people, I saw the power of the Buddha and went forth into homelessness.

Having developed the four qualities of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation, I have reached the destruction of the taints (Arahantship).

When I was ordained, when I became an Arahant, and when I am to attain Parinibbāna—on those occasions, a rain of perfume fell.

The fragrance of my body always excels and surpasses that of precious sandalwood, jasmine, and blue water-lily. Likewise, it overwhelms all other kinds of perfumes and spreads throughout various lives.

My defilements have been burned away... I have followed the instructions of the Buddha.

After attaining Arahantship, reflecting on the suffering of self-mortification he experienced while ordained among the ascetics of other sects, and the happiness of meditation (jhāna) and so forth attained after ordaining in the Dispensation, he declared his final knowledge (Arahantship) by reviewing his own practice, saying thus:

"If a man desiring his welfare applies himself to unsuitable exertion (self-mortification) and continues to practice it, he cannot attain his welfare; such exertion is indeed a sign of my misfortune.

Evil defilements have been uprooted and conquered. If one were to abandon even one (factor such as heedfulness), one would be like a loser. If one were to abandon all (factors), one would be like a blind man due to not seeing what is even and what is uneven.

One should speak only of what one would do; one should not speak of what one would not do. The wise recognize the one who speaks without practicing.

Just as a beautiful flower that is colorful but lacks fragrance (is useless), so too are well-spoken words fruitless for one who does not act accordingly."
42:
“Just as a beautiful flower, possessed of color and fragrance, [gives fragrance to the wearer], so too, well-spoken words are fruitful for one who practices accordingly.” He spoke these five verses.

Among those verses, 'ayoga' refers to the two extremes that should not be pursued or associated with. Here, the meaning should be understood as self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga). One who engages oneself in that practice is called 'yuñjanto'. 'Kiccamicchako' refers to one who, while desiring the welfare of both the present and the cycle of rebirths, practices in 'ayoga' (wrong practice) which is the opposite of that welfare; such a person cannot reach the desired welfare and happiness. Therefore, [he thinks], "That I, being deceived by the views of sectarians, exerted myself in what should not be practiced, is my ill-fortune and unmeritorious nature." This shows that he exerted himself in the wrong practice because of being deluded by past kamma.

Because of their nature to oppress, lust and so on are called 'agha' (suffering/evil). The cycle of rebirth (saṃsāravaṭṭa), which is the occurrence of these evils, is called 'aghagataṃ'. Overcoming wholesome states is called 'vijitaṃ'. In the phrase 'aghagataṃ vijitaṃ', it is recited without dropping the nasal sound (niggahīta). It means being in such a state without having removed those evils (abbūḷhaṃ) and without having completely eradicated the defilements (kilesa). If one were to abandon the one and only, foremost heedfulness (appamāda) or right effort, that person would be like a wretched person (kāḷakaṇṇī). If one were to abandon all five faculties (indriya)—faith (saddhā), energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā)—which mature liberation (vimutti), and if one discards them without developing them, one would be like a blind person who cannot see what is even or uneven (right or wrong).

'Yathā' is a particle used for comparison. 'Ruciraṃ' means beautiful. 'Vaṇṇavantaṃ' means endowed with color and form. 'Agandhakaṃ' means lacking fragrance, like the pālibhaddaka, kaṇṇikā, jayā, and sumanā flowers. 'Subhāsitā vācā' refers to the words of the Buddha, the Tipiṭaka, which are like flowers endowed with color and form. Just as the fragrance of a scentless flower does not spread to the body of the wearer, so too, for one who listens respectfully to these words but does not practice accordingly, they cannot bring the fragrance of learning and the fragrance of practice, and thus become fruitless. Therefore, it was said, "Well-spoken words are fruitless for one who does not practice." 'Sugandhakaṃ' means having fragrance, like the sumanā, campaka, and nīluppala flowers. 'Evaṃ' means just as the fragrance spreads on the body of one who wears such a flower, so too, the well-spoken words known as the Tipiṭaka Buddha-word...
43:
...one also practices well through respectful listening and so on. For one who does not practice respectfully and does not do what should be done regarding that Dhamma, it cannot bring the fragrance of learning and the fragrance of practice, and thus becomes fruitless. Therefore, it was said, "So, well-spoken words are fruitless for one who does not practice."

'Sugandhaka' refers to flowers such as jasmine (sumanā), campaka, and blue lotus (nīluppala). In this way, just as the fragrance spreads on the body of the wearer of that flower, so too, for one who does what should be done regarding the well-spoken words known as the Tipiṭaka Buddha-word through respectful listening and so on, it is fruitful for that person. Because it can bring the fragrance of learning and the fragrance of practice, it is of great fruit and great benefit. Therefore, one should practice according to the advice; one should be one who speaks as he acts and acts as he speaks. The remaining words are as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Subhūti is Finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Girimānanda

"Vassati devo" and the following verses are the verses of the Venerable Girimānanda. What is the background story? This elder also had performed great merit under previous Buddhas and had accumulated meritorious deeds in various existences. In the time of Sumedha Buddha, he was born into a noble family. Upon reaching adulthood, while living as a householder, his wife and children passed away. Pierced by the thorn of grief, he entered the forest. The Teacher (the Buddha) went there and preached the Dhamma. When the thorn of grief was removed, he, with a devoted mind, worshipped with fragrant flowers, paid homage with the five-point prostration, and praised the Buddha with hands raised in anjali to his head.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In the time of our Buddha, he was born as the son of King Bimbisāra's chaplain (purohita) in Rājagaha and was named Girimānanda. When he reached the age of discretion, he saw the Buddha's majesty during the Teacher's visit to Rājagaha. Having gained faith, he ordained. While practicing the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma), he stayed in a village monastery for a few days and then went to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Teacher. King Bimbisāra, hearing of the elder's arrival, approached him and invited him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please reside right here; I shall support you with the four requisites."
44:
(King Bimbisāra) went away and, due to being busy with many affairs, did not remember (to build the monastery). Thinking, "The Elder is living in the open air," the deities prevented the rain out of fear that the Elder would get wet. The King, reflecting on the reason for the lack of rain, had a small hut built for the Elder. While living in that small hut, the Elder obtained a suitable dwelling (senāsana-sappāya), gained concentration, balanced his energy, applied himself to insight meditation, and attained Arahantship. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"My wife has passed away; my son has gone to the cemetery.
My mother, father, and brother have died; they were all cremated on a single pyre.
Burning with that grief, I became thin and pale.
My mind was distracted, afflicted by that sorrow.
Pierced by the dart of grief, I entered the forest.
Eating fallen fruits, I lived at the foot of a tree.
The Buddha named Sumedha, the Conqueror who puts an end to suffering,
Desiring to rescue me, came into my presence.
Hearing the sound of the footsteps of Sumedha, the Great Sage,
I raised my head and looked up at the Great Sage.
When the Great Hero arrived, joy arose within me.
At that time, seeing the Leader of the World, my mind became one-pointed.
Regaining mindfulness, I offered a handful of leaves.
The Buddha, the One with Vision, sat there out of compassion.
Having sat there, the Buddha Sumedha, the Leader of the World,
Preached the Dhamma to me, which dispels the dart of grief.
'Uninvited they came from there; without permission they departed from here.
As they came, so they went. What lamentation can there be in that?
Just as traveling beings, when it rains,
Seek shelter with their belongings to avoid getting wet...'"
45:
"...When the rain ceases, the travelers go wherever they wish. In the same way, your parents have gone. Why lament over their departure? Just as guests arrive and then depart, moving to and fro, so too your parents have gone. Why lament over their departure?

Just as a snake leaves behind its old, worn-out skin and moves on, so too your parents have left their bodies behind in this life.

Having understood the words of the Buddha, I abandoned the dart of grief. Generating joy, I paid homage to the most excellent Buddha. Having paid homage to the Buddha, I worshipped Sumedha, the Leader of the World, with mountain jasmine flowers (girimallikā) that were as fragrant as divine scents.

Having worshipped the Fully Enlightened One, I placed my joined palms on my head, and recollecting his supreme qualities, I praised the Leader of the World.

'O Great Hero, you have crossed over (the ocean of saṃsāra). O Omniscient One, Leader of the World, Great Sage, you rescue all beings through your knowledge.

O Great Sage, you completely cut off doubt and indecision. O One with Vision, through your knowledge, you have set me upon the Path.'

Arahants who have attained mastery, endowed with the six higher powers and great psychic potency, wise ones who travel through the air, were surrounding him at that moment.

There were also disciples who are trainees (sekha) and those established in the fruits (phalaṭṭha). Like lotuses blooming at sunrise, your disciples flourish.

Like the great ocean that cannot be disturbed, you are incomparable and difficult to surpass. Thus, endowed with knowledge, O One with Vision, you are immeasurable.

Having paid homage to the Conqueror of the World, the One with Vision and great fame, and bowing to all directions, I departed, backing away.

Passing away from the deva world, with clear comprehension and established mindfulness, I wandered through various existences and entered a mother's womb."
46:
"Having left the home life, I went forth into homelessness.
Being energetic, wise, and meditative, I dwelt frequenting secluded places.

Having exerted effort in meditation and having pleased the Great Sage,
I wander at all times like the moon freed from a dense cloud.

I am devoted to seclusion, peaceful, and without acquisitions (nirūpadhi).
Having fully understood all taints (āsavas), I dwell free from taints.

Thirty thousand aeons ago, I worshipped the Buddha.
Since then, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

My defilements have been burnt away... I have followed the teaching of the Buddha."

Then, as if the rain deity were rejoicing at the Elder Girimānanda's attainment of Arahantship, it rained. The Elder, as a way of urging the rain and declaring his attainment of Arahantship, spoke these five verses:

"The deity rains according to his well-sung song. My small hut is well-thatched, pleasant, and shielded from the wind.
In it, I dwell at peace. So, if you wish, O deity, rain down!

The deity rains according to his well-sung song. My small hut is well-thatched, pleasant, and shielded from the wind.
In it, I dwell with a peaceful mind. So, if you wish, O deity, rain down!

The deity rains... in it, I dwell free from lust...

The deity rains... in it, I dwell free from hatred...

The deity rains according to his well-sung song. My small hut is well-thatched, pleasant, and shielded from the wind.
In it, I dwell free from delusion. So, if you wish, O deity, rain down!"

Thus, he spoke these five verses.
47:
In those verses, 'yathāsugītaṃ' means in accordance with one's own beautiful rain-song, in accordance with one's own excellent sound of rain. Indeed, just as a cloud is not beautiful if it merely rains without thundering, and it is also not beautiful if it rises with thousands of layers of clouds, thundering and flashing lightning but does not rain; it is said, "The rain-god rains in accordance with his beautiful rain-song" because it is only beautiful when it rains in such a manner (both thundering and raining). Therefore, it is said in the scriptures: "O Pajjunna, thunder!" and "Both thundering and raining." "I dwell in that hut" means I dwell within that hut with the posture of the Noble Abiding (Ariyavihāra). "One with a peaceful mind" means one whose mind is well-pacified through the concentration of the fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala-samādhi).

Accepting the Elder's repeated encouragement with great respect, the rain-god Valāhaka caused a great rain to fall, filling the lowlands and the highlands.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Girimānanda Thera is finished.

## 4. The Commentary on the Verses of Sumana Thera

The verse beginning with "Yaṃ patthayāno" is that of the Venerable Sumana Thera. As for its origin... this Elder had also performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various lives. Ninety-five aeons ago, in an empty aeon (suñña-kappa) when no Buddha appeared, he was born into a family home. Upon reaching maturity, he saw a Paccekabuddha afflicted by illness and offered him a yellow myrobalan (harītaka). Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a householder's family in the Kosala kingdom and was named Sumana, growing up in comfort. His maternal uncle had ordained, become an Arahant, and lived in the forest. When Sumana came of age, his uncle ordained him and gave him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for his temperament. While striving in that meditation, he attained the four jhānas and the five superknowledges (abhiññā). Then the Elder taught him the method of insight (vipassanā). Before long, he developed insight and was established in the fruit of Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"Yellow myrobalan, emblic myrobalan, mango, rose-apple, belleric myrobalan, jujube, marking nut, and bael fruit—I brought these myself."
48:
"Seeing the Sage (Muni) who had reached the mountain cleft, delighting in jhāna and practicing meditation,
Seeing the Great Sage who was severely afflicted by illness and was alone without a companion,

I took a yellow myrobalan and offered it to that Paccekabuddha. Just by eating that medicine, the illness was pacified at that very moment.

The Buddha (Paccekabuddha), freed from distress, expressed appreciation (anumodanā) to me because of that gift of medicine and the pacification of the illness.

'Whether you are a god or a human, or born in any other life, may you be happy everywhere, and may illness never come to you,' he said.

Having said this, the Sage, the Self-become (Sayambhū), the Unconquered, the Wise One, rose into the sky like a king of swans in the air.

From the time the yellow myrobalan was given to the Great Sage, the Self-become, until this birth, no illness has ever arisen in me.

This is my last birth; the final existence is proceeding. The three knowledges (tevijjā) have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Ninety-four aeons ago, I gave medicine then; I do not know of any woeful state. This is the fruit of giving medicine.

My defilements have been burnt away... etc... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

After being established in the fruit of Arahatship, one day he went to attend to his uncle, the Elder. The Elder asked about his attainment, and he replied to the Elder:

"The preceptor (upajjhāya) supported me, who was desiring the Deathless (Amata), in whatever Dhamma he wished for me among the Dhammas; I have done what was to be done.

I have reached and realized the Dhamma myself, which is not based on hearsay (anītiho). Possessing pure knowledge and being free from doubt, I declare this in your presence.

I know my past lives (pubbenivāsa); the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) has been purified. My own goal (Arahatship) has been reached; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

I, being diligent, have practiced the three trainings (sikkhā). Established in your teaching, I have much learning (bahussuta); all taints (āsava) are exhausted. Now there is no further rebirth. You, Venerable Sir, admonished me by establishing me in pure conduct, and you looked after and supported me with compassion. Your instruction was not in vain. The resident pupil has completed his training."

In those verses, 'Yaṃ patthayāno dhammesu upajjhāyo anuggahi amataṃ abhikankhantaṃ' means: among the faultless states such as Samatha and Vipassanā, the preceptor supported me, who was desiring Nibbāna, by giving me advice on whatever Dhamma he desired for me. 'Katā kattabbakaṃ mayā' means: I have completed the sixteen tasks such as full understanding (pariññā) for the sake of attaining that Nibbāna. Therefore, the four paths (magga) have been reached and realized. 'Sayaṃ dhammo anītihoti' means: the realization of the Dhamma of Nibbāna and the Fruit (Phala) by oneself alone (not merely by hearing from others). Self...
49:
"I have practiced the threefold training of my diligent self; I am well-versed in your teaching. All my taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

You have exhorted me with the noble practice, showing compassion and favor. Your advice was not in vain; I, your resident pupil, have trained in the threefold training." With these five verses, he roared his lion's roar, declaring his final knowledge.

In those verses, "The preceptor, desiring that Dhamma for me, favored me who was longing for the deathless" means: among the blameless states such as serenity and insight, the preceptor, desiring that Dhamma for me, favored me who was longing for the deathless Nibbāna by way of giving advice. "I have completed what was to be done" means: for the sake of attaining that Nibbāna, I have completed the sixteenfold task, such as full understanding (pariññā).

Therefore, the fourfold path-dhamma has been reached and realized. "Having seen the Dhamma for oneself, not by hearsay" means: having realized for oneself the Dhamma of Nibbāna and the Dhamma of fruition, not merely hearing it from others. The noble path arises while cutting off doubt known as 'it was thus, so it is said.' Therefore, he said, 'possessing pure knowledge and being free from doubt,' etc. Therein, 'visuddhañāṇo' means one with pure knowledge because of purity from all defilements. 'Tavantike' means in your presence.

'Sadattho' means Arahantship. 'Sikkhā' means the training in higher virtue and so on. 'Sussutā' means well-heard due to the fulfillment of great learning in the scriptures (pariyatti) and great learning in penetration (paṭivedha). 'Tava sāsane' means standing in your advice and instruction.

'Ariyavatā' means by undertaking the practice of very pure virtue and so on. 'The resident pupil has trained in the trainings' means: because of living the holy life in your presence, I am a resident pupil who has trained in the trainings of higher virtue and so on.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sumana Thera is finished.
50:
## 5. Vaḍḍhattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Sādhū hi" is that of the Venerable Vaḍḍha Thera. What is its origin? This one also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits that were the basis for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn into a householder's family in the city of Bharukaccha. Named "Vaḍḍha," he grew up in due course. Then his mother, having developed a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding the cycle of rebirth, entrusted her son to relatives, ordained among the bhikkhunīs, and by practicing insight meditation, attained Arahantship. Later, when her son reached maturity, she had him ordained under the Elder Veḷudanta. That monk Vaḍḍha, having learned the Buddha's word, became a learned Dhamma-preacher and carried the burden of study (ganthadhura). One day, thinking, "I will go see my mother alone, wearing only my inner robe," he went to the bhikkhunīs' quarters. Seeing him, his mother rebuked him, saying, "Why have you come here alone, wearing only your inner robe?" Being rebuked by his mother, he felt spiritual urgency, thinking, "I have done something improper." He returned to the monastery, sat in his daytime resting place, practiced insight, and attained Arahantship. Manifesting the perfection of his mother's advice, he declared his final knowledge thus:

"My mother was indeed good; she showed me the goad.
Having heard the words of her who gave me birth and being exhorted by her,
With energy aroused and mind directed toward Nibbāna, I reached the supreme enlightenment.

I am an Arahant, worthy of offerings, possessing the three knowledges, a seer of the deathless.
Having conquered the army of Namuci, I live free from taints.

Whatever taints I had, both internal and external,
All have been cut off without remainder, and they will not arise again.

The courageous sister spoke this meaning.
Indeed, the forest of craving no longer exists in me.

Suffering has been brought to an end; this is my last physical frame.
The cycle of birth and death has ceased; now there is no more rebirth." He spoke these verses.

In those verses, "Sādhū hi kira me mātာ patodaṃ upadaṃsayī" means: My mother is truly good; she showed me the goad of instruction. With that instruction, she sharpened my energy. She struck the head, which is the noble limb of wisdom. "Yassā" means of that mother of mine. "Sambodhiṃ" refers to Arahantship. The connection (yojanā) here is: My mother having exhorted me, and having heard the words of my mother's instruction, while I lived with energy aroused and mind directed toward Nibbāna, I reached the supreme fruit of Arahantship. Having reached that, he is called "Arahā" because of being far from defilements. He is "Dakkhiṇeyyo" because he is like a field for planting merits. He is called "Tevijjo" because he obtained the three knowledges. He is called "Amataddaso" because he realized Nibbāna.
51:
In these verses, it means: "My mother showed me the goad, which is the instruction. By that instruction, she stimulated my effort and struck (urged) me on the head, which is the limb of wisdom. How excellent!" "Yassā" means "of that mother of mine." "Sambodhi" refers to the fruit of Arahatship. Here is the connection (yojanā): Being exhorted by my mother and hearing her words of instruction, I lived with aroused effort and a mind directed towards Nibbāna, and thus reached the supreme and highest fruit, Arahatship.

Because he has reached Arahatship, he is "Arahaṃ" because he is remote from defilements. He is also "Dakkhiṇeyya," worthy of noble offerings, because he is like a fertile field for merit. He is "Tevijja" because he has attained the three knowledges, such as the knowledge of past lives. He is "Amataddasa" (one who sees the deathless Nibbāna) because he has realized Nibbāna. Having conquered the defilement-army of Māra with the army of the Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma, he lives happily, free from cankers (āsavas).

Now, to make the meaning of "anāsavo" (one free from cankers) clearer, he spoke the verse beginning with "Ajjhattañca." The meaning of that verse is: The internal cankers (ajjhatta-āsava) arising within oneself and the external cankers (bahiddha-āsava) arising externally existed before the attainment of the Ariyan Path. All those cankers have been destroyed without remainder by the Ariyan Path, and now they will never arise again at any time.

Now, taking his mother's words as a hook (aṅkusa) and having attained Arahatship himself, he spoke the verse beginning with "Visāradā" to praise his mother. There, "Visāradā" means one who is definitely free from fear and hesitation. Thus, wishing to express that both he and his mother are true-born children of the Teacher through the attainment of Arahatship, he addressed his mother as "Bhaginī" (sister) and spoke these words of instruction. There is no need to wonder whether this mother who exhorted me in this way is not only confident but also lacks any bond of craving (taṇhā) towards me or her son. It is true that the thicket (vanatha) of craving, such as ignorance, no longer exists in your mental continuum. Such a mother urged me towards Nibbāna, the end of existence.

Now, to show "I have practiced exactly as urged by my mother," he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "Pariyantakataṃ." The meaning of that verse is very easy to understand.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Vaḍḍha Thera is finished.
52:
## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Nadīkassapa Thera

The verse beginning with "Atthāya vata me" is that of the Venerable Nadīkassapa Thera. As for its origin: This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome roots that were a strong support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various lives. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a good family. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw the Teacher wandering for alms. With a devoted mind, he offered a mango fruit, the color of realgar (manosilā), which was the first fruit from a mango tree he had planted himself.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha as the brother of Uruvela Kassapa. When he reached maturity, having a desire for liberation and no wish for the household life, he went forth as an ascetic. Along with three hundred ascetics, he built a hermitage and lived on the banks of the Nerañjarā River. Because he lived on the riverbank and belonged to the Kassapa clan, he became known by the name "Nadīkassapa."

The Blessed One granted him and his followers ordination through the "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, monk) formula. All of this is already mentioned in the Khandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga. That Venerable Elder was established in the fruit of Arahatship at the end of the Blessed One's discourse on the Ādittapariyāya Sutta.

Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna:
"To the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Chief of the World, the Possessor of Tādi-virtue,
Who was wandering for alms, bearing supreme fame,
I took the best fruit with a clear and devoted mind,
And offered it to the Teacher, the Hero worthy of offerings.
O Chief of bipeds, Chief of the World, Bull among men,
By that deed, having abandoned victory and defeat, I have reached the unshakable state.
In the hundred thousandth aeon ago, because of the gift I gave then,
I have not known any woeful state; this is the fruit of that supreme gift.
My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

After being established in the fruit of Arahatship, at a later time, reviewing his own practice and wishing to declare his attainment of Arahatship by way of praising the total eradication of wrong view, he said:
53:
The Buddha truly went to the Nerañjarā River for my benefit. Having heard the Dhamma of that Buddha, I have abandoned wrong views.

I used to perform various sacrifices, high and low; I also performed fire oblations. Thinking, 'This sacrifice alone is the way to purification,' the worldling, lacking the eye of wisdom, became utterly blinded.

Plunging into the thicket of views, I was deluded by misapprehension. Being blind through ignorance and lacking wisdom, I regarded what is not the way to purification as the way to purification.

Now, my wrong views are abandoned, and all existences are destroyed. I make offerings to the Buddha, the supreme recipient of offerings, and I pay homage to the Tathāgata.

All my delusions are abandoned, and craving for existence is destroyed. The cycle of birth and wandering is exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

He recited these five verses.

In those verses, 'atthāya vata me' means truly for my benefit, for my welfare. 'Buddho' refers to the Omniscient Buddha. 'nadiṃ nerañjaraṃ agā' means he came to the river called Nerañjarā; it means he approached the hermitage of my brother, Uruvela Kassapa, on the bank of that river.

Now, to clarify the meaning already stated, the words beginning with 'yassāhaṃ' are said. 'yassa' means of that Buddha, the Blessed One. 'dhammaṃ sutvānā' means having heard the Dhamma connected with the Four Noble Truths, perceiving it through the sense-door of hearing. 'micchādiṭṭhiṃ vivajjayiṃ' means I have abandoned the distorted view that arises in the manner of 'purification comes through sacrifices and so on.'

To expand upon the meaning of 'micchādiṭṭhiṃ vivajjayiṃ,' the words beginning with 'yajiṃ' are said. Therein, 'yajiṃ uccāvace yaññe' means I performed various well-known sacrifices such as Somayāga and Vājapeyya. 'aggihuttaṃ juhiṃ ahaṃ' means I tended the fire, presenting oblations by way of performing those sacrifices. 'esā suddhīti maññanto' means thinking, 'Through this, my purification from Saṃsāra will occur,' because that act of sacrifice and fire-tending was considered the cause of purification. 'andhabhūto puthujjano' means being a worldling who is utterly blinded by the darkness of ignorance due to the lack of the eye of wisdom. Because it is difficult to overcome, like a forest thicket or a mountain thicket, 'view' itself is called a 'thicket' (gahana).
54:
Because it is difficult to overcome and difficult to cross, view itself is called a thicket; because of plunging into that thicket of views, one is called 'diṭṭhigahanapakkhanda.' 'parāmāsena' means by the distorted conviction known as misapprehension, through the power of grasping, 'Only this is the truth,' having overstepped the true nature of things. 'mohito' means led to a state of delusion. 'asuddhiṃ maññisaṃ suddhiṃ' means I regarded sacrifices and so on, which are not the cause of purification from Saṃsāra, as the cause of purification. Regarding the reason for such thinking, he said 'andhabhūto aviddasū.' Because he had become blinded by ignorance, and for that very reason, not knowing or seeing the Dhamma and non-Dhamma, or what is appropriate and inappropriate, he thought in that way—this is the meaning.

'micchādiṭṭhi pahīnā me' means that for such a person as me, having heard the Dhamma discourse containing the Four Noble Truths in the presence of the Teacher and practicing accordingly, all wrong views have been abandoned by me through the power of abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna) via the Right View of the Noble Path. 'bhavā' means all existences, such as the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava) and so on, have been destroyed, utterly demolished by the sword of the Noble Path. 'juhaāmi dakkhiṇeyyaggiṃ' means having abandoned the fires such as the āhuneyya fire, I worship and serve the Fully Enlightened One, named the 'Fire Worthy of Offerings' (dakkhiṇeyyaggi), because he is worthy of the supreme offerings of the world including the devas, and because he burns away all evil. This service of mine to the 'Fire Worthy of Offerings' (the Buddha) is the mere act of paying homage to the Teacher, without regard for curds, fresh butter, buttermilk, ghee, and so on; thus he said, 'namassāmi tathāgataṃ.' Alternatively, 'juhaāmi dakkhiṇeyyaggiṃ' means I serve and attend to myself, who has become like the 'Fire Worthy of Offerings' by making the offerings of donors yield great fruit and by burning away unwholesome states; having done so, I conduct myself. Although in the past I worshipped the fire-deity, now I pay homage to the Tathāgata.

'mohā sabbe pahīnā me' means all delusions, consisting of various types such as ignorance regarding the Truth of Suffering, have been abandoned and cut off by me. For that very reason, the word 'me' should be brought forward and applied to the three phrases: 'bhavataṇhā padālitā' (craving for existence is destroyed), 'vikkhīṇo jātisamsāro' (the cycle of birth is exhausted), and 'natthi dāni punabbhavo' (now there is no more rebirth).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Nadī Kassapa Thera is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Gayā Kassapa Thera

The verses beginning with 'pāto majjhanhikaṃ' are those of the Venerable Gayā Kassapa Thera. What is the background of their origin? This Gayā Kassapa Thera had also performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome roots that serve as a powerful support for the fruit of Arahantship in various lives. Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was born into a good family. Upon reaching maturity, he became wise and, with a desire for liberation, renounced the household life and entered the life of an ascetic...
55:
Having built a hermitage in the forest, he lived subsisting on forest roots and fruits. At that time, the Blessed One, alone and without a companion, went near that ascetic’s hermitage. Seeing the Blessed One, with a mind full of devotion, he approached, paid homage, and standing in a suitable place, observed the proper time and offered the Buddha delightful jujube fruits.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In the time of this Buddha’s appearance, he was reborn into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, with a desire for liberation, he abandoned the household life, went forth as an ascetic, and lived in Gayā with two hundred other ascetics. Because he lived in Gayā and belonged to the Kassapa clan, he became known as Gaya-Kassapa. This Gaya-Kassapa, along with his followers, received the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination from the Blessed One. While being exhorted with the discourse of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta, he was established in Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

''At that time, I was clad in antelope skin and wore bark garments;
Filling my carrying-pole with jujube fruits, I brought them to my hermitage.
At that time, the Buddha Sikhī was alone and without a companion;
Knowing all times, He came to my hermitage.
Having inspired faith in my own heart and paid homage to the One of Good Vows,
Raising them with both hands, I offered the jujube fruits to the Buddha.
Thirty-one aeons ago from this present aeon, I gave that fruit at that time;
Because of that merit, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering jujube.
My defilements have been burnt away... the round of rebirths is exhausted... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.''

Having been established in Arahantship, reflecting on his own practice and wishing to make his attainment of Arahantship known by way of praising the washing away of evil, he uttered:

''In the morning, at noon, and in the evening—three times a day—
I descended into the water at the Gaya river-ghat named Gayā-phaggu.
Whatever evil I had committed before in other births,
I shall now wash away that evil in this river—such was my view in the past.''
56:
''Having heard the well-spoken words, the passage endowed with Dhamma and meaning,
I reflected wisely on the true and factual meaning.

''I have washed away all evils; I am stainless, self-controlled, and pure.
I am the heir of the Pure One (the Buddha), the Buddha's own heart-born son.

''Having entered the stream of the Eightfold Path, I have washed away all evils.
I have attained the Three Knowledges, and the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.''

He uttered these five verses.

Among them, the brief meaning of the first verse is as follows: I descended into the water three times a day—in the morning at sunrise, at noon, and in the evening. In so descending, I did not descend just anywhere or at any time; rather, I practiced the annual ritual of descending into the water at the Gaya-ghat, which is regarded by the multitude as the 'place for washing away sins,' during the time of the Gayā-phaggu, which is the full moon of the month of Phagguna when the moon is in the Uttara-phagguṇī asterism.

Now, to show the intention with which he practiced descending into the water at that time, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Yaṃ mayā.' The meaning of that verse is: 'Whatever evil kamma I had accumulated in other previous births, I now wash away, remove, and cleanse that evil in this Gaya-ghat, at this time of Gayā-phaggu, by this act of descending into the water.' In the past, before coming to the Buddha's teaching, I was one who held such a view, such a perverted vision.

'Dhamma-attha-sahitaṃ padaṃ' is an exposition (niddesa) where the case endings are not elided. It refers to a collection endowed with both the Dhamma and the meaning. Having heard the Buddha's words—speech that is associated with the Dhamma and the meaning in the beginning, middle, and end, and is spoken in a way that is thoroughly and definitely leading out of suffering (niyyānika)—I reflected wisely on the meaning of suffering and so forth, which is 'tatha' (true) because of its ultimate reality as shown by the Blessed One, and 'yāthāvaka' (factual) because there is no deviation in the cause of its arising and ceasing as appropriate, by way of it being fully understood and so on: 'Suffering is to be fully understood, the origin is to be abandoned, cessation is to be...'
57:
It means that one has reflected on the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha-sacca) to be realized and the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca) to be developed, seeing and penetrating them with the eye of wisdom.

Because of such penetration of the Truths, I am one whose evils have all been washed away by the water of the Noble Path. Because of that washing, I am 'Nimmala' (Stainless), as there is no stain of lust and so forth. Because of pure conduct of body, speech, and mind, I am 'Payata' (Exerted), 'Suci' (Pure), and 'Suddha' (Clean). I am a 'Dāyāda' (Heir) because I have received the inheritance of the supramundane Dhamma from the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is purified from all stains of defilements along with their latent tendencies and who gives the inheritance of the supramundane Dhamma. I am his 'Orasa putta' (breast-born son), a true son born from the noble birth produced by the exertion of the heart, which has its origin in the Buddha's knowledge of teaching.

Again, to clarify his state of being one who has bathed (snātaka) in the ultimate sense, he spoke the final verse beginning with 'Ogayhā'. In that verse, 'Ogayhā' means having entered or plunged into. 'Aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ sotaṃ' refers to the stream of the Path composed of the eight factors such as Right View. 'Sabba pāpaṃ pavāhayiṃ' means I have washed away all stains of evil without remainder; by washing with the stream of the Noble Path, I have become a 'snātaka' in the ultimate sense. For that very reason, I have attained the three knowledges (tevijjā) and fulfilled the Buddha's teaching, as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Gaya-Kassapa Thera is finished.

## 8. The Commentary on the Verses of Vakkali Thera

The verse beginning with 'Vātarogābhinīto' is that of the Venerable Vakkali Thera. As for the background: This venerable one also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various lives. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Upon reaching maturity, he went to the monastery with lay devotees who were visiting the Teacher. Standing at the edge of the assembly while listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those liberated by faith (saddhādhimutta). Aspiring for that position himself, he performed a great almsgiving for seven days and made a resolution. The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, gave him the prophecy.

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Teacher. They named him Vakkali. When he reached maturity, he learned the three Vedas and became proficient in the arts of the Brahmins. Upon seeing the Teacher, he was never satisfied with gazing at the perfection of the Teacher's physical form (rūpakāya) and followed the Teacher everywhere. Thinking, 'If I live in the household life, I will not have the opportunity to see the Teacher at all times,' he ordained under the Teacher. Excluding the time for meals and personal hygiene, he spent the rest of his time...
58:
Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Teacher. They named him Vakkali. When he reached maturity, he learned the three Vedas and became proficient in the arts of the Brahmins. Upon seeing the Teacher, he was never satisfied with gazing at the perfection of the Teacher's physical form (rūpakāya) and followed the Teacher everywhere. Thinking, 'If I live in the household life, I will not have the opportunity to see the Teacher at all times,' he ordained under the Teacher. Excluding the time for meals and personal hygiene, he spent the rest of his time standing where he could see the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala), abandoning all other duties and just gazing at the Blessed One. The Teacher, awaiting the maturation of Vakkali's knowledge, said nothing for a long time while Vakkali wandered about just gazing at his form. Then one day, he said: 'Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this foul body? Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me; he who sees me sees the Dhamma. Indeed, Vakkali, seeing the Dhamma, one sees me; seeing me, one sees the Dhamma.'

Even though the Teacher spoke thus, the elder could not leave the sight of the Teacher to go elsewhere. Then the Teacher thought, 'This monk will not realize the Truths without gaining spiritual urgency (saṃvega).' On the day of entering the rains retreat, he dismissed the elder, saying, 'Go away, Vakkali.' Being dismissed by the Teacher and unable to stay in his presence, the Venerable Vakkali thought, 'What is the use of my life if I do not get to see the Teacher?' and climbed the precipice of Mount Gijjhakūṭa. The Teacher, knowing this, thought, 'If this monk does not receive consolation from me, his supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the Paths and Fruits will be destroyed.' To show himself, he emitted a radiance and spoke this verse:

'The monk who is full of joy and has faith in the Buddha's teaching,
May reach the peaceful state, the happiness of the stilling of formations.'

Having spoken this verse, he stretched out his hand, saying, 'Come, Vakkali.' The elder thought, 'I have seen the Ten-Powered One, and I have received the call "Come".' Generating powerful joy and rapture, and not even knowing he was moving, he leaped into the air towards the Teacher. While still on the mountain with his first step...
59: It is stated in the Anguttara Commentary and the Dhammapada Commentary that while reflecting on the recited verse, he suppressed joy while in the air and attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights. However, in this commentary, it is said: "Vakkali, what is the use of [looking at] this foul body?" Having been thus admonished by the Blessed One, he dwelt on Vulture Peak Mountain (Gijjhakūṭa) and practiced insight meditation (Vipassanā). Because his faith (saddhā) was too strong, he could not enter the path of insight. The Blessed One, knowing this, purified and gave him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Again, before he could bring insight to its peak, he developed a wind-ailment (vātābādha) due to a deficiency in food. Knowing that he was being oppressed by the wind-ailment, the Blessed One went there and, wishing to inquire, said: "Afflicted by wind disease, dwelling in the rustling forest, in this harsh place where requisites are hard to find, how will you manage, monk?" Hearing these words, the Elder recited four verses: "Suffusing my body with great joy and bliss, enduring even harsh conditions, I shall dwell in the forest. Developing the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment, I shall dwell in the forest. Seeing companions who are energetic, resolute, always firm in effort, harmonious, and united [in view and virtue], I shall dwell in the forest. Recollecting the Fully Enlightened One, the Supreme, the Tamed, the Concentrated, without sloth day and night, I shall dwell in the forest." In those verses, "vātaroogābhinīto" means brought to a state of being unable to follow one's own will due to wind disease, or oppressed by wind disease. "Tvaṃ" is an address to the Elder. "Viharaṃ" means dwelling in that posture. "Kānane vane" means in the great forest (mahā-arañña) that rustles. "Paviddhagocare" means where the four requisites are difficult to obtain. Because of the absence of suitable medicines like ghee for the wind disease and because of the roughness of the ground, the harsh place is called "lūkhe". "Kathaṃ bhikkhu karissasi" means "Monk, how will you be able to dwell?" thus the Blessed One asked.
60: Upon hearing the Blessed One's question, the Elder Vakkali, wishing to manifest his happy dwelling through unworldly joy and happiness, recited the verse beginning with "Pītisukhena". In that verse, "pītisukhena" refers to joy characterized by uplifting and joy characterized by suffusing, along with the bliss (sukha) associated with that joy. Therefore, it is said to be "vipulena", meaning noble. "Pharamāno samussayaṃ" means suffusing the entire body without gap with the refined material forms (rūpa) produced by the aforementioned joy and bliss. "Lūkhampi abhisambhonto" means overcoming and enduring the difficult-to-bear harshness of requisites, which arises from forest dwelling and has austere practice as its cause. "Viharissāmi kānane" means "I shall dwell in the forest, a place far from people, with the bliss of Jhana and the bliss of insight." Therefore, it was said: "He experiences bliss with the body," and: "Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates, one obtains joy and happiness; for those who know, that is the Deathless." "Bhāvento satipaṭṭhāne" means producing and developing the four foundations of mindfulness, such as mindfulness of the body, which are included in the Path. "Indriyāni" refers to the five faculties, such as faith, included in the Path. "Balāni" likewise refers to the five powers, such as faith. "Bojjhaṅgāni" likewise refers to the seven factors of enlightenment, such as the mindfulness factor of enlightenment. By the word "ca" (and), the four right efforts, the four bases of power, and the eight path factors are included. Since these qualities are inseparable from the foundations of mindfulness, etc., by taking the foundations of mindfulness, they are also taken. "Viharissāmi" means "I shall dwell, developing the aforementioned factors of enlightenment, with the bliss of the Path, the bliss of Fruition achieved through that attainment, and the bliss of Nibbāna." "Āraddhavīriye" refers to those who have energy exerted by way of the four right efforts. "Pahitattte" refers to those whose minds are directed toward Nibbāna. "Niccaṃ daḷhaparakkame" refers to those who have constant, firm endeavor. "Samagge" means harmonious by way of absence of dispute and by way of physical unity. "Sahite" means seeing fellow practitioners who are united by commonality of view and virtue. By this, the attainment of good friendship (kalyāṇamitta) is shown. "Anussaranto sambuddhaṃ" means "I shall dwell, recollecting the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) because he has known all dhammas rightly by himself, the Supreme because he is the best of all beings, the Tamed because he is tamed by the supreme taming, and the Concentrated because he is established in unsurpassed concentration, being one without sloth, day and night, at all times, in the manner of 'Itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ...'." By thus showing the manner of exertion in the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha, it implies repeated exertion in the universal meditation subject (sabbattha-kammaṭṭhāna).
61:
By showing the manner of practice in the recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati), he speaks of the repeated application in the meditation for all purposes (sabbatthaka-kammaṭṭhāna). By the previously mentioned meditation, he speaks of the repeated application in the meditation to be maintained (pārihāriya-kammaṭṭhāna).

Having spoken thus, Elder Vakkali, exerting effort in insight (vipassanā), attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"One hundred thousand aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, a Leader arose, named Anoma, immeasurable, known by the name Padumuttara.

He had a face like a lotus, a complexion as pure as a lotus. Like a lotus untainted by water, he was untainted by the world.

That Hero had eyes like lotus petals, and was as lovely as a lotus. He had a fragrance superior to a lotus, therefore he was called Padumuttara.

He was the eldest in the world, free from vanity, like an eye for the blind. He had a peaceful appearance, was a treasury of virtues, and an ocean of compassion and wisdom.

Once that Great Hero, worshipped by Brahmās, Asuras, and Devas, in the midst of people crowded with gods and men, that Supreme Conqueror—

With his fragrant mouth and sweet voice, pleasing the entire assembly, praised his own disciple:

'This bhikkhu Vakkali, in his resolute faith, in his wisdom, and in his great desire to see me—there is no other like him.'

Then, I was a son of a Brahmin in the city of Haṃsavatī. Hearing those words, I delighted in that position.

Having invited that stainless Tathāgata along with his disciples, and having fed them for seven days, I then offered gifts of robes.

Prostrating with my head at the feet of that ocean of infinite virtues, immersed and filled with joy, I spoke these words:

'O Sage, that monk whom you praised on the seventh day from now as the foremost among those with faith—O Sage, may I be like him.'"
62: 'When this was said, the Great Hero, the Great Sage of unobstructed vision, uttered these words in the midst of the assembly: "Behold this young man, wearing fine cloth, his body adorned with a golden sacrificial thread, who captivates the eyes and minds of people. In the future, he will be the foremost disciple among those resolute in faith under the Great Sage Gotama. Whether as a deva or a human, he will wander through rebirth happily, free from all feverish torments and endowed with all wealth and retinues. One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka line, will arise in the world. This man will be a disciple of that Teacher, an heir to the Dhamma, a heart-born son, created by the Dhamma, named Vakkali." Through that special deed and through my intentions and aspirations, I left the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Wandering through various existences, being happy in all lives, I was born into a certain family in the city of Sāvatthī. Delicate as butter, tender as a young sprout, while I was still a young infant lying on my back, my parents, terrified by the fear of ogres— Placed me at the feet of the Great Sage with anxious hearts. They said, "Lord, we give this child to you; O Leader, be his refuge." Then the Sage, the refuge of the fearful, accepted me with his soft and tender hand, which was marked with the wheel-sign and net-like lines. From then on, being protected by the protection of the Buddha—who himself needs no protection—I grew up happily, freed from all enmity. If separated from the Well-Gone One, I could not endure it even for a moment. At the age of seven, I went forth into the homeless life." '
63:
I lived without ever being satisfied, gazing at the physical form of the Buddha, which was born of all the perfections, possessed dark blue eyes, was noble, and was suffused with all beauty.

Knowing my delight in the Buddha's form, the Conqueror then admonished me: 'Enough, Vakkali! Why do you delight in this form that is cherished by fools?'

'He who sees the True Dhamma, that wise one sees me. He who does not see the True Dhamma does not see me, even though he is looking at me.'

'This body is full of infinite faults; it is like a poisonous tree. It is the abode of all diseases, a mere mass of suffering.'

'Therefore, being disenchanted with the physical form, observe the rise and fall of the five aggregates. You will easily reach the end of the defilements that cause impurity.'

Thus admonished by the Leader, the seeker of welfare, I climbed Gijjhakūṭa Mountain and meditated in a mountain cave.

While I was standing at the foot of the mountain, the Great Sage comforted me, saying 'Vakkali!' Hearing that word of the Conqueror, I was filled with joy.

I leaped from the mountain cliff, which was more than a hundred fathoms high. At that time, by the power of the Buddha, I reached the ground safely.

The Buddha again taught the Dhamma of the rise and fall of the aggregates. Having understood that Dhamma, I attained Arahantship.

Then, in the midst of a vast assembly, the Great Sage, who has reached the end of conduct and possesses great wisdom, declared me foremost among those liberated by faith (saddhādhimutta).

Whatever meritorious deed I performed a hundred thousand aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, since then I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.

My defilements are burnt away... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.

After attaining Arahantship, the Elder Vakkali recited these very verses to declare his attainment. Later, the Teacher, seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, placed the Elder Vakkali in the foremost position among those liberated by faith.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vakkali is finished.

The verse beginning with 'Uggacchāmi' is the verse of the Elder Vijitasena. This Elder Vijitasena also had performed special merit under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that was a strong support for Arahantship in various lives. In the time of the Buddha Atthadassī, he was born into a noble family, and upon reaching maturity, he renounced the household life and became an ascetic. While in the forest, he saw the Buddha Atthadassī traveling through the air. With a heart full of faith, he stood with palms joined. The Buddha, knowing the ascetic's inclination and underlying tendencies, descended from the sky. The ascetic offered sweet fruits that were pleasing to the heart. Out of compassion, the Buddha accepted them. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in the time of this Buddha Gotama, he was born into a family of elephant trainers in the Kosala kingdom and was named Vijitasena.
64:
## 9. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vijitasena

The verse beginning with 'Olaggesāmi' is the verse of the Venerable Elder Vijitasena. The story of his origin is as follows: This Elder also had performed merit under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that was a strong support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various lives. In the time of the Buddha Atthadassī, he was born into a noble family, and upon reaching maturity, he renounced the household life and became an ascetic. While living in the forest, he saw the Buddha traveling through the air. With a heart full of faith, he stood with palms joined, showing signs of devotion. The Buddha, knowing the ascetic's inclination, descended from the sky. The ascetic offered sweet fruits that were pleasing to the heart, and the Buddha accepted them out of compassion.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and when this Buddha appeared, he was born into a family of elephant trainers in the Kosala kingdom, named Vijitasena, and became endowed with wisdom. Two of Vijitasena's maternal uncles, named Sena and Upasena, who were master elephant trainers, heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, gained faith, ordained, and while fulfilling the duty of insight meditation, attained Arahantship. Vijitasena also achieved complete mastery in the art of elephant training. Having an inclination for liberation, his mind was not attached to the household life. After witnessing the Twin Miracle of the Teacher, he gained faith and ordained under his uncles. While practicing insight meditation according to their instructions, his mind strayed from the path of insight and wandered among various external objects. Wishing to admonish his own mind, he recited these verses:

'O mind, I will restrain your going, just as an elephant is restrained at a gatepost. I will not let you be joined to evil, to the net of sensual desire born of the body.

Being restrained, you shall not go, like an elephant that does not find an opening in the gate. O wicked mind, you shall not wander repeatedly, delighting in evil.

Just as a strong elephant trainer turns an untamed, newly caught elephant against its will, so shall I turn you.

Just as an excellent charioteer, skilled in training noble horses, tames a thoroughbred, so shall I tame you, being established in the five powers.'

In these verses, 'Olaggesāmi' means I will block or restrain. 'Te' means you; here the word 'te' is in the genitive case used in the sense of the accusative. Alternatively, it should be understood as 'te gamanaṃ' (your going). In the word 'hatthinaṃ', the meaning should be understood as 'hatthiṃ' (elephant). By the word 'citta', he is addressing his own mind. Wishing to show the manner in which he intends to restrain that mind, he said 'āṇidvāreva hatthinaṃ'. What is called 'āṇidvāra' is the gate of a city surrounded by walls...
65:
## 
“O mind, I shall bind you firmly with the rope of mindfulness; with effort, I shall discipline you. Restrained by the yoke of energy, you shall not go far from me.” Thus, he spoke this verse.

In that verse, ‘olaggetthāmi’ means I will block or prevent. ‘Te’ is the genitive case used in the sense of the second case (accusative) ‘taṃ’ (you). Or it should be understood by supplying the remaining words ‘te gamanaṃ’ (your going). In the word ‘hatthinaṃ’, the meaning ‘hatthiṃ’ (elephant) should be noted. With the word ‘citta’, he addresses his own mind. Desiring to show the manner of restraining that mind, he said, “āṇidvāreva hatthinaṃ” (like an elephant at the gate-bolt).

The ‘āṇidvāra’ is a small gate of a walled city. When the bolt (āṇi) is inserted into the hole of the crossbar, it cannot be opened even by those inside without the mechanism. Through it, beings such as humans, cattle, horses, and buffaloes cannot exit. Even an elephant wishing to go outside the city is prevented from going by the mahout through enticement. Alternatively, ‘āṇidvāra’ is a gate with a crossbar. There, having placed the crossbar (paligha) horizontally, they insert the bolt called the wooden pin into the head of the crossbar.

‘Pāpe’ means I will not engage that mind in unwholesome states such as covetousness (abhijjhā) that arise regarding forms and so on. ‘Kāmajāla’ means being like a net of sensual pleasures. Just as the nets of fishermen and hunters enable them to do as they wish with fish and other creatures, so too a mind that falls into improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) fulfills the will of Māra. Through that mind, Māra causes beings to fall into harmful things. ‘Sarīraja’ means that which arises in the body. In the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra bhava), the mind is called ‘sarīraja’ because its activity is dependent on the physical body.

“You are restrained and shall not go” means: O wicked mind, being restrained by me with the goad and hook of mindfulness and wisdom, you shall not now go as you please; you will not get to act according to your desire through the power of improper attention. How?
