Like an elephant that does not find a gate opening, or like an elephant that does not find a gate opening to exit from the city or from an elephant enclosure. ‘Cittakali’ means the very wicked mind. ‘Punappunaṃ’ means repeatedly (here and there). ‘Pasakkā’ is by the power of repeatedly looking at and being distracted by sensual pleasures. ‘Pāparato’ means delighting in evil deeds; you shall not go now as you did before; the meaning is that I will not allow you to go in that way.
66:
## 
‘Adanta’ refers to one not yet trained in elephant skills. ‘Navaggaha’ refers to an elephant that has been recently captured. ‘Aṅkusaggaha’ is the elephant trainer (mahout). ‘Balavā’ is one who is strong, endowed with both physical strength and the strength of wisdom. ‘Āvatteti akāmaṃ’ means causing to turn back (retreat) through restraint even against its will. Just as that mahout causes the aforementioned elephant to turn back, I too shall cause this wicked mind to retreat by restraining it from misconduct.

‘Varahayadamakusalo’ is one skilled in disciplining noble horses. For that reason, he is the most excellent charioteer, the most distinguished among those who tame horses; he disciplines the thoroughbred (ājāniya) horse according to the place and time using gentle and harsh methods, making it disciplined and free from attachment. Established in the five powers such as faith and so on, I shall discipline that mind by restraining lack of faith (assaddhiya) and the like.

I shall bind this wicked mind to the post of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) with the rope of mindfulness, preventing it from going outside its internal range (gocara). While bound to that meditation post, I shall discipline you with effort and purify you from the stains of defilements.

Just as a horse, yoked and restrained by a skilled charioteer, does not go beyond the yoke, so you, O mind, being restrained by my yoke of energy, because of my respectful and continuous practice, will not be able to act otherwise and will no longer be able to go far outside this internal object. Indeed, for one devoted to meditation, any object other than the meditation subject is ‘far’ in terms of characteristics, even if it is nearby. In this way, the Elder, restraining his own mind with these verses, developed insight and attained Arahantship.

Thus it is said in the Elder’s Apadāna:

“I saw the Buddha, who had a golden complexion and was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
Walking through the forest, as beautiful as a Sal tree in full bloom.

Having spread a mat of grass, I made a request to the Buddha:
‘May the Buddha have compassion on me; I wish to offer alms-food.’”
67:
The Buddha, who is compassionate, merciful, a seer of benefit, and of great fame, knowing my thought, descended to my hermitage.

Having descended, the Sambuddha sat on a spread of leaves. Taking a bhallaṭaka fruit, I offered it to the Best of Buddhas.

While I was looking on, the Victor then partook of it. Having gained confidence in that Buddha, I then paid homage to the Victor.

In the eighteen hundredth aeon ago, I gave that fruit. Since then, I have not known a bad destination; this is the result of the gift of fruit.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Even when declaring his attainment of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa), he spoke these verses.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Vijitasena is finished.

## 10. The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Yasadatta

The verses beginning with "Upārambhacitto" are those of the Venerable Yasadatta. As for the background: This elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that was a strong support for Nibbāna in various lives. Indeed, in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born in a Brahmin family and reached the pinnacle of Brahminical arts and sciences. Renouncing sensual pleasures, he became an ascetic and lived in the forest. One day, seeing the Teacher, with a clear mind, he raised his hands in salutation and praised him. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, he was born in the royal family of the Mallas in the Malla kingdom and was named Yasadatta. When he came of age, he went to the city of Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and traveled together with the wandering ascetic Sabhiya. In due course, he reached Sāvatthī and approached the Blessed One. While the questions asked by Sabhiya were being answered, he himself sat listening, looking for a flaw, thinking, "I will find and point out a fault in the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama." Then the Blessed One, knowing his mental disposition, at the end of the teaching of the Sabhiya Sutta, wishing to give him advice, said:
68:
The one with a fault-finding mind, unwise, hears the Victor's teaching; he is as far from the True Dhamma as the sky is from the earth.

The one with a fault-finding mind, unwise, hears the Victor's teaching; he wanes from the True Dhamma like the moon in the dark fortnight.

The one with a fault-finding mind, unwise, hears the Victor's teaching; he dries up in the True Dhamma like a fish in little water.

The one with a fault-finding mind, unwise, hears the Victor's teaching; he does not flourish in the True Dhamma like a rotten seed in a field.

But he who with a joyful mind hears the Victor's teaching, having exhausted all taints, realizing the unshakable Arahantship, reaching supreme peace, attains Nibbāna without taints—thus he spoke these five verses.

In those verses, 'upārambhacitto' means having a mind that seeks to criticize, with the intention of finding fault. 'Dummedho' means a person without wisdom. 'Ārakā hoti saddhammā' means such a person is as far from the True Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti-saddhamma) as the sky is from the earth, let alone from the True Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-saddhamma). For one who is engaged in contentious talk such as "You do not know this Dhamma and Vinaya," where can there be the peaceful and subtle True Dhamma of practice?

'Parihāyati saddhammā' means he wanes from the ninefold supramundane Dhamma and even from the preceding True Dhamma such as faith. 'Parisussati' means he dries up because of the absence of wholesome states such as zest (pīti) and joy (pāmojja), which have the function of nourishing the body and mind. 'Na virūhati' means he does not reach growth or increase. 'Pūtikaṃ' means (a seed) that has reached a state of rot due to the absence of being smeared with cow dung, etc.

'Tuṭṭhena cittena' is an instrumental case in the sense of a characteristic; it means having become delighted and joyful. 'Khepetvā' means having completely cut off. 'Akuppataṃ' means Arahantship. 'Pappuyya' means having reached. 'Paramaṃ santiṃ' means Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna).
69: To show that for this Elder, the attainment of Nibbāna was merely a matter of time and that he had no attachment to any object and was free from taints, it was said: "parinibbātināsavo" (one who attains Nibbāna, free from taints). Having received such admonition from the Teacher, he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), ordained, and after practicing insight (vipassanā), soon attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: "I saw the Best of Men, shining like a blooming Kaṇikāra flower, like a lit lamp-tree, and as beautiful as Jambu-river gold. Having set aside my water-pot, bark-robe, and vessel, and placing the antelope skin over one shoulder, I praised the Excellent Buddha. O Great Sage, you have crossed over, having destroyed the darkness of delusion and the entanglement of the net of delusion, and having shown the light of knowledge. You lift up this entire world; you are supreme. In all the destinations of the world, there is no comparison to your knowledge. Because of that knowledge, you are called 'Omniscient' (Sabbaññū). I pay homage to you, the Great Hero, who possesses unobstructed Omniscience. One hundred thousand aeons ago, I praised the Excellent Buddha. Due to the merit of praising that knowledge, I have never known a miserable rebirth. My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out." Even when declaring his Arahantship, the Elder recited these very verses. ## The Commentary on the Verses of Yasadatta Thera is finished. ## 11. Commentary on the Verses of Soṇakuṭikaṇṇa Thera. "Upasampadā ca me laddhā" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Soṇakuṭikaṇṇa. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Blessed Padumuttara, he was a wealthy merchant in the city of Haṃsavatī, established in great prosperity and power. One day, seeing the Teacher surrounded by a hundred thousand Arahants...
70:
## 
Seeing the Padumuttara Buddha entering the city with the great splendor and power of a Buddha, he was inspired in heart; he paid homage and stood with joined palms. In the evening, he went to the monastery with the lay followers and, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who speak eloquently (kalyāṇavākkaraṇānaṃ). Aspiring for that same position himself, he gave a great gift and made a resolution. Seeing that there would be no obstacles to his resolution, the Teacher prophesied: 'In the future, in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha named Gotama, you will be the foremost among those who speak eloquently.'

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout that life until death, and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he ordained in the dispensation during the time of Vipassī Buddha. Fulfilling his major and minor duties, he sewed and offered a robe to a monk. Again, in a world empty of Buddhas, he became a tailor in the city of Bārāṇasī and repaired and offered the torn edge of a Paccekabuddha's robe. Thus, having performed merits in various lives, when this Buddha appeared, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy merchant in the city of Kuraraghara in the Avanti country. They named him Soṇa. Although he should have been called 'Koṭikaṇṇa' because he wore ear ornaments worth a crore (koṭi), he became known as 'Kuṭikaṇṇa'.

As he gradually grew up and established his household, the Venerable Mahākaccāna was residing at Pavatta Mountain, supported by his family. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Elder, he became established in the refuges and the precepts, and supported him with the four requisites. Later, feeling spiritual urgency regarding saṃsāra, he went forth in the presence of the Elder. With great difficulty and effort, having gathered a group of ten monks, he received higher ordination (upasampadā). After living in the presence of the Elder for a short time, he took leave of the Elder and went to Sāvatthī to pay homage to the Teacher. Having obtained the opportunity to stay in the same Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) with the Teacher, and being requested at dawn, he recited the sixteen suttas of the Aṭṭhakavagga. The Teacher gave him a 'Sādhu' (Well done!). At the conclusion of the inspired verse (udāna) beginning with 'Seeing the danger in the world' (Udāna 46, Mahāvagga 258), he developed insight and attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

'The Buddha named Padumuttara, the Conqueror, worthy of offerings brought from afar, entered the city at that time with a hundred thousand Arahants. As the Buddha, who was peaceful and such (tādi), entered the city, the jewels shone and a great sound arose. By the power of the Buddha, the drums sounded without being struck; the harps played by themselves as the Buddha entered the city. I pay homage to the most excellent Buddha, the Great Sage Padumuttara. Having seen the miracle, I gained faith in him. "Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Buddha! Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Dhamma! Oh, how wonderful is the perfection of our Teacher!" (he praised). Even inanimate musical instruments play by themselves.'
71:
## 
'The Conqueror named Padumuttara, worthy of offerings brought from afar, entered the city at that time with a hundred thousand controlled ones.

As the Buddha, who was peaceful and such, entered the city, the jewels shone, and at that very moment, great sounds arose.

By the power of the Buddha, the drums sounded without being struck; the harps played by themselves as the Buddha entered the city.

I pay homage to the most excellent of Buddhas, the Great Sage Padumuttara. Having seen that miracle, I gained faith in that Buddha.

How wonderful is the Buddha! How wonderful is the Dhamma! How wonderful is the perfection of our Teacher! Even inanimate musical instruments play by themselves.

In the aeon a hundred thousand years ago, I then obtained that perception (of the Buddha). Due to the fruit of that perception of the Buddha, I do not know any miserable destination.

My defilements have been burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.' (Thus he proclaimed).

Having been established in Arahantship, following the method instructed by his preceptor, he requested five boons from the Teacher: higher ordination in the border regions with a group of five including a Vinaya-expert as the fifth, constant bathing, the use of leather mats, the wearing of multi-layered sandals, and being away from the triple robes. Having received these from the Teacher, he returned to his place of residence and reported the matter to his preceptor. This is the summary here. The details should be understood according to the method in the Udāna Commentary. In the Aṅguttara Commentary, however, it is said: 'Having become a monk, he took a meditation subject from his preceptor, developed insight, and attained Arahantship.'

Later, while dwelling in the bliss of liberation, he reflected on his own practice and, filled with joy, uttered this inspired utterance:

'I have obtained higher ordination, and I am liberated and free from taints. I have seen that Blessed One, and I have lived together with him in the monastery.

For much of the night, the Blessed One spent time in the open air. Then the Teacher, skilled in dwelling, entered the monastery.'
72:
"The Blessed Gotama, having spread his double-layered robe, lies down in the rock cave like a lion king, free from great and small fears.

Then, the Elder Soṇa, a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One and a speaker of beautiful words, recited the True Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.

'Having fully understood the five aggregates, and having developed the Eightfold Path, having reached the supreme peace of Nibbāna, I shall attain Parinibbāna, free from taints.' Thus he recited these five verses.

Among those verses, 'I have also obtained the higher ordination' refers to both the higher ordination he obtained himself by difficultly assembling a ten-member Sangha of monks, and the higher ordination allowed by the Teacher in all border regions by a group of five with a Vinaya-holder as the fifth, granted as a boon. The word 'ca' (and) has a cumulative sense; by that word 'ca', it also includes other boons obtained from the Teacher. 'Being free from taints, I am liberated from defilements' means being liberated through the Path of Arahatship from all defilements along with their bases; therefore, it means being one without taints, such as the taint of sensual desire. 'I have also seen that Blessed One' means: for what purpose did I travel from the country of Avanti to the city of Sāvatthī? I have now seen that Blessed One whom I had never seen before. 'I have also stayed together in the monastery' means not only did I obtain the sight of the Blessed One, but I also stayed together with the Teacher in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) of the monastery, as the Teacher, noting the reason, allowed me to stay. Regarding 'viharē' (in the monastery), some teachers say it means 'near the monastery.'

'Much of the night' means the Blessed One spent much of the night in the open air, during the first watch by way of teaching the Dhamma to the monks and purifying their meditation subjects, and during the middle watch by way of dispelling the doubts of devas and Brahmas. 'Skilled in dwelling' means being skilled in the divine dwelling, the Brahma-dwelling, the imperturbable dwelling, and the noble dwelling. 'Entered the monastery' means he entered the Fragrant Chamber to dispel the fatigue arisen from sitting and walking for a very long time.

'Having spread the double-layered robe, he lies down' means having prepared the fourfold double-layered robe, he took the lion's posture. Therefore, it is said: 'The Blessed Gotama, like a lion in a rock cave, free from great and small fears...' Therein, by the word 'Gotama', he praises the Blessed One by his lineage. 'Like a lion in a rock cave' means as if in a cave of a stone mountain. Just as the lion king, the king of beasts, due to his great majesty, is free from great and small fears and lies on his right side with one foot overlapping the other..."
73:
"...lying on the right side with one foot overlapping the other. Thus, because the defilements that are the causes of mental terror, horripilation, and trembling have been completely cut off, the Blessed Gotama lies down free from fear and dread—this is the meaning.

'Tato' means afterwards. It means that after lying down like a lion king and then rising from that sleep, he was urged by the Teacher, saying, 'Monk, let the Dhamma be clear to you to speak' (Udāna 46). 'Kalyāṇavākkaraṇo' means having beautiful speech, an order of speech endowed with auspicious marks. 'Soṇa recited the True Dhamma' means the Elder Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa recited the sixteen suttas of the Aṭṭhakavagga (The Octad Chapter) in the presence of the Buddha, the Best of Buddhas, the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Elder spoke of himself as if he were another person.

'Having fully understood the five aggregates' means having fully understood the five aggregates of clinging through the three types of full understanding; while thus understanding them, having developed the Noble Eightfold Path, and having reached the supreme peace of Nibbāna, he remains free from taints. Because he thus remains, it means he will now attain Parinibbāna by way of Nibbāna without remainder.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa is Finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kosiya

"Yo ve garūnaṃ" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Kosiya Thera. As for the background: This Elder was also one who had performed merit under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome deeds that serve as a support for liberation from the round of rebirths in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born into a good family, and upon reaching maturity, he saw the Teacher one day and, with a devoted mind, offered a piece of sugarcane. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, he was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha, and was named Kosiya after his lineage. When he reached maturity, he constantly approached the Venerable General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) and listened to the Dhamma. Having gained faith in the Dispensation, he ordained and, practicing meditation, attained Arahatship before long. Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 2.44.44-49):"
74:
In the city of Bandhumatī, I was once a gatekeeper. I saw the Buddha, who had reached the end of all dhammas and was free from the dust of defilements.

With a clear and joyful mind, I took a piece of sugarcane and offered it to the Great Sage, Buddha Vipassī.

Ninety-one aeons ago, because of the merit of offering that piece of sugarcane, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of offering a piece of sugarcane.

My defilements have been burnt away... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.

Upon reaching Arahatship, reflecting on his own practice and praising living under a teacher and associating with the virtuous, he spoke thus:

"The wise one who is receptive to the words of teachers, and abiding in those words, develops love for them; he is called a devoted wise man, and knowing the dhammas, he would possess distinguished qualities.

When great adversities arise, they do not shake the one who stands in reflection; he is called a powerful wise man, and knowing the dhammas, he would possess distinguished qualities.

One who is steady like the ocean, free from craving, of deep wisdom, and a perceiver of subtle meanings; he is called an unshakable (asanhāriya) wise man, and knowing the dhammas, he would possess distinguished qualities.

One who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and a practitioner of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma; he is called such a wise man, and knowing the dhammas, he would possess distinguished qualities."
75:
"One who knows the meaning of what is spoken, and having known the meaning, acts accordingly; he is called a wise man of inner meaning (atthantara), and knowing the dhammas, he would be endowed with distinguished qualities." He spoke these five verses.

In those verses, 'yo' refers to anyone among the four assemblies, such as the khattiyas. The word 've' expresses clarity. 'Garūnaṃ' refers to wise and virtuous ones like the Buddha, who are endowed with noble qualities such as virtue. 'Vacanaññū' means one who knows the words of advice of those virtuous ones, practices as instructed, and knows the benefits of that practice. 'Dhīro' means one endowed with steady wisdom. 'Vase ca tamhi janayetha pemaṃ' means abiding in the advice and instructions of the teachers, practicing as instructed, and thinking, 'Indeed, through this advice, I have escaped this suffering of birth and so forth,' thus generating love and respect for that advice. The explanation of these two points clarifies the meaning already stated by the two words 'garūnaṃ vacanaññū dhīro'. 'So' means the wise one who knows the advice is called 'devoted' (bhattima) because of practicing as instructed, and 'wise' (paṇḍita) because of not transgressing the advice even for the sake of life. 'Ñatvā ca dhammesu visesī assa' means that such a practitioner, by knowing the Four Noble Truths through that very practice, would possess distinguished qualities in mundane and supramundane dhammas, such as the three knowledges, the six higher powers, and the attainment of analytical insight.

'Yaṃ' refers to the person. Even when manifest dangers such as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, as well as hidden dangers such as lust, which are called 'āpadā' (adversities) because they cause obstacles to practice, arise and are very powerful, they cannot shake or disturb him in any way. Why? 'Paṭisaṅkhayantaṃ' means because he stands in the power of reflective wisdom. 'So' means that one who cannot be shaken even by very firm adversities is called 'powerful' (thāmavā), 'steady' (dhitimā), and 'of firm effort' (daḷhaparakkamo). He is also called 'wise' (paṇḍita) because he is endowed with the power of wisdom that overcomes the entire side of defilements. Thus, the phrase 'ñatvā ca dhammesu visesī assa' has the same meaning as stated before.
76:
"Samuddova thito" means one who has the nature of standing like the ocean. How? Just as the great ocean near the base of Mount Sineru, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, remains unmoving and unshakeable despite the natural winds blowing from the eight directions, so too he remains unmoving and unshakeable by the winds of defilements and the winds of sectarian views. Because of his penetration of the profound and subtle meanings of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) and so forth, which cannot be attained by those who have not accumulated the requisites of knowledge, he is one of deep wisdom (gambhīrapañño) and a seer of subtle meanings (nipuṇatthadassī). Such a person is called "Asamhāriyo" because he cannot be moved by defilements or by anyone such as Devaputta Māra. He is also called a wise man (paṇḍita) for the reasons mentioned above. The rest is as previously explained.

"Bahussuto" means one who is learned due to extensive knowledge of the scriptures (Pariyatti). He is called "Bahussuto" because he has heard much, such as the Sutta and Geyya. He is also a "Dhammadharo" (bearer of Dhamma) because he preserves that very Dhamma without loss, like lion's fat kept in a golden vessel. "Dhammassa hoti anudhammacārī" means that having known the meaning and the text of the Pariyatti Dhamma as heard and learned, he practices the Dhamma that is appropriate for the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma), known as the preliminary practice consisting of the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and the meditation on foulness (asubhakammaṭṭhāna). Thus he is an "Anudhammacārī." He wanders practicing with the aspiration to penetrate the paths and fruits, thinking, "Today, even today."

"So tādiso nāma ca hoti paṇḍito" means that the person who, depending on a particular teacher, becomes learned (bahussuto), a bearer of Dhamma (dhammadharo), and a practitioner of Dhamma (anudhammacārī), is called wise (paṇḍita) because he is similar to that teacher and similar in practice. Such a person, having known, would possess distinguished qualities in the Dhamma. This statement has the meaning already described.

"Atthañca yo jānāti bhāsitassa" means the person who knows the meaning of the Pariyatti Dhamma spoken by the Fully Enlightened One. Knowing it, he understands, "In this place, virtue (sīla) is taught; in this place, concentration (samādhi); in this place, wisdom (paññā)." Having known the meaning as stated in various places, he acts and practices according to the instructions of the Teacher. "Atthantaro nāma sa hoti paṇḍita" means such a person is one who knows the meaning. Because of the reason of knowing the meaning, he becomes wise by relying merely on the knowledge of the meanings of virtue and so forth. The rest is as previously explained.
77:
In these verses, in the first verse, by the words "Yo ve garūnaṃ" and so forth, the distinguished nature having faith (saddhā) as its support is stated. In the second verse, by the words "Yaṃ āpadā" and so forth, the nature having energy (viriya) as its support is stated; in the third verse, by the words "Yo ve samuddova thito" and so forth, the nature having concentration (samādhi) as its support is stated; in the fourth verse, by the words "Bahussuto" and so forth, the nature having mindfulness (sati) as its support is stated; and in the fifth verse, by the words "Atthañca yo jānāti" and so forth, the distinguished nature having wisdom (paññā) as its support is stated. This should be understood.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Kosiya Thera is finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of Fives (Pañcaka Nipāta) is finished.
78:
## 6. Chakka Nipāta
## 1. Uruvelakassapattheragāthāvaṇṇanā
In the Book of Sixes, the verses beginning with "Disvāna pāṭihīrāni" are the verses of the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa Thera. What is the origin of this Elder? He too was one who had performed extraordinary merit under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome deeds as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth (vivaṭṭūpaniဿaya) in various existences. Born into a noble family during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he listened to the Dhamma from the Teacher upon reaching maturity. Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position (etadagga) among those with a large following, he himself aspired to that position, performed a great offering, and made a resolution. The Blessed One, seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, prophesied: "In the future, in the dispensation of Gotama Buddha, you will be the foremost among those with a large following."

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life in that existence, he passed away and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Ninety-two aeons ago from this Bhadda Kappa, he was born as a half-brother of Phussa Buddha. He had two other younger brothers. All three brothers honored the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with the highest offerings, performed wholesome deeds throughout their lives, and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Long before the appearance of our Buddha, they were born as brothers in a brahmin family in Vārāṇasī. Being born in succession, all three were named 'Kassapa' by virtue of their clan. Upon reaching maturity, they learned the three Vedas. Among those brothers, the eldest had 500 young men as followers, the middle one 300, and the youngest 200. Searching for the essence in their scriptures, they saw only mundane benefits and thus took pleasure in renunciation.

Among them, the eldest brother went to the Uruvela forest with his followers and became an ascetic, becoming known as 'Uruvela Kassapa'. The one who became an ascetic at a bend in the great river Ganges became known as 'Nadī Kassapa'. The one who became an ascetic at Gayāsīsa Hill became known as 'Gayā Kassapa'.

While they were living in those various places as ascetics, after many days had passed, our Bodhisatta went forth in the Great Renunciation and penetrated Omniscient Knowledge. In due course, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana), established the five monks of the group of five (pañcavaggī) in Arahantship, disciplined the 55 companions headed by the youth Yasa, and dispatched the 60 Arahants saying, "Go forth, O bhikkhus, on a journey." After disciplining the Bhaddavaggiya group, he went to the dwelling place of Uruvela Kassapa. Entering the fire-chamber to stay, he disciplined Uruvela Kassapa along with his followers through 3,500 miracles, beginning with the subduing of the serpent (nāga) in that fire-chamber, and caused them to go forth as monks. Knowing of Uruvela Kassapa's monkhood, the other two brothers also came with their followers and became monks under the Blessed One. All those monks became 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks, carrying bowls and robes created by psychic power. The Blessed One took those one thousand monks to Gayāsīsa and, while staying on a stone slab, established them all in Arahantship through the discourse of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: "The Buddha named Padumuttara, the Knower of the whole world, the One with five eyes, appeared one hundred thousand aeons ago from this Bhadda Kappa. The Buddha, the Trainer, the Teacher, the Savior, skilled in teaching, rescued many people. The Protector..."
79: Having entered (the fire-shed), beginning with the subduing of the Naga performed in that fire-shed, the Buddha disciplined Uruvela Kassapa along with his followers through three thousand five hundred miracles and ordained them. Knowing of his ordination, the other two brothers also came with their followers and were ordained in the presence of the Teacher. All of them became Ehi Bhikkhus, bearing bowls and robes created by psychic power. The Teacher, taking those thousand monks, went to Gayāsīsa, and while sitting on a stone slab, he established all of them in the fruit of Arahantship through the Ādittapariyāya Sutta. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: 'The Conqueror named Padumuttara, the Sage who knew the whole world, the Knower of all things, the Visionary, arose a hundred thousand aeons ago from this [aeon]. The Buddha, who is a teacher, an instructor, a savior of all beings, and skilled in teaching, saved many people. Compassionate, merciful, and seeking the welfare of all beings, he established all the ascetics who came to him in the five precepts. Thus, it was free from confusion, empty of other sectarians, and adorned with such Arahants who possessed mastery and the virtue of patience. That Great Sage, fifty-eight cubits high, resembling a golden pillar, was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. At that time, the lifespan was a hundred thousand years; staying for that long, that Buddha saved many people. Then, I was a brahmin in the city of Haṃsavatī, esteemed as a good man; approaching the Light of the World, I heard the Dhamma teaching. Then, in the midst of a great assembly, hearing [the Buddha] appoint a disciple with a great following to the foremost position, I was delighted. Inviting the Great Conqueror with a large retinue, I gave a gift along with a thousand brahmins. Having given a great gift and paying homage to the Leader, standing at a respectful distance, being joyful, I spoke these words.'
80: 'Venerable Sir, through my faith in you and the merit of my aspiration, may I have a large following in whatever life I am born.' Then the Teacher, with a voice as sweet as the roar of a king elephant and as melodious as the song of the Karavīka bird, said to the assembly: 'Look at this brahmin. Look at this brahmin who has a golden complexion, great arms, face and eyes like lotuses, a sharp mind, who is joyful and has faith in my virtues. This brahmin aspires to the position of the monk named Sīhaghosā. In the future, he will achieve that heart's desire. A hundred thousand aeons from this Bhadda-kappa, a Buddha named Gotama by clan, born in the Okkāka dynasty, will arise in the world. An heir to his Dhamma, like a son born from his breast, created by the Dhamma, a disciple of the Buddha named Kassapa by clan will arise.' Ninety-two aeons from this Bhadda-kappa, the peerless, incomparable, matchless Buddha named Phussa, who leads the world to the noble Nibbāna, arose. That Buddha also dispelled all darkness, untangled the great tangle, and satisfied the world of devas and humans by raining down the rain of the deathless Nibbāna. At that time, we were sons of the king in the city of Bārāṇasī. All three of us brothers were very close to the great king. We had bodies perfected by energy, great strength, and were unconquerable by enemies on the battlefield. At that time, when a rebellion occurred at the border, the king said to us: 'Come, go to the border, clear out the strength of the forest-dwelling thieves, make my kingdom safe, and then return.' Then we said: 'Great King, if you give us the opportunity to serve the Buddha, we will carry out your benefit.' Then, having received the boon, sent by our father the king, we went to the border, made them lay down their arms and brought peace, and then returned to the king.
81: We requested the king for the opportunity to serve and attend to the Buddha, the Lord of the World, the Conqueror of defilements. Having obtained that opportunity, we honored that Buddha for the rest of our lives. We donated expensive clothes, exquisite and tasty food, delightful dwellings and beds, and beneficial medicines. We offered those things, acquired righteously, to the Buddha along with the Saṅgha. Being virtuous, compassionate, and having minds devoted to meditation, we served the Buddha with a heart of loving-kindness constantly. When that Buddha, the pinnacle of the world, attained Parinibbāna, we also performed offerings as much as we could. When we died from that life, we reached the Tusita heaven and enjoyed great happiness there. This is the fruit of the Buddha-pūjā. Just as a magician shows various skills in a performance, I also wandered through the round of rebirths and was once a king ruling over the Videha kingdom. Because of the words of the naked ascetic named Guṇa, I held wrong views and stepped onto the path to hell. However, because of the words of my daughter Rucā, and by accepting the advice of the Brahma King Nārada, when I was advised in many ways by Brahma King Nārada, I abandoned that evil wrong view. In that life, I especially fulfilled the ten paths of wholesome action, and when I gave up the body, I reached the heavenly realm as if returning to my own home. When I reached this final birth, I was born into a wealthy brahmin family in the city of Bārāṇasī. Fearing death, sickness, and old age, I entered the great forest and, seeking the state of Nibbāna, became an ascetic. At that time, my two brothers also became ascetics with me. Having built a hermitage in the Uruvelā forest, I lived there. Since I was a Kassapa by lineage and lived in the Uruvelā forest, I was known as 'Uruvela Kassapa'.
82:
“My brother named Nadī Kassapa lived near the river. Gayā Kassapa lived in the region of Gayā, according to the name of his dwelling place. The youngest brother had two hundred disciples, the middle brother had three hundred, and I had a full five hundred disciples. All those disciples followed my will. Then, the Buddha, the foremost in the world, the trainer of those to be tamed, came to me and, performing various miracles, disciplined me. I became an Ehi Bhikkhu monk along with a thousand followers. Together with all those disciples, I attained the fruit of Arahatship. Those disciples and many other disciples surrounded me. I am also capable of preaching the Dhamma. Therefore, the Buddha placed me in the foremost position (Etadagga) in the midst of a large assembly. Oh, how wonderful! The meritorious deed performed towards the Buddha has become fruitful for me. My defilements have been burnt away... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.”

Having attained the fruit of Arahatship and reflecting on his own practice, he uttered this lion's roar with a brave voice like a lion king:

“Even though I saw the miracles of the famous Buddha Gotama, I did not bow down for that long, being deceived by envy and pride. The Buddha, the trainer of those to be tamed, knowing my thoughts, urged me. Then, a wonderful sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) that made my hair stand on end arose in me. The small successes in gains and honor that I had obtained previously as a matted-hair ascetic (Jaṭila), I abandoned then and went forth in the Conqueror's teaching. Previously, I was content with sacrifices and prioritized the sensual realm, but later I have completely uprooted lust, hatred, and delusion. I know my past lives, my divine eye is purified, I am possessed of psychic powers and know the minds of others, and I have attained the divine ear.”
83:
“For the sake of that benefit—the path, the fruit of Arahatship, and Nibbāna—
I have gone forth from the home life to the homeless life of a monk.
That benefit, which is the destruction of all fetters,
the fruit of Arahatship and Nibbāna, I have now attained.”
He uttered these six verses.

In those verses, “disvāna pāṭihīrāni” means having seen the three thousand five hundred miracles, starting with the taming of the Naga king. The words “pāṭihīraṃ”, “pāṭiheraṃ”, and “pāṭihāriyaṃ” are the same in meaning but differ only in their literal form. “Yasassino” means (of the Buddha) whose fame is spread according to the truth in the world including the devas, as in “Itipi so Bhagavā” and so on. “Na tāvāhaṃ paṇipatiṃ” means that as long as the Buddha did not rebuke me, saying, “Kassapa, you are not yet an Arahat, nor have you entered the path to Arahatship, nor do you have the practice by which you would be an Arahat or enter the path to Arahatship,” I did not humble myself. Why? Because I was deceived by envy (issā) and pride (māna). “If I become a disciple of this ascetic Gotama, my gains and honor will decline, and they will increase only for this ascetic Gotama”—thus, I was deceived by envy, characterized by the inability to endure the prosperity of others, and by pride, characterized by arrogance, thinking, “I am a leader of a sect, recognized by many people.”

“Mama saṅkappamaññāya” means knowing my wrong thoughts. When the Buddha performed miracles that surpassed the human state (uttarimanussadhamma), seeing those various miracles, I thought, “The Great Ascetic Gotama is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty,” yet I still had the wrong thought, “But he is not an Arahat like me.” Knowing this, the Buddha waited for the ripening of my knowledge and remained indifferent. Later, in the middle of the Nerañjarā River, he cleared the water all around and walked on the dusty ground. Even when he stood on the boat brought there, I thought, “He is of great psychic power,” but again had the wrong thought, “But he is not an Arahat like me.” Knowing this is the meaning. “Codesi narasārathi” means that at that time, knowing the ripening of my knowledge, the Teacher, the trainer of those to be tamed, rebuked and disciplined me, saying, “You are not an Arahat,” and so on. “Tato me āsi saṃvego, abbhuto lomahaṃsano” means that because of the aforementioned rebuke, which had never happened before for such a long time, and because it occurred with the bristling of hair, a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) called “wonderful and hair-raising” arose in me. It was the arising of saṃvega along with the path and fruit, thinking, “Though I was not an Arahat, I mistakenly thought I was.”

“Jaṭilabhūtassa” means at the time of being an ascetic. “Siddhi” means the fulfillment of gains and honor. “Parittikā” means reaching a small state. “Tāhaṃ” is “taṃ ahaṃ”, meaning “I [abandoned] that fulfillment of gains and honor.” “Nirākatvā” means abandoning it without lingering when spiritual urgency arose due to the Buddha’s rebuke. Some say “siddhi” means psychic power accomplished through meditation (bhāvanā). However, that statement is not appropriate because at that time, the Elder Uruvela Kassapa had not yet attained jhāna. That statement is true. “Kāmadhātupurakkhato” means...
84:
Because I had thought, “I am an Arahant,” there arose in me saṃvega (spiritual urgency), which is the arising of knowledge accompanied by ottappa (moral dread).

‘Jaṭilabhūtassa’ means to one who has become an ascetic. ‘Siddhi’ means the success of gain and honor. ‘Parittikā’ means reaching a state of insignificance. ‘Tāhaṃ’ means ‘that [gain and honor] I...’. ‘Tadā’ refers to the time when saṃvega arose due to the Blessed One’s admonition. ‘Nirākatvā’ means having discarded, having abandoned, or being without regard. Some say, “Iddhi means the psychic power accomplished through meditation.” That statement is not appropriate, because at that time he (Uruvela-Kassapa) had not yet attained jhāna. For that very reason, it was said, “kāmadhātu-purakkhato” (preoccupied with the sensual realm).

‘Yaññena santuṭṭho’ means being content with sacrifice, perceiving one’s task as finished, thinking, “Having offered the sacrifice, I shall enjoy heavenly bliss; this much is enough.” ‘Kāmadhātu-purakkhato’ means standing with the sensual world as one’s priority through the sacrifice, with craving arisen by taking the sensual happy realm as an object. If that sacrifice is associated with the taking of life (pāṇātipāta), one cannot attain a happy destination through it. This is because the result of an unwholesome deed does not manifest as a desired or pleasant result. However, due to the wholesome intention (kusala cetanā) such as giving (dāna) involved in that sacrifice, one may reach a happy destination when the conditions are met. ‘Pacchā’ refers to the time after ordaining as an ascetic, when he abandoned the views of the ascetics through the Teacher’s instruction and applied himself to the meditation on the Four Noble Truths. ‘Samūhaniṃ’ means that by exerting effort in vipassanā (insight), he completely eradicated greed, hatred, and delusion through the sequence of the Paths.

Since this Elder became one possessed of the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā) even while eradicating greed and so forth through the Noble Path, he spoke the words beginning with “Pubbenivāsaṃ jānāmi” to show his state of possessing the six higher powers. In those words, ‘Pubbenivāsaṃ jānāmi’ means knowing and realizing through the knowledge of recollecting past lives—like a myrobalan fruit on the palm of the hand—the aggregates that occurred in the past lives of himself and others, and the matters connected with those aggregates. ‘Dibbacakkhu visodhitaṃ’ means the divine eye knowledge has been purified; it means that through meditation, he obtained and purified the knowledge capable of clearly perceiving forms—whether divine or human, distant, concealed, or extremely subtle—just like a natural form coming into the range of the natural eye. ‘Iddhimā’ means possessing psychic powers such as the power of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi) and the power of transformation (vikubbana-iddhi); it means he is an attainer of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (iddhividha-ñāṇa). Because he knows the minds of others in their various states, such as being with lust, he is called ‘Paracittaññū’ (knower of others' minds); it means he is an attainer of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa). ‘Dibbasotañca pāpuṇiṃ’ means he also attained the divine ear knowledge.
85:
“That goal of mine has been attained, the destruction of all fetters.” This means that through the attainment of the Noble Path, I have reached my own benefit and the supreme benefit (Nirvana), which is the destruction of all fetters, or that which is to be obtained by such destruction. It should be understood that with this verse, the Elder made his declaration of supreme knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Uruvela-Kassapa is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Tekicchakāri

The verse beginning with “Atihitā vīhī” is that of the Venerable Elder Tekicchakāri. As for the background: this Elder had also performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merits in various births. Ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born into a good family and, upon reaching maturity, became proficient in the science of medicine. He cured the Elder named Asoka, who was the attendant of the Blessed One Vipassī, of an illness, and out of compassion, he also prepared medicine for other beings oppressed by disease.

Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha-era, he was born as the son of a Brahmin named Subuddha. Because physicians protected him by removing dangers during his time in the womb, they gave him the name “Tekicchakāri” (The Protected by Medicine). That youth Tekicchakāri grew up learning the branches of knowledge and arts suitable for his family. At that time, the minister Cāṇakka, seeing the maturity of Brahmin Subuddha’s wisdom and his skill in means regarding affairs, became envious, thinking, “If this man gains a footing in this royal house, he will overcome me.” He then had King Candagutta cast the Brahmin into prison. Hearing that his father had entered prison, Tekicchakāri became afraid and fled. He went to the presence of Elder Sāṇavāsī, told the Elder the reason for his terror, and after ordaining, he took a meditation subject. He lived as an open-air dweller (abbhokāsika) and a sitter (nesajjika), practicing the recluse's Dhamma without regard for cold or heat. In particular, he developed the four Brahma-vihāras (divine abodes).

Seeing the monk Tekicchakāri, the evil Māra thought, “I shall not let him escape my realm.” Wishing to make his mind wander, Māra went to the Elder in the guise of a field guard during the harvest time and, wishing to mock him, said:
“O monk, the grains have been brought in, and the rice has reached the threshing floor. Alms food cannot be obtained either. What shall I do?”

The Elder, hearing Māra’s words, said:
“Recollect with devotion the Blessed One, who is endowed with immeasurable virtues. With a body pervaded by pīti (rapture), be always joyful and glad.”
86:
Having ordained and taken up a meditation subject, he undertook the ascetic practices of living in the open air (abbhokāsika-dhutaṅga) and the sitter's practice (nesajjika-dhutaṅga). Without regarding cold or heat, he exerted himself solely in the monk's duties (samaṇadhamma). Specifically, he devotedly practiced the meditation on the Divine Abidings (brahmavihāra-bhāvanā). Seeing him, the evil Māra thought, "I will not let him transcend my domain," and wishing to distract him, he approached the Elder in the guise of a field guard during harvest time and spoke thus, intending to mock him:

"The grains have been stored in the granary, and the fine rice has reached the threshing floor. Yet I cannot get even a morsel of food; what shall I do?"

Hearing these words, the Elder said:
"Recollect the Buddha, who is endowed with immeasurable virtues, with a confident heart; with a body pervaded by rapture (pīti), you shall be constantly joyful.

Recollect the immeasurable Dhamma with a confident heart; with a body pervaded by rapture, you shall be constantly joyful.

Recollect the immeasurable Saṅgha with a confident heart; with a body pervaded by rapture, you shall be constantly joyful."

Hearing this, Māra said:
"You dwell in the open air; these winter nights are very cold. Do not be afflicted by the hardship of the cold; enter the monastery and stay with the door-leaves closed."

Then the Elder said:
"I shall dwell attaining the four immeasurables (appamaññā); I shall dwell happily through those states. Dwelling unshaken, I cannot be afflicted by the hardship of the winter cold."

In those verses, "atihitā vīhi" means the grains have been brought into the granary and stored, or have been brought home from the threshing floor. Here, by the term "vīhi" (grain/paddy), other types of grain should also be included. As for fine rice (sālī), since it is generally included among the superior grains, it is said, "khala-gatā sālī." This means it has reached the threshing floor and remains there in heaps or for the purpose of threshing and so on. In this verse, fine rice is mentioned specifically to show it is the most excellent grain. By both terms, it is shown that grain is plentifully present in the village, outside the village, or in the fields. "Na ca labhe piṇḍaṃ" means that even in such a time of plenty (subhikkha) when grain is abundant, I cannot get even a single meal. "Katham-ahaṃ kassaṃ" is a mockery, meaning "What shall I do? How shall I make a living?" Hearing these words, the Elder thought, "This wretch is clearly showing his own evil nature; as for me, the word of advice for me..."
87:
It means the grains have been brought to the granary and stored, or brought from the threshing floor to the house. 'Khala-gatā sālī' means the fine rice has reached the threshing floor, the place for processing grain, and remains there in the form of heaps or for the purpose of threshing and winnowing. The separate mention of fine rice (sālī) here is to show its status as the principal grain. By both [vīhi and sālī], it is shown that grain is fully present both in the village and outside the village. 'Na ca labhe piṇḍaṃ' means that even in this time of plenty when grain is easily obtained, I do not get even a morsel of food. 'Now what shall I do? How shall I live?'—thus [Māra] made a joke and mockery.

Hearing that, the Elder thought, "This wretch has revealed his own nature to me; I should only admonish myself, and I should not say anything [to him]." Thus, applying himself to the recollection of the Three Jewels, he spoke the three verses beginning with 'Buddham-appameyyaṃ'. In those verses, 'Buddham-appameyyaṃ anussara pasanno' means: He is called 'Buddha', the Blessed One, because of the absolute departure of the sleep of ignorance (avijjā) along with its latent tendencies (vāsanā), and because of the blossomed state of his wisdom. He is 'immeasurable' (appameyya) because of the absence of defilements such as greed (rāga) which create measures, because of being endowed with immeasurable virtues, and because of being an immeasurable field of merit. 'Pasanno' means having a confident heart through faith characterized by conviction (okappana). 'Anussara' means to repeatedly maintain mindfulness on the object of the Buddha, such as 'Itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho'. If you do so, you will be one whose body is pervaded by rapture (pīti).

'Satatam-udaggo' means that while one is recollecting, one's body is constantly and at all times pervaded by rapture characterized by pervasion (pharaṇa-pīti), with the body being overwhelmed by the sublime material forms produced by rapture. Being uplifted by uplifting rapture (ubbegā-pīti), may you be one capable of making the body buoyant and leaping into the sky. Through the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), may you experience abundant rapture and joy directed towards the Buddha. The meaning is that when you experience this, you will not be overcome by hunger and thirst, just as you are not overcome by cold and heat.

'Dhammaṃ' refers to the noble supramundane Dhamma. 'Saṅghaṃ' refers to the noble ultimate Saṅgha. The rest is as previously explained. Regarding 'anussara', it should be connected as: recollect the Dhamma as 'Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo', etc., and recollect the Saṅgha as 'Suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho', etc.

Thus, when the Elder had admonished himself by way of urging the recollection of the virtues of the Triple Gem, Māra again, wishing to divert him from his life of seclusion...
88:
Wishing to show himself as one desiring the monk's welfare, he spoke the fifth verse: "You live in the open air." The meaning of that verse is: "O monk, you live in an open space, uncovered by anything. These very cold nights of the winter season, when snow falls, are occurring. Therefore, do not be afflicted or distressed by the cold. Enter a dwelling with its door-leaves closed; in this way, you will live in comfort."

Hearing those words, the Elder, wishing to show, "I have no need to seek a dwelling; I can live happily right here," spoke the sixth verse beginning with "Phusissaṃ." In that verse, "I shall touch the four immeasurables" (phusissaṃ catasso appamaññāyo) means: "I shall attain from time to time and experience the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), which are called 'immeasurables' because they take immeasurable beings as their object." "And being happy through those immeasurables, I shall live in all four postures. Because of living thus, I shall have only happiness at all times, and no suffering. For I shall not be distressed by the cold; even during the 'eight days of interval' (antaraṭṭhaka) when snow falls, I shall not suffer from the cold. Therefore, because ill-will and other causes of mental agitation have been well abandoned, and because there is no more agitation caused by external conditions, I shall live happily and unshaken through the bliss of meditative attainment."

Thus, while the Elder was reciting this verse, he developed insight and realized the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the city of Bandhumatī, I was a well-trained physician. I benefited the sick who were in pain and brought happiness to the multitude. Seeing a monk who was ill, virtuous, and of great majesty, I then offered him medicine with a clear and joyful mind. Because of that medicine, that monk named Asoka, who was the attendant of the Buddha Vipassī and restrained in his faculties, was cured of his illness. In the ninety-first aeon from now, I gave that medicine; because of that gift of medicine, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of offering medicine.

In the eighth aeon from this auspicious aeon, I was a Cakkavatti king named Sabbosadha, endowed with the seven treasures and ruler of the four great islands. I have burned away the defilements... I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching."

Since this story of the appearance of the Elder Tekicchakārī occurred during the time of King Bindusāra, it should be understood that these verses were chanted at the Third Council. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Tekicchakārī is finished.

Sixes (Chakkanipāta), First Group (Paṭhamavagga), 3. Verses of the Elder Mahānāga. The verse beginning with "Yassa sabrahmacārīsu" is that of the Venerable Mahānāga. This Mahānāga, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, and accumulating the causes for liberation from Saṃsāra in various lives...
89:
"In the eighth aeon from this auspicious aeon, I was a Cakkavatti king named Sabbosadha, endowed with the seven treasures and of great fruit.

My defilements have been burned away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

In this story as well, since this Elder appeared during the time of King Bindusāra, it should be understood that these verses were chanted at the Third Council.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Tekicchakārī is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahānāga

The verse beginning with "Yassa sabrahmacārīsu" is that of the Venerable Mahānāga. What is the story of his origin? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit which is the cause for liberation from Saṃsāra in various lives. In the time of the Buddha Kakusandha, he was born in a respectable family. When he reached the age of discretion, one day he entered the forest and saw the Buddha Kakusandha sitting at the foot of a certain tree, enjoying the bliss of jhāna. With a clear and faithful mind, he offered a pomegranate to the Buddha.

Due to that meritorious deed, after wandering through the worlds of gods and humans, in this Buddha-era, he was born in the city of Sāketa as the son of a Brahmin named Madhuvāseṭṭha and was named Mahānāga. When he reached the age of discretion, while the Blessed One was staying in the Añjanavana forest at Sāketa, he saw the miraculous power of the Venerable Gavampati. Having gained faith, he went forth in the presence of that Elder, and abiding by his instruction, he attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"The Great Hero Kakusandha, who had reached the further shore of all dhammas, went into the forest, secluded from the crowd.

I took a fruit, strung it with a creeper, and offered it to the Blessed One who was then meditating in the mountain cleft.

Seeing the God of gods with a clear mind, I gave the fruit to the Hero, the worthy recipient of offerings."
90:
In this very Auspicious Aeon (Bhadda-kappa), I gave a gift of fruit at that time. Since then, I have not known a rebirth in the four woeful states; this is the fruit of the gift of fruit.

My defilements are burnt... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.

The Elder Mahānāga, having reached Arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of liberation (vimutti-sukha), saw the monks of the group of six (Chabbaggiya) living without respect for their fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī). Desiring to give them advice, he recited these six verses:

'If one does not have respect for fellow practitioners,
One declines from the True Dhamma, like a fish in little water.

If one does not have respect for fellow practitioners,
One does not grow in the True Dhamma, like a rotten seed in a field.

If one does not have respect for fellow practitioners,
One is far from Nibbāna in the teaching of the King of Dhamma.

If one has respect for fellow practitioners,
One does not decline from the True Dhamma, like a fish in much water.

If one has respect for fellow practitioners,
One grows in the True Dhamma, like a good seed in a field.

If one has respect for fellow practitioners,
One is near to Nibbāna in the teaching of the King of Dhamma.'

In those verses, 'sabrahmacārīsu' refers to fellow practitioners who are similar in virtue and views, practicing the same noble Dhamma such as virtue. 'Gāravo' means the act of showing respect based on qualities such as virtue. 'Nūpalabbhati' means it does not exist, does not occur, or does not arise. 'Nibbānā' means the exhaustion of defilements due to the extinguishing of defilements. 'Dhammarājassa' refers to the Buddha. For the Buddha is called the 'King of Dhamma' (Dhammarāja) because he delights and satisfies the world, including the devas, with mundane and supramundane Dhamma as appropriate. Here, by the phrase 'in the teaching of the King of Dhamma' (Dhammarājassa sāsane), it is shown that Nibbāna exists only in the Buddha's teaching and not in the teachings of other wanderers. Among them, if one lacks respect for fellow practitioners, just as he is far from Nibbāna, it is shown that he is also far from the Buddha's teaching. 'Bavhodake' means a place with much water. 'Santike hoti nibbānaṃ' means Nibbāna is in the vicinity. The rest of the explanation is as previously stated. These verses were spoken by the Elder Mahānāga when he attained Arahantship.

The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mahānāga is finished.

5. Sixth Division - 1. First Group - 213. Verses of Elder Kulla

The verses beginning with 'Sīvathikaṃ' are the verses of the Venerable Elder Kulla. This Elder also had performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. When our Gautama Buddha appeared, he was born into a wealthy family in the city of Sāvatthī and was named 'Kulla'. When he reached the age of discretion, [he heard] the Buddha's...
91:
It is shown that just as one who lacks respect for fellow practitioners is far from Nibbāna, so too is he far from the teaching of the King of Dhamma. 'Bavhodake' means in a place with much water. 'Santike hoti nibbānaṃ' means Nibbāna is in his presence, very near to him. The rest is as already stated. These very verses were the Elder Mahānāga's declaration of Arahantship (aññā-byākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mahānāga is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kulla

The verses beginning with 'Kullo sivathikaṃ' are the verses of the Venerable Elder Kulla. As for the circumstances of their origin: This Elder also had performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. In this Buddha's time, he was born into a householder's family in Sāvatthī and received the name 'Kulla'. When he came of age, he heard the Dhamma from the Buddha, gained faith, and ordained. That Elder was of a lustful temperament (rāga-carita) and possessed a nature of intense passion. Therefore, defilements frequently overwhelmed his mind. Then the Buddha, knowing his mental disposition, gave him the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) and said, 'Kulla, you should frequently practice by wandering in the cemetery (susāna).'

He entered the cemetery and saw various bloated corpses. Although he could arouse the perception of foulness for a moment, as soon as he left the cemetery, he was again overwhelmed by sensual lust (ကာမရာဂ). Again, the Buddha, knowing this, on one occasion when Kulla went to the cemetery, created and showed him the form of a young woman who had just died and whose skin had not yet decayed. As soon as he saw it, lust immediately arose in his mind as if for a living person of the opposite sex (visabhāga). Then, while he was watching, the Buddha transformed it into a most repulsive, foul-smelling, and disgusting corpse, swarming with worms and oozing impurities from its nine openings. While he was looking at that corpse, his mind became free from lust. Then the Buddha emitted a radiance and, to arouse mindfulness, said:

'Kulla, look at this assembly (body), afflicted by disease, impure, putrid, oozing from above and below, which fools greatly delight in.'
92:
Hearing these words, the Elder Kulla, carefully investigating the nature of the body, gained the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) and attained the first jhāna based on that foulness. Using that first jhāna as a basis, he developed insight (vipassanā) and reached the fruit of Arahantship. Reflecting on his own practice, he recited these verses as an inspired utterance (udāna):

'Kulla has gone to the cemetery and seen a woman's body cast away. He has seen that body thrown in the cemetery, filled with worms and being devoured.

Behold this body, afflicted by disease, impure, putrid, oozing from orifices above and below, and greatly delighted in by fools.

Taking the Mirror of Dhamma to attain the vision of knowledge, I have contemplated this body, which is empty inside and out, and devoid of essence.

As this body is, so is that corpse; as that corpse is, so is this body. As it is below, so it is above; as it is above, so it is below.

As it is by day, so it is by night; as it is by night, so it is by day. As it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before.

The delight of one who has a concentrated mind and rightly contemplates the Dhamma is not found even in the playing of fivefold musical instruments.'

In these verses, 'Kullo' means the Elder speaks of himself as if he were another person.

'Āturaṃ' means being repeatedly oppressed by various kinds of suffering. 'Asuciṃ' means being devoid of purity and being loathsome and repulsive. 'Pūtiṃ' means having a foul odor. 'Passa' means 'behold according to its nature.' 'Kulla' was the name the Blessed One used to address the Elder during the time of instruction. At the time of the inspired utterance, however, the Elder refers to himself. 'Samussayaṃ' refers to the body. 'Uggharantan' means the oozing of impurities from the upper orifices. 'Paggharantan' means the oozing of impurities from the lower orifices and from all around. 'Bālānaṃ abhinanditaṃ' means being delighted in by blind worldlings through the clinging of views and craving, thinking 'I' and 'mine.'

'Dhammādāsaṃ' means the Mirror of Dhamma. Just as beings see the defects and merits of their own faces or bodies in a mirror, so too a practitioner sees the states of defilement and purity within their own being as they truly are through a certain insight knowledge; that insight knowledge is called 'Dhammādāsa' here. Having produced that Mirror of Dhamma in his own being to attain the Eye of Dhamma, which is called Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa)... 'Paccavekkhiṃ imaṃ kāyaṃ' means he contemplated this physical body (karaja-kāya) with the eye of wisdom, seeing it as empty because it is devoid of permanence and essence, and as 'inside and out' by distinguishing between his own being and the beings of others. To show the manner of his contemplation, the words beginning with 'Yathā idaṃ' are connected. In that verse, 'Yathā idaṃ tathā etaṃ' means: just as this corpse, devoid of consciousness, displays various magical-like movements, so too this corpse in the past...
93:
...through that insight knowledge, one sees the states of defilement and purity in one's own being as they truly are; that insight knowledge is called 'Dhammādāsa' (Mirror of Dhamma) in this Dispensation. Having produced that Mirror of Dhamma in his own being to attain the Eye of Dhamma, which is the Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) known as the vision of knowledge... 'Paccavekkhiṃ imaṃ kāyaṃ' means he looked at and contemplated this physical body (karaja-kāya) with the eye of wisdom, seeing it as empty because it is devoid of permanence, essence, and so on, and as 'inside and out' by distinguishing between his own being and the beings of others.

To show the manner in which he looked at and contemplated it, the words beginning with 'Yathā idaṃ' are spoken. In those words, 'Yathā idaṃ tathā etaṃ' means—just as this foul thing called my body displays various magical-like movements because life, heat, and consciousness have not yet departed, so too this corpse in the past was like that before those states departed. Just as this corpse now displays no movement at all because those states have departed, so too my body will surely perish when those states depart. Just as my body now has not yet died and is not lying in the cemetery, and has not yet reached the state of being bloated and so on, so too this corpse now was like that in the past. Just as this corpse now lies in the cemetery and has reached the state of being bloated and so on, so too my body will be like that in the future.

Alternatively, just as my body is impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, repulsive, impermanent, suffering, and non-self, so too is that corpse. Alternatively, just as this corpse has the nature of being impure and so on, and the nature of being impermanent and so on, so too is my body. 'Yathā adho tathā uddhaṃ' means—just as this body below the navel is impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, repulsive, impermanent, suffering, and non-self, so too above the navel it has the nature of being impure and so on. 'Yathā uddhaṃ tathā adho' means—just as it has the nature of being impure and so on above the navel, so too it is below the navel.

'Yathā divā tathā rattiṃ' means—just as this body oozes impure things such as 'eye-wax from the eyes' during the day, so too it is during the night. 'Yathā rattiṃ tathā divā' means—just as this body oozes impure things during the night, so too it is during the day; the meaning is that there is no change into another state by the distinction of time. 'Yathā pure tathā pacchā' means—just as this body was impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive in the past during the time of youth, so too it is in the later time of old age. Just as it has the nature of being impure and so on in the later time of old age, so too in the past...
94:
Even in the time of youth; or just as in the past time when consciousness was present, the nature of impurity and the nature of impermanence existed, so too in the future time when consciousness is absent, it will be the same—thus should the meaning be understood in this context.

"With five-fold musical instruments" (pañcaṅgikena turiyena) refers to instruments such as the one-sided drum, the two-sided drum, the all-around drum, the solid instrument (cymbals), and the hollow instrument (flute). The delight and pleasure arising from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by a powerful person entertained by such five-fold musical instruments cannot be compared. "As for one with a one-pointed mind, rightly contemplating the Dhamma" (yathā ekaggacittassa sammā dhammaṃ vipassato) means that for a practitioner who, having joined serenity and insight (samatha and vipassanā) together, observes the rise and fall of the aggregates through insight with the unified function of the faculties—the kind of delight in the Dhamma that arises for him, not even a sixteenth part of it can be matched by delight in sensual pleasures. For this has been said by the Blessed One:

"Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates,
One attains joy and gladness; that is the Deathless for those who understand it."
(Dhammapada 374)

These very verses were also the Elder Kulla's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kulla is finished.

## 5. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mālukyaputta

The verses beginning with "Manujassa" belong to the Venerable Elder Mālukyaputta. What is the background story? This elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various lives, was reborn in this Buddha-era in the city of Sāvatthī as the son of the royal appraiser (aggāsanika) of King Kosala. His mother was named Mālukyā; he became well-known as Mālukyaputta (son of Mālukyā) because of her name. When he reached the age of maturity, having a desire for liberation, he abandoned the household life and wandered as a paribbājaka (wandering ascetic). While wandering, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, gained faith in the Dispensation, and ordained. While striving in the work of insight, he soon became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers. Out of compassion for his relatives, he went to his relatives' home. The relatives, having served the elder with excellent food and snacks, wishing to tempt him with wealth, placed a great...
95:
...heap of wealth before him and pleaded, "This wealth belongs to you; return to lay life and, while supporting a wife and children with this wealth, perform meritorious deeds." The elder, wishing to change their inclination, stood in the air and preached the Dhamma with these six verses:

"For a human being who lives heedlessly, craving grows like a māluvā creeper.
He leaps from life to life, like a monkey in the forest seeking fruit.

Whomsoever this wretched craving, the entangler in the world, overcomes,
His sorrows grow like bīraṇa grass after rain.

But he who overcomes this wretched craving, so difficult to pass in the world,
Sorrows fall away from him like water drops from a lotus leaf.

I say this to you: may there be good fortune for all of you gathered here!
Dig up the root of craving, as one seeking the fragrant root digs up bīraṇa grass.
Do not let Māra break you again and again, like the stream breaks a reed.

Follow the word of the Buddha; let not the opportune moment (khaṇa) pass you by.
For those who have missed the moment sorrow when they are consigned to hell.

Heedlessness is dust; dust follows upon heedlessness.
Through heedfulness and through knowledge, one should pluck out one's own sting."

With these six verses, he preached the Dhamma. In those verses, "manujassa" means for a being. "Pamattacārino" means for one who lives with heedlessness, characterized by the abandonment of mindfulness; for such a person, neither jhāna, nor insight, nor the paths and fruits increase. Just as the māluvā creeper grows, entwining and surrounding a tree for its destruction, so too craving grows for that person, arising repeatedly in regard to forms and so on, depending on the six sense doors. As it grows, just as the māluvā creeper overwhelms and brings down the tree that is its own support, so too craving causes the person who follows its power to fall into the states of misery (apāya). "So plavati" means that person who is under the power of craving leaps and runs back and forth through various lives. How? Like a monkey in the forest seeking fruit. Just as a monkey seeking forest fruit runs through the forest, catches one branch, lets it go and catches another, lets that go and catches another. Because it is said, "He sits without having caught a branch"...
96:
...does not reach the state of being described as such. In this same way, a person who follows the will of craving, running here and there, does not reach the state of being described as 'having reached the non-arising of craving due to not obtaining an object.'

'Yaṃ' refers to that person. Because of its vile nature, it is called 'jammī' (wretched). Because it has poisonous nutriment, a poisonous cause, poisonous fruit, poisonous utility, and because it is particularly and intensely attached to forms and so on, the craving that arises at the six doors is known as 'visattikā' (the entangler). It overcomes and overwhelms that person. Just as bīraṇa grass grows when it rains repeatedly in the forest, so do sorrows rooted in the round of rebirth grow and increase.

'Yo cetaṃ...pe... duraccayaṃ' means: that person who overcomes and overwhelms this craving, which is of the nature described and is difficult to transcend because it is hard to abandon, from that person, sorrows rooted in the round of rebirth fall away. Just as a drop of water falling on a lotus leaf does not remain, so those sorrows do not remain.

'Taṃ vo vadāmi' means: for that reason, I, the Buddha, tell you. 'Bhaddaṃ vo' means: may there be good fortune for you; do not reach ruin and misfortune like a person who follows the will of craving. 'Yāvantettha samāgatā' refers to all those who have assembled in this place. If one asks, 'What do you say?', it is: dig up the root of craving. Dig up and cut off the mass of defilements such as ignorance, which is the cause of this craving arising at the six doors, with the hoe of the knowledge of the path of Arahatship. For example, just as a man desiring usīra grass digs up the grass named bīraṇa (also called usīra) with a large hoe, so should you dig up the root of that craving. May the Māra of defilements, the Māra of death, and the Māra of celestial beings not destroy you repeatedly, like a swift river current destroys reeds growing on the riverbank.

Therefore, follow the words of the Buddha. Follow the words of the Blessed Buddha spoken as, 'Monks, burn away the defilements, do not be negligent,' and so on. Strive to fulfill the practice according to the instruction. 'Khaṇo vo mā upaccagā' means: the person who does not follow the words of the Buddha...
97:
...for that person, all these moments—the moment of a Buddha's arising, the moment of being born in a suitable place, the moment of attaining right view, and the moment of having the six sense bases unimpaired—pass away. Let that moment not pass you by. 'Khaṇātītā' means those who have missed that moment, or for those persons for whom that moment has passed, they reach hell, and being born in that hell, they grieve for a long time.

'Pamādo rajo' means: negligence, characterized by the relinquishing of mindfulness regarding objects such as forms, is called 'pamāda.' It is called 'dust' (raja) because of its nature to defile and because it is mixed with the dust of lust and so on. 'Pamādānupatito rajo' means: whatever dust of defilements such as lust exists, all of it arises only through the power of negligence. 'Appamādena' means through the practice of diligence (appamāda). 'Vijjāya' means through the knowledge of the highest path (arahattamagga). 'Abbahe sallamattano' means: one should pull out or remove the dart of lust and so on that resides in one's own heart.

## The Explanation of the Verses of Elder Mālukyaputta is Finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Verses of Elder Sappadāsa

The verses beginning with 'Paṇṇavīsati' are those of the Venerable Elder Sappadāsa. How did they arise? This elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit that serves as a support for liberation from the round of rebirth in various existences, was born in this Buddha's era in the city of Kapilavatthu as the son of King Suddhodana's chaplain. His name was Sappadāsa. When he came of age, he gained faith at the assembly of the Teacher's relatives and ordained. However, being oppressed by defilements and unable to attain concentration of mind, he practiced the holy life and felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Later, while taking a weapon, he developed wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) and reached the fruit of Arahatship. Desiring to declare his attainment of Arahatship, he said:

'For these twenty-five years since I ordained, I have not obtained peace of mind even for the duration of a finger-snap.'

'Unable to attain one-pointedness of mind and being oppressed by sensual lust, I left the monastery weeping with my arms raised.'
98:
“I will take a weapon,
What is the use of my life?
How could one like me die
Having renounced the training?

Then, taking a razor,
I sat upon the bed.
The razor was applied (to my neck)
To cut my own throat.

Then, wise attention (yoniso manasikāra)
Arose within me.
The danger (of saṃsāra) became manifest,
And detachment (nibbidā) was established.

Then my mind was liberated (from defilements).
Behold the excellent nature of the Dhamma!
The three knowledges have been attained,
The Buddha’s bidding has been done.”
He recited these verses.

In those verses, “these twenty-five years since I was ordained” means these twenty-five years starting from the time I was ordained. “I did not obtain peace of mind even for the duration of a finger-snap” means that although I have been practicing the holy life for such a long time, I did not obtain even a moment of tranquility of mind or concentration (samādhi), even for the duration of a single finger-snap.
