Regarding this failure to obtain one-pointedness of mind, he states the reason: “being oppressed by sensual desire.” In that context, “aṭṭito” means oppressed or overwhelmed. “Crying with arms raised” means crying out with his face turned upwards and arms raised, thinking, “It is indeed very inappropriate for me to be unable to lift myself out of the mire of defilements after having been ordained in this liberating Dispensation.” “Left the monastery” means he went outside from the monastery where he resided.

To show the intention with which he left, it is said, “I will take a weapon,” and so on. In the phrase “satthāṃ vā āharissāmi,” the word “vā” (or) has the sense of alternative choice. By that word “vā,” various forms of death such as “I will jump from a tree” or “I will die by hanging” are included. “Sikkhaṃ” refers to the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā). “Paccakkhaṃ” means renouncing or giving up. There is also a Pali reading “paccakkhā,” which means by renouncing. “Kālaṃ” means death. The meaning is: how could one like me die by renouncing the training? For renouncing the training is called death in the Discipline of the Noble Ones. As the Blessed One said—
99:
“Monks, for one who renounces the training and returns to the lower life, this is called ‘death’ (in the Discipline of the Noble Ones)” (Majjhima Nikāya). In the reading “sikkhaṃ paccakkhā,” however, he thinks, “How could one like me die by renouncing the training? I shall die only while being possessed of the training.” Therefore, it is connected as: “I will take a weapon; what is the use of my life?”

“Tadā” (then) refers to that time when he was weary of life because of his inability to perform the monk’s duties due to being overwhelmed by defilements. “Khura” means a sharpened razor, or a small knife similar to a razor. “I sat upon the bed” means he entered a private room and sat on the bed for fear of being stopped by others. “Parinīto” means brought near (to the neck), or placed at the neck. “Dhamaniṃ” refers to the throat; they also call it “kaṇṭhadhamani” or “galavalaya” (the windpipe). “Chettuṃ” means for the purpose of cutting.

“Then wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) arose within me” means when he applied the razor to his throat to cut it, thinking “I shall die,” thereafter, while reflecting, “Is my virtue (sīla) flawless?”, he saw his virtue to be unbroken, without holes, and perfectly pure, and joy (pīti) arose. In one with a joyful mind, the body became tranquil; for one with a tranquil body experiencing spiritual happiness, wise attention arose through the power of insight (vipassanā) due to the concentration of the mind. Alternatively, “tato” (thence) means that when a wound was caused by applying the razor to the neck, wise attention arose through the power of insight while suppressing that pain. Now, to show the subsequent arising of the knowledge of the Path, the Fruit, and Reviewing, it is said, “The danger became manifest,” and so on. Its meaning is just as stated below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sappadāsa is finished.

## 7. Katiyānattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

“Uṭṭhehi” and so on are the verses of the Venerable Elder Katiyāna. What is the background? This elder had also performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. In this Buddha’s era, he was born in Sāvatthī as the son of a certain Brahmin of the Kosiya clan...
100:
Katiyāna was born as the son of a Brahmin and was named Katiyāna according to his mother’s clan. When he came of age, he was a lay friend of the Elder Sāmaññakāni; upon seeing the Elder, he was ordained. While performing the monk’s duties, he went up to the walking path (caṅkama) at night, thinking, “I will dispel my sleepiness.” While walking, he was overwhelmed by sleep, and nodding off, he fell down and slept right there on the bare ground. The Teacher, seeing his situation, went there himself and, standing in the air, gave him a sign by calling out, “Katiyāna!” Upon seeing the Teacher, he stood up, paid homage, and stood there filled with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Then the Teacher, wishing to preach the Dhamma to him, said:

“Arise, sit, Katiyāna!
Do not be fond of sleep; be wakeful.
Let not the King of Death, the friend of the heedless,
Conquer you who are lazy, like a hunter (with a trap).

Just like the surge of the great ocean,
So do birth and old age roll over you.
Therefore, make a good island for yourself,
For there is no other refuge for you.

For the Teacher has conquered this path,
Transcending the bonds and the fear of birth and old age.
In the first and last watches of the night, being heedful,
Apply yourself firmly to spiritual practice (yoga).

Release former bonds.
Being a monk who wears the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), is shaven-headed, and eats alms-food,
Katiyāna, do not indulge in play or sleep;
Devote yourself to meditation (jhāya).

Meditate, conquer, Katiyāna!
You are skilled in the paths to security (yogakkhema).
Having reached supreme purity,
You will attain Parinibbāna like a fire extinguished by water.”
101:
“Just as a person who lights a lamp, though the radiance be small, is swayed by the wind like a creeper; even so, Kātiyāna of the Kosiya lineage, do you likewise, without clinging (through craving), strike down and destroy Mara and his fivefold army. Being free from passion regarding the feelings to be experienced, remain here in this very world, cooled of the heat of defilements, awaiting the time for Parinibbāna.” Thus He spoke these verses.

In those verses, “Uṭṭhehi” means: arising from the state of sleep, exert the effort of arousal. Since sleeping belongs to the side of laziness, do not sleep. “Nisīda” means: having sat down cross-legged, keeping the body erect, and establishing mindfulness directed towards the meditation subject, remain so. With the word “Kātiyāna,” He addresses the Elder by name. “Mā niddābahulo ahu” means: do not be one overcome by sleep. “Jāgarassu” means: be one who is awake, devoted to wakefulness. “Mā taṃ alasaṃ” means: may the King of Death not oppress, overwhelm, or crush you—who are lazy and heedless without exerting wakefulness—with the dangers of aging and sickness, just as a hunter oppresses a deer or a bird with a deceptive trap.

The word “Seyyathāpi” should be divided into “Seyyathā” and “api.” “Mahāsamuddavego” is the force of the waves of the great ocean. “Evaṃ” means: just as the force of the great ocean waves, as they rise up successively, overwhelms a man who is unable to cross them; in this same way, birth and aging successively overwhelm you who are oppressed by laziness. “So karohi” means: Dear Kātiyāna, do you create within your own continuity the ‘good island’ known as the Fruit of Arahatship, which cannot be overwhelmed by the four floods. In the phrase “Na hi tāṇaṃ tava vijzteva aññaṃ,” the word “hi” is a particle showing cause. The meaning is: because no other refuge besides that Fruit of Arahatship is found either in this world or in another world, therefore create that island of the Fruit of Arahatship.

“Satthā hi vijesi maggametaṃ” means: Your Teacher, the Buddha, having conquered Mara the son of a deva and others, has won and accomplished that Noble Path—which many sectarians of other views were unable to achieve and were defeated by, which is the cause of that ‘good island,’ and which transcends the five kinds of attachment and the dangers such as birth. Because the Buddha’s...
102:
...inheritance of Dhamma should be taken up by a disciple and not discarded. Therefore, to attain that Dhamma, being heedful, mindful, and possessed of clear comprehension during the first and last watches of the night, devote yourself to the practice of meditation and practice it firmly.

“Release former bonds” means: release and abandon the bonds of a householder and the bonds of sensual pleasures that bound you during your time as a layman; be one without longing for those sensual pleasures. “Wearing the double robe, shaving the head, eating alms food” means: one who wears the double robe, whose head is shaved with a razor, and who habitually eats alms food. These three are stated as the reasons for liberation from former bonds and for not devoting oneself to play, delight, and sleep. Since you live wearing the double robe, with a shaved head, and subsisting on alms food, it is not proper for you to devote yourself to the pleasure of the senses, nor to engage in play, delight, and sleep. Therefore, the connection is: release former bonds, and do not devote yourself to play, delight, and sleep. “Meditate” means: devote yourself to meditation on an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna).

Furthermore, in so devoting oneself, to show the practice of meditation on characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna)—by which meditation one who meditates completely conquers the defilements—He said: “Meditate and conquer.” “You are skilled in the paths to security from the four yokes” means: you are proficient and expert in the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) which are the paths to Nibbāna, the security from the four yokes. Therefore, urging him to meditation, He said: having reached the unsurpassed, pure Nibbāna and Arahatship, you shall attain Parinibbāna. “Like fire by water” means: just as a great mass of fire is extinguished by the falling of a great downpour of water, so will you attain Parinibbāna through the falling of the rain of the Noble Path.

“Light-maker” refers to a lamp. “Small radiance” means having only a little light. “Is bent” means being removed or swayed. “Like a creeper” means like a climbing vine. This is what is meant: Just as a lamp with faint light due to the deficiency of supports such as the wick, or a small creeper, is blown away and destroyed by the wind, so it is with you. O dear one of the lineage similar to Indra, because of being of the Kosiya lineage: destroy and blow away Mara by not coming under his power and by being without clinging. You, thus destroying Mara, with desire and passion vanished regarding all feelings to be experienced, being cooled and at peace even in this very existence due to the absence of the distress and fever of all defilements, await only the time of your own Parinibbāna.

When the Blessed One preached the discourse leading to Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna), the Elder Kosiya developed insight and reached the Fruit of Arahatship. After reaching the Fruit of Arahatship, he recited this verse in the very manner the Buddha had preached. Therefore, these verses are also ‘Verses of Declaration of Gnosis’ (aññābyākaraṇa-gāthā) acknowledging the Elder Kosiya’s attainment of Arahatship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kosiya Ends.
103:
The Blessed One said: "Just as a small creeper is blown away by the wind, you, dear son, should not follow the will of Māra, but without attachment, destroy Māra. While destroying him, being free from passion in all feelings, being cooled in this very life, just await the time of your Parinibbāna." Thus, when the Blessed One preached the Dhamma, leading him to Nibbāna without remainder, that Elder developed insight at the end of the teaching and attained Arahantship. After attaining Arahantship, he recited these verses in the same manner as taught by the Blessed One. These verses became the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kātiyāna is finished.

## 8. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Migajāla

The verses beginning with "Sudisito" are those of the Venerable Migajāla Thera. What is the background? This venerable one had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various lives. When this Buddha appeared, he was reborn in Sāvatthī as the son of the great laywoman Visākhā and was named Migajāla. He went to the monastery, frequently heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and ordained. Having developed insight and attained Arahantship, wishing to declare his final knowledge, he recited:

"Well-taught by the Visionary, the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun; transcending all fetters, destroying all cycles of rebirth.

It is leading out, crossing over, drying up the root of craving; having cut the root of poison, the place of execution, it leads to Nibbāna.

For the breaking of the root of ignorance, it is the destroyer of the machine of kamma; in the grasping of consciousnesses, it is the striking of the diamond-weapon of knowledge.

It makes feelings known without distortion, it releases from grasping; it sees existence with knowledge repeatedly like a pit of glowing coals.

It has great flavor, is very deep, and prevents aging and death. The Noble Eightfold Path calms the suffering of the cycle and is peaceful.

Knowing kamma as kamma and its result as result, it gives the light that sees the nature of dependently originated phenomena as they truly are. It is peaceful, leading to the secure Nibbāna, and is auspicious in the end."

In those verses, "Sudisito" means well-taught by clearly demonstrating the benefits of the present, the future, and the ultimate goal, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be tamed.
104: In those verses, "Sudisito" means well-taught. It is called "Sudisito" because it is taught by way of clearly demonstrating the present benefit, the future benefit, and the ultimate goal, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be tamed. Alternatively, "Sudisito" means rightly taught, signifying the "Svākkhāta" Dhamma taught by way of making clear the process of saṃsāra (pavatti), the cessation of saṃsāra (nivatti), and the causes of both without distortion. "Cakkhumatā" refers to the Blessed One who is endowed with these five eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Buddha eye, and the universal eye. "Buddhena" refers to the Omniscient Buddha. "Adiccabandhunā" is because he is of the lineage of the Sun. In the world, the Khattiya (warrior-noble) lineage is of two kinds: the Solar lineage (Ādiccavaṃsa) and the Lunar lineage (Somavaṃsa). Among them, the Solar lineage should be known as the Okkāka royal lineage. Because they originated from that Okkāka royal lineage, the Sakyans are of the Solar clan (Ādiccagotta). Therefore, the Blessed One is called "Ādiccabandhu" (Kinsman of the Sun). Alternatively, he is "Ādiccabandhu" because he is a kinsman of the Sun; this meaning has been stated below. He is "Sabbasaṃyojanātīto" because he has transcended all fetters such as the fetter of sensual desire. Because he has transcended them, he is "Sabbavaṭṭavināsano" because he destroys and demolishes the cycle of defilements, the cycle of kamma, and the cycle of results. He is "Niyyāniko" because he is the means of exit from the prison of saṃsāra. He is "Uttaraṇo" in the sense of causing one to cross over the great flood of saṃsāra. He is "Taṇhāmūlavisosano" because he dries up ignorance and unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), which are the roots of all cravings such as sensual craving. He is "Visamūlaṃ" because he destroys the penetration of the three Vedas, and because he is the cause of poison-like suffering. He cuts off and completely eradicates the cycle of kamma or the cycle of defilements, which is like a place of execution where beings meet their ruin, and leads them to Nibbāna. The root of ignorance (aññāṇa) is unwise attention and the outflows (āsavas). As it is said, "With the arising of the outflows, there is the arising of ignorance," (M. Ni. 1.103), he taught for the sake of breaking that ignorance with knowledge like a diamond-weapon. Alternatively, according to the words "With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations," etc., this cycle of existence has ignorance as its root; it should be connected as "taught for the sake of shattering it with the diamond of path-knowledge." "Kammayantavighāṭano" means the destroyer of the machine of the self-identity (attabhāva) which is joined by kamma. "Viññāṇānaṃ pariggahe" means when the grasping of consciousness is manifest in the sense-sphere existence, etc., according to one's own kamma—the remaining words should be added. For when rebirth is taken in various existences, the consciousnesses dependent on those various existences are also taken. "Ñāṇavajiranipātano" means destroying those consciousnesses by striking with the diamond of knowledge; it refers to the arising [of path-knowledge] while destroying the consciousnesses that would arise in the seventh existence and so on, when the supramundane Dhamma arises.
105:
Dropping the thunderbolt of knowledge, he breaks those consciousnesses. For when the supramundane Dhamma arises, it arises only by breaking the consciousnesses that are fit to arise in the seventh existence and so forth.

He is called 'Vedanānaṃ viññāpano' because he makes known the three feelings, such as pleasure and so on, correctly according to their true nature as thorns of suffering and as impermanent. He is called 'Upādānappamocano' because he releases the mental continuum from the four types of grasping, such as sensual grasping and so forth. He is called 'Bhavaṃ aṅgārakāsuṃva ñāṇena anupassano' because he repeatedly and clearly sees and shows, through the knowledge of the path of Arahatship, the nine types of existence as being like a pit of glowing coals more than a man's height deep, ablaze with the eleven fires.

He is called 'Mahāraso' (Great Essence) because of his peaceful and sublime nature, and because of the immortal taste that never satiates. Alternatively, he is called 'Mahāraso' because of having great tasks through the function of full understanding (pariññā) and so forth, and because of having great attainment through the power of the fruits of recluseship. He is profoundly deep because he is difficult to enter and find a footing for those who have not accumulated the requisites of perfections. He is called 'Jarāmaccunivāraṇo' because he prevents old age and death by turning back the production of future existence. Now, wishing to show the Dhamma endowed with the aforementioned special qualities in its own form, he said, 'Ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko' (The Noble Eightfold Path), and then said 'Dukkhūpasamano sivo' (The allayer of suffering, the peaceful) and so forth to clarify some of its qualities. The meaning is: he is 'Ariya' (Noble) because of his purity; 'Aṭṭhaṅgika' (Eightfold) because of the combination of the eight factors such as Right View and so forth; 'Magga' (Path) because of seeking Nibbāna; 'Dukkhavūpasamano' because of allaying all the suffering of the round of rebirths; and 'Sivo' because of being secure.

In the doctrines outside this Dispensation, because they are made known by those who are not Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, kamma and its result might be perverted. Without such perversion, by knowing kamma as kamma and result as result among the dependently arisen phenomena through preliminary knowledge (pubbabhāga-ñāṇa), one sees the true light by crushing and destroying the views of eternalism and annihilationism. He shows the light of supramundane knowledge that makes one know thus. Because he is never oppressed by any danger at any time, he goes to the great security of Nibbāna and leads beings there. Therefore, he is called 'Mahākhemangamo'. He is 'Santa' (Peaceful) because of allaying all the distress and fever of defilements. The connection is: the One with Vision (the Buddha) well-taught the Dhamma which is good in the end because it leads to the unshakeable liberation of mind (cetovimutti), the fruit of Arahatship, and to the Nibbāna element without remainder.

Thus, Migajāla Thera, praising the Dhamma of the Noble Ones in various ways, pointed out his own attainment of the fruit of Arahatship. The commentary on the verses of Migajāla Thera is finished. The verses beginning with 'Jātimadena mattohaṃ' are the verses of the Venerable Jenta Thera. This Jenta Thera had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, and in this Buddha's time, he was born in Sāvatthī as the son of the chaplain of King Kosala. He was named Jenta. When he came of age, he became intoxicated with the pride of birth, the pride of wealth, and the pride of power, and he used to oppress others and did not respect his elders.
106:
Thus, Migajāla Thera, praising the Dhamma of the Noble Ones in various ways, showed that he himself had attained that Dhamma by referring to other matters (pointing to the fruit of Arahatship).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Migajāla Thera is Finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Verses of Jenta Thera, the Son of the Chaplain

The verses beginning with "Jātimadena mattohaṃ" are the verses of the Venerable Jenta Thera. What is the account of his origin? This Jenta Thera also had special merit performed in the presence of previous Buddhas, and having accumulated merits such as giving and virtue in various existences, he was born as the son of the chaplain of King Kosala in Sāvatthī when our Buddha appeared. He was named Jenta. When he came of age, he wandered about stiff with pride, intoxicated with the pride of birth, the pride of wealth, the pride of power, and the pride of physical beauty, despising others and not showing respect even to those worthy of honor.

One day, seeing the Teacher teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a large assembly, he approached and thought, "If the recluse Gotama speaks to me first, I will also speak; if he does not, I will not speak," and stood there. Since the Blessed One did not speak first, he himself, out of pride, did not speak and showed a sign of leaving. Then the Blessed One addressed him with a verse:

"Brahmin, pride is not good. For one who seeks benefit here, O Brahmin, whatever purpose you came for, only that should you cultivate." (Saṃ. Ni. 1.201)

He became greatly inspired, thinking, "The recluse Gotama knows my mind," and prostrating with his head at the Blessed One's feet, showing extreme humility, he asked:

"In whom should one not be proud? In whom should one have reverence? To whom should one be respectful? Who should be well-honored?"

The Blessed One answered his question and taught the Dhamma:

"In mother and in father, and also in the eldest brother and sister, in the teacher as the fourth, and in recluses and brahmins (one should not be proud)."

One should not be arrogant or proud toward these people, such as mother and father. You, Jenta the Brahmin, should cultivate reverence, respect, humility, and good worship toward these people, such as mother and father. One should especially bow down to those virtuous ones, such as parents, and to the Arahats who have finished their task, are free from taints, and are peaceful, by humbling one's pride and being one who is not stiff. Because of that teaching, that Brahmin became a stream-enterer, ordained as a monk, and while practicing insight meditation, he reached the fruit of Arahatship, and in praise of his own practice...
107:
“One should not show pride towards them; one should have respect for them. Towards whom should one show reverence? They are well-worshipped. Having abandoned pride and being without stubbornness, one should pay homage to those Arahants who are cooled, who have done what was to be done, who are free from taints (āsavas), and who are supreme.” Thus, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma while answering the question. Due to that teaching, that brahmin became a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Having gone forth as a monk and practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained the fruit of Arahantship. By way of praising his own practice and wishing to declare his attainment of Arahantship, he recited these verses:

“Intoxicated by pride of birth, and by wealth and power,
Intoxicated by pride of physical form and appearance, I used to wander.

I did not consider anyone as my equal, nor anyone as my superior;
A fool destroyed by excessive pride, I was stubborn, with the banner of conceit raised high.

Neither mother nor father, nor others worthy of respect,
Did I ever salute, being stubborn with pride and disrespectful.

Having seen the Leader, the Supreme One, the best of charioteers,
Shining like the sun, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks,

Casting away the nine types of pride and intoxication, with a clear mind,
I paid homage with my head to the Buddha, the Supreme among all beings.

Excessive pride and inferiority complex have been abandoned and well-uprooted;
The conceit ‘I am’ (asmimāna) is completely cut off, and all forms of pride are destroyed.”

In those verses, “jātimadena mattohaṃ” means: Being born in a noble brahmin family, I wandered with stubborn pride, intoxicated by the pride of lineage, thinking, “There is no other like me, born pure from both sides of my parentage.”

“Bhoga-issariyena ca” means: Intoxicated by the pride arising from the possession of wealth and power, I wandered.

“Saṇṭhāna-vaṇṇa-rūpena” means: Perfection of physical stature is called ‘saṇṭhāna’; the brightness and purity of complexion is called ‘vaṇṇa’; the beauty of limbs is called ‘rūpa’. In this explanation, the meaning should be understood as stated below.

“Madamatto” means: By pride other than the types mentioned...
108:
Perfection of stature and circumference is called *saṇṭhāna* (form/stature). Perfection of the skin, such as being fair or golden-hued, is called *vaṇṇa* (complexion). The beauty of the limbs and body parts is called *rūpa* (physical beauty). In this context also, the connection of the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. *Madamaṭṭo* means being intoxicated by forms of intoxication (*mada*) other than those already mentioned.

"Not anyone equal to myself" (*Nāttano samakaṃ kañci*) means he did not consider anyone to be his equal, whether by birth or other factors, nor did he consider anyone superior. The meaning is: "If I did not even consider anyone equal to me, how could there be anyone superior?" "A fool struck by excessive pride" (*Atimānahato bālo*) means: "I am a fool, and because of that foolishness, my virtuous conduct was destroyed by excessive pride (*atimāna*)." Because of this, he was extremely stubborn, like one who has hoisted a banner of pride. Due to the power of that pride, he did not show respect or humility even to his teachers; he was exceedingly stiff, unbending, and possessed a raised banner of conceit.

To make the aforementioned meaning clearer, the words beginning with "mother" (*mātaraṃ*) were spoken. In that context, "others" (*aññe*) refers to elder brothers and the like, as well as recluses and brahmins. "Those esteemed as venerable" (*garusammate*) refers to those who are respected or held in high positions. "Disrespectful" (*anādaro*) means lacking in reverence.

"Seeing the Guide, the Foremost" (*Disvā vināyakaṃ aggaṃ*) means that while wandering about stiff with pride, he saw the Teacher. He is called "Guide" (*Vināyaka*) because he disciplines (*vinayana*) sentient beings for their welfare in this life, the next life, and the ultimate goal, and because he is a leader by his own self-enlightenment (*sayambhū*). He is "Foremost" (*Agga*) because he is the most excellent in the world, including the devas, due to his virtues such as morality (*sīla*). He is the "Supreme Charioteer" (*Sārathīnaṃ varuttamaṃ*) because he disciplines those fit to be disciplined to the utmost degree. He shines like the sun with the radiance of his fathom-wide aura (*byāmappabhā*), preaching the Dhamma surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. Seeing the Teacher, the most excellent of all beings, he was as if awed by the Buddha's power. He abandoned the pride of wealth and other intoxications, such as the thought "I alone am superior, others are inferior," and with a clear and confident mind, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet. This is how the meaning should be connected. One might ask: "How did this Brahmin Jenta, being so stiff with pride, abandon his pride just by seeing the Teacher?" It should not be viewed in that way. He did not abandon pride merely by seeing the Teacher; rather, he abandoned it through the teaching (*desanā*) beginning with "Brahmin, pride is not good." Referring to that teaching, it was said: "Having discarded pride and intoxication, with a clear mind, he prostrated with his head." In the phrase "with a clear mind" (*vippasannena cetasā*), the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of a characteristic attribute (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*).

Excessive pride (*atimāna*) and pride of inferiority (*omāna*) have been abandoned, well-uprooted. The conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) has been completely cut off. All nine types of pride have been destroyed. Among those verses, "I was intoxicated by the pride of birth" (*jātimadena mattohaṃ*) means: "Because I was born into a noble family of chaplain brahmins, and because there is no one else born as purely as I from both parents for seven generations, I wandered about intoxicated and stiff with the pride of my lineage." "And by wealth and power" (*bhoga-issariyena ca*) means: "I wandered about intoxicated by the pride that arose based on the possession of wealth and the possession of authority." Regarding "by stature, complexion, and physical beauty" (*saṇṭhānavannarūpena*): Perfection of stature and circumference is called *saṇṭhāna*. Perfection of the skin, such as being fair or golden-hued, is called *vaṇṇa*. The beauty of the limbs and body parts is called *rūpa*. In this explanation as well, the method of connecting the meaning should be understood as stated below. *Madamaṭṭo* means: "I wandered about intoxicated by forms of intoxication other than those already mentioned."

"Not anyone equal to myself" (*Nāttano samakaṃ kañci*) means he would not consider anyone to be his equal, whether by birth or other factors. The meaning is: "If I did not even consider anyone equal to me, how could there be anyone superior?" "A fool struck by excessive pride" (*Atimānahato bālo*) means: "I am a fool, and because of that foolishness, my virtuous conduct was destroyed by excessive pride." Because of this, he was extremely stubborn, like one who has hoisted a banner of pride. Due to the power of that pride, he did not show respect or humility even to his teachers; he was exceedingly stiff, unbending, and possessed a raised banner of conceit. To make the aforementioned meaning clearer, the words beginning with "mother" (*mātaraṃ*) were spoken. In that context, "others" (*aññe*) refers to elder brothers and the like, as well as recluses and brahmins. "Those esteemed as venerable" (*garusammate*) refers to those who are respected or held in high positions. "Disrespectful" (*anādaro*) means lacking in reverence.

"The Guide, the Foremost" (*Vināyakaṃ aggaṃ*) means that while wandering about stiff with pride, he saw the Teacher. He is called "Guide" (*Vināyaka*) because he disciplines sentient beings for their welfare in this life, the next life, and the ultimate goal, and because he is a leader by his own self-enlightenment. He is "Foremost" (*Agga*) because he is the most excellent in the world, including the devas, due to his virtues such as morality. He is the supreme among those who discipline those fit to be disciplined. He shines like the sun with the radiance of his fathom-wide aura, preaching the Dhamma surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. Seeing the Teacher, the most excellent of all beings, he was as if awed by the Buddha's power. He abandoned the pride of wealth and other intoxications, such as the thought "I alone am superior, others are inferior," and with a clear and confident mind, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet. This is how the meaning should be connected. One might ask: "How did this Brahmin Jenta, being so stiff with pride, abandon his pride just by seeing the Teacher?" It should not be viewed in that way. He did not abandon pride merely by seeing the Teacher; rather, he abandoned it through the teaching beginning with "Brahmin, pride is not good." Referring to that teaching, it was said: "Having discarded pride and intoxication, with a clear mind, he prostrated with his head." In the phrase "with a clear mind" (*vippasannena cetasā*), the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of a characteristic attribute.

The pride that arises as "I alone am superior" is excessive pride (*atimāna*). The pride of one who views others as inferior, thinking "This person is indeed lowly," is called the pride of inferiority (*omāna*). The pride of one who views himself as superior, surpassing others by thinking "I am superior," is called the pride of superiority (*seyyamāna*). The pride that arises as "I am inferior" is called lowly pride (*hīnamāna*). They have been abandoned; "well-uprooted" (*susumūhatā*) means they have been abandoned by the three paths and finally cut off entirely by the Path of Arahatship. The conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) is the pride that arises from the clinging and assumption of "I am" or "I". In the word "all" (*sabbe*), it does not mean only the conceit "I am" based on the five aggregates, but all nine types of pride, such as the pride of superiority, and the infinite varieties of all pride.
109:
The pride that arises as "I alone am superior" is called atimāna (arrogance). The pride of one who regards others as inferior, thinking "These people are indeed lowly," is called "omāna" (lowliness). The pride that arises when one surpasses others and regards oneself as superior, thinking "I am superior," is called seyyamāna atimāna. The pride that arises as "I am inferior" is called hīnamāna omāna. "Pahīnā susamūhatā" means they have been abandoned by the three lower paths and well-uprooted by the path of Arahantship. Asmimāna is the pride that arises by way of grasping the five aggregates as "I", thinking "This is I." "Sabbē" means not only atimāna, omāna, and asmimāna, but indeed all nine types of pride starting with seyyamāna, and all groups of pride which are numerous in their various divisions, have been well-destroyed and uprooted by the path of Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Jenta Thera, the Son of the Chaplain, is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verses of Sumana Thera

The verses beginning with "Yadā navo pabbajito" are those of the Venerable Sumana Thera. What is the background story? This Elder also had performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. In the time of Sikhī Buddha, he was born into a family of florists. Upon reaching maturity, one day he saw Sikhī Buddha and, with a devout heart, made an offering of jasmine flowers. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In this Buddha's era, he took rebirth in the house of a certain lay devotee (upāsaka). That lay devotee was an attendant of the Venerable Anuruddha Thera. Previously, all the children born to that lay devotee had died. Therefore, that lay devotee thought, "If I get a son now, I will have him ordained in the presence of the Venerable Anuruddha Thera." That child was born after ten months, was healthy, and grew up gradually. When he reached the age of seven, his father had him ordained in the presence of the Elder. After ordaining, because he possessed mature wisdom, while practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he soon attained the six higher powers (abhiññā). Wishing to serve the Elder, he took a water pot, saying "I will fetch drinking water," and went to Lake Anotatta by psychic power. At that time, a certain Nāga king of wrong view was covering Lake Anotatta, having coiled himself seven times...
110: ...and spreading a large hood above, did not give the novice Sumana the opportunity to take water. The novice Sumana took the form of a Garuda, subdued that dragon king, took the water, and traveled through the sky towards the Elder's dwelling place. The Teacher, seated in Jetavana, saw him coming in that manner and addressed the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, saying, "Sāriputta, look at this [novice]," and spoke of his virtues in four verses. Then, Venerable Sumana spoke six verses by way of declaring final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa):"When I was newly ordained, seven years of age from birth, I subdued the dragon king of great power with psychic power. I brought water for my preceptor from the great Lake Anotatta; seeing me, the Teacher said this: 'Sāriputta, look at this young boy coming, carrying a water jar, well-concentrated within. With graceful conduct and beautiful posture, he is Anuruddha's novice, confident in psychic power. A noble one made noble by a noble one, well-trained by the good, disciplined by Anuruddha who has done what was to be done. Having reached supreme peace and realized the unshakable, that novice Sumana wishes, "May others not know me."'"Among those verses, the first two were spoken by Venerable Sumana himself, and the remaining four were spoken by the Teacher who wished to praise him. Later, Venerable Sumana combined all of them and spoke them by way of declaring final knowledge. In those verses, 'pannaginda' refers to the dragon king. 'Tato' means at that time. The meaning is: "At that time when I, being newly ordained at seven years from birth, subdued the dragon king of great power with the strength of psychic power and brought water for my preceptor from Lake Anotatta."
111:
Referring to me, my teacher, the Blessed One, spoke these words. Desiring to show this, he said, "Sāriputta, look at this person," and so on. "Ajjhattaṃ susamāhitaṃ" means being well-concentrated within one's own continuity by the highest fruition-concentration (phalasamādhi). "Pāsādikena vattena" means with conduct that inspires faith in those who see it. Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of instrument. "Kalyāṇairiyāpatho" means one possessed of perfect postures. Alternatively, the instrumental case in "pāsādikena vattena" indicates a characteristic (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). The state of a recluse is called "sāmañña." Because it brings about that state of a recluse, it is called "sāmaṇera" or "samaṇuddesa." "Iddhiyā ca visārado" means being very skilled and proficient in the field of psychic powers. "Ājānīyena" means being a noble person (thoroughbred), one who accomplishes his own benefit and the benefit of others, a virtuous person; it refers to the Elder Anuruddha who has completed what was to be done, who is well-disciplined, who accomplishes both mundane and supramundane benefits, or simply one who is well-tamed. "Aggavijjāya vinīto" means disciplined by the wisdom of the fruition of Arahatship, trained or taught by being brought to the state of an Arahant.

That novice Sumana, having reached the noble peace of Nibbāna, having realized it through the attainment of the highest path, and having made it personal for himself, attained the unshakable fruition of Arahatship. Due to the excellence of his fewness of wishes (appicchatā), he strongly desired, "Let no one know me as 'This one is an Arahant' or 'This one is a possessor of the six supernormal knowledges'."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sumana Thera is Finished.

## 11. The Commentary on the Verses of Nhātakamuni Thera

The verse beginning with "Vātarogābhinīto" is that of the Venerable Nhātakamuni. As for the origin: he too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various births. In this Buddha's era, he was born into a Brahmin family in Rājagaha. When he came of age, he reached the completion of sciences and arts, and because he was endowed with the marks of a "Nhātaka" (one who has bathed/graduated), he became known as "Nhātaka." He went forth as an ascetic and lived in a forest area about three yojanas from Rājagaha, subsisting on wild grains like millet and wild rice, and tending the sacrificial fire. The Blessed One, seeing the support (upanissaya) for Arahatship shining within his heart like a lamp inside a jar, went to his hermitage. Seeing the Blessed One, he was filled with joy and delight...
112:
...and offered food according to his own means (millet, wild rice, etc.). The Blessed One partook of that food. After he had offered food in this way for three days, on the fourth day, the Blessed One said, "You are very delicate; how do you subsist on such coarse food?" The Teacher taught the Dhamma, revealing the quality of contentment of the Noble Ones (ariyavaṃsa). Having heard that, the ascetic became a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), went forth, and attained Arahatship. The Blessed One, having established him in Arahatship, departed. While living there, he was later afflicted by a wind-ailment. The Teacher went there and, by way of friendly greeting, asked about his living condition:

"Afflicted by wind-disease, living in the forest,
With discarded food and in a coarse place, how will you fare, O Bhikkhu?"

Thus he spoke the verse. Then the Elder replied:

"Pervading the body with great rapture and bliss,
Enduring even the coarseness, I shall dwell in the forest.
Developing the seven factors of enlightenment, the faculties, and the powers,
Endowed with the subtlety of jhāna, I shall dwell without taints.
Constantly reflecting on the mind freed from defilements,
Pure and undisturbed, I shall dwell without taints.
The taints that used to pierce me, both internally and externally,
Are all cut off without remainder; they will not arise again.
The five aggregates are fully understood; they remain with their roots cut;
The end of suffering (Nibbāna) is reached; now there is no more rebirth."

With these remaining verses, he informed the Teacher of his way of living.

In those verses, "jhānasokhummasampanno" means endowed with the subtle nature of jhāna. "Jhānasukhuma" refers to the formless jhānas (arūpajjhāna); therefore, it means he is an attainer of the eight attainments. By this, he shows his liberation in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutti). Others, however, say that by the word "sokhumma," the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā) in the highest path and fruition is intended. Furthermore, by taking jhāna, he makes clear his liberation in both ways. "Vippamuttaṃ kilesehi" means liberation from all defilements through the liberation of tranquilization (paṭippassaddhivimutti). For that very reason, because of having a pure mind and undisturbed thoughts, he is called "anāvila" (undisturbed). All these three terms refer only to the mind of the fruition of Arahatship. The remaining explanations are as stated before. This verse itself is the Elder's declaration of Arahatship (aññābyākaraṇa). The commentary on the verses of Nhātakamuni Thera is finished.
113:
By attaining jhāna, he manifests his state of being liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutti). "Well-liberated from defilements" means liberated from all defilements through the liberation of complete tranquility (paṭippassaddhivimutti); for that very reason, he has a pure mind, and because of having thoughts that are not turbid, he is said to have a mind free from turbidity. By these three terms, only the fruition-consciousness of Arahantship (arahattaphala-citta) is spoken of. The remaining explanation is exactly as stated in the method below. This verse itself was the Elder's declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Thera Nātakamuni is finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Verses of Thera Brahmadatta

The verse beginning with "Akkodhassa" is that of the Venerable Brahmadatta Thera. As for the background story: he also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, having accumulated merits in various existences, was reborn in this Buddha's era in Sāvatthī as the son of King Kosala, and was named Brahmadatta. When he reached maturity, he saw the majesty of the Buddha at the festival of the Jetavana Monastery and, having gained faith, he ordained. While striving in the practice of insight (vipassanā), he became an Arahant endowed with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā).

One day, while he was wandering for alms in the city, a certain Brahmin insulted him. Although the Elder heard those insults, he remained silent and continued his alms-round. The Brahmin insulted him again. Even though he was being insulted in this way, people said, "This Elder does not say anything at all." Hearing those words, the Elder, wishing to preach the Dhamma to those people, recited these verses:

"For one who is without anger, who is tamed, who lives righteously, who is liberated through right knowledge, who is peaceful and equanimous (tādi)—where can anger exist?

He who reacts with anger to one who is angry makes himself worse by that very reaction. He who does not react with anger to one who is angry wins a battle that is difficult to win.

He who, knowing that the other is angry, remains mindful and calm, practices for the benefit of both—himself and the other.

Those people who are unskilled in the Dhamma consider him a 'fool' who thus heals both himself and the other."
114:
“If anger arises in you, you should reflect on the teaching of the Kakacūpama Sutta (The Simile of the Saw). If craving for tastes arises, remember the Simile of the Son’s Flesh (Puttamansūpama Sutta).

If your mind runs towards sensual pleasures or towards existences, quickly restrain it with mindfulness, like a crop-eating bull is restrained.” Thus, he recited these verses.

In those verses, 'akkodhassa' means for one who is free from anger, for one whose anger has been utterly destroyed by the Path. 'Kuto kodho' means for what reason could anger arise? The meaning is that there is no cause for the arising of anger in him. 'Dantassa' means for one who is tamed by the supreme taming, the taming of the highest Path (aggamagga). 'Samajīvino' means for one who lives evenly by way of bodily composure, etc., having completely abandoned bodily misconduct, etc., and who conducts himself well with clear comprehension established in the seven bases (sattaṭṭhāniya sampajañña). 'Sammad-aññā vimuttassa' means for one who is liberated from all taints (āsavas) after having known the things to be known, etc., through right knowledge. For that very reason, for an Arahant (khīṇāsava) who is peaceful through the calming of all defilements, distress, and fevers, and who has attained the characteristic of equanimity (tādi) towards desirable and undesirable objects, etc.—where can anger exist? Thus, by referring to another, the Elder spoke of his own absence of anger and its causes. Now, wishing to preach the Dhamma by showing the disadvantages of anger and the advantages of non-anger, he spoke the words beginning with “Tasseva”.

In that verse, 'yo kuddhaṃ paṭikujjhati' means that person who reacts with anger to a person who is angry or provoked at him; for that person alone, by that reaction, such as retaliating with insults or striking back, it is very bad and very ignoble in this world due to the censure of the wise, etc., and in the next world due to the suffering of hell, etc. As for the one who does not get angry, there is no need to say that there is no evil due to anger. Some teachers, however, interpret it as “He who reacts with anger towards one who is not angry.” 'Kuddhaṃ appaṭikujjhanto' means he who, knowing an angry person as “This person is angry, overwhelmed by anger,” does not react with anger but endures; he is said to win the battle of defilements which is difficult to win. To show that he not only wins the battle of defilements but also practices for the welfare of both parties, he said, “For the benefit of both... is peaceful.” He who, knowing that another person is provoked and angry, develops loving-kindness or equanimity towards him...
115:
Being mindful and endowed with clear comprehension, he becomes calm and patient, and does not retaliate with anger. Such a person practices for the welfare and benefit of both himself and others, bringing happiness to both worlds.

Fools who are unskilled in the noble conduct of the Dhamma think of such a person—who heals the disease of anger in both himself and others and who is patient—as 'This is an ignorant person who does nothing to one who abuses or strikes him.' This thinking of theirs is due to improper reflection. Some read 'tikicchanaṃ' (healing), meaning having the nature of healing.

Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Elder Brahmadatta, the abusive Brahmin became stirred and gained a clear, confident mind. He asked for the Elder's forgiveness and went forth in his presence. When the Elder gave him a meditation subject, he reflected, 'Loving-kindness meditation (mettā-bhāvanā) is suitable for this monk.' After giving him the meditation on loving-kindness, and wishing to show the method of reflection on the arising of anger and so forth, he spoke the words beginning with 'Uppajje te'.

In that verse, 'Uppajje te sace' means: If, while you are practicing meditation, anger that has been long-accustomed arises in you toward some person, then to calm that anger—
'Monks, even if bandits were to savagely sever you limb by limb with a double-handled saw, if any of you should give way to anger, he would not be a follower of my teaching.'—
Reflect on this advice given by the Blessed One, known as the Simile of the Saw (Kakacūpama). 'Uppajje ce rase taṇhā' means: If craving for tastes such as sweetness arises in you, then to calm that craving—
'Just as a husband and wife might eat the flesh of their own son only to cross a difficult wilderness, so too a monk of good family partakes of alms-food not out of craving for taste, but only for the sake of living comfortably.'—
Repeatedly recollect and reflect on this advice, which is like the eating of a son's flesh (Puttamansūpama).

'Sace dhāvati te cittaṃ' means: If your mind, through improper reflection, runs away due to sensual desire for the five cords of sensual pleasure, or due to longing for existence in the three realms such as the sensual realm, then quickly restrain that wandering mind with mindfulness.
116:
Like a man who ties a crop-eating, wicked bull to a post with a rope to make it follow his will, quickly restrain your mind by tying it to the post of concentration (samādhi) with the rope of mindfulness (sati). Discipline it so that it becomes free from the poison of the defilements. Some teachers, however, say: "The Venerable, while still a worldling (puthujjana), endured the abuse and taught the Dhamma to show the virtues of the Noble Ones to those people. Later, he admonished himself with two verses, developed insight (vipassanā), attained Arahantship, and then spoke these verses to declare his attainment."

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Brahmadatta is finished.

## 13. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Sirimaṇḍa

"Channamativassati" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Sirimaṇḍa. The background story is as follows: This Venerable One had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various lives. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn into a Brahmin family in the city of Saṃsumāragiri and was named Sirimaṇḍa. When he came of age, while the Blessed One was staying in the Bhesakalā Wood, he approached the Buddha, heard the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth, eventually receiving higher ordination. While practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, on a certain Uposatha day, while sitting at the place where the Pātimokkha is recited, he reflected on the meaning of the Pali text at the end of the introduction (Nidāna): "Disclosure brings him comfort." He realized that by not disclosing and instead concealing an offense (āpatti) he had committed, he would fall into successive offenses; because of such concealment, he would not be at ease. Only for a monk who discloses and rehabilitates according to the Dhamma is there comfort. Reflecting on this meaning, he felt inspired, thinking, "How wonderful is the Blessed One's Dispensation! How very pure it is!" He suppressed the rapture (pīti) that had arisen, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. Reflecting on his own practice with a clear and confident mind, and wishing to give advice to the monks, he said:

"The rain pours down on what is covered; it does not pour down on what is open.
Therefore, open up what is covered; thus the rain will not pour down on it."
117:
The world of beings is greatly oppressed by death and surrounded by old age.
The dart of craving has entered the heart, and it is always made to fume with desire.

The world of beings is greatly oppressed by death and also surrounded by old age.
Like a guilty thief who is punished, it is constantly struck, being without protection.

Like masses of flame falling, the three great masses of fire—death, sickness, and old age—fall upon [beings], oppressing and destroying them.
There is no strength to resist those fires, nor is there speed to flee.

One should make the day not in vain, whether with a little or a lot.
Whatever night is given up, that person's life is diminished by that night.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the final night approaches.
It is not the time for you to be negligent.

He spoke these verses.

In those verses, 'channaṃ' means misconduct that is covered, not opened according to reality, and not made manifest. 'Ativassati' means that the rain of offenses (āpatti) and the rain of defilements (kilesa) rain down excessively. The concealment of an offense has such a nature due to shamelessness (alajjī) and so forth. Because of concealment, one might fall into another kind of offense, or again into an offense of the same nature, or into an even more evil offense. Therefore, concealment is said to be the cause of raining. 'Vivaṭaṃ' means that which is made manifest and not concealed. In the word 'nātivassati', 'ati' is merely a prefix, and the meaning is 'it does not rain'. This 'not raining' should be understood as the opposite of the aforementioned meaning, because the mental continuum has been purified. By the word 'tasmā', he reflects on the aforementioned meaning as the cause. The meaning is that for one with concealed misconduct, the rain of offenses etc. rains excessively, while for one with revealed misconduct, it does not rain. 'Channaṃ vivaretha' means that even if a desire to conceal arises due to being a worldling (puthujjana), one should not follow that desire but should reveal it, make it manifest, and remedy it according to the Dhamma. 'Evaṃ' means that by such revelation and practice according to the Dhamma, that concealed misconduct no longer rains with the rain of offenses and defilements, but establishes the person in a state of purity.
118:
Now, wishing to show the grounds for urgency (saṃvegavatthu) which is the cause for heedfulness, saying, "Indeed, one should purify oneself quickly and practice heedfulness (appamāda)," he spoke the verse beginning with "Maccunābbhāhato loko."

In that verse, 'maccunābbhāhato loko' means this entire world of beings is oppressed by death (maccu), which causes one to fall into the entire round of existence, just as an executioner oppresses a thief; one cannot escape from its hands. 'Jarāya parivārito' means this world is surrounded by old age, which has the function of leading to death after birth; it is overwhelmed and ensnared by the mass of old age. 'Taṇhāsalena otiṇṇo' means it is pierced by the dart called craving (taṇhā), which has the characteristic of grasping, like a poison-smeared arrow sunk into the body; it has entered deep into the heart. Indeed, craving is called a 'dart' because it produces pain, pricks within, and is difficult to extract. 'Icchādhūpāyito' means it is made to fume by desire (icchā), which has the characteristic of longing for objects. Indeed, a person desiring that object, whether obtaining the desired object or not, burns with that desire which has the characteristic of constant burning, and thus reaches a state of distress. 'Sadā' means at all times; this word should be applied to all the preceding phrases.

'Parikkhitto jarāya ca' means not only is it oppressed by death, but indeed it is also surrounded by old age. It is hemmed in by old age and encircled by the wall of old age; the meaning is that one cannot transcend that old age. 'Haññati niccamattāṇo' means being without protection and without refuge, one is constantly struck and afflicted by old age and death. For example, just as a thief who has committed a crime and is facing execution is struck by royal authority without protection, similarly, he shows that this world is struck by old age and death.

'Āgacchantaggikkhandhāva' means like great masses of fire that overwhelm a forest when it is burning, these three—death, sickness, and old age—which are like masses of fire because of their sense of constant burning, come oppressing the world of beings. There is no strength or effort in this world to meet and overcome those fires. When they overwhelm quickly, there is no speed to flee. There is no 'speed of legs' in this world to turn one's back and flee to a place where they cannot oppress.
120:
## 14. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sabbakāmi

The verse beginning with "Dvīpādako" is that of the Venerable Sabbakāmi. As for the background: it is said that in the dispensation of the Buddha Padumuttara, having seen an Elder who cleared a blemish (abbuda) that had arisen and restored it to its original state, he made the aspiration: "May I also be able to clear a blemish in the dispensation of a future Buddha and restore it to its original state." Having performed meritorious deeds corresponding to that aspiration, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, while the Blessed One had not yet attained Parinibbāna, he was born in a Khattiya family in the city of Vesālī with the name Sabbakāma. When he reached maturity, his relatives arranged a marriage for him, but because of his inclination toward liberation, he loathed the household life and ordained under the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Venerable Ānanda). While practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, he went to Vesālī with his preceptor and visited his relatives' house. There, his former wife, who was suffering from the pain of separation from her husband, being thin, of poor complexion, unadorned, and wearing soiled clothes, stood to one side weeping after paying homage to him. Seeing her, while the Elder was developing loving-kindness preceded by compassion, defilement suddenly arose due to improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra) toward an object he had previously experienced.

Like a noble steed struck by a whip, he felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He immediately went to a cemetery, took up the sign of foulness (asubha-nimitta), and using the jhāna attained there as a basis, he developed insight (vipassanā) and reached Arahantship. Then, his father-in-law, bringing his daughter who was well-adorned and accompanied by a large retinue, went to the monastery wishing to make him disrobe. The Elder, knowing his intention and wishing to reveal his detachment from sensual pleasures and his lack of clinging to all objects, recited these verses:

"This two-footed body is impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome;
it is full of various corpses and leaks from here and there.

Just as a deer is caught by a snare, a fish by a hook,
or a monkey by glue, so [this body] afflicts worldlings.

Pleasant sights, sounds, tastes, smells, and touches—
these five cords of sensual pleasure are seen in a woman's form.

Those worldlings with lustful minds who indulge in these women,
they increase the dreadful cemetery and accumulate further rebirth."
121:
“Whoever avoids these women as one avoids the head of a snake with one's foot, that person, being mindful, successfully overcomes this attachment (visattikā) in the world. Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and seeing renunciation as safety, having escaped from all sensual pleasures, I have reached Nibbāna, the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya).” These were the verses he uttered.

In those verses, the term 'dvipādako' (two-footed) is used because, although the bodies of legless creatures and others are also impure, this term is used either for emphasis or to show a specific distinction. Alternatively, while other impure bodies are prepared with sour and salty flavors and served as food for humans, the human body is not; therefore, to show its extremely repulsive nature, he said 'dvipādako'. The word 'ayaṃ' (this) refers to the female form that appeared before him at that time. 'Asuci' (impure) means it is purely impure; the meaning is that there is not even a slight amount of purity in this body. 'Duggandho parihariyati' (foul-smelling, it is carried) means that although it is foul-smelling, it is adorned and carried with the scents of flowers, perfumes, and so on. 'Nānākuṇapaparipūro' (filled with various corpses/impurities) means it is filled with various impurities such as hair and so forth. 'Vissavanto tato tato' (flowing from here and there) should be connected as: although they strive to cover the repulsiveness of this body with flower scents and such, that effort is in vain, and it is carried while impurities like saliva and snot flow from the nine openings, and sweat and filth flow from the pores.

To show that even though it is thus repulsive, this body deceives foolish worldlings (andhaputhujjana) with its visual forms and so on, just as a snare deceives deer, he spoke the verse beginning with 'migaṃ'. In that verse, 'migaṃ nilīnaṃ kūṭena' means it is like a hunter oppressing a deer that is hidden or trapped by a deceptive device such as a snare or a net. The word 'iva' (like), which will be mentioned later, should be brought forward and applied here as well. 'Baḷiseneva ambujaṃ' means it is like a fisherman oppressing a fish with a hook baited with food. 'Vānaraṃ viya lepena' means just as a hunter oppresses a monkey with monkey-glue (pitch) smeared on trees or rocks, [these sensual pleasures] deceive and oppress the multitude of foolish worldlings.

As for what things oppress, he said 'rūpā saddā' and so on. The five strands of sensual pleasure, such as visual forms, especially depend on disagreeable objects. They delight the minds of foolish worldlings who are surrounded by unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) based on distorted perceptions. Because they are the basis for defilements and bring about harm, they are said to 'oppress' those people. Therefore, it is said, 'rūpā saddā... are seen in the female form.'
122:
In this context, it should be understood that the mention of 'woman' (itthiggahana) is done for the sake of emphasis. For that very reason, he said, "Those who indulge in these women," and so on. The meaning is: those worldlings whose minds are oppressed by lust and overcome by passion indulge in these women with the perception that they are objects of enjoyment. They repeatedly increase the cycle of rebirth known as the cemetery (kaṭasi)—which is terrifying due to birth and so on, and which is delightful only to the foolish—through repeated rebirth and death. Therefore, he said, "They repeatedly accumulate new existence."

"Whoever avoids these" means that any person who avoids these women, either by suppressing or by cutting off sensual desire (chandarāga), as if treading on the head of a snake with one's foot, that person, being mindful, successfully overcomes the craving called 'visattikā' because they have abandoned all attachment to the world.

"Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures" means seeing the various forms of danger and fault in objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesakāma), as expressed in: "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton, full of suffering and full of despair," and so on. "Seeing renunciation as safety" means seeing renunciation (nekkhamma), the state of a monk (pabbajjā), and Nibbāna—which are the states of having departed from sensual pleasures and existences—as safety and as being free from affliction. He has escaped and is disconnected from all things belonging to the three planes of existence (tebhūmaka dhamma). All things of the three planes are called 'kāma' (sensual/desirable) in the sense of being desired; the Elder is disconnected from those 'kāmas'. Therefore, he said, "I have reached the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya)."

Thus, the Elder preached the Dhamma with the first five verses and declared his attainment of Arahantship with the sixth verse. Upon hearing those words, the father-in-law thought, "This monk is unsullied by all objects; it is impossible to lure him back to sensual pleasures," and he returned by the same path he had come. As for Ven. Sabbakāmi, one hundred years after the Buddha's Parinibbāna, he became the leading Elder (Pathavyā Thera) with one hundred and twenty years of seniority (vassa). He purified the danger to the Sasana created by the Vajjiputta monks of Vesālī and led the Second Council (Dutiya Saṅgīti). He then instructed Tissa Mahābrahmā, saying, "Purify the danger that will arise in the future during the time of King Dhammāsoka," and then attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa nibbāna-dhātu).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Ven. Sabbakāmi is finished.

## The Commentary on the Group of Six (Chakkanipāta) is finished.
123:
Having conducted the Council and having commanded the Great Brahma Tissa to prevent and ward off the dangers that would arise during the reign of King Dhammāsoka in the future, he attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without any remaining physical substrate (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). The explanation of the verses of the Elder Sabbakāmī is finished. The explanation of the Book of Sixes (Chakkanipāta) is finished.

## 7. Sattakanipāta
## 1. Sundarasamuddattheragāthā-vaṇṇanā
In the Book of Sevens, the verse beginning with "Alaṅkatā" is that of the Venerable Sundarasamudda. How did it arise? This Elder, too, had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating merit in various births. When our Buddha appeared, he was born in the city of Rājagaha as the son of a very wealthy merchant. His name was Samudda. Because of his physical beauty, he was known as Sundarasamudda. While in his youth, seeing the Buddha's majesty as He entered Rājagaha, he gained faith and, with the desire for liberation, went forth as a monk. Having received higher ordination and undertaken the dhutaṅga practices, he went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī. Having learned the practice of Vipassanā from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta), he lived devoted to his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

On a festival day in Rājagaha, the Elder's mother saw other merchant sons enjoying the festivities with their wives, all adorned and prepared. Remembering her son, she wept. Seeing her weeping, a certain courtesan asked the reason. The mother told her the reason. Hearing this, the courtesan said, "I will bring him back; just see my womanly power." The mother replied, "If that is so, I will make you his wife and the mistress of this household," and sent her off with much wealth.

That courtesan went to Sāvatthī with a large retinue and, staying in a house where the Elder went for alms, daily had others offer him alms respectfully. She herself would appear adorned, wearing golden sandals. Then one day, seeing the Elder passing by the door, she removed her golden sandals, approached him with joined palms, and invited him with various sensual temptations. Hearing her words, the Elder thought, "The mind of a worldling is unstable; I must make an effort right now." Standing right there, he intensified his meditation and became an Arahant with the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā). Referring to that courtesan, this was said:

Adorned, well-dressed, wearing garlands and decorated,
With feet dyed with lac, and wearing sandals, the courtesan (spoke these words):
124:
"Descending from her sandals, with joined palms in front, that courtesan spoke to me with gentle and soft words, smilingly:

'You have gone forth while young; stay in my instruction. Enjoy human sensual pleasures; I will give you wealth. I promise you truly, or else I shall bring fire and swear. When we both become old, leaning on staffs, we shall both go forth. Thus, we shall be winners in both worlds.'

Seeing that courtesan with joined palms, adorned and well-dressed, like a snare of Death set out—then, wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) arose in me. The danger (of sensual pleasures) became apparent, and revulsion (nibbidā) was firmly established. Then my mind was liberated (from defilements). Behold the excellent nature of the Dhamma! The three knowledges (tevijjā) have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

In those verses, 'māladhārī' means a woman wearing flower garlands and wreaths. 'Vibhūsitā' means one whose body is decorated with flowers, perfumes, and ointments to fill in any deficiencies. By the word 'alaṅkatā', ornamentation with bracelets, rings, necklaces, etc., is intended. 'Alattakakatāpādā' means one whose feet are dyed with lac the color of mature jasmine flowers. This is a compound word (samāsa). The long vowel (dīgha) in 'alattakakatāpādā' is used for the sake of metrical ease in the verse. In a non-compound form, the word 'tassā' should be understood as remaining. 'Pādukāruyha vesikā' means a woman who lives by her beauty (a courtesan), wearing golden sandals in the manner described; the word 'standing' (ṭhitā) is understood as remaining.

'Pādukā oruhitvānā' means descending from the sandals, having removed the golden sandals. 'Pañjalīkatā' means having raised joined palms. That courtesan spoke to me, or spoke of her own accord without waiting for a sequence of words. 'Saṇhena' means with smooth words. 'Mudunā' means with sweet words. Although 'vacanena' (with words) is not explicitly mentioned, it should be understood as such because 'abhāsatha' (spoke) is used.
125:
“You were young and youthful when you went forth as a monk” means that you were a young person, a mere youth, when you entered the monkhood. It points out that one who goes forth should only do so upon reaching the seventh decade (after reaching sixty years of age). “Abide in my teaching” means “Abide by my word.”

If one asks what that word is, it says, “Enjoy human sense pleasures.” For one who wishes to enjoy sense pleasures, the perfection of appearance, the perfection of age, the perfection of retinue, and the perfection of wealth are desired. Among these four, if one should say, “Where shall I find the perfection of wealth?”, she says to such a person, “I will give you wealth.” One might think, “How can this word be believed?” To make that monk believe, she says, “I truly promise you; otherwise, I will bring fire to you.” The meaning is: “There is this word I have promised, ‘Enjoy human sense pleasures, I will give you wealth.’ I solemnly swear that this word is indeed true. If you do not believe me, I will even bring fire and swear an oath by means of fire.” “Victory in both places” means that by ordaining only when both of us are old, there is victory in both [the present and the future]. The intention is: “Let us enjoy wealth until the time we must rely on a staff (old age). By enjoying in this way, we do not lose out on wealth in this world, and since we will ordain later, we will not lose out on wealth in the next world either.” “For that reason” means because of that cause; it is due to the words spoken by that courtesan who invited him with sense pleasures, saying “You are still young,” and “When we are old,” etc. Taking those very words as a goad, the Elder practiced the Dhamma of a recluse and fulfilled his own goal. The remaining words are just as explained below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sundarasamudda Thera is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya Thera

The verse beginning with “Pare ambāṭakārāme” is the verse of the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya Thera. The background story is as follows: In the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, this Elder was born into a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having reached the proper age, while sitting and listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher at that moment appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those with sweet voices. Aspiring to that position himself, he offered a great gift (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and prayed, “O, may I also in the future become the foremost among those with sweet voices in the dispensation of a Buddha like this monk.” The Buddha, seeing that there were no obstacles for him, gave the prophecy. That person performed meritorious deeds throughout his life in that existence and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the time of the Buddha Vipassī, he became a cuckoo bird with beautiful wings, and in the King's garden, with its beak, a sweet mango...
126:
“...may I also become the foremost among those with sweet voices in the dispensation of a Buddha like this monk,” he made this aspiration. The Buddha, seeing that there were no obstacles for him, gave the prophecy and departed.

That person performed meritorious deeds throughout his life in that existence and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the time of the Buddha Phussa, he became a cuckoo bird with beautiful wings. While carrying a sweet mango from the King's garden in its beak, he saw the Teacher and, with a devoted mind, thought, “I will offer this.” The Teacher, knowing the bird's mind, took his bowl and sat down. The cuckoo bird placed the ripe mango in the bowl of the Ten-Powered One. The Teacher partook of that mango. That cuckoo bird, having a devoted mind, spent seven days in that very joy and happiness (pīti-sukha). Due to that meritorious deed, he became one with a sweet voice.

In the time of the Buddha Kassapa, when efforts were being made to build a stupa (cetiya), they asked, “What size shall we make it?” Some said, “Let us make a stupa seven leagues (yojana) in size.” Others said, “This is too large.” They then suggested six leagues, but again it was said, “This too is too large.” When they suggested five, four, three, or two leagues, this person, who was then a master carpenter (jeṭṭhavaḍḎhakī), said, “Come, sirs, it is proper to build it so that it will be easy to maintain in the future.” Measuring and encircling it with a rope, he stood at a distance of one gāvuta and said, “Let each side be one gāvuta; the stupa will be one league in circumference and one league in height.” The people followed the master carpenter's words. Thus, he had set a limit (measure) for the Buddha who is measureless (in virtues). Due to that karma, in every existence where he was born, he had a body that was shorter in stature than others.

That person was born into a wealthy family in the city of Sāvatthī in the time of our Teacher and was named Bhaddiya. Because he was extremely short, he was known as Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and ordained. He became a learned Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika) and preached the Dhamma to others with a sweet voice.

Then, on a festival day, a certain courtesan traveling in a carriage with a brahmin saw the Elder and laughed, showing her teeth. The Elder, taking the bones of her teeth as a sign (nimitta), gave rise to meditative absorption (jhāna). Using that jhāna as a basis, he developed insight (vipassanā) and became a Non-Returner (anāgāmī). While living with constant mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati), one day, upon receiving an exhortation from the Venerable General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), he was established in Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

“The Buddha named Padumuttara, who has the five eyes regarding all phenomena and who leads veneyya beings to Nibbāna, appeared one hundred thousand aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa. At that time, I was a wealthy son in the city of Haṃsavatī. While wandering in saṃsāra, I heard that Buddha, the supreme in the world, preaching the Dhamma. He praised a disciple who was foremost among those with sweet voices. Hearing that Dhamma talk, joy and happiness arose in me. I performed meritorious deeds, paid homage at the Buddha's feet, and prayed for that position. Then the Buddha gave the prophecy that my heart's desire would be fulfilled.”
127:
The Victorious Buddha named Padumuttara, who possessed the five types of vision regarding all phenomena and who leads beings to Nibbāna, appeared one hundred thousand aeons ago from this present one.

At that time, I was the son of a wealthy merchant in the city of Haṃsavatī. While walking for exercise, I arrived at a monastery (Saṅghārāma). Then, that Buddha, the Light of the World, while preaching the Dhamma, praised a certain disciple who was the foremost among those with sweet voices. Having heard those words and being filled with joy, I made an offering to the Great Sage, paid homage at the Teacher's feet, and aspired for that same position (Etadagga).

Then, in the midst of the Saṅgha, the Buddha prophesied: "In the future, your heart's desire will be fulfilled. One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama, born of the Okkāka clan, will appear in the world. His heir in the Dhamma, a true spiritual son, created by the Dhamma, will be a disciple named Bhaddiya."

Due to that well-performed wholesome deed and my intentional aspiration, I left my human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Ninety-two aeons ago from now, the Victorious Buddha named Phussa appeared, who was difficult to approach by those with wrong views, invincible to the enemies of defilements, and supreme in all the world. He was endowed with conduct (caraṇa), great in stature, upright, and majestic. Seeking the welfare of all beings, he liberated many from their bonds.

In the Nandārāma grove of that Buddha, I was a cuckoo named Phussa. I lived in a mango tree near the Gandhakuṭī. At that time, seeing the Victorious One, the Supreme One worthy of offerings, as he was going for alms, I gladdened my mind and sang with a sweet voice. Then, going to the royal garden, I took a cluster of well-ripened, golden-skinned mangoes and offered them to the Fully Enlightened Buddha.
128:
At that time, knowing my mind, the Victorious Buddha, the Great Compassionate One, the Leader, reached out and took the bowl from the hand of his attendant.

With a joyful heart, I offered the cluster of mangoes to the Great Sage. After placing them in the bowl, I gracefully performed a salutation with my wings.

Singing with a charming, pleasant, and beautiful voice as an offering to the Buddha, I went to my nest and lay down.

Then, as I was joyful and had an aspiration rooted in love for the Buddha, a hawk came and killed me with a malicious mind.

After passing away from that life, I experienced great happiness in the Tusita heaven. By the power of that wholesome deed, I reached the human world.

In this Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), the Buddha named Kassapa by clan, who had a great following and fame, and was the best among those who speak, appeared.

Having made the Dispensation (Sāsana) shine, overcoming those of wrong views, and disciplining those who were ready to be guided, he entered Parinibbāna along with his disciples.

When that Supreme One of the world had entered Parinibbāna, many people, being devoted, built a stupa to honor the Buddha, the Teacher.

"Let us build a stupa seven leagues high, adorned with the seven kinds of jewels, for the Great Sage," they consulted among themselves.

At that time, I was the general of King Kiki of Kāsi. Regarding the stupa of the Buddha of immeasurable qualities, I spoke of a limit (restriction).
