Then, because of my words, they built the stupa of the Hero of Men only one league high, adorned with various jewels.

Due to that well-performed deed and my intentional aspiration, I left my human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Now, in this final birth, I was born into a wealthy merchant family in the noble, prosperous, and affluent city of Sāvatthī.
129:
Seeing the Sugata (the Happy One) entering the city, with a mind full of devotion, I ordained and not long after, attained Arahantship.

Because of that deed of setting a limit on the size of the stupa, I was born with a short body (Lakuṇḍaka), deserving of being looked down upon by others.

Because I honored the Great Buddha with a sweet voice, I reached the foremost position among monks with sweet voices.

Through the offering of fruit to the Buddha and the recollection of his virtues, I am endowed with the fruits of recluseship and live free from taints (āsavas). My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Later, wishing to declare his attainment of Arahantship:

"In the excellent Ambāṭaka garden grove, the Elder Bhaddiya, having uprooted craving along with its roots, meditates excellently right there in that forest.

Some delight in drums, lutes, and cymbals. But I delight in the teaching of the Buddha at the foot of a tree.

If the Buddha were to grant me a boon, and if I were to receive that boon, I would choose constant mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) for the sake of the whole world."

He recited these three verses.

In those verses, "Pare" means noble, excellent, or distinguished. This word "Para" conveys the sense of "excessive" or "great," as in "paraṃ viya mattāya" and so on. "Ambāṭakārāme" means in the garden of this name. That place is delightful, being endowed with shade and water and adorned with forest groves; therefore, it is specifically called "Pare" (excellent). Some also say, "In the Ambāṭaka forest, the forest marked by Ambāṭaka trees." "Vanasaṇḍhamhi" means in the forest grove, in a forest thick with trees, bushes, and creepers. "Bhaddiyo" is the name of the Elder; he refers to himself as if he were another person. "Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha" means...
130:
The root of craving is ignorance. Therefore, it means uprooting that craving along with ignorance by the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga). In that verse, 'Bhaddo va jhāyati' means being a good person (Bhadda) through supramundane virtue and so forth, and because the task to be done is completed in that very forest, he meditates with the Fruition-absorption (Phalajhāna) of Arahatship by way of dwelling happily in the present life.

Having shown his delight in seclusion by saying that he spends time with the bliss of Fruition and meditative attainments, he shows the same meaning by way of contrast with the verse 'Ramanteke'. In that verse, 'mudingehi' means with five-fold drums; 'vīṇāhi' means with harps such as the Nandinī; 'paṇavehi' means with small drums. Some who enjoy sensual pleasures delight in these. Their delight is not noble and is associated only with harm. 'Ahañca' means 'But I, alone, delight in the dispensation of the Buddha; because of that very delight, I dwell greatly delighting at the foot of a tree.'

Having thus praised his delight in seclusion, now, to praise the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) by which he reached Arahatship, he spoke the verse 'Buddho ce me'. The meaning of that verse is: If I were to request a boon from the Blessed One, saying 'Venerable Sir, I ask a boon from the Blessed One,' and if the Blessed One, without rejecting it by saying 'Bhikkhu, the Tathāgatas have surpassed boons,' were to grant the boon as requested, and if that boon were to fulfill my intention and reach the pinnacle of my heart's desire—the Elder speaks by way of supposition—'Venerable Sir, may all beings at all times develop the meditation of mindfulness directed to the body.' Showing that 'I would take as a boon the constant development of mindfulness directed to the body for the whole world,' he said: 'Gaṇhehaṃ sabbalokassa, niccaṃ kāyagataṃ satiṃ'. Now, wishing to praise the one whose defilements are exhausted by disparaging those whose defilements are not yet exhausted:

Those who measured me by my appearance,
And those who followed me by my voice,
Possessed of desire and lust,
Those people do not know me.

The fool, who does not know the internal,
And does not see the external,
Being completely obstructed,
Is indeed carried away by the voice.

He who does not know the internal,
But sees clearly the external,
Seeing only the fruit externally,
He too is carried away by the voice.
131:
“He knows the Dhamma within himself,
And he sees specifically the Dhamma in others.
Seeing without any obstruction,
He is not carried away by the voice.”
He spoke these four verses.

In those verses, ‘Ye maṃ rūpena pāmiṃsu’ means those unwise people who measured (disparaged) me as inferior by my unattractive and lowly appearance, and by my body made of Dhamma, thinking “Wisdom is like the outward appearance.” They despised me, thinking “This one is inferior,” and judged me by limitations. And those beings who followed me by way of praise with a sweet voice (‘ye ca ghoseṇa anvagū’) and thought of me as having many qualities—that thought of theirs is wrong. Indeed, I should not be despised by mere appearance, nor should I be thought of as having many qualities by mere voice. Therefore, those people who are under the influence of desire and lust do not know me. Those two types of people, being under the influence of desire and lust and having unabandoned desire and lust, do not know my Dhamma, I who have completely abandoned desire and lust.

The nature of one like me is not their range. To show that this is because they do not distinguish and know the objects within themselves or externally, he said ‘ajjhattaṃ’ and so on. ‘Ajjhattaṃ’ means the phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense-bases (āyatana) within one's own continuity. ‘Bahiddhā’ means the phenomena in the continuity of others. Alternatively, ‘ajjhattaṃ’ means the qualities such as the aggregate of virtue of the Asekhas (Noble Ones) within me. ‘Bahiddhā’ means the occurrence of material phenomena and the occurrence of eye-consciousness and so forth associated with the perfection of my (Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya's) deportment and so on. ‘Samantāvaraṇo’ means a person whose knowledge is obstructed and who is possessed of obstructions on all sides because of not knowing the internal and external in this way. That fool, whose intellect is led by others, is carried away, led, and pulled by the voice and words of others.

‘Bahiddhā ca vipassati’ means that a person who does not know himself in the manner described, but sees specifically externally by following what has been heard or by investigating the perfection of deportment and so forth. He thinks, “He might be possessed of special qualities.” He too, seeing the fruit externally, taking only the fruit by way of method, is carried away by the voice of others in the manner described. He also does not know one like me.

But the one who knows the qualities such as virtue within himself and within the Arahant, and sees specifically the possession of special qualities by carefully noting the practice and conduct in that person's external continuity—‘anāvaraṇadassāvī’ means seeing without any obstruction, he is able to see the qualities of the Noble Ones. That person is not carried away by the mere voice of others. Why is that?...
132:
One who is capable of seeing and knowing virtue, who sees things as they truly are, is not carried away by the mere sound of others' voices.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Bhadda

The verses beginning with "Ekaputto" are those of the Venerable Elder Bhadda. As for the circumstances of their origin: This Elder Bhadda, it is said, made offerings of the four requisites such as robes to the Blessed One Padumuttara and the Saṅgha of one hundred thousand bhikkhus. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and when this Buddha appeared, he was reborn in a wealthy merchant family in the city of Sāvatthī.

His parents, being childless, made offerings and prayers to deities but did not obtain a child. They then approached the Teacher and made a vow: "Venerable Sir, if we obtain a single son, we shall offer him to serve you." Having made this request, they departed. Knowing the Teacher's intention, a certain son of the devas whose life span had ended was commanded by Sakka, the king of devas, "Be reborn in such-and-such a family," and he was reborn in that family. They named him Bhadda.

When the boy reached the age of seven, his parents adorned him and brought him to the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, this is the boy we obtained after making a request to you; we now offer him to you." The Teacher commanded the Elder Ānanda, "Ordain this boy." After giving this command, he entered the Gandhakuṭī. The Elder ordained him and briefly explained the gateway to Vipassanā (insight meditation). Because he was endowed with strong supporting conditions (upanissaya), while he was practicing Vipassanā, he intensified his meditation even before the sun had risen and became an Arahant with the six supernormal powers (chalabhiññā). Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The multitude approaches the Buddha Padumuttara, the Great Sage of loving-heart, the supreme leader of the whole world.

All people give food and drink, both hard and soft, to the Teacher, the unsurpassed field of merit.

I, too, shall give a gift to the God of gods, the Such-like One, having invited the Excellent Buddha and the unsurpassed Saṅgha."
133:
"Those people whom I had sent invited the Tathāgata and the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the unsurpassed field of merit.

I prepared a golden throne worth a hundred thousand, covered with a large rug, and a seat suitable for the Buddha, of great value, with cushions, linen, and cotton cloths.

Padumuttara, the Knower of the Worlds, the God of gods, the Bull among men, approached my door surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Having gone out to meet the Sambuddha, the Renowned Lord of the World, with a clear and joyful mind, I invited Him into the house.

With a clear and joyful mind, I satisfied the hundred thousand bhikkhus and the Buddha, the Leader of the World, with the most excellent food.

Padumuttara, the Knower of the Worlds, the Recipient of offerings, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, spoke these verses:

'Whoever has given this golden seat covered with a large rug, I shall praise him; listen to my words.

He will exercise the sovereignty of devas seventy-four times, and surrounded by celestial nymphs, he will enjoy prosperity.

He will dwell upon the earth as a regional king a thousand times, and fifty-one times he will be a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).

In all his births and origins, he will be of noble birth. Later, urged by his pure root of merit, he will ordain and become a disciple of the Teacher by the name of Bhaddiya.'

Now, I am devoted to seclusion, dwelling in a remote lodging. I have attained all fruits, and today I have abandoned all defilements.

Knowing all my virtues, the All-Knowing Lord of the World, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, placed me in the foremost position (etadagga).

The four analytical insights, the eight deliverances, and the six supernormal powers have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."
134:
The Blessed One, knowing that the Elder Bhaddiya had attained the six supernormal powers, said, "Come, Bhadda." At that very moment, the Elder Bhaddiya approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood near the Teacher with palms joined. That itself became his higher ordination (upasampadā). This kind of ordination is known as 'Buddhūpasampadā' (Ordination by the Buddha). The Elder, declaring his attainment of Arahantship by way of recounting his life from birth, spoke these verses:

"I was an only son, dear to my mother and dear to my father, obtained through many religious observances and prayers.

Out of compassion, desiring my welfare and seeking my benefit, both my father and mother offered me to the Buddha.

'This son was obtained with difficulty; he is delicate and was raised in comfort. We give him to you, O Lord, as a servant to the Conqueror' (they said).

The Teacher, having accepted me, said this to Ānanda: 'Ordain him quickly; he will be a noble thoroughbred (ājāniya).'

After the Teacher, the Conqueror, had me ordained, he entered the monastery. Before the sun had set, my mind was liberated (from the taints).

Then the Teacher, having emerged from seclusion, said to me, 'Come, Bhadda.' That was my higher ordination.

At the age of seven from birth, I obtained higher ordination. I have reached the three knowledges (tevijjā). Oh, how excellent is the nature of the Dhamma!"

In those verses, "vatacariyāhi" (through religious observances) means through practices such as drinking only milk or fasting, after hearing the words of ascetics and brahmins who said, "By doing this, you will obtain a son." "Āyācanāhi" (through prayers) means through prayers to deities and the request made to the Teacher. In this context, this (the request to the Buddha) is the primary cause. The Elder mentioned the other matters to show the conduct of his parents and to show that he was obtained with difficulty.
135:
"Te" refers to the parents. "Upanāmayuṃ" means they brought [him] near [to the Buddha] (offered him).

"Sukhedhito" means one who has been raised in comfort (sukhasaṃvaddhita). "Te" means "your". "Paricārakaṃ" refers to an attendant (kiṃkāra) who looks after what needs to be done.

"Hessatyājāniyo ayaṃ" means "This boy will be a noble person (ājāniya) in my Dispensation; therefore, ordain him quickly this very day." He spoke these words.

"Pabbājetvāna" means having been ordained by the Elder Ānanda. "Vihāraṃ" refers to the Gandhakuti (the Fragrant Chamber). "Anoggatasmiṃ sūriyasmiṃ" means even before the sun had set. "Tato cittaṃ vimucci me" means that shortly after beginning the practice of insight (vipassanā), in just a moment, my mind was liberated from all taints (āsavas), and I became one whose taints are exhausted (an Arahant).

"Tato" means after the exhaustion of my taints. "Nirākatvā" means having set aside the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) that he had entered, and having emerged from it. Therefore, it is said, "paṭisallānavuṭṭhito" (risen from seclusion). "Sā me āsūpasampadā" means that the very words "Come, Bhadda," spoken by the Teacher directed at me, were my higher ordination (upasampadā). Thus, at the age of seven from birth, I attained higher ordination; in saying this, he shows the special favor bestowed upon him by the Teacher and the liberating nature of the Dispensation. Therefore, it is said, "Aho dhammasudhammatā" (Oh, how wonderful is the excellence of the Dhamma!).

In this context, although he had already declared his state as one whose taints are exhausted by saying "my mind was liberated," the subsequent mention of "attaining the three knowledges (tevijjā)" is to demonstrate a portion of mundane supernormal knowledge for the purpose of explaining the state of possessing the six supernormal powers (chalabhiññā). Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna, "The six supernormal powers have been realized."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Bhadda Thera is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Sopāka Thera

The verses beginning with "Disvā pāsādachāyāyaṃ" are those of the Venerable Sopāka Thera. What is the background story? This [Elder] had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Siddhāttha, he was born into a brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he achieved mastery in the sciences and arts of the brahmins. Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he abandoned the household life and was ordained as an ascetic.
136:
He lived on a certain mountain. The Teacher, knowing that his death was near, went to him. Seeing the Blessed One, he felt a clear and joyful mind. Desiring to express his intense rapture and joy, he prepared and offered a seat made of flowers. The Teacher sat there, delivered a discourse connected with impermanence (aniccatā), and then departed through the air even as the ascetic was watching. The ascetic abandoned the view of permanence he had previously held, established the perception of impermanence in his heart, and after passing away, was reborn in the deva world. Wandering between the worlds of devas and humans, in this Buddha-arising, he was born into a Sopāka (outcaste) family in Rājagaha. He became known by the name Sopāka because of his birth. However, some teachers say, "He was born in a merchant family, and 'Sopāka' was merely his name." This statement contradicts the Apadāna Pali, which says, "When the final birth arrived, I came to a Sopāka womb."

When the boy Sopāka was four months old, his father died, and his uncle (father's younger brother) raised him. In due course, he reached the age of seven. One day, the uncle became angry, thinking, "He is quarreling with my own son." He took Sopāka to a cemetery, tied his two hands together with a rope, and with that same rope, tied him firmly to a corpse. He left, thinking, "Let the jackals and others eat him." Because he was in his final birth, by the power of the boy's merit, the uncle could not bring himself to kill him personally, nor could the jackals and other creatures harm him. At midnight, the boy lamented thus:

"What destination (gati) is there for me who is without refuge? Who is a kinsman to me who is without kin? Who will be the giver of fearlessness to me, who is bound in the midst of the cemetery?"

At that time, the Teacher, while surveying the sentient beings (veneyya) who are his kin, saw the supporting condition (upanissaya) for Arahantship shining within the boy's heart. Spreading forth a radiance to arouse mindfulness, he spoke thus:

"Come, Sopāka, do not fear. Look at the Tathāgata. I shall deliver you, just as the moon is delivered from the mouth of Rāhu."

By the power of the Buddha, the boy's bonds were severed. At the conclusion of the verse, he became a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and stood before the Gandhakuti. His mother, not seeing her son, questioned the uncle. When he did not tell her what had happened, she went wandering here and there in search of him. Thinking, "The Buddhas can see the past, future, and present; if I approach and ask the Buddha, I will surely know about my son," she went to the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One, by his psychic power, kept the boy Sopāka hidden. [Then the mother said,] "Venerable Sir..."
137:
While searching for her son, that mother thought, "The Buddhas know the past, future, and present. It would be good if I approach the Blessed One and learn about my son's situation." She then went to the Buddha. The Blessed One, having concealed the boy with his psychic power, was asked by the mother: "Venerable Sir, I do not see my son. Does the Blessed One know of his whereabouts?"

Thereupon, the Buddha preached the Dhamma (Dhammapada 288):
"Sons are no protection, nor is a father, nor are kinsmen. For one seized by the King of Death, there is no protection among relatives."

Upon hearing this Dhamma, the mother became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). The boy also attained Arahatship. This account is stated in the Apadāna (Ap. Thera 1.2.112-123) as follows:

"While I was clearing a mountain cave in the great forest of a noble mountain, the Blessed One named Siddhattha came into my presence."

"Having seen the Buddha, the Foremost of the World, endowed with such qualities, who had arrived there, I spread out a carpet of flowers and offered him a flower-seat."

"The Blessed One Siddhattha, the Leader of the World, sat upon the flower-seat and, knowing my destiny (gati), spoke on the nature of impermanence (anicca)."

"Impermanent indeed are formations (saṅkhārā), subject to arising and passing away. Having arisen, they cease; their subsiding is bliss."

"Having said this, the All-Knowing One, the Foremost of the World, the Bull among Men, the Hero, rose into the sky like a king of swans in the air."

"Abandoning my own views, I developed the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā). After developing it for just one day, I passed away right there in that practice."

"Having enjoyed the two types of prosperity (human and divine), and being urged by the root of my past merit, I was born into a Sopāka family when I reached my final birth."

"I went forth from the home life into the homeless state. At only seven years of age from birth, I attained Arahatship."

"With energy exerted and a mind directed toward Nibbāna, well-established in the precepts, I pleased the Great Naga (the Buddha) and received higher ordination (upasampadā)."
138:
“In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, I performed that good deed. Since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of offering flowers.

“In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, I developed that perception of impermanence. For me, who developed that perception of impermanence, the destruction of the taints (arahatship) has been reached.

“The four analytical insights... pe... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled,” he declared.

Then the Blessed One withdrew his psychic power. The female lay devotee, seeing her son and having a joyful and happy mind, heard of her son Sopāka's attainment of Arahatship, and after letting him remain as a monk, she departed. The Elder Sopāka approached the Blessed One while He was walking back and forth in the shade of the Gandhakuṭi, and after paying homage, he followed Him in the walking meditation. The Blessed One, wishing to grant the Elder higher ordination, asked ten questions beginning with “What is one?” The Elder Sopāka, understanding the Blessed One's intention and aligning his answers with the Buddha's Omniscience, answered those questions beginning with “All beings subsist on food” (Khuddakapāṭha 4.1). Because of this, those questions became known as the Kumārapañhā (The Boy's Questions). The Buddha, pleased with the Elder's explanation of the questions, granted him higher ordination. Therefore, that higher ordination became known as the Pañhavyākaraṇūpasampadā (Higher Ordination through Answering Questions). The Elder Sopāka, manifesting his own history and wishing to declare his attainment of Arahatship, recited this:

“Having seen the Buddha, the Foremost of Men, walking back and forth in the shade of the Gandhakuṭi, I approached the Blessed One there and paid homage to that Supreme Man.

“Placing my robe over one shoulder and joining my palms in reverence, I followed the walking meditation behind the Blessed One, the Stainless One, the Foremost of all beings.

“Then the Buddha, the Knower, the Expert in questions, asked me questions. I, too, answered the Teacher without trembling and without fear.

“When the questions were answered, the Tathāgata rejoiced. Looking at the Saṅgha of monks, He spoke this meaning:

“‘Great is the gain for those people of Aṅga and Magadha whose requisites—robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines—this Sopāka enjoys. Great is the gain for those who perform the duties of welcoming and showing respect to him,’ He said.”
139:
“Dear Sopāka, from today onwards, approach to see me. Dear Sopāka, let this [answering of questions] alone be your higher ordination (upasampadā).”

“I obtained higher ordination at the age of seven from birth and bear my final body. Oh, how wonderful is the excellent nature of the supramundane Dhamma!” Thus he spoke these verses.

In those verses, ‘pāsādachāyāyaṃ’ means in the shadow of the Gandhakuṭi (Fragrant Chamber). ‘vandiṃ’ means I paid homage. ‘saṃharitvāna pāṇayo’ means joining both hands in the shape of a lotus bud, referring to making the añjali salutation. ‘anucaṅkamissaṃ’ means walking to and fro, following the Blessed One as he was walking. ‘virajaṃ’ refers to the Blessed One who is free from the dust of defilements such as lust (rāga).

‘pañhe’ occurs in the Kumārapañha (The Novice's Questions). ‘vidū’ refers to the All-knowing (Sabbaññū) Blessed One who has known what should be known. Because the trembling and fear that arose thinking, ‘The Blessed One is questioning me,’ had been abandoned and uprooted by the path of Arahantship, he answered without trembling and without fear.

‘ye sāyam’ means this Sopāka of the people of Aṅga and Magadha. ‘paccayaṃ’ refers to medicinal requisites for the sick. ‘sāmīciṃ’ refers to respectful conduct such as coming out to welcome.

In the word ‘azzadagge’, the letter ‘d’ is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhi), meaning starting from today or from today onwards. There is also a Pali reading ‘azzatagge’, meaning starting from today's state. ‘dassanāyopasaṅkama’ means approach to see me without thinking, ‘This person is of low birth’ or ‘He is very young in age.’ ‘esā ceva’ refers to the answering of questions done by that Sopāka in accordance with my omniscient knowledge. It should be construed as: “Let this answering of questions itself be your higher ordination.” There is also a Pali reading ‘laddhā me upasampadā’. In the view of the teachers who read ‘laddhāna upasampadaṃ’, it means by the seventh year or being seven years of age. What is not mentioned here is easily understood.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sopāka is Finished.
140:
## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sarabhaṅga

The verses beginning with “Sare hatthehi” are those of the Venerable Elder Sarabhaṅga. What is the origin story (uppatti)? This venerable one also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, having accumulated merit that is a supportive condition for liberation from the round of suffering in various existences, was reborn in this Buddha's era as the son of a certain Brahmin in the city of Rājagaha. His name, which came from his family lineage, was “Anabhilakkhita.” When he reached maturity, he renounced sensual pleasures, became an ascetic (tāpasa), and lived in a leaf-hut he made by breaking sara reeds himself. From that time on, he was known by the name “Sarabhaṅga.”

Then, the Blessed One, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, saw his supportive condition for attaining the fruit of Arahantship. He went to that place and preached the Dhamma. Having gained faith, he ordained and, while practicing Vipassanā, soon attained Arahantship and continued to live in that same place. Later, the leaf-hut he had made during his time as an ascetic became old and dilapidated. Seeing this, people said, “Venerable sir, why do you not repair this small hut?” The Elder, wishing to make clear the whole matter by saying, “It is no longer possible to do now as I did during my time as an ascetic,” spoke these two verses:

“I used to break reeds with my hands and live in a hut I made. Because of that, the name ‘Sarabhaṅga’ was given to me by conventional designation.

Now it is not proper for me to break reeds with my hands; training rules have been prescribed for us by the glorious Gotama.”

In those verses, “sare hatthehi bhañjitvā” means that in the past, during his time as an ascetic, he cut sara reeds with his hands, made a grass hut, and lived there, performing sitting and lying down. “tena” means because of breaking the reeds to build the hut. “sammutiyā” means that the name “Sarabhaṅga” came about through a conventional designation consistent with the meaning (anvatthasammuti).

“na mayhaṃ kappate azza” means that now, for me who has received higher ordination, it is no longer proper or suitable to break sara reeds with my hands. Why? As stated in “sikkhāpadā no paññattā, gotamena yasassinā,” it shows that we do not transgress the training rules prescribed by our Teacher, the Blessed One, even for the sake of life.
141:
Having thus shown the reason for not repairing the grass hut in one way, he now wishes to show it in another way, and spoke this verse:

"Sarabhanga did not see the whole, complete disease before. Now that disease is seen, by the follower of the word of the God of gods."

In that verse, 'sakalaṃ' means all. 'Samattaṃ' means complete, without remainder in every part. 'Rogaṃ' (disease) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā), which are like a disease because they are painful in the sense of being oppressive due to the nature of suffering (dukkha-dukkhatā) and so forth. 'Nāddasaṃ pubbe' means he did not see it in the time before receiving the instruction of the Teacher. 'Soyam rogo diṭṭho, vacanakarenātidevassa' means that Sarabhanga, who follows the instruction of the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)—the Supreme God (Atideva) who stands surpassing all gods, namely conventional gods (sammuti-deva), gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva), and gods by purity (visuddhi-deva), through his own virtues such as morality (sīla)—has seen and fully understood that disease known as the five aggregates through Path-wisdom (magga-paññā) accompanied by Insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). By this, he shows: how can one who has no regard even for the 'hut' of his own physical body repair an external grass hut?

Now, wishing to declare his own attainment of Arahantship, saying, "The path by which I have seen this disease of the physical body as it really is, is the path common to all Buddhas. Their teaching of the Dhamma is like refined gold cut in the middle; established in that path, I have reached the end of suffering," he said:

"By the very path Vipassī went, by the very path Sikhī and Vessabhū,
Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa, by that straight path Gotama went.

Free from craving, without clinging, the seven Buddhas are established in the destruction [of suffering];
By those who are the Dhamma-become, such as they are, this Dhamma was taught.

Out of compassion for living beings, the four Noble Truths were taught:
Suffering, the Origin, the Path, and Cessation, which is the end of suffering."
142:
"In which [Nibbāna] the endless suffering of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) ceases. With the breaking up of this body and the exhaustion of the life-faculty, there is no further rebirth. I am well-released in every way."

He spoke these verses.

In those verses, "yeneva maggena" means by the Noble Eightfold Path which is the preliminary stage. "Gato" means reached Nibbāna or attained Parinibbāna. "Vipassī" is Vipassī the Perfectly Enlightened One. "Kakusandhā" is an expression without case-ending. There is also a reading "Kakusandhakoṇāgamanā". "Tenañjasena" means by that very straight path of the Noble Path.

"Anādānā" means without clinging (anupādānā) or without rebirth. "Khayogadhā" means established in Nibbāna or merged into Nibbāna. "Yehiyaṃ desito dhammo" means this teaching of the Dispensation (sāsana-dhamma) was taught and proclaimed by the seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones. "Dhammabhūtehi" is so called because they have the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya), because they are of the nature of Dhamma, because they have arisen from the nine supramundane (lokuttara) states, or because they have reached the Dhamma. "Tādibhi" means those who have reached the state of 'tādi' (steadfastness) regarding desirable and undesirable objects.

With "cattāri ariyasaccāni" and so forth, he shows the Dhamma taught by those Buddhas. Therein, "cattāri" is the numerical limit. "Ariyasaccāni" is the showing of the defined Dhamma. According to the word-meaning, they are "Ariya-sacca" because they are noble (ariya) and are truths (sacca) in the sense of being unerring. Or, they are the truths of the Noble One (the Blessed One) because they were taught by him, or they are truths that make one noble.

The five aggregates of clinging are called "dukkha" (suffering) because they are loathsome and empty of essence. Craving (taṇhā) is called "samudaya" (origin) because suffering arises from it. The eight factors such as Right View are called "magga" (path) because it goes along killing the defilements, or because it is sought by those desiring Nibbāna. Nibbāna is called "nirodha" (cessation) because there is no obstruction (rodha) known as the wandering in saṃsāra here, or because there is no obstruction for the person when this Nibbāna is attained, or because suffering ceases here. Therefore, he said "dukkhasankhayo" (the end of suffering). This is just a summary here; the details should be understood in the manner stated in the Visuddhimagga.

"Yasmiṃ" means when that cessation, Nibbāna, is attained. "Nivattate" means when there is the development of the Noble Path, the endless suffering of birth and so forth in this saṃsāra does not proceed but is cut off. That cessation was taught by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones who are the Dhamma-become.

With "bhedā" and so forth, he shows his own attainment of Arahantship in detail, indicating the full understanding of the Truth of Suffering by saying "I have seen the disease." In the whole verse, the connection (yojanā) in the phrase "yasmiṃ nivattate dukkhaṃ" is as follows: In the saṃsāra called the continuity of aggregates, there is this endless suffering such as rebirth. Because of the exhaustion of this life-faculty and the breaking up of the five aggregates called the body, there is no more renewed existence (punabbhava) which causes repeated birth apart from this suffering. Therefore, I am well-released from all defilements and from all existences.

## The Commentary on Sarabhanga Thera Gāthā is finished.
## The Commentary on the Book of Sevens (Sattakanipāta) is finished.
143:
Because they are the embodiment of Dhamma, the Buddhas who are of the nature of Dhamma have taught this Dhamma—thus it should be construed. By the words "Bhedā" and so forth, "The disease has been seen," he shows his own attainment of Arahantship in its true form, which was indicated in the full understanding of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca).

In the text "Yasmiṃ nibbattate dukkhaṃ", the construction for the entire verse is as follows: In this saṃsāra, which is known as the succession of aggregates and so forth, this endless suffering such as rebirth arises. Apart from this occurrence of suffering, it is called renewed existence (punabbhava) because it causes repeated becoming. Due to the exhaustion of this life faculty (jīvitindriya) and the destruction of the collection of the five aggregates called the body, there is no further rebirth in the future. Therefore, in every respect, I am well-liberated and detached from all defilements and all existences.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sarabhaṅga Thera is finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of Sevens is finished.
144:
## 8. The Book of Eights

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Mahākaccāyana Thera

In the Book of Eights, the verse beginning with "Kammaṃ bahukaṃ" is that of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana Thera. What is the background story of this Elder? This Mahākaccāyana Thera also had performed special meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. In the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was born into a wealthy householder's family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Upon reaching maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw a monk being placed in the foremost position among those who could explain in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Teacher. He himself desired that position, made an aspiration, and performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna), wandering through the realms of gods and humans. In the time of Sumedha Buddha, he became a Vidyādhara (knowledge-holder). While traveling through the air, he saw the Teacher sitting in a forest grove in the Himālaya mountains and, with a devout heart, made an offering of Kaṇikāra flowers.

Due to that meritorious deed, he revolved only in happy destinations (sugati). In the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was born into a respectable family in Bārāṇasī. When the Buddha passed away into Parinibbāna, he made an offering of a golden brick worth a hundred thousand at the site where the golden stūpa was being built, and made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, may my body be golden in color in every life I am born." Apart from that, he performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans during the interval between two Buddhas. When our Gotama Buddha appeared, he was born in the house of the chaplain of King Caṇḍapajjota in the city of Ujjeni. On the naming day, his mother said, "My son is golden in color; he has come taking his own name," and named him "Young Kañcana." When he grew up, he learned the three Vedas and, after his father's death, obtained the position of chaplain. He was known as "Kaccāyana" by his lineage. King Caṇḍapajjota, hearing that a Buddha had appeared, sent him saying, "Teacher, go there and bring the Teacher here." That Kaccāyana, along with seven others, approached the Teacher. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, he, together with the seven people, was established in Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

The Buddha named Padumuttara, free from defilements and craving, the conqueror of the unconquerable enemy, the leader of gods and humans, appeared a hundred thousand eons ago from this eon.
The one who is energetic, with eyes like lotus petals, with a face pure like the full moon, resembling a golden mountain, with a radiance like sunlight,
who attracts the eyes of beings, adorned with all noble marks, who has transcended all paths of speech, worshipped by gods and humans,
who makes beings realize the Four Noble Truths, the master of speech, with a sweet voice and a mind connected with compassion,
the Buddha, who is courageous in the assemblies, taught the sweet Dhamma connected with the Four Noble Truths.
He rescued beings sinking in the mire of delusion.
At that time, I was an ascetic living in the Himālayas, practicing alone. While traveling to the human world through the air, I saw the Buddha.
145: The Victor named Padumuttara, free from craving, the conqueror of the unconquered, the conqueror of the five Maras, the Leader, the pinnacle of the world, arose a hundred thousand eons from now. The Hero, with eyes like lotus petals, with a face pure like the full moon, resembling a golden mountain, with a radiance like the sunlight—that Blessed One—who attracts the eyes of beings, adorned with noble marks, transcending all paths of speech, the Lord honored by humans and gods. The Fully Enlightened One, who makes beings realize the Four Truths, the Master of Speech, with a sweet voice, with a mind-stream connected to compassion, confident in the assemblies—the Fully Enlightened One—taught the sweet Dhamma associated with the Four Truths. He rescues beings submerged in the mire of delusion. At that time, I was an ascetic living in the Himālayas, practicing alone. While traveling through the world of human habitation by air, I saw the Victorious Buddha. Approaching the presence of that Blessed One, I heard the Dhamma teaching while the Hero was praising the great virtues of a disciple. "I do not see any other disciple in this Dispensation who, like this Kaccāyana, can please the assembly and me by explaining in detail the Dhamma taught by me in brief. Therefore, monks, remember that this Kaccāyana is the foremost in that position." Then, hearing those delightful words, I was amazed. I went to the Himālayas, brought a collection of flowers, and having worshipped the Buddha, the Refuge of the World, I prayed for that position. Then, knowing my intention, the Buddha, who had abandoned the defilements, spoke the prophecy: "Behold this noble sage, with skin like molten gold, with hair pointing upwards, with full shoulders, standing firm with joined palms, joyful, with very clear eyes, with an intention established in the virtues of the Buddha, born of the Dhamma, with a noble heart, resembling one sprinkled with the nectar of immortality."
146:
Having heard of Kaccāna's virtues, I remained aspiring for that position. In the future time, in the dispensation of the Great Sage Gotama, I shall be a disciple of the Teacher named Kaccāna, an heir to his Dhamma, born of the Dhamma, and created by the Dhamma. Being very learned, of great wisdom, and knowing the Sage's intent, I shall reach that position just as I was prophesied by him.

One hundred thousand aeons ago, I performed that meritorious deed. Since then, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of honoring the Buddha. I have wandered through only two states of existence: the world of devas and the world of humans. I have gone to no other destination; this is the fruit of honoring the Buddha. I have been born into only two types of noble families: the Khattiya and the Brahmin. I have never been born into a low family; this is the fruit of honoring the Buddha.

Now, in my final birth, I was born in the city of Ujjeni, in the family of the chaplain to the fierce King Pajjota. I am the son of the Brahmin Tiriṭivaccha, skilled and a master of the three Vedas. My mother's name was Candimā, and I am Kaccāna, possessing a noble golden complexion.

Sent by the King to investigate the Buddha, I saw the Leader, a heap of virtues, who is like the gateway to the city of liberation. Having heard his pure words, which dry up the mud of the rounds of rebirth, I attained the peaceful Deathless Nibbāna along with my seven companions. Having become one who knows the intent of the Sugata of great wisdom, I was placed in the foremost position (Etadagga), my aspirations fully realized. My defilements have been burnt away... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.

Then the Teacher stretched out his hand and said, 'Come, monks!' At that very moment, they became like elders of sixty years' standing, with hair and beards only two finger-breadths long, and bearing robes and bowls created by psychic power. Thus, the Elder, having fulfilled his own purpose, said, 'Venerable Sir, King Pajjota...'
147:
"...wishes to pay homage to your feet and to hear the Dhamma." Thus he informed the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Monk, you yourself go there; even when you go, the King will be inspired." According to the Teacher's command, the Elder went there as the eighth member of the group, inspired the King, established the Dispensation in the Avanti country, and then returned to the Teacher's presence. One day, seeing many monks who had abandoned their recluse duties and were living negligently, delighting in activities, delighting in company, and following the craving for tastes, he gave them advice by way of these verses:

"One should not undertake many works; one should avoid crowds and not strive (for material gain). The monk who is anxious and greedy for tastes loses the benefit (such as virtue) that brings happiness.

The wise have known this—the homage and worship in families—to be 'mud.' Honor is a subtle thorn, difficult to extract; it is hard for a base person to give up."

In those verses, "One should not undertake many works" (kammaṃ bahukaṃ na kāraye) means one should not start large new construction projects, such as building new dwellings, which are obstacles to the practice of a recluse. However, small tasks with little effort, such as repairing broken parts, should indeed be done as a way of honoring the Teacher's words. "One should avoid crowds" (parivajjeyya janaṃ) means one should avoid people in the sense of delighting in company. Or, one should avoid such a person who is a bad friend (akalyāṇamitta), by whose association, service, and attendance, wholesome states decline and unwholesome states increase. "One should not strive" (na uyyame) means one should not strive for the sake of obtaining the four requisites by means of ingratiating oneself with families. For this reason, "The monk who is anxious and greedy for tastes loses the benefit that brings happiness" (so ussukko rasānugiddho atthaṃ riñcati yo sukhādhivāho) means a monk who is greedy for tastes, under the power of craving for tastes, and intent on obtaining requisites, is anxious to ingratiate himself with families. He is happy when they are happy and sad when they are sad, and he personally involves himself in their affairs. In such a case, he loses the benefit of virtue and so on, which brings the happiness of Samatha, Vipassanā, the Path, the Fruit, and Nibbāna. In effect, it means he separates himself from those benefits.

Thus, having advised with the first verse, "Avoid delighting in activities, delighting in company, and greed for requisites," he now spoke the second verse, wishing to censure the desire for honor and offerings. Its meaning is: There are acts of homage and worship performed by householders out of reverence for the virtues of monks who have come for alms. The Buddhas and other Noble Ones have known such worship to be "mud" because of its sense of causing one to sink and its sense of defilement. Because worldlings find it difficult to know the nature of the desire for honor, and because it is oppressive, pierces within, and is hard to give up, that honor is a subtle thorn that is difficult to extract.
148:
The Noble Ones, beginning with the Buddha, have declared it as 'mud' (*paṅka*) because it causes those with undeveloped minds to sink and because it makes them defiled. The desire for honor and offerings (*sakkāra*) among blind worldlings, whose aggregates are not fully understood, is difficult to comprehend; because it causes affliction, pierces within, and is difficult to extract, they have declared it as a subtle and hard-to-extract 'dart' (*salla*). For this very reason, a base person finds it difficult to abandon such honor and offerings because he does not practice the path of abandoning them. By abandoning the desire for honor and offerings, the honor and offerings themselves are abandoned; therefore, it is shown that one should make an effort to abandon that desire.

One should not resort to evil deeds such as killing or binding for the sake of another's property; nor should one resort to such evil deeds oneself, for these beings are the kin of their own deeds.

One does not become a thief merely by the words of another, nor does one become a sage (*muni*) merely by the words of another. As one knows oneself to be pure or impure, so do the gods know him.

'We here in this world must go to the presence of Death'—others do not realize this. Among them, those wise ones who do realize that 'we are going near to Death,' through such realization, their harming of others (quarrels) are stilled.

A wise person, even when reaching the exhaustion of wealth, can live by a blameless livelihood; but a person without wisdom, even if possessing wealth, cannot live in accordance with the Dhamma.

A wise man hears all sounds with his ears and sees all forms with his eyes; yet the wise one should not discard everything seen or heard.

Though having eyes, let him be as if blind; though having ears, as if deaf; though having wisdom, as if mute; though strong, as if weak. Furthermore, when a matter concerning one's benefit arises, let him lie as if dead.

The Elder Mahākaccāyana spoke these six verses by way of instruction to King Pajjota. It is said that the king, believing the words of Brahmins, was performing animal sacrifices. Without investigating cases, he punished those who were not thieves, perceiving them as thieves; and in legal proceedings, he made non-owners owners and owners non-owners. Then the Elder, to turn him away from those evils, spoke the six verses beginning with 'Na parassa'.
149:
Among those verses, 'Na parassūpanidhāya, kammaṃ maccassa pāpakaṃ' means that one should not personally perform, nor cause others to perform, unwholesome deeds such as killing or binding by referring to or for the sake of another being. 'Attanā taṃ na seveyya' means that one should not commit that evil unwholesome deed oneself. Why? 'Kammabandhū hi mātiyā' means that these beings are the heirs of the deeds they have committed. Therefore, one should not perform any evil deed oneself, nor cause others to perform it.

'Na pare vacanā coro' means that just as one does not become a thief merely by the words of another without committing theft oneself, likewise, one does not become a sage (*muni*)—one with perfectly pure conduct of body, speech, and mind—merely by the words of another. In this context, the word 'pare' is presented without dropping the case ending. However, some teachers say that 'pare' is stated by dropping the 'saṃ' ending where it should have been 'paresaṃ'. 'Attā ca naṃ yathā vedī' means that the being's own mind (*citta*) knows truly, 'I am pure' or 'I am impure.' 'Devāpi naṃ tathā vidū' means that the gods of purity (*visuddhideva*) and the gods by rebirth (*upapattideva*) also know him in that same way. Therefore, only oneself and such gods are the valid standard in knowing the state of purity or impurity, and beings overwhelmed by desire and hatred are not the standard.

'Pare' refers to those in this world, excluding the wise, who do not know wholesome and unwholesome deeds, blameful and blameless actions, karma and its results, the foulness of the body, and the impermanence of formations (*saṅkhāra*). They do not know, 'We are constantly and continuously approaching death.' 'Ye ca tattha vijānanti' means those wise ones in that human realm who do know, 'We are approaching death.' 'Tato sammanti medhagā' means that those who know in this way practice for the stilling of harming others. It means that they themselves do not harm or oppress others, nor do others harm them. You, however, for the sake of livelihood, accuse non-thieves as thieves, and by punishing them, you make owners non-owners, oppressing them with the loss of property due to your lack of wisdom. Even without acting in such a way, a wise person still lives. Even if wealth is exhausted, one of a wise nature is content with whatever is available and lives a blameless life. His living is indeed true living. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'The life of wisdom, they say, is the best life.' But a foolish person...
150:
One who, through the lack of wisdom, fails to achieve the benefits of both the present life and the future life, does not truly live even if they possess wealth; because of the occurrence of blame and so forth, they cannot be called one who is living. One who destroys the wealth they have acquired due to ignorance of the proper means cannot even sustain their life.

The Elder reportedly spoke these four verses to the King in a dream. Having seen the dream, the King woke up while still paying homage to the Elder. When the night had dawned, he approached the Elder, paid respects, and related the dream exactly as he had seen it. Hearing this, the Elder recited those verses again and exhorted the King with two verses beginning with "He hears everything with the ear."

Among those verses, "He hears everything with the ear" means that in this world, a person who is not deaf hears with the ear everything that comes into the range of hearing, whether it be well-spoken or ill-spoken. Similarly, one who is not blind sees with the eye all forms, whether beautiful or ugly; this is the nature of the sense faculties. In that context, "The wise person should not discard everything seen or heard" is merely an illustration. This is because a wise person, endowed with wisdom, should not discard, abandon, or take everything that is seen or heard. Rather, having scrutinized the faults and merits therein, one should discard only what should be discarded and take only what should be taken.

Therefore, when one who has sight sees something that should be discarded, even though they have eyes, they should be as if blind, not seeing. Similarly, when hearing something that should be discarded, even though they have ears, they should be as if deaf, not hearing. "A wise person should be like one who is mute" means that although one is wise in discernment and skilled in speech, one should be like a mute regarding things that should not be spoken. Although endowed with strength and power, one should be like a weak person (the letter 'ra' is a euphonic conjunction) regarding things that should not be done, as if incapable.

Then, "When a matter of benefit arises, one should sleep like a corpse" means that when a duty to be performed by oneself arises and is present, even if one sleeps with the kind of sleep like a corpse, that duty must still be brought to completion; it must not be allowed to fail. Alternatively, "When a matter of benefit arises" means when an unbeneficial matter that should not be done by oneself arises and is present, one should sleep like a corpse; even after sleeping, that matter must simply not be done. For a wise person should not do what is improper. Thus exhorted by the Elder, the King abandoned what should not be done and became one who exerted effort only in what should be done.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahākaccāyana is finished.
151:
## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Sirimitta Thera

The verse beginning with "Akkodhana" is the verse of the Venerable Sirimitta Thera. What is the story of its origin? This Elder also had performed special merit under previous Buddhas and, having accumulated wholesome deeds that are a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various lives, was reborn in this Buddha's era in the city of Rājagaha as the son of a wealthy householder; he received the name Sirimitta. It is heard that his mother was the sister of Sirigutta. His story appears in the Dhammapada Commentary (Garahadinna Vatthu). That Sirimitta, the nephew of Sirigutta, upon reaching maturity, gained faith when the Blessed One tamed the elephant Dhanapāla. Having ordained and practiced the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship before long.

One day, he ascended the seat to recite the Pātimokkha and, sitting while holding an ornate fan, preached the Dhamma to the monks. While preaching, wishing to analyze and show the most noble qualities, he said:

One who is not angry, does not bear a grudge, is without deceit, and is free from slander—such a monk, if he practices in this way, does not sorrow after passing away.

One who is not angry, does not bear a grudge, is without deceit, is free from slander, and always guards the doors of the sense faculties—if a monk practices in this manner, he does not sorrow after passing away.

One who is not angry, does not bear a grudge, is without deceit, is free from slander, and is of good virtue—if that monk practices in this way, he does not sorrow after passing away.

One who is not angry, does not bear a grudge, is without deceit, is free from slander, and has good friends—if that monk practices in this way, he does not sorrow after passing away.

One who is not angry, does not bear a grudge, is without deceit, is free from slander, and has good wisdom—if that monk practices in this way, he does not sorrow after passing away.

He whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable and well-established, and whose virtue is good, loved by the Noble Ones, and praised;

He who has faith in the Saṅgha and has an upright vision—they say that such a person is not poor; his life is not in vain.
152:
Therefore, a wise person, remembering the teachings of the Buddhas, should repeatedly apply themselves to faith, virtue, confidence, and the vision of the Dhamma. He spoke these verses.

Among those verses, 'akkodhana' means one who is not prone to anger. Even when a cause for anger arises, he remains established in patient endurance and does not give rise to anger. 'Anupanāhī' means one who does not harbor a grudge. Based on an offense committed by others, he does not harbor anger in the form of "He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me," and so on. He is 'amāyo' because of the absence of deceit (māyā), which has the characteristic of concealing existing faults. He is 'rittapesuṇa' because he is free from slanderous speech. 'Sa ve tādisako bhikkhu' means a monk of such a nature, of such a kind, endowed with the aforementioned qualities. By practicing in this way, he does not grieve in the next world because there is no cause for grief. He is 'guttadvāra' (guarded in the sense-doors) because his doors, such as the eye-door and the body-door, are guarded, closed, and restrained. 'Kalyāṇasīla' means one who has good virtue, very pure virtue. 'Kalyāṇamitta' means one who has good friends endowed with the characteristics of being: "Dear, respectful, venerable, a speaker, patient of words, a speaker of deep discourse, and not urging one to an improper place." 'Kalyāṇapañña' means one who has good wisdom. Although there is no such thing as "bad" wisdom, this is said with reference to the wisdom that leads to liberation (niyyānika-paññā).

Thus, in this context, having shown the right practice through the verse based on a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), starting with non-anger and so on by way of suppressing and cutting off anger etc., he now spoke the words beginning with 'Yassa saddhā' to show the right practice through a verse based on a person, highlighting the accomplished supramundane faith and so on. The meaning of that verse is: For a person, the faith in the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One, which arises through the method beginning with 'Iti pi so bhagavā' and is attained through the Path (magga), is unshakeable and well-established because of that very Path. (The word 'atthi' should be brought in and connected here.) 'Ariyakanta' means virtue that is loved and cherished by the Noble Ones because it is not abandoned even in another life. 'Pasamsita' means having virtue that is praised, lauded, and commended by the Buddhas and others. That virtue is the virtue to be observed by laypeople.
153:
The virtue of monks is of two kinds. Among them, the virtue of laypeople refers to the virtue of the five precepts that can be observed by laypeople. The virtue of monks refers to the entire virtue of fourfold purification (catupārisuddhi-sīla), starting from the ten precepts. All this virtue should be known as "good virtue" (kalyāṇa) because it is not violated by way of being unbroken and so on, and is not misapprehended by craving or views.

"Saṅghe pasādo yassatthi" means: for which person there is faith and confidence in the Noble Saṅgha, which is unshakeable and well-established, through the method beginning with "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples has practiced well." This should be connected accordingly. "Ujubhūtañca dassanaṃ" means: for which person there is a vision that is straight, not crooked, and free from the crookedness of views and defilements—namely, the two kinds of vision: the vision of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-dassana) and the vision of mind-and-matter along with their causes—which is unshakeable and well-established. This should be connected. "Adaliddo" (not poor): the Buddhas and other Noble Ones call such a person "not poor" because of the possession of these very pure riches: the wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, and the wealth of wisdom. "Amoghaṃ tassa jīvitaṃ" means the life of such a person is not in vain; it is fruitful because of the attainment of benefits such as those in the present life and in the future.

"Tasmā" means: since a person endowed with the aforementioned qualities of faith and so on is called "not poor and having a life not in vain," therefore, (reflecting) "I too should be of such a nature." "Saddhañca... pe... sāsanaṃ" means: a son of good family, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas spoken as "The non-doing of all evil" and so on, should apply himself to and develop faith of the described varieties, virtue, and the confidence that is the cause of liberation due to right decision in the Dhamma, which is the cause for seeing the Dhamma.

Thus, the Elder, while showing the qualities existing in himself by way of preaching the Dhamma to the monks, declared his attainment of Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sirimitta is Finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mahāpanthaka.

The verses beginning with "Yadā paṭhamamaddakkhi" are those of the Venerable Mahāpanthaka. What is the background? This Venerable Mahāpanthaka was a wealthy householder in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. One day, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Buddha, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those skilled in liberation from the burden through wisdom. Desiring that position for himself, he offered a great gift (mahādāna) for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and said, "Venerable Sir, seven days ago, you appointed this monk as the foremost among those skilled in liberation from the burden through wisdom in your Dispensation."
154:
## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mahāpanthaka

The verse beginning with "Yadā paṭhamamaddakkhiṃ" belongs to the Venerable Elder Mahāpanthaka. What is the origin of this Elder? It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, this Mahāpanthaka was a wealthy householder in the city of Haṃsavatī. One day, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those skilled in liberation through perception (saññā-vivaṭṭa-kusalānaṃ). Aspiring for that same position, he performed a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and made a prayer: "Venerable Sir, seven days ago from today, You appointed a certain monk to the foremost position, saying, 'This monk is the foremost among those skilled in liberation through perception in my Dispensation.' By the power of this meritorious deed, may I also become foremost in the Dispensation of a future Buddha, just like that monk."

His younger brother also performed a meritorious deed in the presence of the Blessed One in the same manner and made an aspiration according to the method mentioned, based on two factors: the creation of a mind-made body and skill in the liberation of mind (ceto-vivaṭṭa-kosalla). Seeing that the aspirations of both would be fulfilled without obstacle, the Blessed One prophesied: "In the future, after one hundred thousand aeons, your aspirations will be fulfilled in the Dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama."

Both of them performed meritorious deeds for the rest of their lives in that existence and, after passing away, were reborn in the celestial world. Among them, the wholesome Dhamma practiced by Mahāpanthaka in the intervening existences is not mentioned. Cūḷapanthaka, however, ordained in the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa and practiced the white kasina (odāta-kasiṇa) for twenty thousand years before being reborn in the celestial city. In the Apadāna, it is stated: "Cūḷapanthaka became a hermit during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara and, while living in the Himālaya, saw the Blessed One and worshipped Him with a flower umbrella." While they were wandering through the realms of devas and humans, one hundred thousand aeons passed. Then, our Teacher attained Omniscience, set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and resided in the great monastery of Veḷuvana, depending on the city of Rājagaha.

At that time, in the city of Rājagaha, the daughter of the merchant Dhana formed an intimacy with her own slave. Fearing her relatives, she took her portable wealth and fled with that slave to live in another place. Dependent on that slave, she conceived a child, and when the pregnancy was mature...
155:
Thinking, "I will go to my relatives' house to give birth," she gave birth to a son on the way. Her husband made her turn back, and they lived in their former residence. Since the son was born on the road (pantha), they named him "Panthaka." When that child was at the age of running about, she conceived a second child due to the same person. When the pregnancy was mature, she gave birth to a son on the way just as before. Her husband made her turn back, and they named the elder son "Mahāpanthaka" and the younger son "Cūḷapanthaka," continuing to live in their usual place. As the boys gradually grew up, they pleaded, "Mother, please show us our grandfather's family." So, she sent the boys to her parents. From then on, the boys grew up in the house of the merchant Dhana. Among them, Cūḷapanthaka was very young. Mahāpanthaka, however, went to the Blessed One with his grandfather. Upon seeing the Teacher, he immediately gained faith. Having heard the Dhamma and being endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), he desired to ordain and asked his grandfather for permission. The grandfather informed the Teacher of the matter and had him ordained as a novice. After ordaining, he learned much of the Buddha's word and, upon reaching the age of twenty, received higher ordination. While practicing meditation with wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), he specifically attained the four formless jhānas (arūpajjhāna). Emerging from those jhānas, he applied himself to insight meditation (vipassanā) and attained the fruit of Arahatship. Thus, he became the foremost among those skilled in liberation through perception. Spending his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition (phala-sukha), one day he reviewed his own practice and, with joy arising from the attainment he had achieved, he uttered this lion's roar:

"When I first saw the Teacher, the Fearless One, then spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in me upon seeing the Best of Men."

"One who would push away the arriving glory with hands or feet, having pleased such a Teacher, would then miss the opportunity."

"Then I abandoned son and wife, wealth and grain; having cut off hair and beard, I entered the homeless life."

"Endowed with the training and livelihood, well-restrained in the senses, worshipping the Perfectly Enlightened One, I lived undefeated."
156:
Then a resolution arose in my mind, a desired aspiration: "I shall not sit down even for a moment as long as the thorn of craving is not pulled out."

Behold my energetic effort! The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's bidding has been done.

I know my past dwellings (pubbenivāsa). The divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) has been purified. I am an Arahant worthy of offerings, liberated and free from acquisitions (nirūpadhi).

Furthermore, at the end of the night, towards sunrise, having dried up all craving, I sat down cross-legged. Thus, he spoke these verses.

In those verses, "yadā" means at which time. "Paṭhamaṃ" means for the first time. "Addakkhiṃ" means I saw. "Satthāraṃ" means the Blessed One. "Akutobhayaṃ" means fearless. The meaning here is: because all causes of fear were abandoned at the foot of the Bodhi tree, and because there is no fear from anywhere, He is called "akutobhaya" (fearless). Because He instructs the veneyya (those to be tamed) according to their suitability with the supreme benefits of this life, the next life, and the ultimate goal, He is called "Satthā" (the Teacher), the Fully Enlightened One. At which time I first went with my grandfather and saw Him; having seen that Supreme Man, the foremost individual in the world including the devas, then because of that seeing, and after that seeing, saṃvega (spiritual urgency) arose in me, and knowledge accompanied by dread (ottappa) was born, thinking: "For so long a time, I have not had the opportunity to see the Teacher or to hear the Dhamma."

Showing that I, in whom saṃvega had arisen, thought in this way, he spoke the verse beginning with "Siriṃ hatthehi." The meaning of that verse is: just as a man desiring wealth might drive away and reject with his hands and feet the Goddess of Fortune (Siri) who has come to his bed in person, saying, "I will live in your presence as a servant," such an unfortunate man, having encountered such a Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, and having obtained this ninth opportune moment (khana), would miss it by not following His instruction. The intention is: "I, however, shall not do so." Therefore, he said, "Tadāhaṃ...pe... anagāriyaṃ."

In that verse, "chaḍḍayiṃ" means I abandoned. There is also a reading "chaḍḍiyaṃ." Now, did this elder not ordain without taking a wife? If so, why did he say, "I abandoned wife and children"? For example, if a man cuts down a tree that has not yet borne fruit, by that cutting he is said to be deprived of the fruits that would have been obtained. In this way, the completion should be understood. "Sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno" means: in that training called the higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the monks live together; they have a common livelihood and common conduct. Being endowed with that sājīva (livelihood) which is the code of training rules prescribed by the Blessed One, it means fulfilling the training and completing both without transgressing the sājīva. By that Pali, he shows his standing in the extremely pure Pātimokkha virtue...
157:
Why did he say, "I have also abandoned wife and children"? Just as a man who cuts down a tree that has not yet borne fruit is deprived of the fruits that would have been obtained from it had it not been cut, so too should this be understood in its completeness.

"Sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno" means being endowed with the higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) and with the sājīva (livelihood), which is the code of training rules prescribed by the Blessed One, in which monks live together with a common livelihood and similar conduct. It means being one who is complete in the state of training, fulfilling the training and not transgressing the sājīva, thus accomplishing both. By this, he shows his established state in the extremely pure Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla. "Indriyesu susaṃvuto" means well-restrained in the senses, with the mind as the sixth. The meaning is that he has the doors of the senses, such as the eye, well-closed with the door-panel of mindfulness (sati), by way of preventing the occurrence of covetousness (abhijjhā) and so on, which tend to arise in the objects such as forms.

By thus showing the perfection of Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla and Indriya-saṃvara-sīla, the perfection of the other virtues is also shown by implication. After the elder showed his own perfection in the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla), he spoke of his devotion to the meditation of the recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati) with the words "namassamāno Sambuddhaṃ." "Vihāsiṃ aparājito" means he lived as one undefeated by the Maras of defilements (kilesamāra) and so on. The meaning is that until he reached Arahantship, he was not overcome by those defilements; on the contrary, he lived overcoming them.

"Tato" means because of that—because he possessed extremely pure virtue, was greatly devoted to the Teacher, and stood in the practice of overcoming defilements. "Paṇidhi" means resolution or aspiration. Or it is the directing of the mind. "Āsi" means it occurred. "Cetaso abhipatthito" means desired by my mind. What was the nature of that resolution? He said: "I shall not sit down even for a moment as long as the thorn of craving is not pulled out." The meaning is that this was my mental aspiration: "As long as the thorn of craving is not extracted from my heart by the pincers of the Highest Path (aggamagga-saṇḍāsa), I shall not sit down even for a moment; I shall not take a sitting posture."

Having thus resolved in his mind and developed meditation, passing the night only by standing and walking, he emerged from the formless attainments (arūpa-samāpatti) and, establishing insight (vipassanā) by way of the jhana factors, he realized Arahantship. Therefore, he said the words beginning with "tassa me." "Nirūpadhi" means one who is free from acquisitions because of the absence of acquisitions of defilements (kilesūpadhi) and so on. "Ratyāvivisāne" means at the end of the night portion (at dawn). Marking the sunrise, having dried up all the thorns of craving, such as sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā), with the Highest Path, he sat down cross-legged because he was released from his vow of "I shall not sit until the thorn of craving is pulled out."
158: At the time of dawn, which is the end of the night, marking the sunrise, he dried up the entire stream of craving, including sensual craving and so forth, with the Path of Arahantship. Having been released from his vow, "I shall not sit down as long as the thorn of craving is not yet pulled out," he sat down cross-legged. The meaning of the remaining words is clear. ## The Commentary on the Verses of Mahāpanthaka Thera is finished. ## The Commentary on the Book of Eights is finished.
159:
## 9. Navakanipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Bhūta

In the Book of the Nines (Navakanipāta), the verse beginning with "Yadā dukkha" is that of the Venerable Bhūta Thera. What is the account of its origin? This Elder Bhūta had also performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit that serves as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences, was reborn in a Brahmin family during the time of Siddhattha Buddha. He received the name "Sena" and reached the age of discretion. One day, having seen the Teacher and with a mind full of faith and joy, he praised him with four verses beginning with "Usabhaṃ pavaraṃ."

Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this current Buddha's era, he was reborn as the son of a wealthy merchant in a village near the gate of the city of Sāketa. It is said that a certain yakkha, who was prone to killing, had devoured all the children born to that merchant. However, because this child was in his final birth (pacchimabhavika), the spirits (bhūta) took up his protection. The yakkha, meanwhile, had gone to serve King Vessavaṇa and did not return. On the day of the naming ceremony, they named him "Bhūta," reasoning that "by doing so, the spirits (bhūta) will protect him out of compassion."

That youth Bhūta grew up without any dangers due to the power of his own merit. Everything concerning him, such as "he had three palaces," should be understood in the same way as the description of the wealth of the clansman Yasa. When he reached maturity, while the Teacher was residing in Sāketa, he went to the monastery along with some lay followers. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and ordained. While living in a cave on the banks of the river named Ajakaraṇī, he established insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"Who, having seen the Buddha—who is like a bull, noble, heroic, a great seeker, a conqueror, and of golden hue—would not be inspired with faith?

Just as the Himavant is immeasurable, and the ocean is difficult to cross, likewise the meditative absorption (jhāna) of the Buddha is difficult to cross. Who, having seen that Buddha, would not be inspired with faith?

Just as the earth is immeasurable and adorned with various forest garlands, likewise the virtue (sīla) of the Buddha is immeasurable. Who, having seen that Buddha, would not be inspired with faith?"
160:
"Just as the sky is incalculable, likewise the knowledge (ñāṇa) of the Buddha is incalculable. Who, having seen that Buddha, would not be inspired with faith?

The Brahmin named Sena, having praised the most excellent Siddhattha Buddha, the unconquered, with these four verses,

Did not fall into woeful states (duggati) for ninety-four aeons, but enjoyed immense happiness and success in the good realms (sugati).

Because I praised the Leader of the World ninety-four aeons ago, I do not know of any birth in the four woeful states; this is the fruit of that praise.

In the fourteenth aeon, there were four wheel-turning monarchs (cakkavatti) named Uggata, endowed with the seven treasures and great power.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Having attained Arahatship, at a later time, out of compassion for his relatives, he went to Sāketa. Being attended to by them for a few days, he stayed in the Añjana Grove. When he wished to return to his original dwelling place, he showed signs of his departure. His relatives pleaded with the Elder, saying, "Venerable Sir, please stay right here; you will not be weary, and we shall increase in merit."

The Elder, wishing to make known his delight in seclusion (viveka) and his peaceful living in that place, spoke these verses:

"When the wise man knows aging and death as suffering, while the ignorant worldlings remain attached to the aggregates of clinging; having fully understood that suffering, he meditates with mindfulness. He finds no delight greater than that.

When, having abandoned craving (taṇhā)—the bringer of suffering, the poisonous one (visattikā), the carrier of the mass of suffering produced by obsession and conceit—he meditates with mindfulness. He finds no delight greater than that."
161:
"When, having seen with wisdom the most excellent Path—which is safe, eightfold, and the purifier of all defilements—he meditates with mindfulness. He finds no delight greater than that.

When he develops the peaceful Nibbāna—which is sorrowless, stainless, unconditioned, the purifier of all defilements, and the cutter of the bonds of fetters. He finds no delight greater than that.

When the drum of the clouds thunders in the sky, and the path of the birds is filled with raindrops on all sides, and the monk, having gone to a mountain cave, meditates. He finds no delight greater than that.

When, sitting on the bank of rivers crowded with flowers and adorned with various forest garlands, he meditates joyfully. He finds no delight greater than that.

When at midnight in the silent forest, while the rain falls and the fanged beasts roar, and the monk, having gone to a mountain cave, meditates. He finds no delight greater than that.

When, having restrained his own thoughts, relying on a mountain cleft within the mountain range, free from distress and free from thorns, he meditates. He finds no delight greater than that.

When, being happy, the destroyer of stains, thorns, and sorrow, without bolts, without underbrush, and without arrows, he meditates having brought all taints (āsavas) to an end. He finds no delight greater than that."

Thus, he recited these verses.
162:
## In these verses, by way of word-connection, this is the explanation of the meaning of the first verse.

The ripening of the aggregates is called aging (*jarā*). The breaking and dissolution of the aggregates is called death (*maraṇa*). In this context, by the heading of aging and death, the phenomena (*dhammā*) possessing aging and death are included. Ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) who possess ignorance (*avijjā*) and do not know according to reality that "this aging and death is suffering," are attached to, bound to, and clinging to the group of five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*). Having distinguished that suffering with the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*) accompanied by insight wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), saying "This is suffering, this much is suffering, there is nothing beyond this," the wise monk, mindful and clearly comprehending in this Dispensation (*sāsana*), meditates with the contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) at whatever time.
