He does not find, he does not obtain a delight superior to or more excellent than that delight in insight or that delight in the path and fruit (*magga-phala*). Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates, one obtains joy and gladness; for those who know, that is the Deathless (*amata*)."

"Better than sole sovereignty over the earth, better than going to heaven, better than lordship over all the worlds, is the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*)."

Having thus shown the delight in seclusion (*viveka-rati*) by way of the breakthrough of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*), he now spoke three verses starting with the second to show that delight by way of the breakthrough of abandoning (*pahānābhisamaya*), etc. Among those verses, 'dukkha-avahana' means bringing about suffering in the future, having the meaning of producing suffering. 'Visattikā' refers to craving (*taṇhā*). That craving is called 'visattikā' because it is widespread (*visata*), because it is vast (*visāla*), because it is pervasive (*visata*), because it schemes (*visakkati*), because it carries poison (*visa*), because it is deceptive (*visamvādikā*), because it has poison as its root (*visamūla*), because it has poison as its fruit (*visaphala*), because it has poison as its enjoyment (*visaparibhoga*). Alternatively, that craving is called 'visattikā' because it is spread out (*vitthata*) among forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, as well as among lineages and groups.

'Papañca-saṅghāta-dukkhādhivāhinī': Lust (*rāga*), etc., and conceit (*māna*), etc., are called 'proliferations' (*papañca*) because they expand the continuity of beings in *saṃsāra*. These very things are called 'assemblage' (*saṅghāta*) in the sense of being a collection of the suffering of occurrence, and they are called 'suffering' (*dukkha*) because they have the nature of distress and fever. Thus, they are 'the suffering of the assemblage of proliferations' (*papañca-saṅghāta-dukkha*). Because it carries or produces that suffering, it is called 'the carrier of the suffering of the assemblage of proliferations' (*papañca-saṅghāta-dukkhādhivāhinī*). 'Pahantvāna' means having completely cut off that craving by the Noble Path.
163:
It is called 'safe' (*khemaṃ*) because it is not oppressed by the defilements (*kilesa*) that cause danger, through their complete cutting off. It is called 'attained by the path of twice-four factors' (*dve-caturaṅga-gāminaṃ*) because it leads the noble ones to Nibbāna by means of the eight factors starting with Right View. Here, it should be understood that the case ending is not dropped (*vibhatti-alopa*) for the sake of the verse's meter. It is called 'the best of paths' (*magguttamaṃ*) because it is superior to all paths, such as those leading to rebirth in the fine-material realm (*rūpa-bhūmi*). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Of paths, the Eightfold Path is the best," etc. It is called 'the purifier of all defilements' (*sabba-kilesa-sodhanaṃ*) because it purifies beings from all the stains of defilements. 'Paññāya passitvā' means having penetrated through the breakthrough of development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*) by means of penetrative wisdom (*paṭivedha-paññā*).

Because of the absence of the causes of sorrow, and because it is the cause for the absence of sorrow for a person, there is no sorrow in this Nibbāna; thus it is called 'sorrowless' (*asokaṃ*). Similarly, because it is free from the dust of lust, etc., it is called 'dustless' (*virajaṃ*). Because it is not conditioned by any cause, it is called 'unconditioned' (*asaṅkhataṃ*). It is called 'the peaceful state' (*santaṃ padaṃ*) because it is the subsiding of all defilements and all suffering, and because it is to be reached and attained by those oppressed by the suffering of *saṃsāra*. It is called 'the purifier of all defilements' (*sabba-kilesa-sodhanaṃ*) because it is the cause for purifying the continuity of beings from all stains of defilements. 'Bhāveti' means knowing by means of the breakthrough of realization (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*). This is said by attributing the distinction obtained in the object of a person who frequently brings about the breakthrough of realization with Nibbāna as the object, to the object (Nibbāna) itself. It is called 'the cutter of the bonds of fetters' (*saṃyojana-bandhana-chidaṃ*) because it cuts the bonds known as fetters. Here, the cause is metaphorically spoken of as the agent, just as the truths that make one a noble one are called 'Noble Truths' (*ariya-sacca*). Just as in the previous verses it was connected as "whenever he meditates, then he finds no delight superior to that delight," so here it is connected as "whenever he develops, then he finds no delight superior to that delight in development."

Thus, the Elder, without bringing himself forward, declared his attainment of Arahantship by praising the penetration of the Four Truths through four verses. Now, wishing to show the comfort of the secluded nature of the place where he dwells, he spoke the verse beginning with "Yadā nabhe". In that verse, 'nabhe' means in the sky. Because of its smooth and deep sound, the cloud itself is the 'cloud-drum' (*megha-dundubhi*). It is called 'filled with showers' (*dhārākulā*) because it is crowded with streams flowing from all around. It is connected as 'in the sky, the path of birds' (*vihagapathe nabhe*) because it is the path of travel for birds. 'Tato' means than the delight in jhāna.
164:
*Kusumākulānaṃ* refers to [rivers] covered with flowers fallen from trees. *Vicittavāneyyavaṭaṃsakānaṃ* means rivers that possess various beautiful wild flower garlands, as they are born in the forest; it means rivers having various kinds of wild flower crests. One who has a good mind through the power of supramundane states (jhāna) is called *Sumana*; he meditates.

*Nisīthe* means at night. *Rahitami* means in a secluded place free from the congestion of people. *Deve* refers to the clouds. *Gaḷantami* means while the streams of rain are pouring down. *Dāṭhino* refers to hostile creatures such as lions and tigers. They are called *Dāṭhino* because they carry fangs as weapons. The phrase "the fanged ones roar" is included only to show the seclusion from people.

*Vitakke uparundhiyattano* means having restrained wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts arising in one's own continuity by the power of the opposite [wholesome states]. Alternatively, the word *attano* should be connected with *vindati* as "he no longer finds a delight more excellent than that [jhāna bliss] for himself." *Nagantare* means between mountains. *Nagavivaraṃ* means a mountain cave or a mountain slope. *Samassito* means depended upon or approached. *Vītaddaro* means one who is free from the distress of defilements. *Vītakhilo* means one who has abandoned the five mental spikes (*cetokhila*).

*Sukhī* means one who is happy through the bliss of jhāna and so on. *Malakhilasokanāsano* means one who dispels the stains such as lust, the five mental spikes, and the sorrow caused by reasons such as separation from relatives. *Niraggaḷo* means: ignorance (*avijjā*) is called a bolt (*aggaḷa*) because it prevents entry into the city of Nibbāna; because of the absence of that [ignorance], he is "without a bolt" (*niraggaḷo*). *Nibbanatho* means one without craving. *Visallo* means one whose darts, such as lust, have been removed. *Sabbāsave* means all the taints, such as the taint of sensuality. *Byantikato* means one who has brought them to an end by the Noble Path; when such a person meditates for the sake of dwelling happily in the present life, he finds no delight more excellent than that delight of jhāna—this is the connection. Having spoken thus, the Elder went to the banks of the Ajakaraṇī River.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Bhūta is finished.

## The Commentary on the Section of Nines is finished.
165:
## 10. Dasakanipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kāḷudāyī

In the Section of Tens, the verses beginning with "Aṅgārino" are those of the Venerable Elder Kāḷudāyī. What is the origin of these verses? This Elder Kāḷudāyī was also born into a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain monk to the foremost position among those who inspire confidence in families (*kulappasādaka*). He performed a corresponding meritorious deed and aspired to that position.

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took conception in a minister's house in Kapilavatthu on the very day our Bodhisatta took conception in his mother's womb. Since he was born on the same day as the Bodhisatta, they laid him on a roll of fine cloth on that day and brought him to serve the Bodhisatta. Indeed, these seven—the Bodhi tree, Rāhula's mother, the four great treasure jars, the state elephant, the horse Kaṇṭhaka, the minister Channa, and the minister Kāḷudāyī—were called "co-natals" (*sahajāta*) because they were born on the same day as the Bodhisatta. Later, on the naming day, because he was born on a day when the whole city was in a state of high spirits (*udagga*), they named him Udāyī. However, because he was slightly dark-complexioned, he was known as Kāḷudāyī. He grew up playing childhood games with the Bodhisatta.

In later times, the Lord of the World (the Buddha) went forth on the Great Renunciation, gradually attained Omniscience, and set the Noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion. While He was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery near the city of Rājagaha, King Suddhodana heard that news and sent a minister accompanied by a thousand men, saying, "Bring my son here." That minister went to the Teacher at the time of the Dhamma teaching, stood at the edge of the assembly, and while listening to the Dhamma, attained Arahantship along with his followers. Then the Teacher stretched out his hand and said, "Come, monks" (*Ehi bhikkhavo*). At that very moment, they all became like elders of sixty years' standing, bearing miraculously created bowls and robes. From the moment they attained Arahantship, Noble Ones remain in a state of equanimity; therefore, they did not convey the King's message to the Ten-Powered One. The King, thinking, "The group of soldiers who went has not returned, nor is any news heard," sent another minister...
166:
The King sent a minister along with a thousand men. That minister acted in the same way [as the previous ones]. In this manner, he sent nine thousand men along with nine ministers; all of them attained Arahantship and remained silent.

Then the King thought: "So many people, out of a lack of affection for me, have said nothing to bring the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) here. However, this Udāyī is of the same age as the Ten-Powered One, was a childhood playmate in the dust, and has affection for me. I will send him." Having summoned him, he said, "Dear Udāyī, go to Rājagaha with a retinue of a thousand men and bring the Ten-Powered One back."

While departing, Udāyī said, "Your Majesty, if I am allowed to ordain, I shall bring the Blessed One here." The King replied, "Do whatever is necessary, but show me my son." He went to Rājagaha, stood at the edge of the assembly during the Blessed One's sermon, and upon hearing the Dhamma, attained Arahantship along with his retinue and was established in the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, Monk) ordination. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"To the Buddha Padumuttara, the Chief of the World, the Such-like (Tādi),
Who was then traveling on a long journey, wandering for the Dhamma.
Taking a well-bloomed lotus, a blue lily, and jasmine, 
And taking excellent food, I offered them to the Teacher.
The Great Hero partook of that excellent food, the fine meal,
And taking those flowers, he showed them to the people.
'This noble flower born in water, desired, delightful, and beloved in the world—
He who gave me this flower has performed a deed most difficult to do.
He who offered the flowers and gave me the excellent food,
I shall praise him; listen to my words.
Eighteen times he shall exercise the kingship of the devas;
Blue lilies, lotuses, and jasmines, even more than that.
By the result of his merit, endowed with divine fragrance,
A canopy shall be formed in the sky and shall be held up at that very moment.'"
167:
"And twenty-five times he shall be a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). Five hundred times he shall rule the earth as a sovereign king.

In a hundred thousand aeons from now, born in the Okkāka clan,
A Teacher named Gotama by lineage shall arise in the world.

Devoted to his own task of wholesome meditation, urged by his pure roots (merit),
He shall be a kinsman who brings joy to the Sakyans.

Later, having ordained, urged by his pure roots,
Fully understanding all taints (āsavas), he shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints.

Having attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), finished his task, and being taintless,
The Buddha Gotama, the kinsman of the world, shall appoint him to this foremost position (Etadagga).

With a mind directed toward meditation, peaceful, and free from acquisitions (upadhi),
He shall be a disciple of the Teacher, known by the name Udāyī.

Lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and disparagement (makkha) have been destroyed.
Having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.

I have pleased the Fully Enlightened One, being energetic and wise.
The Fully Enlightened One, being pleased, has appointed me to the foremost position.

The four analytical insights... I have followed the Buddha's teaching."

Upon attaining Arahantship, he thought, "Now is not yet the time for the Ten-Powered One to go to his ancestral city. Only when spring arrives, the forests are in bloom, and the ground is covered with green grass will it be the time to travel." Waiting for the time, when spring arrived, wishing to praise the beauty of the journey to the Teacher's ancestral city, he said:

"Venerable Sir, now the trees, seeking fruit, have shed their old leaves and appear like glowing embers.
They shine all around like flames, O Great Hero;
It is the time to visit your relatives."
168:
"The trees have bloomed, they are delightful to the heart; the scent of blossoms wafts in all directions. Like shedding old leaves and longing for fruit, O Great Hero, it is time to depart from this city of Rājagaha.

Venerable Sir, the season is pleasant for a long journey, being neither too cold nor too hot. May the Sakyans and Koliyans see you crossing the Rohiṇī River, facing the west.

The farmer plows the field, longing for the harvest; he sows the seed with hope. Merchants go to the sea, seeking wealth. I stand with a certain longing; may that longing of mine be fulfilled.

Again and again, they sow the seed; again and again, the king of devas (the rain) falls. Again and again, the farmers plow the field; again and again, grain reaches the kingdom.

Again and again, beggars wander; again and again, lords of giving (donors) give. Having given again and again, the lords of giving reach the heavenly realm again and again.

A hero of great wisdom is born in a certain clan; that hero truly brings benefit to seven generations of his lineage. I believe that You, the God of gods, are capable; because of You, the Sage of true name has arisen.

The father of the Great Seer, the Buddha, is named Suddhodana; the mother is named Māyā. She who carried the Bodhisatta in her womb, after the breaking up of the body, rejoices in the Tusita heaven.

That Gotamī Māyādevī, having passed away from this human world, is endowed with divine sensual pleasures. Surrounded by those hosts of devas, she rejoices in the five strands of sensual pleasure."
169:
“I am the son of the Buddha, the Angīrasa, who is unassailable, peerless, and endowed with the quality of suchness (tādi). O Great Sakyan, you are the father of my father. O King of the Gotama lineage, you are rightfully my grandfather.” Thus he spoke these verses.

In those verses, ‘angārino’ means that because the blossoms and shoots of the trees have a red coral-like color like glowing embers, they are called ‘angārino’. The meaning is that it is as if they are showered with a rain of embers by the very red flowers and sprouts. ‘Idāni’ means at this time. ‘Dumā’ means trees. ‘Bhadante’ is derived from the analysis ‘bhaddaṃ ante etassa’, dropping one letter ‘da’. It is a term of address for the Teacher who is endowed with special qualities and is the supreme among those with such qualities. Therefore, ‘bhadante’ is a term of address for the Teacher. Although it is a nominative case ending in ‘e’, it should be understood here in the sense of the vocative (sambodhana). Therefore, it is said, “Bhadante is a term of address.” Some say, “It is another word with the same meaning as the word bhadda.” They are called ‘phalesino’ because they seek fruits. Even for inanimate trees, the actions of the animate are attributed, just as one says, ‘the house wishes to fall’; the meaning is the time of attaining the fruit, when efforts are made to take the fruits. ‘Chadanam vippahāya’ means having abandoned old leaves and possessing full mature leaves (new leaves).

‘Te’ refers to those trees. ‘Accimantova pabhāsayanti’ means they illuminate all directions as if they have the flame of a lamp or like a blazing fire. ‘Samayo’ means time, and the remaining word ‘anuggahāya’ (for the sake of favor) is included. ‘Mahāvīra’ is an address to the Buddha of great prowess. ‘Bhāgī rasānaṃ’ means possessing the collection of the essence of meaning (attharasa), etc. For it was said by the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta): “The Blessed One is a possessor of the essence of meaning and the essence of Dhamma.” Both ‘Mahāvīra’ and ‘Bhāgī’ should be understood as terms of address. If the reading is ‘Bhāgīrathānaṃ’, it means for the benefit of the Sakyans, who are called Bhāgīratha because they were born in the lineage of the ancient king named Bhagīratha.

‘Dumāni’ refers to trees, spoken with a change of gender. ‘Samantato sabbadisā pavanti’ means they bloom in all directions and on all sides, and because they bloom in such a way, they waft their fragrance to all directions. ‘Āsamānā’ means desiring and wishing to take.
170:
Having shown the delightfulness of the journey through the beauty of the trees, he now shows the perfection of the season with “Nevātisītaṃ” and so forth. “Sukhā” means a pleasant and desirable season by being neither too cold nor too hot. “Utu addhaniyā” means a season suitable for traveling a long distance.

“Let the Sakyans and Koliyans see you... crossing the Rohiṇī facing west” means the river named Rohiṇī flows from the north to the south between the Sakyan and Koliyan territories. The city of Rājagaha is to the southeast of that river. Therefore, when going from Rājagaha to Kapilavatthu, one crosses that river facing the west. That is why it is said, “Let them see you... crossing.” By saying, “Let the inhabitants of the Sakyan and Koliyan territories see the Blessed One crossing the river named Rohiṇī facing west,” he urges the Blessed One by requesting Him to go to Kapilavatthu.

Now, desiring to reveal his own aspiration through similes, he spoke the verse beginning with “Āsāya kasate”.
A farmer plows the field with hope, desiring the fruit (harvest).
With the hope of fruit, the sower casts and plants the seed.
Merchants seeking wealth travel by boat across the ocean to reach other lands with the hope of wealth.
With whatever hope I stand here. (Likewise, I stand here with the hope and request for the Blessed One to go to the city of Kapila.)
May that hope of mine be fulfilled; you should go to Kapilavatthu—this is the meaning. Here, the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) is called ‘hope’ (āsā) because of its similarity to hope.

To show the reason for requesting many times by praising the journey and so forth, the words beginning with “Punappunaṃ” are spoken. Its meaning is: if the nursery is not successful with just one sowing, farmers sow the seed again and again, a second and third time. Pajjunna, the king of devas, does not rain only once but rains again and again from time to time. Farmers do not plow only once but plow again and again to make the dust and mud soft for the perfection of the crop. Humans, not being satisfied with gathering grain once, saying “this is enough,” bring rice and other grains to be stored in granaries again and again, and thus it reaches the kingdom.
171:
Beggars, when they beg, do not go to families just once, but wander and approach them again and again. When asked, the lords of alms (donors) also do not give just once, but give again and again. In this way, by giving gifts again and again and accumulating merit consisting in giving, the lords of alms repeatedly reach the heavenly realm; they go to the world of devas by way of rebirth. Therefore, I too request again and again: "May the Blessed One fulfill my heart's desire"—this is the meaning.

Now, to show the purpose for which he requests the Teacher to go to Kapilavatthu, he spoke the verse beginning with "Vīro have". The meaning of that verse is: In whatever family a hero—one who is energetic, of great prowess, and of great wisdom—is born, there, indeed, he purifies the seven generations of ancestors through right practice. This is a worldly saying or a superior claim among others. However, the Blessed One, being the supreme deity among all devas, is called the Deva of devas. I believe that by restraining from evil and establishing in goodness, he is able to purify even beyond those seven generations. Why? Because you, Venerable Sir, are born through the Noble Path and know the two benefits of the present and the cycle of rebirths, thus you have the unerring name "Sacca" (Truth). Because you, Venerable Sir, are born of the Noble birth, the state of a Sage (Muni) exists. Or, a Sage is so called because of the meaning of knowing one's own benefit and the benefit of others, and both this world and the world beyond; thus he has the unerring and true name "Muni". Or, he is called "Muni" because of the wisdom of the Path of Arahantship. You, Venerable Sir, who have the unerring and true names of "Samaṇa", "Pabbajita", and "Isi", are born. Therefore, because it is the cause for beings to obtain absolute benefit, we request the Blessed One's journey to that city of Kapilavatthu—this is the meaning.

Now, when "seven generations" (sattayuga) is mentioned, to show the father's generation, the passage beginning with "Suddhodano nāma" was spoken. He is named Suddhodana because his livelihood consists of pure food. Indeed, the Buddha's father has extremely pure conduct of body, speech, and mind, and an extremely pure livelihood. Why? Because he is endowed with the fulfillment of past aspirations. "Māyā nāma" means: because she was endowed with excellence in family, appearance, virtue, and conduct, she had the quality of being told by relatives and friends, "Do not go" (Mā yāhī—because they cherished her), thus she received the name "Māyā". "Pariharitvā" means having carried (in the womb). "Kāyassa bhedā" means after the breaking up of her own body, which was like a shrine for the world including the devas (after death). "Tidivamhi" means in the Tusita heaven.

That Queen Māyā Devī is praised by her lineage as "Gotamī". "Dibbehi kāmehi" means by the divine objects of sensual pleasure belonging to the Tusita realm. "Samangībhūtā" means being endowed with. "Kāmaguṇehi" means by the strands of sensual pleasure. Again, by the word "kāmaguṇehi", it means by various kinds of objects of sensual pleasure.
172:
Furthermore, with the words "by means of the strands of sensual pleasure," he shows that one is made to enjoy various kinds of objective sensuality. "By those" means in whichever group of devas one is born; it refers to those groups of Tusita devas, or otherwise to those strands of sensual pleasure. The reference in the feminine gender, "being endowed with and surrounded by," is made with reference to the female state or the state of a deity achieved in a previous existence. However, rebirth as a deity (upapatti) occurs only in the male form.

Thus, being requested by the Elder, the Blessed One, seeing that many would attain distinction upon his going there, set out on the road leading to Kapilavatthu from Rājagaha by way of a leisurely journey, surrounded by twenty thousand taintless ones (Arahants). The Elder went to Kapilavatthu by psychic power and stood in the air in front of the King. Seeing an appearance never seen before, the King asked, "Who are you?" Desiring to show, "If you, O King, do not know me, the son of the minister whom you sent to the Blessed One, then know me thus," he spoke the concluding verse:

"I am the true son of the Buddha, who is unassailable, peerless, and endowed with the virtue of patience, the one named Angīrasa.
O Sakyan King, you are the father of my father (the Buddha).
O King of the Gotama lineage, you are rightfully my grandfather."

In that verse, "Buddhaassa puttomhi" means: because of being born from the breast of the Omniscient Buddha, I am a true-born son. "Asayhasāhino" means: because before the Great Enlightenment, he carried out the entire requisites of enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) and the great compassion which could not be endured or carried out by others besides the Great Bodhisatta; and because after that, he endured and overcame the five Māras who cannot be endured or overcome by others; and because by knowing the divisions of inclinations, underlying tendencies, characters, and dispositions, etc., he accomplished the Buddha's duty—consisting of instruction for the benefit of beings in the present life, the future life, and the ultimate sense—which is unassailable by others; or because of being one who acts excellently in that Buddha's duty, he is called "Asayhasāhī." "Angīrasassa" means: because of being endowed with the fulfillment of virtues such as morality. Other teachers say, "Because of having an aura emanating from his limbs." Some teachers, however, say that the two names "Angīrasa" and "Siddhattha" are specifically to be taken.
173:
Some teachers say that the two names Aṅgīrasa and Siddhattha are specifically taken. "Appaṭima" means the incomparable (anūpama). He is called "Tādi" because he has reached the state of suchness (tādilakkhaṇa) regarding desirable and undesirable objects. "Pitupitā mayhaṃ tuvaṃsi" means: by way of the noble birth (ariyajāti), the Buddha is my father; by way of worldly convention, you, Great King, are his father. He addresses the King as "Sakka" by way of his birth. "Dhammena" means by nature; by combining the natures of the two births—the noble birth and the worldly birth—he addresses the King by his lineage as "Gotama." "Ayyakosi" means you are the grandfather. In this verse, the Elder, by saying "I am the son of the Buddha," etc., declared his attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.

After making himself known in this way, the King, joyful and delighted, had him sit on a costly throne. When the King filled his bowl with food of various excellent flavors he had prepared and offered it, the Elder showed a sign of wanting to leave. When asked, "Why do you wish to go? Please eat first," he replied, "I will go and eat in the presence of the Teacher." When asked, "Where is the Teacher?", he replied, "He has set out on the journey to see you, Great King, accompanied by twenty thousand monks." The King said, "Venerable Sir, please eat this almsfood; and until my son reaches this city, please take almsfood from here to him."

The Elder, having finished his meal, preached the Dhamma to the King and his retinue. Even before the Teacher arrived, he inspired the entire royal household with great faith in the Triple Gem. Then, while everyone was watching, he sent the bowl full of food intended for the Teacher into the sky, and he himself rose into the air, brought the almsfood, and placed it in the Teacher's hand. The Teacher partook of that almsfood. In this way, as the Teacher traveled the sixty-league journey at the rate of one league per day, the Elder brought food from the King's palace every day and offered it. Then the Blessed One, saying, "You have inspired faith in the entire household of my father, the Great King," placed him in the foremost position (aggaṭṭhāna) among those who inspire faith in families (kulappasādakānaṃ).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Kāḷudāyi Thera is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Ekavihāriya Thera
The verses beginning with "Purato pacchato vā" are those of the Venerable Ekavihāriya Thera. This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. In the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was born in a respectable family, and upon reaching maturity, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. Gaining faith, he ordained, entered the forest, and lived in seclusion.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the celestial and human worlds for one Buddha-interval. When our Buddha appeared...
174:
## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Ekavihāriya Thera

The verses beginning with "Purato pacchato vā" are those of the Venerable Ekavihāriya Thera. What is the origin? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. In the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was born in a respectable family, and upon reaching maturity, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. Gaining faith, he ordained, entered the forest, and lived in seclusion.

Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the celestial and human worlds for one Buddha-interval. In this Buddha's era, after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, he was born as the younger brother of King Dhammāsoka. It is said that King Asoka the Great, two hundred and eighteen (218) years after the Teacher's Parinibbāna, was consecrated as the sole ruler of the whole of Jambudīpa. He appointed his younger brother, Prince Tissa, as the viceroy and by a certain means made him very devoted to the Dispensation. One day, while out hunting in the forest, Prince Tissa saw the Great Elder Yonaka Mahādhammarakkhita sitting while being fanned by a noble elephant with a sal branch. Seeing this, great faith arose in him, and he thought: "Oh, how wonderful! If only I too could ordain like this Great Elder and live in the forest!"

The Elder, knowing the Prince's thought, rose into the air while the Prince was watching, and standing on the unbroken surface of the water in the pond at Asokārāma, he hung his robes in the air and began to bathe. The Prince, seeing the Elder's psychic power, was deeply inspired. Returning from the forest to the palace, he informed the King, "I will ordain." The King pleaded with the Prince in many ways to turn him away from his intention to ordain, but could not. The Prince, becoming a lay follower (upāsaka) and longing for the bliss of ordination, said this:

"Whether in front or behind, if no other is found,
It is exceedingly pleasant for one living alone in the forest.

Come now, I shall go alone to the forest praised by the Buddha;
It is pleasant for a monk who dwells alone and is resolute in mind.

I shall quickly enter the delightful forest, which brings joy to practitioners (yogis),
Frequented by elephants in rut, seeking my own goal alone."
175:
“In the well-blossomed, cool Sītavana, in the cool mountain glen, having washed my limbs, I will walk alone.

Alone, without a companion, in the delightful great forest, when shall I dwell, having completed my task and being free from taints (āsavas)?

May my desire to do so be fulfilled; I myself will accomplish it, for no one else can do it for another.” Thus he recited these six verses.

In those verses, ‘purato pacchato vā’ means that if no other person is seen either in front or behind (since the word ‘vā’ has a disjunctive sense), there is great ease and mental happiness. For one who dwells alone without a companion, ‘vane vasato’ (for one dwelling in the forest) refers to one whose heart is drawn by a long-practiced inclination for seclusion. Such a person, weary of the social life of living surrounded by crowds day and night, and valuing the bliss of seclusion greatly, speaks thus.

‘Handa’ is a particle in the sense of renunciation; by this word, he expresses the firm resolve of going to the forest which is to be done now. ‘Eko gamissāmi’ means, in accordance with the words ‘Householder, the Tathāgatas delight in secluded dwellings,’ etc., I will go alone without a companion to the noble forest praised by the Buddhas, with the intention of dwelling there. The meaning is that for a monk who is accustomed to dwelling alone without a companion in postures such as standing, whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna, and who practices the three trainings such as the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the forest brings ease, is desirable, and brings happiness.

‘Yogī-pītikaraṃ’ means it brings the joy (pīti) of jhāna and vipassanā to yogis who are devoted to meditation, due to the absence of noise and such. It is delightful (rammaṃ) because it is suitable for seclusion, being free from incompatible objects. ‘Matta-kuñjara-sevitaṃ’ means a forest frequented by noble elephants in rut; by this, he shows the seclusion from people due to it being a vast forest. ‘Atthavasī’ means here ‘attha’ refers to the practice of a recluse (samaṇadhamma). Being under its influence, he thinks, ‘How indeed might that be mine?’ ‘Supupphite’ means well-blossomed. ‘Sītavane’ means in the cool forest because it is endowed with shade and water. By both terms, only the delightfulness of the forest is shown.
176:
“Supupphite” means well-blossomed. “Sītavane” means in the cool forest because it is endowed with shade and water. By both terms, he clearly shows only the delightfulness of that forest. “Girikandare” means in the glen within the mountains. “Kaṃ” means water, and a low place carved by that water is called “kandara.” In such a cool mountain glen, having dispelled the heat and having sprinkled and bathed his body, he says, “I will walk alone,” thereby showing his independent way of life, not relying on anyone else in any place.

“Ekākiyo” means alone, without a companion. “Adutiyo” means without a second, because of the absence of the companion known as craving (taṇhā). Indeed, craving is called a “companion” because it never leaves a man. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “A man with craving as his companion wanders for a long time in saṃsāra.”

“Evaṃ me kattukāmassa” means for me who desires to exert in meditation after going to the forest by the method already mentioned, such as “Now I will go alone.” “Adhippāyo samijjhatu” means may this mental wish (manoratha), “When shall I dwell, having completed my task and being free from taints?” reach completion and be fulfilled. Since the attainment of Arahatship is not achieved by mere prayer, nor can it be accomplished by another, he said: “I myself will accomplish it, for no one else can do it for another.”

Thus, knowing the firm resolve of the Vice-regent for ordination, King Asoka had the road leading to the Asokārāma monastery decorated. He then had the prince adorned with all ornaments and led him to the monastery with a great army and great royal majesty. The prince went to the meditation hall and ordained in the presence of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita. Many hundreds of people followed him and ordained. Aggibrahmā, the king’s nephew and husband of Princess Saṅghamittā, also followed him and ordained. After ordaining, being joyful and happy, and wishing to manifest the task he must perform, he said:

I bind on this armor (of energy), I will enter the forest;
I will not emerge from there until I reach the destruction of taints.

While the cool, fragrant breeze blows,
Sitting on the mountain peak, I will shatter ignorance (avijjā).
177:
"In the forest covered with flowers, and in the cool mountain cave, happy with the bliss of liberation, I shall delight in Giribbaja." He spoke these three verses.

In those verses, "esa bandhāmi sannāhaṃ" means "I bind this armor of energy (viriya); I bind it with the armor of energy that is regardless of body and life." This is the intended meaning: For example, just as a brave man, when enemies appear, desiring to conquer them, abandons other tasks and prepares for battle by putting on armor and so on, and does not return from the battlefield until he has conquered the enemies; even so, I, to conquer the enemies of defilements (kilesa), disregarding even a burning head or clothes, put on the armor of the fourfold right effort (sammappadhāna-viriya). I will not abandon the secluded place suitable for the victory over defilements until I have conquered them. Therefore, it is said, "I will enter the forest; I will not come out from there until I have reached the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya), which is the fruit of Arahantship."

With the words "mālute upavāyante" and so on, he speaks of the suitability of the forest for the development of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). The connection is "I shall delight in Giribbaja." He speaks with a future sense, thinking, "I shall delight in Rājagaha, which is surrounded by five mountains." The rest is very easy to understand.

Having said this, while the Elder entered the forest and practiced the recluse's Dhamma, he went to the Kalinga country with his preceptor. There, a skin disease (cammikābādha) arose on the Elder's feet. Seeing that affliction, a doctor said, "Venerable sir, please seek some ghee (sappi); I will treat it." The Elder, without seeking ghee, practiced only the work of insight (vipassanā), and the disease increased. The doctor, seeing the Elder's indifference toward the affliction, sought the ghee himself and cured the Elder. Being cured, he attained Arahantship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In this Bhadda-kappa, the Buddha named Kassapa by clan, a kinsman of Brahma, of great fame, the best of speakers, arose.

He was free from proliferation (nippapañca), unsupported by craving or views (nirālamba), with a mind like the sky. Dwelling much in the abiding of emptiness (suññatā-vihāra), he was such a one (tādī), delighting in signless insight (animitta-vipassanā), and a master of the five masteries (vasī)."
178:
"With an unattached mind, free from defilements, not mixing with families or groups, of great compassion, a hero, skilled in the means of discipline.

Exerting for the welfare of others, disciplining the world including the devas, (showing) the path leading to Nibbāna, the destination that dries up the mud of the rounds of rebirth.

(Teaching the Dhamma) which is deathless, of supreme delight, and which prevents old age and death, that Buddha, the Savior of the world, sat in the midst of a great assembly.

The Lord with a voice like the karavīka bird, with a Brahma-voice, the Tathāgata, rescuing those who are lost and without a leader from the great whirlpool of saṃsāra.

I saw the Leader of the world, preaching the stainless Dhamma. Having heard his Dhamma, I went forth into the homeless life.

Having gone forth then, contemplating the Victor's teaching, I lived alone in the delightful forest, being oppressed by social contact.

Physical seclusion (sakkāyavūpakāsa) became the cause (for the attainment of the path and fruit) for me, who sees danger in social contact and possesses mental seclusion (manasavūpakāsa).

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been done."

After reaching Arahantship, while the Elder was dwelling there in the forest, the King, spending ten billion in wealth, had the Bhojakagiri Vihāra built and made the Elder reside there. While dwelling there, at the time of his Parinibbāna, he spoke the final verse:

"I am one whose resolve is fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day. All taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth."

He spoke this final verse. The meaning of that verse is clear. That very verse was the Elder's declaration of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Ekavihāriya is finished.
179:
## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mahākappina

"Anāgataṃ yo paṭikacca passati" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Mahākappina. What is its origin? It is said that in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who give exhortations to the monks. Having performed a corresponding meritorious deed, he aspired to that position.

After performing meritorious deeds for the rest of his life in that existence and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Vārāṇasī during the time of the Buddha Kassapa. Upon reaching maturity, he became the leader of a group of a thousand men and had a large monastery built and decorated with a thousand chambers. All those people also performed meritorious deeds for the rest of their lives and, with that lay devotee as their leader, were reborn in the deva realm along with their wives and children. For the interval between one Buddha and another, they wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Among them, the leader of the group was reborn in a royal house in the city named Kukkuṭa in a border region, even before our Buddha appeared. His name was Kappina. The remaining men were reborn in the families of ministers in that same city. Upon the death of his father, Prince Kappina ascended the throne and became known as King Mahākappina. Being a seeker of knowledge, he would send messengers early in the morning through the four gates, saying, "Wherever you see those of great learning, return from there and inform me."

At that time, our Teacher had appeared in the world and was dwelling near the city of Sāvatthī. Then, merchants living in Sāvatthī took goods produced in Sāvatthī, went to that city, stored their goods, and thinking, "We shall see the King," had their arrival announced to the King with gifts in their hands. The King had the merchants summoned, and as they stood there having offered their gifts and paid homage, he asked, "Where have you come from?" "From Sāvatthī, O King," they replied. "Is your country prosperous? Is the King righteous?" he asked. "Yes, O King," they replied. "What kind of Dhamma is currently prevailing in your region?" he asked. "O King, it is not proper to speak of that with unwashed mouths," they replied. The King had water brought in a golden pitcher. They rinsed their mouths, and facing the direction of the Ten-Powered One, they raised their hands in salutation and said, "O King, in our region, the Jewel of the Buddha..."
180:
(The merchants) said, "...has arisen." As soon as the King heard the word "Buddha," joy (pīti) arose, pervading his entire body. From that moment, he asked, "Friends, did you say 'Buddha'?" "O King, we said 'Buddha'," they replied. Having made them say it three times, and thinking, "The word 'Buddha' is immeasurable," he became devoted to that very word, gave them a hundred thousand (coins), and asked, "Tell me more news." "O King, the Jewel of the Dhamma has arisen in the world," they replied. Hearing that as well, he gave another hundred thousand in the same manner and asked, "Tell me more news." "O King, the Jewel of the Saṅgha has arisen in the world," they replied. Hearing that too, he gave another hundred thousand in the same manner and, thinking, "I will go forth as a monk in the presence of the Blessed One," he departed from that very place. The ministers also departed in the same way.

That King Mahākappina, together with the thousand ministers, reached the bank of the Ganges and made an Act of Truth: "If the Teacher is truly the Samma-sambuddha, who has realized the Four Noble Truths without error, let not even the hooves of these horses be wetted by water." He then crossed the overflowing Ganges River on the surface of the water. In the same manner, he crossed another river half a league wide, and upon reaching the third great river named Candabhāgā, he crossed that great river as well by that same Act of Truth.

The Teacher also, having emerged from the Attainment of Great Compassion at dawn on that very day, surveyed the world and saw, "Today, King Mahākappina, having abandoned a kingdom of three hundred leagues, will come to me with a retinue of a thousand ministers to go forth as a monk." Thinking, "It is proper for me to go and welcome them," he performed his morning bodily duties, wandered for alms in Sāvatthī surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, and after the meal, having returned from the alms round, he himself traveled through the air. He sat cross-legged at the foot of a great banyan tree in a place facing the landing site where they would arrive on the bank of the Candabhāgā River, and emitted the six-colored Buddha-rays. As they were coming up from that landing site, they saw the Buddha-rays darting here and there, and upon seeing the Blessed One, they came to a conclusion just by the sight: "This is surely the Teacher for whose sake we have come." From the place where they saw him, they bowed down and approached the Blessed One, acting with great reverence. The King held the Blessed One's ankles, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place together with the thousand ministers. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to them. At the conclusion of the teaching, he, along with his followers, was established in Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

The Buddha named Padumuttara, who has reached the further shore of all phenomena, appeared like the sun rising in the stainless sky of the month of Kattika. That Blessed One caused the lotuses of those to be led (veneyya) to bloom with the rays of his teaching. The Blessed One, with the rays of his knowledge, dried up the mud of defilements. He dispelled the fame of the heretics just as the sun dispels the light of fireflies. He made clear the light of the meaning of the Truths just as the sun makes jewels manifest. Just as the ocean is the repository of jewels, the Blessed One is the repository of virtues.
181:
The Victorious One named Padumuttara, who has reached the further shore of all phenomena, appeared like the sun rising in the stainless sky during the month of Kattika. With the rays of his teaching, that Blessed One caused the lotuses of those to be enlightened (veneyya) to bloom. That Leader of men and gods, with the rays of his wisdom, dried up the mud of defilements. Just as the sun dispels the light of fireflies, he dispelled the fame of the sectarians. Just as the sun makes jewels manifest, he made manifest the light of the meaning of the Four Noble Truths. Just as the ocean is the source of jewels, he is the source of virtues. Just as the rain god pours down upon beings, he rained down with the cloud of Dhamma.

At that time, I was a judge in the city named Haṃsavatī. Having approached the Buddha named Padumuttara, I heard the Dhamma. (I heard the Dhamma of the Blessed One) who, while praising the virtues of the disciple named Katāvī, who was skilled in advising the monks, made my heart rejoice. Having heard that Dhamma, being inspired and joyful, I invited the Tathāgata, offered food to him along with his disciples, and aspired for that position.

Then the Blessed One, whose gait was like that of a king of swans and whose voice was like the sound of a swan, said: "Look at this great minister, who is courageous in judgment. This minister, who lies prostrate at my feet, whose hair stands on end with joy, who has the complexion of a dark rain cloud, who has full shoulders, who has a clear eyes and face, who is accompanied by a large retinue, who is engaged in the king's service, and who is famous, with a joyful mind, aspires for the position of the monk Katāvī. Because of this act of prostration, generosity, and aspiration, this person shall not go to a state of misery for a hundred thousand aeons. Having enjoyed the prosperity of a god among gods and greatness among humans, he shall reach Nibbāna through the remaining merit. A hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born in the Okkāka family, will appear in the world."
182:
"He will be a disciple of that Teacher, an heir to the Dhamma, a breast-born son, created by the Dhamma, named Kappina by name."

From there, having performed meritorious deeds well-done in the dispensation of the Victorious Buddha, I left the human body and went to the Tusita heaven.

After ruling as a king of gods and a king of men for hundreds of times, I was born into a potter's family near the city of Bārāṇasī.

Together with a thousand followers and my wife, I attended to and honored five hundred Paccekabuddhas.

Having offered them food for the three months of the rainy season, I later offered them sets of triple robes. When we passed away from there, we all reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

When we all passed away from that heaven, we reached the human world again and were born in the city of Kukkuṭavatī near the Himālaya mountains.

I became a famous prince named Kappina. The others were born into ministerial families and surrounded me.

While I was enjoying the happiness of kingship and was endowed with all my desires, I heard the news of the Buddha's arising as told by merchants.

"The Buddha, the peerless and unique person, has arisen in the world. That Blessed One reveals the True Dhamma, the deathless and supreme happiness.

His disciples are well-practiced, well-liberated, and free from taints (āsavas)." Having heard the good words of those merchants and having honored them,

I abandoned the kingdom and, together with the ministers, being one who cherishes the Buddha, I went forth. Seeing the Mahācandā river, which was full to the brim,

without a foothold, without a support, difficult to cross, and flowing swiftly, I recollected the virtues of the Buddha and crossed over safely.

"If the Buddha, the Knower of the world who has reached the end of the world, has indeed crossed the stream of existence, by this word of truth, may my journey be successful."
183:
"If the Path leads to the peace of Nibbāna, and if Nibbāna is indeed absolute happiness, by this word of truth, may my journey be successful.

If the Saṅgha has crossed the difficult wilderness and is the unsurpassed field of merit, by this word of truth, may my journey be successful."

As soon as the noble act of truth was made, the waters moved away from the path. Then I crossed over easily to the delightful riverbank.

I saw the Buddha sitting there, like the rising sun, like a shining golden mountain, like a brilliant lamp-tree.

I beheld the Buddha, like the moon accompanied by stars, surrounded by his disciples, like Sakka raining down the stream of the rain of his teaching.

Having prostrated along with the ministers, I sat at one side. Then, knowing our inclination, the Buddha taught the Dhamma.

Having heard the stainless Dhamma, we said to the Victor: "O Great Hero, we are weary of existence; please grant us ordination."

The Buddha said: "Monks, the Dhamma is well-expounded for the ending of your suffering; lead the holy life."

As soon as he spoke, we all took on the appearance of monks, became fully ordained, and became Stream-enterers (Sotāpannas) in the Dispensation.

From there, going to the Jetavana monastery, the Leader exhorted me. Being exhorted by the Victor, I attained Arahatship.

At that time, I exhorted a thousand monks. Those who followed my exhortation also became free from taints (arahants).

The Victor, pleased with that quality, placed me in the foremost position (Etadagga) among the great multitude, saying: "Kappina is the foremost among those who exhort the monks."

The deed performed a hundred thousand aeons ago has shown its fruit to me here. Like the speed of a released arrow, I have burnt away my defilements.

My defilements are burnt away... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.
184:
After all of them attained Arahantship, they requested ordination from the Blessed One. The Blessed One said to them, "Come, monks (Etha, bhikkhavo)." That very call became their novice ordination (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā). The Blessed One, taking those one thousand monks, traveled through the air to the Jetavana Monastery.

On another day, the Blessed One asked the disciples of that Elder, "Monks, does the Elder Kappina preach the Dhamma to you?" The monks replied, "Venerable Sir, he does not. That Elder lives without concern, devoted only to the bliss of the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra); he does not give even a word of advice."

The Blessed One had the Elder summoned and asked, "Dear Kappina, is it true that you do not give even a word of advice to your disciples?" "It is true, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Brahmin, do not do so. From today onwards, preach the Dhamma to the disciples who approach you," the Blessed One commanded.

"Very well, Venerable Sir," the Elder replied, accepting the Blessed One's words with great respect. With just a single instruction, he established the one thousand monks in Arahantship. Therefore, when the Blessed One was appointing his great disciple Elders to their respective positions in order, he placed that Elder in the foremost position among those who advise monks (bhikkhu-ovādaka). On another day, the Elder, wishing to advise the bhikkhunīs, spoke these verses:

"He who sees both the beneficial and the harmful
In advance, before they arrive—
Whether an enemy or a well-wisher,
Looking for a flaw, they do not see it.

"For him whose mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati)
Is complete and well-developed,
Practiced step-by-step just as taught by the Buddha,
He illuminates this world like the moon released from a cloud.

"Indeed, my mind is pure, immeasurable, and well-developed.
Liberated and penetrating, it illuminates all directions.

"A wise person lives even if his wealth is exhausted;
But without wisdom, even a wealthy person does not truly live.

"Wisdom decides what is heard; wisdom increases fame and renown.
A person endowed with wisdom in this world finds happiness even in sufferings."
185:
"This nature of death is not something of today only; it is not a wonder, nor is it something that has never happened before. Where one is conceived and born, in that very existence one shall surely die; what wonder is there in that? For one who is born, death is certain immediately after life. All beings born in this world die. Beings, having been born, have the nature of reaching death.

"Weeping for the dead does not serve the purpose of their life, nor does it bring renown or worldly benefit to those left behind. Such weeping is not praised by recluses, brahmins, or wise men. By weeping, one harms the eyes and the body; appearance, strength, and wisdom decline. The enemies of the one who weeps rejoice, while well-wishers who desire his benefit cannot be happy.

"Therefore, one should desire to have wise and learned persons in the family. By the power of the wisdom of such wise ones, they can accomplish all their tasks, just as one crosses a full river with a boat."

He spoke these verses. In those verses, 'anāgataṃ' means that which has not yet arrived or is not yet known. 'Paṭikacca' means beforehand. 'Passati' means looking and contemplating. 'Atthaṃ' means the task. 'Taṃ dvayaṃ' means both the beneficial and the harmful. 'Viddesino' means enemies. 'Hitesino' means good friends. 'Randhaṃ' means a hole, a flaw, or a defect. 'Samekkhamānā' means those who are searching.

The meaning is this: A person who sees, investigates, and scrutinizes with the eye of wisdom—just as I do—both the beneficial and harmful tasks before they arrive; his flaws cannot be seen by enemies with ill intentions or by friends with good intentions. Such a wise person is one of flawless conduct. Therefore, you all should be such persons.

Now, wishing to show the virtues of the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) to engage them in that meditation, he spoke the second verse beginning with 'Ānāpānasati yassa'. In that verse, 'āna' is the out-breath, and 'apāna' is the in-breath. In this context, with mindfulness as the forerunner, the development of concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā) associated with that mindfulness of breathing is intended. 'Yassa' means of that practitioner (yogi). 'Paripuṇṇā subhāvitā' means being complete at all times due to the fulfillment of the four foundations of mindfulness and the sixteen aspects, and being well-developed through the fulfillment of the seven factors of enlightenment and true knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti). 'Anupubbaṃ paricitā yathā buddhena desitā' means practiced, cultivated, and developed step-by-step as taught by the Blessed One in the manner of 'mindfully he breathes in,' and so on. 'Somaṃ lokaṃ pabhāseti abbhā muttova candimā' means that practitioner, being liberated from impurities such as clouds...
186:
Āna means exhalation. Apāna means inhalation. Mindfulness that has exhalation and inhalation as its causal object is called ānāpānasati. In this context, with mindfulness as the head, the development of concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā) associated with that mindfulness is intended. "Yassa" means "of that yogi."

"Paripuṇṇā subhāvitā" means being fully perfected at all times through the fulfillment of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and the sixteen modes, and being well-developed and increased through the fulfillment of the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti). "Anupubbaṃ paricitā, yathā buddhena desitā" means being practiced, cultivated, and developed in sequence, just as the Blessed One taught, starting with "He, mindful, breathes in," and so forth.

"Somam lokaṃ pabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā" means that just as the moon, freed from impurities such as clouds, illuminates this world of space (okāsa-loka) with its moonlight, so too that practitioner (yogāvacara), freed from the impurities of defilements such as ignorance (avijjā), illuminates and makes manifest the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka) within their own continuum and the continua of others with the light of knowledge. Therefore, the meaning is that the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati-bhāvanā) should be cultivated by you.

Now, wishing to show the fruitfulness of engaging in meditation by using himself as an example, he spoke the third verse beginning with "Odātaṃ vata me cittaṃ." The meaning of that verse is: My mind is indeed truly pure because of the departure of the impurities of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Just as one abandons passion (rāga) and so forth, which create limits, and realizes the limitless Nibbāna, so too, because of such development, the limitless (Nibbāna) has been well-developed. For that very reason, the Four Noble Truths have been penetrated and realized. Having withdrawn from the entire mass of defilements, and having crossed over doubt regarding the truths such as the truth of suffering and views such as the view of the past (pubbanta-diṭṭhi), and because of the absence of the darkness of delusion (moha) in all phenomena, all directions are bright and clear. Therefore, he shows that you too should develop such a mind.

To show that wisdom resulting from meditation is of great benefit to people through the purification of mental impurities and so forth, and that other types of wisdom are also beneficial, he spoke the fourth verse beginning with "Jīvate vāpi sappañño." The meaning of that verse is: Even if his wealth is exhausted, a person of a wise nature, being content with whatever he gets, lives indeed with a blameless livelihood. His life is truly called living. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "They say that living by wisdom is the best life."

A person of poor intellect, however, because of the lack of wisdom, ruins the benefits of the present and the future...
187:
...(or even if they have wealth), they cannot be said to be living. Their life is merely a descent into the lower realms (apāya). Because of knowing what is not the cause and because of destroying the wealth they have obtained, they cannot sustain their life. Therefore, the meaning is that you should also fulfill protective wisdom (pārihārika-paññā) with heedfulness.

Now, to show the advantages of wisdom, he spoke the fifth verse beginning with "Paññā sutavinicchinī." In that verse, "Paññā sutavinicchinī" means that wisdom has the nature of deciding what has been heard. Regarding the meanings that have reached the ear-door as they were heard, it produces a decision such as: "This is unwholesome, this is wholesome; this is blameworthy, this is blameless."

"Kittisilokavaddhanī" means it increases fame, which is praise in one's presence, and reputation, which is the nature of renown spreading among the people. For it is only for the wise person that fame and so forth arise, because of being praiseworthy by the wise. "Paññāsahito" means being endowed with protective wisdom (pārihārika-paññā) and insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā). "Api dukkhesu sukhāni vindati" means that through right practice regarding the aggregates (khandha) and sense bases (āyatana) etc., which are inherently suffering, and through the penetration and realization of their true nature, one obtains even spiritual (nirāmisa) happiness.

Now, wishing to preach the Dhamma associated with impermanence and conducive to the state of being steadfast (dhīra) to those bhikkhunīs, he spoke the remaining verses beginning with "Nāyaṃ ajjatano dhammo." The summary of the meaning of those verses is: This Dhamma, which is the nature of birth and death of beings, is not something that has just arisen today; it is not a wonder because of its constant occurrence, nor is it a strange thing because it is not something that has never happened before. Therefore, in whatever world a being is born, that being will certainly die. Since death is natural, how could there be anything strange about it? There is no other cause for momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa). The reason is that for one who is born, death is certain after life; immediately after birth, death from life is inevitable because the arisen aggregates (khandha) certainly break up.

The worldly conventional term "living" used here is uncertain (anekantika) because it depends on many conditions for its sustenance. Since this is so, beings born here die; for such is the nature of living beings. This is the natural state of beings. "Yadidaṃ jātānaṃ maraṇaṃ" means that death follows after birth.
188:
At that time, among those bhikkhunīs, some had minds bound by grief. Therefore, to dispel their grief, the words beginning with "Na hetadatthāya" were spoken. In those words, "Na hetadatthāya matassa hoti" means that the weeping of others for the sake of the life of one who has passed away cannot result in the life of that deceased person, nor does it serve the benefit of anyone else. For those who weep, weeping on account of the deceased person brings neither fame nor purity. "Na vaṇṇitaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇehi" means it is not an act praised by the wise; rather, it is an act censured by the wise.

To show that these are not the only disadvantages of weeping, but that there are others as well, the verse beginning with "Cakkhuṃ sarīraṃ upahanti" was spoken. Then, to prevent such harms as grief and to encourage those bhikkhunīs to associate with good friends, the concluding verse beginning with "Tasmā" was spoken. In that verse, "Tasmā" is used because weeping afflicts the eyes and the body of the person who weeps; and because of that weeping, complexion, strength, and wisdom decline; the enemies of that weeping person become joyful and delighted, while friends who wish for their welfare become distressed. Therefore, the wise, who are endowed with wisdom which is the essence of the Dhamma, should desire learned persons who reside in their own clan and make them those who visit their homes, in order to fulfill the learning based on the benefits of the present life and so forth. "Yesaṃ" means that just as people cross a river overflowing with currents by means of a boat through the power of the wisdom of the wise and learned, so too do sons of good family cross over their own affairs and reach the other shore. The connection of the meaning is that one should desire such persons to reside in one's clan.

In this way, the Elder, having preached the Dhamma to those bhikkhunīs, dismissed them. Those bhikkhunīs, established in the Elder's advice, dispelled their grief, practiced appropriately, and fulfilled their own welfare.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Mahākappina Thera is finished.
189:
## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Cūḷapanthaka Thera

The verse beginning with "Dandhā mayhaṃ gati" is that of the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka Thera. How did it arise? Regarding the circumstances of its origin, it has already been told in the Mahāpanthaka story in the Aṭṭhakanipāta. The following is the specific detail. The Venerable Mahāpanthaka, having attained Arahantship and spending his time in the supreme bliss of Phalasamāpatti, thought, "How can I establish Cūḷapanthaka in this bliss as well?" The Elder approached his grandfather, the merchant Dhana, and said, "Great Merchant, if you permit, I would like to ordain Cūḷapanthaka." "Venerable Sir, please ordain him," he replied, and so the Elder ordained Cūḷapanthaka. While established in the ten precepts and staying with his elder brother—

"Look at Angīrasa (the Buddha) shining,
Like the sun glowing in the sky,
Like a fragrant red Kokanuda lotus,
Blooming in the morning with its scent unfaded."

Though he tried to learn this verse, he was unable to do so for four months. Whatever words he learned did not remain in his heart. Then the Venerable Mahāpanthaka said to him, "Panthaka, you are unfit for this Sasana. If you cannot learn even a single verse in four months, how will you bring the work of a monk to its consummation? Leave this monastery." Expelled by the Elder, Cūḷapanthaka stood weeping near the gateway.

At that time, the Teacher was staying in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Then Jīvaka sent a man, saying, "Invite the Teacher together with five hundred monks." At that time, the Venerable Mahāpanthaka was the assigner of meals (bhattuddesaka). When requested, "Venerable Sir, please accept the meal for five hundred monks," the Venerable Mahāpanthaka said, "I accept for the rest, excluding Cūḷapanthaka." Hearing this, Cūḷapanthaka became exceedingly distressed. The Teacher, knowing his mental exhaustion, thought, "Cūḷapanthaka will realize through the means I provide," and showing himself in a place not far from him, asked, "Panthaka, why are you weeping?" "Venerable Sir, my elder brother is expelling me," he replied. "Panthaka, do not worry. In my Sasana, there is monkhood for you. Come, take this piece of cloth and contemplate, 'Taking away impurity, taking away impurity' (rajoharaṇaṃ)," and the Teacher gave him a clean piece of cloth created by psychic power.

Cūḷapanthaka sat rubbing the piece of cloth given by the Teacher with his hand, saying, "Taking away impurity, taking away impurity." As he rubbed the cloth, it reached a state of being soiled. Rubbing it again, it became like a cloth used for wiping soot. Because Cūḷapanthaka's wisdom had matured, he thought, "This piece of cloth was originally pure, but because of this body (upādinnaka-rūpa), it has become soiled. Therefore, it is impermanent. Just as this cloth is impermanent, so too is the mind." Contemplating rise and fall (khaya-vaya), he developed jhāna based on that sign, and then, developing insight (vipassanā) based on jhāna, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna—
190:
He sat down, rubbing with his hand the piece of cloth given by the Teacher, [contemplating], "Rajoharaṇaṃ, rajoharaṇaṃ" (Taking away impurity, taking away impurity). As he rubbed it, the cloth became soiled. Rubbing it again, it became as dirty as a rag used for wiping a cooking pot.

Because his wisdom was mature, Cūḷapanthaka thought: "This piece of cloth was originally pure. Because of this clung-to body (upādinnaka-sarīra), it has become soiled and changed. Therefore, just as this cloth is impermanent, so too is the mind." Contemplating rise and fall, he attained the jhānas on that very sign (nimitta). Using the jhānas as a basis for insight (vipassanā), he attained Arhatship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Victor named Padumuttara, worthy of receiving offerings brought from afar, was then dwelling in seclusion from the group in the Himalayas.

I too was then living in a hermitage in the Himalayas; I approached the Great Hero, the Leader of the World, who had recently arrived.

Taking a flower-parasol, I approached the Bull among Men; I warded off [other sensory] dangers before the Buddha who was entering concentration.

Raising the flower-parasol with both hands, I offered it; the Blessed One, the Great Sage Padumuttara, accepted it.

All the devas, being joyful, came to the Himalayas; they uttered cries of 'Sādhu', saying, 'The One with Vision will express appreciation (anumodanā).'

Having said this, those devas approached the Best of Men, while the noble lotus-parasol remained held in the air [over the Buddha].

'This hermit raised a hundred-petaled lotus-parasol and offered it to me; I shall praise the merit of that hermit, listen to my words.' (Thus the Buddha spoke).

'For twenty-five aeons, he will exercise the sovereignty of devas; and thirty-four times, he will be a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).

In whatever state of birth he wanders, whether as a deva or a human, whenever he stands in the open, a lotus will [automatically] provide him shade.'"
191:
" 'In a hundred thousand aeons from now, the Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka lineage, will arise in the world.

When the Dispensation (Sāsana) shines forth, he will obtain human birth; among those with mind-made bodies (manomaya-kāya), he will be the most excellent.

There will be two brothers, both named Panthaka; both having experienced the supreme goal of Arhatship, they will illuminate the Dispensation.'

That person was I, who at the age of eighteen, went forth from home to the homeless life; yet I did not attain any distinction in the Dispensation of the Son of the Sakyans.

My progress in wisdom was slow; because I had disparaged [the slow-witted] in the past, I was treated with contempt; even my elder brother expelled me, saying, 'Go home now.'

Being thus expelled, I stood at the gate of the monastery with a troubled mind, yet still longing for the state of a monk.

The Blessed One came to that place and stroked my head; taking me by the arm, He led me into the monastery.

Out of compassion for me, the Teacher gave me a foot-wiping cloth; He said, 'Resolve upon this pure cloth,' and I remained in one place making that resolution.

Taking that foot-wiping cloth in my hands, while I contemplated its color which had become like a red lotus, my mind was liberated from the taints (kilesas), and I attained Arhatship.

In creating mind-made bodies, I have reached the pinnacle in all respects; having fully understood all taints (āsavas), I dwell free from taints.'

'The four analytical insights... (etc.) I have followed the instructions of the Buddha.'"

Together with the Path of Arhatship, the Three Piṭakas and the five higher knowledges (abhiññā) came to that venerable one. The Teacher, together with five hundred monks less one, went and sat on the prepared seats in Jīvaka's house. Cūḷapanthaka, however, did not go because he had not yet been invited for the alms-meal. When Jīvaka began to offer the gruel, the Teacher covered the bowl with His hand. When asked, "Venerable Sir, why do you not accept it?", He said, "Jīvaka, there is one monk left at the monastery." Jīvaka sent a man, saying, "Go, fellow, and invite the venerable one sitting at the monastery."

The Elder Cūḷapanthaka created a thousand monks, each differing from the other in appearance and posture, and sat there. That man, seeing many monks at the monastery, returned and told Jīvaka, "There are more monks at the monastery than in this Saṅgha; I do not know which venerable one to invite." Jīvaka asked the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, what is the name of the monk sitting at the monastery?" When He said, "Jīvaka, his name is Cūḷapanthaka," Jīvaka commanded again, "Go, fellow, ask 'Who is the monk named Cūḷapanthaka?' and bring him." The man went to the monastery and asked, "Venerable sirs, who is the monk named Cūḷapanthaka?" All thousand monks said, "I am Cūḷapanthaka, I am Cūḷapanthaka." The man returned again and reported this matter, and Jīvaka...
192:
"... Fetch (that venerable one) and come," (he ordered). Cūḷapanthaka Thera also created a thousand monks, none of whom were identical to each other in appearance or posture, and sat there. The man, seeing the great number of monks in the monastery, returned and said to Jīvaka, "There are many more monks in the monastery than this Saṅgha of monks; I do not know which venerable one to invite."

Jīvaka asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, what is the name of the monk sitting in the monastery?" "Jīvaka, his name is Cūḷapanthaka," the Buddha replied. "Go, friend, ask 'Who is Cūḷapanthaka?' and bring that venerable one," Jīvaka ordered again. The man went to the monastery and asked, "Venerable sirs, which one is Cūḷapanthaka?" "I am Cūḷapanthaka," all thousand monks replied simultaneously. The man returned and informed Jīvaka of the situation.

Jīvaka, being one who had penetrated the Four Noble Truths, realized through deduction, "The venerable one must possess psychic powers." He said, "Go, friend, and say to the very first one who speaks, 'The Blessed One calls for you,' and take hold of the corner of his robe." The man went to the monastery and did as instructed; at that moment, the created monks vanished. He then escorted the Elder.

At that moment, the Blessed One accepted the rice gruel and various snacks. After finishing the meal, when the Blessed One returned to the monastery, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall: "How wonderful is the power of the Buddhas! Indeed, they could make even one who was unable to learn a single verse for four months become one of such great psychic power in just a short moment."

The Blessed One, hearing the conversation of those monks, came and sat on the Buddha's seat. He asked, "Monks, what are you discussing?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, Cūḷapanthaka has now established himself in my instruction and received the supramundane inheritance; in the past, however, he received a mundane inheritance." At the request of the monks, he then told the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka.

Later, while the Blessed One was seated on the Dhamma throne surrounded by the assembly of Noble Ones, he placed Cūḷapanthaka in the foremost position among those monks who create mind-made bodies and those skilled in mental transformation (cetovivaṭṭa). On another occasion, when asked by the monks, "How did you, being so dull-witted, penetrate the Truths?" he revealed his practice, starting from the time his elder brother expelled him:

"My progress was slow; formerly, I was despised.
My brother even expelled me, saying, 'Go home now!'"
193:
While the Blessed One was seated on the Dhamma throne surrounded by the assembly of Noble Ones, he placed the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka in the foremost position among those monks who create mind-made bodies and those skilled in mental transformation (cetovivaṭṭa). On a later occasion, when the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka was asked by the monks, "How did you, being so dull-witted, penetrate the Four Noble Truths?" he spoke as follows, wishing to reveal his practice starting from the time his elder brother expelled him:

"My progress was slow; formerly, I was despised. My brother even expelled me, saying, 'Go home now!' Being thus expelled, I stood at the gate of the monastery, dejected, yet still longing for the Dispensation. The Blessed One came there and stroked my head; taking me by the arm, he led me into the monastery. Out of compassion, the Teacher gave me a clean foot-wiping cloth, saying, 'Meditate on this well-resolved foot-wiping cloth in a suitable place.'

Having heard the words of the Blessed One, I dwelt delighting in the Dispensation; I fulfilled the concentration of the path of Arahatship for the attainment of the supreme goal of Arahatship. I know my past lives; the divine eye has been purified. The three knowledges (tevijjā) have been attained; the Buddha's bidding has been done. Having created myself a thousandfold, I, Panthaka, sat in the delightful Jīvaka's mango grove until the time for the meal was announced. Furthermore, the Teacher sent a messenger to me to announce the time for the meal; when the time was announced, I approached the Buddha through the air. Having paid homage to the Teacher's feet, I sat to one side; knowing that I was seated, the Teacher accepted my homage. The Blessed One, worthy of the supreme offerings of the whole world, worthy of offerings brought from afar, the field of merit for mankind, accepted the gift offered by Jīvaka."

He spoke these verses. In those verses, *dandhā* means dull, being weak in the sense of being unable to learn a four-line verse in four months. *Gati* means the course of wisdom. *Āsi* means it was. *Paribhūto* means despised and insulted as "one of muddled mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension" for that very reason. *Pure* means formerly, during the time of being a worldling. In the phrase *bhātā ca*, the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction; it means not only was I despised, but my brother also expelled me, saying, "Panthaka, you are unintelligent, rootless (ahetuka), I think; therefore, you are unable to bring the monk's task to its peak. You are not worthy of this Dispensation; go to the perpetual state of a householder."

*Saṅghārāmassa* means of the monastery; *koṭṭhake* means near the gate; *dummano* means with a dejected heart. *Sāsanasmiṃ apekhavā* means having longing for the Blessed One's Dispensation, implying he had no desire to return to lay life. *Bhagavā tattha āဂစ္ဆိ* means the Blessed One, whose mind was urged by great compassion and who wished to favor me, at whichever gate...
194:
The elder brother said, "You are incapable, not worthy of this Sasana; go now to your grandfather's house," and expelled him. 'Bhātā' means by the brother (bhātarā). 'Koṭṭhake' means near the gateway. 'Dummano' means having reached a state of unhappiness (domanassa). 'Sāsanasmim apekkhavā' means having regard for the Blessed One's Sasana and not wishing to return to lay life.

The Blessed One came to that place. Driven by great compassion and wishing to favor me, the Blessed One came to that gateway where I was standing. Having come, He comforted me, saying, "Panthaka, I am your teacher, not Mahāpanthaka. Your renunciation was intended for Me." He then stroked my head with His palm, which was adorned with fingers that were soft, slender, and long like a golden net, glorious like a blooming lotus, and marked with the wheel-mark, as if to show, "Now he will become my son."
