Saying, "Why are you standing here?" He took me by the arm with His hand, which was fragrant with the scent of sandalwood, and led me into the Saṅghārāma. He gave me a piece of foot-wiping cloth. It means He gave it saying, "Contemplate this as 'rajoharaṇaṃ' (dirt-remover)." Some read it as "adāsi pāda-puñchanim." Some teachers say, "He gave a piece of foot-wiping cloth." This is inappropriate because He gave the piece of cloth by creating it through psychic power.

He said, "Having well-established this pure piece of cloth by contemplating 'rajoharaṇaṃ, rajoharaṇaṃ,' sit in a secluded spot at the front of the Gandhakuṭi and establish it; thus, make the mind concentrated and proceed."

Having heard the words of that Blessed One, I remained delighted in that Sasana and its instruction, and practiced as I was taught. While practicing, I fulfilled concentration for the attainment of the noble fruition of Arahatship. 'Uttamattha' refers to the fruition of Arahatship. It means that to attain that Arahatship, I produced the fine-material jhānas through the power of kasiṇa-preliminary work, and then, establishing insight based on jhāna, I fulfilled the concentration of the highest path (Arahatship) through the sequence of the paths. Here, 'concentration' (samādhi) includes general concentration from access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) up to the concentration of the fourth path. The concentration of the fruition of Arahatship is taken by the term 'uttamatttha.' Because this venerable one is exceedingly skilled in concentration, it is said, "I fulfilled concentration." As for the other Mahāpanthaka Thera, he is skilled in the immaterial...
195:
That statement is true. Because of his skill in concentration, this Venerable Cūḷapanthaka is called 'one skilled in the liberation of mind' (cetovivaṭṭa-kusala). Mahāpanthaka, however, because of his skill in insight, is called 'one skilled in the liberation through perception' (saññāvivaṭṭa-kusala). Between these two, one elder is skilled in the characteristics of concentration, while the other is skilled in the characteristics of insight. One delights in concentration, the other in insight. One is skilled in summarizing the factors (anga), the other in summarizing the objects (ārammaṇa). One is skilled in defining the factors, the other in defining the objects—so it is explained.

In fact, Cūḷapanthaka is called 'skilled in the liberation of mind' because he attained the four fine-material jhānas with excellence. Mahāpanthaka is called 'skilled in the liberation through perception' because he attained the four immaterial jhānas with excellence. Alternatively, the former, Cūḷapanthaka, having attained the fine-material jhānas and emerging from the jhāna factors, reached Arahatship; thus he is called 'skilled in the liberation of mind.' The other, Mahāpanthaka, having attained the immaterial jhānas and emerging from the jhāna factors, reached Arahatship; thus he is called 'skilled in the liberation through perception.'

To say more: when creating a mind-made psychic body, other individuals create three or four or many, but they make them all identical to themselves. They create them while performing a single type of action. This elder, however, created a thousand monks with a single thought-advertence (āvajjanā). He did not make even two monks identical in body, nor did he make them perform the same type of action. Therefore, he is called the foremost (agga) among those who create mind-made bodies.

Now, to show the special attainment he reached, he said the words beginning with "Pubbenivāsaṃ jānāmi" (I know past lives). Although this elder possessed the six higher knowledges (abhiññā), in order to show that higher knowledge which is of great help in attaining the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), he said, "I know past lives, the divine eye is purified," and then "The three knowledges have been attained." Indeed, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) are of great help to the practice of insight. Other knowledges are not as helpful.

'Sahassakkhattuṃ' means a thousand. Some say "a thousand times." But the elder created a thousand mind-made bodies with a single thought-advertence, not by creating them one after another. He created those persons to be unlike each other and performing various tasks. If asked, "Is such psychic creation possible for other disciples (sāvaka) as well?" the answer is that it is not possible for all disciples. However, due to the perfection of his aspiration (abhinīhāra), only this Venerable Cūḷapanthaka could do this. That is why he was placed in the foremost position (etadagga) in this regard for this reason. "Panthako nisīdi" (Panthaka sat down) is speaking of himself as if he were another person. "Ambavane" means in the Mango Grove monastery donated by Jīvaka. "Vehāsā" is in the ablative case, meaning "through the sky." The letter "da" is inserted for euphonic junction. "Atha" means "after I had sat down." "Paṭiggahī" means "He accepted the noble water of donation." "Āyāgo sabbalokassa" means "the object of sacrifice for the entire world including the devas..."
196:
It was in the monastery built by Jīvaka. In the word "vehasādupaṅkamiṃti," "vehasā" is the use of the ablative case in the sense of the instrumental, meaning "vehasena" (by way of the sky); the letter "da" is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhi). "Atha" means after my sitting. "Paṭiggahī" means he accepted the noble water of donation (dakkhiṇodaka). "Āyāgo sabbalokassa" means that because he is worthy of the highest offerings from the entire world including the devas, he is the place where offerings should be brought and sacrificed. "Āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho" means he is the one who accepts noble offerings by making them yield great fruit. "Paṭiggaṇhittha dakkhiṇaṃ" means he accepted the noble offering consisting of various items such as gruel and food brought by Jīvaka.

Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal, commanded the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, "Perform the appreciation (anumodanā)." That Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, having attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), stirred the word of the Buddha—the Tipitaka—as if grasping Mount Sineru and churning the great ocean, and gave the appreciation according to the Teacher's intention. Although he was endowed with such strong supporting conditions (upanissaya), this venerable one had been unable to learn even a single four-line verse for four months, being oppressed by such remnants of past karma (kammapilotikā). Seeing the perfection of his supporting conditions, the Teacher directed him towards wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) in accordance with his past practices. Indeed, while the Blessed One was sitting in Jīvaka's house, knowing that "Cūḷapanthaka's mind is concentrated; his insight (vipassanā) has entered the path," he manifested himself exactly as he was sitting and, wishing to show, "Panthaka, just as this piece of cloth is soiled and covered with dust, there is another kind of soilure and dust in the discipline of the Noble Ones," he spoke these verses:

"Lust is called dust, but actual dust (reṇu) is not called dust;
'Dust' is a designation for lust.
Having abandoned this dust, the monks
Live in the teaching of the One who is free from dust.

"Hatred is called dust... (and so on) ...live in the teaching.

"Delusion is called dust... (and so on) ...live in the teaching of the One who is free from dust."

He spoke these three verses of radiance (obhāsa-gāthā). At the conclusion of the verses, Venerable Cūḷapanthaka attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges and supernormal powers.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Cūḷapanthaka is Finished.
197:
## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Kappa Thera

The verse beginning with "Nānākulamalasampuṇṇo" is that of the Venerable Kappa Thera. As for the background: This venerable one had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit in various lives. In the time of Siddhattha Buddha, he was born into a wealthy family. After his father's death, upon reaching maturity, he decorated a wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha) with various colorful and exquisite garments, numerous ornaments, precious gems, flower garlands, and so forth, and offered it to the Teacher's stupa. Due to that meritorious deed, he wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, he was born into a provincial royal family in the Magadha country. After his father's death, he was established in kingship and lived greatly attached to and greedy for sensual pleasures. The Blessed One, emerging from the attainment of great compassion and surveying the world, saw him appearing in the net of his knowledge. Reflecting on "What will happen?", he knew, "If this king hears a discourse on foulness (asubhakathā) from me, his mind will become detached from sensual pleasures, he will ordain and attain Arahantship." Thus, he traveled there through the air and taught as follows:

Full of various kinds of impurities, born from a great heap of excrement,
Like a ripened cesspool, like a great boil, like a great wound.

Full of pus and blood, immersed in a pit of dung,
This body, with liquids trickling out, always flows with putrid matter.

Bound together by sixty large sinews, plastered with the coating of flesh,
Wrapped in the garment of skin, this putrid body is useless.

Joined together by a collection of bones, tied with the strings of tendons,
Due to the combination of many (elements and bases), it maintains its postures.

Constantly moving towards death, in the presence of the King of Death,
Man, who goes wherever he desires, must discard this body right here in this world.

This body is covered by ignorance, tied by the four bonds (gantha),
Sinking in the four floods (ogha), this body is overwhelmed by the net of latent tendencies (anusaya).

Joined with the five hindrances, afflicted by thought (vitakka),
Followed by the root of craving, it is shrouded by the darkness of delusion.
198:
## 
"This body revolves, bound by the machine of kamma; prosperity ends in ruin, and through separation, it falls into decay.

Foolish worldlings cherish this body, thinking 'it is mine.' They increase the dreadful cemetery and take up new existence again.

The wise who avoid this body like a snake smeared with dung, having vomited the craving that is the root of existence, will attain Parinibbāna, free from taints."

With these verses, He preached the discourse on foulness (asubha-kathā) to King Maṇḍalika. Having heard the discourse on foulness, which explained the true nature of the body in various ways and in accordance with reality in the presence of the Blessed One, King Maṇḍalika became weary of, ashamed of, and disgusted with his own body. With a stirred heart, he paid homage to the Blessed One and requested ordination, saying, "Venerable Sir, I wish to receive ordination in the presence of the Blessed One." The Blessed One commanded a monk standing nearby, "Go, monk, ordain this man, grant him higher ordination, and bring him back." That monk gave him the meditation on the five parts ending in skin (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. At the very end of the shaving of his hair, he attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the presence of the noble stupa of the Blessed One Siddhattha, I hung exquisite cloths and set up a wish-fulfilling tree (kappa-rukkha).

In whatever state I was reborn, whether as a deity or a human, a wish-fulfilling tree stood beautifying my door.

I and my retinue, whoever were dependent on me, always took cloths from that tree and wore them.

Ninety-four aeons ago, I set up that tree. Since then, I have not known a woeful state; this is the fruit of offering a wish-fulfilling tree.

Seven aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, there were eight powerful wheel-turning kings (cakkavatti) named Suceḷa, endowed with the seven jewels.

The four analytical insights... the teaching of the Buddha has been carried out."
199:
## 
Having attained Arahantship and received higher ordination, that elder approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and while sitting in a suitable place, recited those same verses to declare his attainment of Arahantship. Because of this, those verses became known as Theragāthā.

In those verses, 'nānākulamalasaṃpuṇṇo' means a body full of various kinds of impurities that are its parts; it is filled with various impure components such as hair, body hair, and so on. 'Mahāukkārasambhavo': 'ukkāra' refers to a cesspool. For as long as the mother's age [during pregnancy], the mother's womb is intended here as a 'great cesspool' because of its similarity to a latrine that has been cleaned for that duration. 'Mahāukkārasambhavo' means one whose place of birth or origin is that womb. 'Candanikaṃvā': 'candanika' is a place for discarding wash-water, filth, and other impurities. It means a place of such a nature, filled with impure things up to the knees. 'Paripakkaṃ' means matured or old. Therefore, it shows that this body is of such a nature, just as at the gate of a Caṇḍāla village in the summer, when it rains with large drops, a ditch (candanikā-vāṭa) stands surrounded by water, filled with various corpses such as urine, excrement, bones, skin, tendons, saliva, and snot, stirred with muddy water, swarming with various kinds of worms after a few days, boiling from the heat of the sun, emitting foam and bubbles on top, deep blue in color, extremely foul-smelling, and disgusting, such that no one would dare to approach or look at it.

Because it is always associated with the cause of suffering, because it oozes impure things, and because it has the nature of swelling, maturing, and breaking due to birth, aging, and death, it is called 'mahāgaṇḍo' (a great boil), like a large abscess. Because it is followed by painful feelings in all respects, because it endures the strikes of wounds, and because it oozes impure things, it is called 'mahāvaṇo' (a great wound), like a large old sore. 'Gūthakūpena gāဠိတော' means filled only with excrement in a cesspool. There is also a reading 'gūthakūpanigāဠှိတော', which means one who has come out of a cesspool. 'Āpopaggharaṇo kāယော သဒါ သန္ဒတိ ပူတိကံ' means this body has the nature of always oozing with the liquid element (āpo-dhātu). In that oozing, it only flows with foul and impure things such as bile, phlegm, sweat, and urine; it never flows with anything pure.

'Saṭṭhikaဏ္ဍရသမ္ဗန္ဓော' means starting from the upper part of the neck, there are twenty tendons binding the body, with five each on the front, back, right, and left sides of the body; and those binding the hands and feet, with five each on the front and back sides of them...
200:
Because it is bound and entwined in every way by sixty large tendons connected to the limbs, it is called 'saṭṭhikaṇḍarasambandha' (connected by sixty tendons). 'Maṃsalepanalepita' means smeared with the plaster called flesh, smeared with nine hundred pieces of flesh. 'Cammakañcukasaṇṇaddha' means completely covered, entwined, and delimited by the casing called skin. 'Pūtikāya' means a body that has a foul smell in every way. 'Niratthaka' means a useless body. While the bodies of other beings may be useful through the use of their skin, tendons, etc., the human body is not useful in that way. 'Aṭṭhisaṅghātaghaṭita' means joined and connected by a collection of more than three hundred bones. 'Nhārusuttanibandhana' means constantly bound by nine hundred tendons which are like threads. Due to the meeting of those tendons, and due to the harmonious combination of the four great elements, the life faculty, in-breath and out-breath, consciousness, and so on, it brings about postures such as standing, like a mechanical machine, just as threads meet and harmonize.

'Dhuvappayāto maraṇāya' means definitely journeying for the sake of death, proceeding towards death from the moment of conception. For that very reason, it stands in the presence of death, which is the King of Death (Maccu-rāja). 'Idheva chaḍḍayitvāna' means having abandoned the body in this very world, this being goes to the place of its desire; therefore, it shows that one should not have attachment, thinking, "This body must be abandoned and gone from."

'Avijjāya nivuto' means covered by the hindrance of ignorance, thus the fault is hidden; the meaning is, if the fault were seen in another way, who would develop attachment to this body? 'Catuganthena' means bound by the four bonds such as the bodily bond of covetousness, entwined by the state of being bound. 'Oghasaṃsīdana' means sinking in the four floods such as the flood of sensual desire by the state of being flood-prone. Because they repeatedly lie latent in the mental continuum by way of not being abandoned, sensual lust and so on are called 'anusaya' (underlying tendencies). Because it is overwhelmed and oppressed by the net of those underlying tendencies, it is called 'anusayajālamotthata'. The letter 'ma' is a word-connector; it is spoken by making it long for the sake of ease in reciting the verse. Because it is joined and inclined towards the five hindrances such as sensual desire, it is called 'pañcanīvaraṇe yutto'; here, the locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. Because it is attended by wrong thoughts such as thoughts of sensual desire, it is called 'vitakkena samappito'. It is followed by the root of existence called craving. It is covered by the obstruction called delusion (sammoha). All this is said in reference to the physical body (karaja-kāya) together with consciousness. In the Pali passages such as "Monks, the body of the Tathāgata stands with the cord that leads to existence cut," and "This body and the name-and-form outside," it is called 'kāya'. In the Pali passages such as "Thus it is full of various kinds of filth" and "Covered by ignorance," this body exists in the manner already described. Even though it exists, it is joined by the machine of kamma, the machine called kamma consisting of good and bad deeds. Just as one is unable to go to a place of safety, because of such agitation, it revolves in the happy and unhappy realms.
201:
Because it is attended by wrong thoughts such as thoughts of sensual desire, it is called 'vitakkena samappito' (attended by thought). 'Taṇhāmūlenānugato' means following by the root of existence called craving. 'Mohacchādanachādito' means covered by the obstruction called delusion (sammoha). All this is said in reference to the physical body (karaja-kāya) together with consciousness.

The individual existence (attabhāva) with consciousness is called 'kāya' in the Pali scriptures such as: "Monks, the body of the Tathāgata stands with the cord that leads to existence cut; this body and the name-and-form outside." "Thus this body exists" means this body arises in the manner described in the Pali scriptures such as "full of various kinds of filth" and "covered by ignorance." While it so arises, it remains joined by the machine of kamma called kamma consisting of good and bad deeds. Or, just as one is unable to go to a place of safety, because of such agitation, it revolves in the happy and unhappy realms.

"Sampatti ca vipatyantā" means the prosperity and happiness obtained in this revolving end in ruin. All youth ends in old age, all health ends in sickness, all life ends in death, and all meeting ends in parting. Therefore, He said: "nānābhāvo vipajjati" (it perishes in various ways). 'Nānābhāvo' means separation. That separation occurs in various ways, sometimes by the power of the one who separates, and sometimes by the power of the one to be separated from.

"Yemaṃ kāyaṃ mamāyanti" means those foolish worldlings who, regarding this unattractive, impermanent, unstable, painful, and coreless body as "this is mine," cherish it and give rise to desire and lust. Those people, through rebirth and so on, and through hell and so on, repeatedly increase saṃsāra—which is called a cemetery, fearful and terrifying, and enjoyed by the unwise—through birth, death, and so on. Therefore, He said: "ādiyanti punabbhavaṃ" (they take up renewed existence).

"Yemaṃ kāyaṃ vivajjenti gūthalittaṃva pannagaṃ" means, for example, just as a man desiring happiness and wishing to live, upon seeing a snake with fierce poison in dung, avoids it and does not cling to it because it is loathsome or because it is dangerous; in the same way, wise men of good family avoid and abandon this body—which is loathsome due to its impurity and dangerous due to its impermanence and so on—by abandoning desire and lust. They, having vomited and discarded ignorance and craving for existence, which are the roots of existence, and having abandoned them completely, will become entirely free from taints and attain Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element with residue and the Nibbāna element without residue.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Kappa is finished.

10-Dasakanipāta, 38-Upasenatheragāthā. The verses beginning with "Vivittaṃ appampi santi" are the verses of the Venerable Upasena. It is heard that this Venerable Upasena, in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara...
202:
## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Upasena Vangantaputta

"Vivittaṃ appanigghosaṃ" and so forth is the verse of the Venerable Elder Upasena. What is its origin? It is said that this Venerable Upasena was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Upon reaching maturity, he went to the presence of the Teacher and, while listening to the Dhamma, saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the foremost position among those who are pleasing in every way (samantapāsādika). He performed a great act of merit for the Teacher and aspired to that position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was born in this Buddha's era in the village of Nālaka in the womb of the Brahmin lady Rūpasārī, and was named Upasena.

When he reached maturity, he learned the three Vedas. After hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he gained faith and went forth into the homeless life. When he had reached one year of seniority (vassa) after his higher ordination, thinking, "I shall increase the Noble lineage," he ordained a young man in his presence and went with that disciple to the Teacher. When the Teacher heard that he was the preceptor of that monk who had not yet completed a single year of seniority, he rebuked him, saying, "Vain man (mogha-purisa), you have turned too quickly toward abundance (of followers)."

Thinking, "Now, just as I have been rebuked by the Teacher because of my followers, I shall also be praised by the Teacher because of my followers," he strove in the practice of insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahatship. Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna:

"I approached the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Chief of the World, the Bull among Men, the Supreme Man, as he sat in a mountain cave.

Seeing a Kaṇikāra flower, I cut it at the stem, and having decorated a parasol with it, I offered it to the Buddha.

I also gave alms-food, excellent food with fine flavors. In that cave, I fed nine monks, with the Buddha at the head.

The Great Hero, the Self-Enlightened One, the Supreme Person, expressed appreciation (anumodanā) thus: 'By this gift of a parasol, by the offering of excellent food,

And by that clarity of mind, you shall enjoy prosperity. Thirty-six times you shall be the King of Gods and exercise divine sovereignty.

Twenty-one times you shall be a Wheel-turning Monarch. As for the status of a regional king, it shall be vast and beyond counting.'"
203:
"One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka line, will appear in the world.

In the dispensation of that Buddha, you will reach the state of a human. You will be an heir to his Dhamma, a legitimate son, created by the Dhamma.

By the name Upasena, you will be a disciple of the Teacher. He will place you in the foremost position among those who are pleasing in every way (samantapāsādika).

This is my final existence; all births have been uprooted. Having conquered Māra and his host, I bear this final body.

The four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā)... and so forth (have been realized); the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled," thus he said.

Even after reaching Arahatship, he himself undertook and practiced all the ascetic qualities (dhutaṅga) and encouraged others for that purpose. Therefore, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position among the monks who are pleasing in every way. At a later time, when a dispute arose in Kosambī and the Saṅgha of monks was split in two, a certain monk who wished to avoid that dispute asked, "Now a dispute has arisen and the Saṅgha is split; how should I practice?" Desiring to explain the practice to him, starting from living in seclusion, he spoke these verses:

A monk should resort to a dwelling that is secluded, with little noise, and inhabited by wild beasts, for the sake of solitary meditation.

Having brought rags from dust heaps, from cemeteries, and from the streets, and having made a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) from them, he should wear coarse robes.

With a humble mind, going from house to house in continuous alms-round (sapadāna), a monk should wander for alms with guarded sense-doors and well-restrained.

He should be content even with coarse food and should not crave many other flavors. The mind of one who is greedy for flavors does not delight in meditation (jhāna).

Being of few desires, content, and secluded, the sage should live without socializing with both householders and the homeless.
204:
A wise monk should present himself as if he were dull or mute. In the midst of the Saṅgha, he should not speak excessively.

That monk should not revile anyone; he should avoid causing harm. He should be one who is restrained in the Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla (virtue of restraint according to the Disciplinary Code). He should also be one who knows the proper measure in the food he consumes.

He should be skilled in giving rise to a mind that has a well-grasped sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta). He should devote himself to the practice of serenity (samatha-bhāvanā) and, at the proper time, also to the practice of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā).

Endowed with steadfast energy and perseverance, he should always be constantly engaged in meditation (bhāvanā). A wise monk should not live complacently [abandoning effort] without having reached Nibbāna, which is the end of suffering.

For a monk who lives in this manner and desires purity, all taints (āsavas) are exhausted, and he attains Nibbāna. Thus, the Buddha spoke these verses.

In those verses, "vivitta" (secluded) refers to a place such as a forest that is secluded from people. "Appanigghosa" (quiet) refers to a place that is silent and free from the roar of sound. "Vāḷamiganisevita" (haunted by wild beasts) refers to a place frequented by wild animals such as lions, tigers, and leopards. By this, the Buddha shows seclusion from people by indicating the nature of remote lodgings (panta-senāsana). "Senāsana" (lodging) here means a dwelling place suitable for sleeping and residing. "Paṭisallānakāraṇā" (for the sake of seclusion) means for the purpose of seclusion; withdrawing the mind from various objects to make it adhere well only to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

After thus showing contentment with lodgings suitable for meditation, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "saṅkārapuñjā" to show contentment with robes and other requisites. "Saṅkārapuñjā" means from a heap of rubbish, from a place where refuse is discarded. "Āhatvā" means having brought or collected. "Tato" means with those collected pieces of cloth; here, the ablative case (pañcamī vibhatti) is used in the sense of the instrumental case (karaṇa). "Lūkhaṃ" (coarse) refers to unrefined clothing that is poor in quality of thread or dye. "Dhāreyya" means he should wear or carry it as a robe; by this, contentment with robes is spoken of.

"Nīcaṃ manaṃ karitvāna" (having made the mind humble) means having made the mind one in which pride and arrogance are destroyed, by remembering the instruction of the Buddha (Sugata) such as: "Monks, among the ways of living, this life of begging is the lowest..." (Itivuttaka 91, Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.80). "Sapadānaṃ" means...
205:
...wandering in order from house to house without skipping any house. Therefore, the Buddha said "kulā kulaṃ." "Kulā kulaṃ" means wandering from one family to another in the sequence of houses. "Piṇḍikāya" means for the sake of mixed alms-food; by this, contentment with alms-food is spoken of. "Guttadvāro" means one who has well-closed and guarded sense doors, such as the eyes. "Susaṃvuto" means well-restrained due to the absence of restlessness of hands and feet.

In the phrase "lūkhena pi vā" (or even with coarse [requisites]), the word "api" is used in a conjunctive sense, and the word "vā" is used in an alternative sense. One should be well-satisfied with whatever is easily obtained, whether it be coarse or meager. Therefore, the Buddha said "nāññaṃ patthe rasaṃ bahuṃ." "Nāññaṃ patthe rasaṃ bahuṃ" means he should not long for or desire any taste other than what he has received, such as sweets, nor should he desire abundant or excellent food. By this, contentment with medicinal requisites (gilāna-paccaya) is also shown. To state the reason for preventing greed for tastes, the Buddha said: "The mind of one who is excessively greedy for tastes does not delight in jhāna." The meaning is: for one who does not fulfill the restraint of the senses, how can there be concentration of a scattered mind?

After thus showing the practice of effacement (sallekha-paṭipatti) regarding the four requisites, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "appiccho ceva" to show the remaining subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu). Therein, "appiccho" (having few desires) means having no desire for the four requisites. By that term, the Buddha speaks of the displacement (vikkhamphana) of the arising of craving for the four requisites. "Santuṭṭho" (content) means one who is content with whatever is obtained of the four requisites. It is said: "One who does not grieve for the past, does not long for the future, and sustains himself with the present is called 'content'."

"Pavivitto" (secluded) means one who is physically secluded and withdrawn, having abandoned the company of the crowd. Mental seclusion (citta-viveka) and others will be discussed later. The verb "vase" (should dwell) should be applied to all the terms. He is called a "muni" (sage) because of being endowed with the qualities of sagehood (moneyyadhamma). "Asaṃsaṭṭho" (unassociated) means one who is not mixed with others due to the absence of seeing, hearing, conversing, eating together, or physical contact. "Ubhayā" (with both) means not being associated with both householders and the homeless (monks). This word "ubhayā" is a nominative form used in the sense of the instrumental. 

"Attānaṃ dassaye tathā" means that even if he is not dull or mute, he should present himself as if he were dull or mute. By this, the Buddha speaks of the abandonment of impudence (pāgabbhiya). In the phrase "jaḷo vā mūgo vā," the vowels are shortened for the sake of the verse's meter. The words "ca" and "vā" have a conjunctive meaning. "Nātivelaṃ sambhāseyya" means he should not speak excessively; he should be one who speaks in moderation (mattabhāṇī). "Saṅghamajjhamhi" means in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks or in a group of people. "Na so upavade kañci" means that person should not revile anyone...
206:
The words 'ca' and 'vā' have the sense of conjunction (aggregation). "Nātivelāṃ sambhāseyya" means one should not speak excessively beyond the limit; one should be a person who speaks knowing the measure. "Saṅghamajjhamhī" means in the midst of the community of monks or in the midst of a group of people.

"Na so upavade kañcī" means that monk with the aforementioned practice should not disparage anyone—whether low, middle, or high—with words. "Upaghātaṃ vivajjaye" means he should avoid harming or harassing others with the body. "Saṃvuto pātimokkhasmiṃ" means he should be restrained in the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint; it means his body and speech should be guarded by the Pātimokkha restraint. "Mattaññū cassa bhojane" means he should be one who knows the measure in food regarding seeking, receiving, consuming, and relinquishing.

"Suggahītanimittassa" means he should be one who has a well-grasped sign of concentration, noting the manner at that time: "When I attended to it in this way, my mind became concentrated." There is also a reading "Suggahītanimitto so," which means "that yogi."

"Cittuppādakovido" means he should be skilled in the causes of the arising of the sluggish mind and the restless mind, thinking, "For one practicing thus, the mind becomes sluggish" or "It becomes restless." Indeed, when the mind is sluggish, the enlightenment factors of investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), energy (vīriya), and rapture (pīti) should be developed; when the mind is restless, the enlightenment factors of tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā) should be developed. However, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (sati) is desired in all circumstances. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, at the time when the mind is sluggish, that is the time for developing the investigation of states enlightenment factor," and so forth.

"Samathaṃ anuyuñjeyya" means he should develop serenity meditation; he should produce unarisen concentration and increase and expand the arisen concentration until reaching mastery (vasībhāva). "Kālena ca vipassanaṃ" means he should practice insight (vipassanā) at the proper time, making it part of penetration (nibbedha) only, without making it part of decline or stability, and without exhausting the attained concentration through attachment.

Alternatively, "Kālena ca vipassanaṃ" means that one practicing serenity should practice insight to attain the Noble Path without shrinking back when that serenity has become firm. As it is said:

"Alternatively, by the gain of concentration or by a secluded lodging, a monk attains confidence, though not yet having reached the destruction of taints."
207:
Therefore, the words "Vīriyasātaccasampanno," etc., were spoken. Constancy is called 'sātacca'; it means one who is endowed with the constancy of energy, who has constant energy, and whose effort is always exerted. "Yutta-yogo sadā siyā" means he should always be devoted to meditation. "Dukkhantaṃ" means he should not come to confidence or go [to the thought that taints are destroyed] without having reached Nibbāna, which is the end and cessation of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha). It means he should not be one who is negligent, saying, "I have pure virtue, I am a gainer of jhāna, a gainer of direct knowledge, and I stand having brought insight to its peak."

For a monk living in this way—by the method ending in being devoted to application through insight by means of resorting to secluded lodgings and so forth—who desires purity, namely, the purification of knowledge and vision, the ultimate purity of Nibbāna, and Arahantship, and who sees danger in Saṃsāra, all taints (āsavas) such as the taint of sensual desire are destroyed; they reach cessation. By the very destruction of those taints, he attains the two types of Nibbāna: with residue (sa-upādisesa) and without residue (anupādisesa).

In this way, the Elder, under the guise of giving advice to that monk, declared his own attainment of Arahantship by showing how he himself had practiced accordingly.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta is finished.

## 7. (Apara)-Gotamattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

The verses beginning with "Vijāneyya sakaṃ atthaṃ" are the verses of the Venerable Apara-Gotama. What is the background story? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, having accumulated merit that is a support for liberation in various births, was born in a high-class Brahmin family in Sāvatthī even before the arising of our Blessed One. When he reached the proper age, he became a master of the three Vedas, learned the ways of debate, and finding no one who could speak superior to his own doctrine, he wandered about devoted to contentious talk with various people.

Then our Blessed One, having arisen in the world and turned the noble Wheel of Dhamma, gradually trained those to be tamed such as Yasa and others, and came to Sāvatthī at the invitation of Anāthapiṇډika. At that time, having gained faith when the Teacher accepted the Jetavana monastery, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and requested ordination.
208:
The Teacher commanded a certain monk who practiced the dhutaṅga of alms-round, "Monk, ordain this person." While being ordained by that monk, that person attained Arahantship at the very end of the shaving of the hair. He went to the Kosala country, lived there for a long time, and then returned to Sāvatthī. Many wealthy Brahmin householders approached and sat near that venerable one, asking, "In this world, there are many recluses and brahmins who profess purification from Saṃsāra. Among them, whose doctrine is liberating? By practicing in what way can one be purified from Saṃsāra?" The Elder, wishing to clarify that matter to them, said:

One should know one's own benefit and should look into the Teaching (Pāvacana) proclaimed by the Buddha.
One should consider what is suitable in this Dispensation for one who has entered the state of a monk.

In this Dispensation, having good friends, undertaking the extensive training rules,
and the desire to listen to the instructions of teachers who are worthy of respect—this is suitable for a monk.

Reverence for the Buddhas, respect for the Dhamma as it really is,
and esteem for the Saṅgha—this is suitable for a monk.

Being endowed with proper conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara), having a pure livelihood that is blameless and clean,
and well-establishing one's mind—this is suitable for a monk.

Being endowed with the virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla) and the virtue of avoidance (vāritta-sīla), having an inspiring deportment,
and constant exertion in the mind associated with insight—this is suitable for a monk.

Forest dwellings that are secluded and free from the noise of people
should be resorted to by a sage; such resorting is suitable for a monk.

Possessing virtue, great learning, investigating the dhammas as they really are,
and penetrating the Four Noble Truths—this is suitable for a monk.

One should develop the perception of impermanence (anicca), the perception of non-self (anatta), and the perception of foulness (asubha),
as well as the perception of disenchantment with the world. Such development is suitable for a monk.
209:
...is suitable for a monk. Forest dwellings that are secluded and free from the noise of people should be resorted to by a monk. Such a forest dwelling is suitable for a monk. Virtue, great learning, investigating the dhammas as they really are, and penetrating the Four Noble Truths are suitable for a monk. One should develop the perception that "all formations are impermanent," the perception that "all dhammas are non-self," the perception that "the body is not beautiful," and the perception of disenchantment with the world. Such development is suitable for a monk.

One should develop the seven factors of enlightenment, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the Noble Eightfold Path. Such development is suitable for a monk.
A monk should abandon craving, should break and destroy the taints (āsava) along with their roots, and should live liberated from defilements. Such living is suitable for a monk.
He spoke these verses.

In those verses, "One should know one's own benefit" means a wise person should investigate and know their own welfare as it really is. When investigating, one should also look into the Teaching (Pāvacana)—the doctrine—proclaimed in this world by many recluses and brahmins and by the Fully Enlightened One. Among those doctrines, one should look with the eye of wisdom for the Dhamma that leads out of suffering (niyyānika). These recluses and brahmins of various sects, being wrongly attached, speak contradictory words to one another, such as "permanent" for the impermanent, "self" for the non-self, and "the path of purification" for the path that is not pure. Therefore, their doctrine is not liberating. The Fully Enlightened One, however, having known as it really is through his self-attained knowledge, proclaims: "All formations are impermanent, all dhammas are non-self, Nibbāna is peace." Therefore, one should look at the greatness of the Dispensation, thinking, "Only the Teacher's doctrine is liberating." This is the meaning.

A son of good family who has entered the state of a monk (sāmañña) should also look into the matters and tasks that are suitable and appropriate for the state of a monk in this Dispensation. What are those matters? "Having good friends in this Dispensation," and so on. It should be connected as: "Having good friends in this Dispensation is suitable for a monk." The same method applies to the remaining terms. Depending on a good friend, one can abandon the unwholesome, develop the wholesome, and carry oneself purely. "Undertaking the extensive training" means exerting oneself in the trainings such as higher virtue (adhisīla) which leads to Nibbāna. "Listening to the instructions of teachers" means the desire to hear the advice of good friends such as teachers and preceptors (upajjhāya), and performing services for them. This refers to associating with good friends and so on.

"Reverence for the Buddhas" means the application of reverence and great esteem for the Omniscient Buddhas, thinking, "The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One." "Respect for the Dhamma as it really is" means respectfully honoring the Noble Dhamma as it really is. "Esteem for the Saṅgha" means cherishing the Noble Saṅgha. This is indeed the act of showing respect to the Triple Gem. "Endowed with proper conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara)" means abandoning misconduct (anācāra), which is transgression by body and speech, and abandoning the six unsuitable places (agocara) for alms-round, such as the houses of prostitutes; and being endowed with proper conduct (ācāra), which is non-transgression by body and speech, and proper resort (gocara), which is a suitable place for receiving alms. This is the meaning. "Purity of livelihood (ājီva-suddhi)" means the purity of life for one who abandons improper ways of seeking requisites that are censured by the Buddha, such as playing bamboo flutes, and instead makes use of blameless requisites.
210:
Reverence for the Buddhas (*sagāravatā*) means being endowed with respect, and performing acts of reverence and high esteem toward the Buddhas, who know all things, with the thought: "The Blessed One is the one worthy of offerings, the one who has rightly known all things by himself." Respect for the Dhamma in its true sense (*apaciti*) means the respectful worship of the *ariya-dhamma*. High esteem for the Saṅgha (*cittīkāra*) means cherishing the *ariya-saṅgha*. This should be understood as the act of showing respect and high esteem toward the Triple Gem.

Being endowed with conduct and resort (*ācāragocarayutto*) means abandoning improper conduct (*anācāra*), which is defined as bodily and verbal transgression, and abandoning the six improper resorts (*agocara*), such as the dwellings of courtesans and so on, which are unsuitable places to visit for the sake of alms and other needs; and instead being endowed with proper conduct (*ācāra*), defined as bodily and verbal non-transgression, and proper resort (*gocara*), which are suitable places to visit for the sake of alms and other needs. Purified livelihood (*ājīvo sodhito*) means that for one who abandons wrong livelihood (*anesana*), such as giving bamboo and other practices censured by the Buddha, and instead makes use of requisites that have arisen blamelessly, their livelihood is especially purified. Because it is thus purified, such a person is not censured by the wise. Properly establishing the mind (*cittassa ca saṇṭhapanaṃ*) means properly establishing the mind by way of "seeing only what is seen" and so on, so that greed and other defilements do not arise toward sense objects like forms through the sense doors like the eye. These three are: perfection in conduct and resort, purification of livelihood, and guarding the doors of the sense faculties.

*Cāritta* is the virtue (*sīla*) that must be fulfilled through performance, while *vāritta* is the virtue that must be fulfilled through non-performance (abstinence). Inspiring deportment in postures (*iriyāpathiyaṃ pasādanīyaṃ*) refers to the clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) associated with postures, which brings about the inspiration of others and is the cause for perfection in appearance. Exertion in the higher mind (*adhicitte ca āyogō*) means the repeated practice and development of tranquility (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

*Āraññakāni* refers to places belonging to the forest, and *pantāni* refers to secluded places. Virtue (*sīla*) refers to the fourfold purification virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). Although it was mentioned separately below, it is mentioned here collectively without distinction. Great learning (*bāhusaccaṃ*) is the state of being very learned. Such learning is of great benefit to one who exerts themselves in meditation; for a person who is frequent in right investigation regarding skillfulness in the factors of enlightenment, the incomparable state of peace, and being endowed with the higher mind, the exertion in tranquility and insight reaches fulfillment. Investigation of phenomena as they really are (*dhammānaṃ pavicayo yathābhūtaṃ*) means the investigation of mental and material phenomena through their non-perverted specific characteristics and general characteristics. By this statement, the Buddha speaks of insight (*vipassanā*), which is the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*). Realization of the truths (*saccānaṃ abhisamayo*) means the penetration of the noble truths, such as suffering, by way of the realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*) and so on.

To show how that realization of the truths occurs, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "One should develop" (*bhāveyya*). In that context, "one should develop impermanence" (*bhāveyya ca aniccaṃ*) means one should develop the perception of impermanence in all formations (*saṅkhāra*), as shown in the passages: "All formations are impermanent" and "Whatever form there is—past, future, or present." Perception of non-self (*anattasaññā*) should be understood as developing the perception of non-self that arises as "All things are non-self," because they do not follow one's will.
211:
Whether without distinction, as in "Whatever form there is—past, future, or present," or with distinction, one should develop, produce, and increase the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) in all formations. The construction "one should develop the perception of non-self" (*anattasaññaṃ bhāveyya*) applies to the perception of non-self that proceeds as "All things are non-self." The same applies to the remaining perceptions. Perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*) is the perception that proceeds as "they are foul," because of the oozing of the impurities of defilements, whether in the physical body or in all formations of the three planes of existence. This perception is surrounded by the perception of suffering (*dukkhasaññā*); therefore, it should be understood that the perception of suffering is also included by this very perception of foulness. Non-delight in the world (*loke ca anabhirati*) means the perception of non-delight in all the world, that is, in the formations of the three planes of existence. By this, the Buddha speaks of the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*) and the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*).

Showing that one who is thus devoted to the development of insight should increase these qualities while exerting effort in that insight, the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with "And one should develop the factors of enlightenment" (*bhāveyya ca bojjhaṅge*). Its meaning is: the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgā*) are the qualities such as mindfulness, because they are the harmony of the sevenfold qualities for enlightenment (*bodhi*), or because they are the factors of a person who possesses that enlightenment. These are the seven factors of enlightenment beginning with mindfulness, the four bases of power beginning with desire (*chanda*), the five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*), the five powers which are also faith and so on, and the Noble Eightfold Path by way of right view and so on. By the word "and" (*ca*), the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) are also included; thus, one should develop, produce, and increase all the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*). Among them, their production at the moment of the first path, and their increase at the moments of the higher paths, is suitable for a monk who is a recluse.

Showing that one who thus develops the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment realizes the truth of the path (*magga-sacca*) by way of realization through development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*), and likewise realizes the truth of the origin (*samudaya-sacca*) by way of realization through abandoning (*pahānābhisamaya*), and the truth of cessation (*nirodha-sacca*) by way of realization through witnessing (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*), the Buddha spoke the concluding verse: "One should abandon craving" (*taṇhaṃ pajaheyya*). In that verse, "one should abandon craving" means one should utterly cut off all craving, including the varieties such as craving for sensual pleasures, by means of the Noble Path. *Mona* refers to wisdom; one is called a sage (*muni*) because of being endowed with that wisdom. "One should shatter the taints along with their roots" (*samūlake āsave padāleyya*) means one should break and utterly cut off all taints, such as the taint of sensual desire, along with their roots, such as the underlying tendency to sensual lust. "One should dwell fully released" (*viharēyya vippamutto*) means being thus released in every way because of the abandoning of all defilements...
212:
One should dwell having realized Nibbāna, the cessation which is the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi). "Etam" means that such a dwelling is appropriate and suitable for a monk who has calmed all evil.

In this way, by praising the practice suitable for a monk, the Elder explained the nature of the Dispensation as leading out of suffering, and the nature of outside doctrines, which are the opposite, as not leading out of suffering. Having heard this Dhamma, those brahmins of great wealth (mahāsāla) gained great faith in the Dispensation and established themselves in the refuges and so forth.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the (Other) Elder Gotama is finished.
## The Commentary on the Book of the Tens is finished.
213:
## 11. Ekādasanipāta
## 1. Saṅkiccattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

In the Book of the Elevens, the verse beginning with "Kiṃ tavattho vane tāta" is the verse of the Venerable Elder Saṅkicca. What is its origin? This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, and having accumulated wholesome merit which is a support for the liberation from the round of rebirths in various existences, he took rebirth in a wealthy brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. While he was in the womb, his mother died of an illness. When her body was taken to the cemetery and cremated, the womb did not burn. When people poked the belly with spikes, they struck the corner of the child's eye. After poking it, they covered it with embers and left. The belly area burned, but on top of the embers, the child remained like a golden image, as if lying in the heart of a lotus. Indeed, for a being in his final birth (pacchimabhavika), even if pressed down by Mount Sineru, there is no such thing as the end of life as long as he has not attained Arahantship.

The next day, people going to the cremation ground saw the child lying there and were filled with wonder and amazement. They took the child, entered the village, and asked the fortune-tellers. The fortune-tellers said, "If this child lives the household life, seven generations of his family will be impoverished. If he ordains, he will wander surrounded by five hundred monks." The relatives said, "Let it be; when he grows up, we will have him ordained under our master, the Elder Sāriputta." Because the corner of his eye was cut by a spike (saṅku), they called him "Saṅkicca" and later he was known as Saṅkicca.

When he reached the age of seven, having heard about his mother's death while he was in the womb and his own experience in the womb, he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and said, "I will ordain." The relatives said, "Very well, dear," and took him to the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, and handed him over, saying, "Venerable Sir, please ordain this child." The Elder gave him the meditation on the five parts of the body (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna) and ordained him. At the very end of the hair-shaving, he attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). While dwelling in the forest with thirty monks, he saved those monks from the hands of robbers, and having disciplined those robbers himself, he ordained them. In another monastery with many monks...
214:
After disciplining and ordaining those robbers, while dwelling in another monastery with many monks, he saw those monks engaged in disputes and said, "I will go elsewhere," and took leave of the monks. This is the summary here; the details should be understood as they appear in the Dhammapada Commentary (Saṅkicca Sāmaṇera Vatthu). Then, a lay follower who wished to serve him, requesting him to stay nearby, spoke the first verse:

"Dear, what is the use of your living in the forest like Mount Ujjuhāna in the rainy season?
Are the gadflies delightful to you?
For one who meditates, is not seclusion alone what is desired?"

Having heard those words, the Elder said:
"Just as in the rainy season the Veramba wind clears away the clouds,
my perceptions associated with seclusion clear away [unwholesome thoughts].

The white-colored, egg-born [vulture] that makes its home and wanders in the cemetery,
arouses mindfulness in me regarding this body, based on dispassion.

That monk whom others do not protect, and who does not protect others,
that monk indeed lives happily, being without longing for sensual pleasures.

Those mountains with clear waters, large rocky slabs, filled with forest cattle and deer,
covered with moss—they delight me.

I have lived in forest regions, in canyons and caves,
and in secluded dwellings frequented by wild beasts.

'May these beings be killed, may they be slaughtered, may they come to suffering,'
I do not recall such an ignoble thought associated with ill-will.

I have served the Teacher, the Buddha; I have fulfilled the Buddha's Dispensation;
the heavy burden has been laid down; the lead to existence (bhavanetti) has been uprooted.

The purpose for which I went forth from home into homelessness,
that purpose has been attained: the destruction of all fetters."
215:
I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life. I await the time [of death] just as a hireling awaits [the completion of his work].

I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life. I await the time [of death], being clearly comprehending and mindful. Thus he spoke these verses.

In those verses, regarding the phrase 'Kiṃ tavattho vane', the word 'Kiṃ' is used with a shift in gender. It means 'What benefit is there for you in the forest?' The word 'Tāta' (dear/son) is used because Saṅkicca was a young novice, and he is addressed as if he were a son. Regarding 'Ujjuhāno va pāvuse', it is said that there is a mountain named Ujjuhāna. That mountain is covered with thickets, has many ponds and ravines, and has water flowing in various places; it is an unsuitable place during the rainy season. Therefore, it means 'What benefit is there for you on Mount Ujjuhāna in the rainy season like this?'

In this regard, some teachers say, 'There is a type of bird named Ujjuhāna that cannot withstand the cold and stays hidden in the forest bushes during the rainy season.' According to those teachers, it means 'What benefit is there for you in the forest during the rainy season, like the Ujjuhāna bird?' Regarding 'Verambhā ramaṇīyā te', it should be connected as 'How are they delightful to you when the Verambha winds are blowing?' Some teachers say, 'Verambha is the name of a mountain cave or a slope.' That place is suitable for coming and going, free from the crowding of people, and endowed with shade and water; thus it is delightful and suitable for living in the forest.

Why is this? Because for those who practice jhāna, seclusion is what is desired. Such meditators desire seclusion anywhere. Therefore, it means, 'Dear son, do not go to a distant forest area, but stay only in Verambha.' The meaning here is: only when meditators obtain a lodging that is conducive to seclusion and comfortable for living do they achieve jhāna and so on; if they do not obtain it, they do not achieve them. Therefore, in such cold weather, while it is not possible to live in just any forest, it is possible to live in caves, mountain slopes, and so on.

When the lay devotee spoke thus, the Elder, wishing to show that 'only the forest and such places delight me', spoke the words beginning with 'Yathā abbhāni'. The meaning is: just as the Verambha wind drives away, throws down, and carries off the clouds in the rainy season, even so, perceptions associated with seclusion pervade my mind and pull it only towards the place of seclusion.
216:
How so? The crow, which is not white but black in color, born from an egg, having its dwelling in the cemetery, and wandering in that very place, arouses in me mindfulness of the body associated with dispassion. It is heard that one day the Elder, seeing a human corpse being pecked by a crow, attained the perception of foulness (asubhasaññā); referring to that attainment, he spoke thus. By this, he shows his desire to live only in the forest because of the total absence of desire and lust for the body. In the word 'Yañcā', the syllable 'ca' has the sense of a collective; by that 'ca', he shows, 'Listen also to another reason for my living in the forest.' Because of living in loving-kindness and because of having requisites that are not objects of greed, there is no one to be guarded, and thus other servants and so on do not have to guard him; and because that monk does not have to guard others as a source of any anxiety or hindrance—due to the absence of such things, that monk truly sleeps happily. Because that monk has entirely cut off sensual desire, he is without longing for the objects of sensuality and sleeps happily anywhere. For such a person, because there is no recurring doubt or all-around suspicion, it is the same whether in the forest or in the village.

Now, to show the delightfulness of mountains, forests, and so on, and his previous dwelling there, he spoke the words beginning with 'Acchodikā'. There, 'vasitaṃ me' means 'I have lived there before'. 'Vāḷamiganisevite' means in the forest inhabited by wild beasts such as lions and tigers.

'Saṅkappaṃ nābhijānāmi' means 'I do not recall ever giving rise to an evil intention, such as: Let these various beings be killed by weapons like arrows and swords, let them be oppressed by being struck with fists and so on, or let them reach suffering by any other means.' Thus, he shows his dwelling in loving-kindness (mettāvihāritā) by stating that he has never given rise to an unnoble, evil intention involving ill-will and cruelty associated with anger, and that wrong thought has never arisen before.

Now, with the words beginning with 'Pariciṇṇo', he shows that he has completed his task. There, 'pariciṇṇo' means the Teacher has been served by following his advice and instructions. 'Ohito' means laid down. 'Garuko bhāro' refers to the very heavy burden of the aggregates. 'Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ' means he does not desire death, thinking 'How will my death be?' 'Nābhinandāmi jīvitaṃ' means he does not desire life, thinking 'How may I live for a long time?' By this, he shows that he has an equal mind towards both death and life. 'Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi' means he is awaiting the time of Parinibbāna; it carries the sense of being weary [of the world].
217: 'Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ' means 'I do not desire death, thinking "How indeed will my death be?"' 'Nābhinandāmi jīvitaṃ' means 'I do not desire life, thinking "How indeed may I live for a long time?"' By this, he shows the state of having an equal mind towards both death and life. 'Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi' means 'I only await the time of Parinibbāna.' 'Nibbisam' refers to one who is weary or one who works for hire. 'Bhatako yathā' means: just as a hireling, while performing another's work, does not delight in the completion of the work but, while doing the work, only looks forward to the time when the day will end; even so, though I do not delight in life, I sustain this physical body, and though I do not delight in death, I await the final time. The remaining words are just as previously explained. ## The commentary on the verses of the Elder Saṅkicca is finished. ## The commentary on the Book of the Elevens is finished.
218:
## 12. Dvādasakanipāta
## 1. Sīlavattheragāthāvaṇṇanā

In the Dvādasakanipāta, the verse beginning with 'Sīlameva' belongs to Venerable Sīlava. What is its origin? This Venerable Sīlava had also made aspirations under previous Buddhas, accumulating merit that is the basis for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of King Bimbisāra and was named Sīlava. When the prince came of age, King Ajātasattu, wishing to kill him, placed him on a fierce, rutting elephant and attempted various means to end his life, but was unable to do so. This was because he was a pacchimabhavika (one in his last birth), and as long as he had not yet attained the fruit of Arahantship, no life-threatening danger could occur in the interim. Seeing this situation, the Blessed One commanded Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, 'Bring Prince Sīlava here.' The Elder, by his psychic power, brought him along with the elephant. The prince descended from the elephant, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat in a suitable place. The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma according to his disposition. Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith, ordained, and while practicing the work of Vipassanā, he soon attained Arahantship and resided in the Kosala country.

Then, King Ajātasattu again commanded his men, 'Go and kill him.' While those men stood in the presence of the Elder, they heard the Dhamma discourse he preached, were moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), and with a settled mind, they ordained. The Elder (preached to them as follows):

'In this world, one should train only in virtue that is well-practiced.
For virtue, when cultivated, brings all forms of success.

A wise person, desiring the three types of happiness—
praise, the acquisition of wealth, and joy in heaven after death—should guard virtue.

For the virtuous person gains many friends through restraint;
But the immoral person, practicing evil, falls away from friends.

The immoral person receives blame and ill-repute;
The virtuous person always receives fame, reputation, and praise.'
219:
'Virtue is the beginning of wholesome states, and their foundation. It is like the mother of good qualities. It is the chief of all dhammas. Therefore, one should purify virtue.

Virtue is the boundary and the restraint; it is the delight of the mind. It is like the ford (crossing place) for all Buddhas. Therefore, one should purify virtue.

Virtue is incomparable strength; virtue is the supreme weapon. Virtue is the most excellent ornament; virtue is a wonderful armor.

Virtue is a great bridge; virtue is the matchless scent. Virtue is the most excellent ointment, the fragrance of which wafts in all directions.

Virtue is the foremost bundle of provisions; virtue is the supreme travel food. Virtue is the most excellent conveyor (vehicle) by which one can go in all directions.

The fool who is not established in virtue receives blame in this very life, and after death, he suffers in the states of deprivation. He is miserable everywhere.

The wise person who is well-established in virtue receives fame in this very life, and after death, he rejoices in heaven. He is joyful everywhere.

In this world, virtue alone is supreme, but the person with wisdom is even more excellent. Among humans and gods, victory is achieved through virtue and wisdom.'

With these verses, he taught the Dhamma.

In those verses, regarding the phrase 'Sīlamevidha sikkhetha', 'idha' is merely a particle. In this world of beings, a son of good family who desires his own welfare should first train only in virtue, which is divided into cārittasīla (virtue of performance) and vārittasīla (virtue of avoidance). When training, he should train by making that virtue well-practiced, extremely pure, and complete, without letting it be broken or flawed. The phrase 'asmiṃ loke' means that among the dhammas to be practiced in this world of formations (saṅkhāraloka), one should train in virtue first. Because virtue is also the foundation for the attainment of right view (diṭṭhisampatti), he said 'Sīlaṃ hī' and so on. In that context, the word 'hi' indicates the reason. Because virtue, when cultivated and practiced...'
220:
Virtue that is guarded brings all these forms of prosperity—human prosperity, celestial prosperity, and the prosperity of Nibbāna—to the being who possesses it; it bestows them.

To show in detail the meaning of the brief statement "Virtue bestows all prosperity," he said "One should protect virtue," and so on. In that context, "should protect" means one should keep it secure. Indeed, one who abstains from taking life and so forth, and who fulfills major and minor duties, is said to protect that virtue because he overcomes the states opposing it. "The wise person" refers to the demonstration of the means of protection; for it is only through the power of wisdom that one's undertaking and non-violation of virtue can be achieved. "Desired" means having a wish. "Three kinds of happiness" refers to either the three types of bliss or the cause of bliss being intended as "happiness." "They praise" refers to fame or the praise of the wise. "Gaining joy" means obtaining satisfaction and delight. Some also read it as "gaining wealth," meaning the acquisition of material riches. For a virtuous person, due to diligence, acquires a great mass of wealth. "After death" means after passing away. "Delighting in heaven" should be connected as: also desiring to delight in the heaven world through the desired sensual pleasures. The construction is: one should protect virtue, desiring praise and the acquisition of wealth in this world, and delighting in divine prosperity in the next world.

"Through restraint" means through the restraint of the body and so forth. Indeed, one who is restrained from bodily misconduct and so forth does not harm anyone and, being like one who gives the gift of fearlessness, becomes beloved and dear, thereby gaining friends. "Departs" means it goes away or fades. "The evil-doer" refers to one who commits bad deeds such as taking life. Beings who desire their own welfare do not associate with an immoral person; instead, they avoid them.

"Avaṇṇa" means lack of virtue or face-to-face blame. "Akitti" means lack of reputation or ill-fame. "Vaṇṇa" means virtue or quality. "Kitti" means fame or widespread renown. "Pasaṃsa" means face-to-face praise.

"Beginning" means the root or source. It is true that virtue is the beginning and root of wholesome states. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Therefore, monk, you should first purify the very beginning of wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? It is well-purified virtue." "Foundation" means the basis or ground. Virtue is the foundation for all superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma). Therefore, He said: "Established in virtue," and so on. Being like a mother to the good states such as tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā)...
221:
Virtue is like a mother and has the meaning of generating (wholesome states). "Pamukhaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ" means it is the chief or foremost of all blameless states such as joy (pāmojja), and it is like a gateway for their arising. Because it is the beginning and so forth, it is said "Therefore." "Should purify" (visodhaye) means one should fulfill it by making it unbroken, unperforated, unspotted, and unspeckled.

It is called "Velā" (boundary or shore) in the sense that it is not to be transgressed by misconduct. Or, it is called "Velā" because it destroys immorality (dussīlya). Virtue is called "restraint" (saṃvara) because it closes the gateway for the arising of bodily misconduct and so forth. It is called "exhilaration" (abhihāsana) because it gladdens the mind without any cause for remorse. It is like a ford (tittha) for all Buddhas—Disciple Buddhas, Private Buddhas, and Fully Enlightened Buddhas—both in washing away the stains of defilements and in entering the great ocean of Nibbāna.

Virtue is an incomparable strength and the power of an army in crushing the army of Mara. It is the supreme weapon for cutting through the states of defilement. It is called an "ornament" (ābharaṇa) in the sense of beautifying the body of qualities. It is the "best" because it is always an excellent substance, and it is a wonderful "armor" (kavaca) because it protects life. Some also read it as "abbhidaṃ," which means unbreakable.

It is a "bridge" (setu) in the sense of not sinking due to defilements while crossing the great flood of the lower realms and the great flood of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra). "Mahesakkho" means having great power. It is an unsurpassed "scent" because it wafts in all directions against the wind and because it captivates the minds of all people. Therefore, He said: "By which scent of virtue, the one endowed with it wafts in all directions." "Disodisā" means the ten directions.

"Sambala" refers to provisions or a lunch pack. Just as (yathā) a man who carries a lunch pack does not suffer from the pain of hunger during his journey, so too (evaṃ) one endowed with virtue, having taken the provision of pure virtue, does not suffer in whatever place he reaches while traveling through the wilderness of saṃsāra. Therefore, virtue is called the supreme provision. Furthermore, virtue is called the excellent travel rations (pātheyya) because it is not shared with thieves and because it produces the desired prosperity in various lives. It is called the vehicle "ativāha" because it leads to the desired destination. Virtue is the supreme vehicle because it is the cause of reaching the desired goal without being harassed by anyone.
222:
Because it is the cause for reaching the desired destination, virtue (sīla) is the supreme vehicle (ativāha). By means of this vehicle, when traveling in various directions, whether to a place never reached before or to a familiar destination (gati), one goes to those various places with ease.

In this world, one who has a mind corrupted by lust (rāga) and the like, and who is of evil heart, receives blame and reproach as "one without virtue, one of wicked nature." In the world beyond, in the planes of misery (apāya), such a person also receives blame from the minions of King Yama, being called "a wretched man," and so forth. Not only does he receive blame, but indeed, the fool is unhappy in all places—in this world because his mind is defiled by practicing misconduct (duccarita), and in the world beyond because of the arising of suffering such as karmic punishments. Why is this? It is because of the inability to properly establish the mind in virtues and the lack of concentration.

In this world, one with a joyful mind receives fame as "a good person, one of virtue, one of good conduct." In the world beyond, in the heavenly realm, he also receives fame, such as "This good person was virtuous and of good conduct; therefore, he has attained the company of the gods." Not only does he receive fame, but indeed, the wise person, endowed with fortitude and having a mind well-concentrated in virtues, is joyful in all places—in this world because of practicing good conduct (sucarita), and in the world beyond because of obtaining prosperity.

In this Dispensation, virtue alone is supreme. Virtue is of two kinds: mundane (lokiya) virtue and supramundane (lokuttara) virtue. Among them, mundane virtue brings about a distinguished rebirth among the great wealthy khattiyas and the like in the sense-sphere world, as well as in the heavenly and Brahma realms; it is also the cause for obtaining gains and so forth. Supramundane virtue, however, causes one to transcend the entirety of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). Therefore, virtue is indeed supreme. Thus it has been said:

"By low holy life, one is born in a royal family;
By middling, to the state of a deity;
And by the highest, one is purified."

"Monks, if a monk should desire: 'May I be a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,' he should fulfill the virtues. Monks, the mental aspiration of a virtuous person succeeds because of its purity."
224:
He was born into the family of flower-scavengers (scavengers of refuse) for hundreds of lives and made his living in that very manner. In this present age when our Gautama Buddha appeared, he was born again into a family of flower-scavengers and made his living by cleaning excrement, living in poverty without even enough food or clothing.

Then, during the last watch of the night, the Blessed One entered the Attainment of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti), which is the habit of the Buddhas. Having emerged from that attainment and surveying the world with His Buddha-eye, He saw within Sunīta’s heart the strong sufficing condition (upanissaya) for the Fruit of Arahantship, shining like a lamp inside a jar. When the night had brightened into morning, the Blessed One adjusted His lower robe, took His bowl and robes, and, surrounded by the community of monks, entered the city of Rājagaha for alms. The Blessed One proceeded along the very street where Sunīta was performing his work of cleaning excrement.

Sunīta, having gathered piles of leftovers, excrement, and rubbish here and there, placed them in baskets and was carrying them on a shoulder-pole. Seeing the Teacher approaching surrounded by the community of monks, he became greatly afraid and his heart was agitated. Finding no way to proceed and no place to hide, he set his shoulder-pole against a wall and stood pressing himself against the wall as if trying to merge into it, with his hands joined in reverence. Some even say, "He wished to escape through a hole in the wall."

When the Teacher reached him, He thought: "This Sunīta is afraid of Me, who has come urged by his own past merit. Because of his low birth and humble work, he is even ashamed to face Me. Now, I shall dispel his fear." Then, with a noble and deep Brahma-voice, as melodious as the song of the karavīka bird, which could resonate through the whole city, He called out, "Sunīta!" and said, "What is the use of this miserable livelihood? Would you be able to ordain as a monk?"

Upon hearing those words of the Teacher, Sunīta felt as if he were being sprinkled with the nectar of immortality and experienced sublime joy and happiness. He replied, "Blessed One, if even someone like me can obtain ordination in this Dispensation, why should I not ordain? May the Blessed One please ordain me." The Teacher said, "Come, monk (Ehi Bhikkhu)." At that very moment, through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' formula, he obtained the state of a novice and a fully ordained monk. Bearing the bowl and robes created by psychic power, he stood near the Teacher like a senior elder of sixty years' standing.

The Blessed One took him to the monastery and taught him a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). He first attained the eight meditative attainments and the five supernormal powers, then developed insight and became an Arahant endowed with the six supernormal powers. Deities such as Sakka and the Brahmas approached and worshipped that Elder Sunīta. Therefore, it is said:

Seven hundred noble deities and the Brahma approached the noble one...
225:
"Those seven hundred noble deities, as well as Brahma and Indra (Sakka), having approached, worship with confident hearts the noble Sunīta, who has overcome birth and old age," and so forth.

The Blessed One, seeing him preceded by the host of deities, smiled and, wishing to praise him, taught the Dhamma with the verse beginning with "By austerity, by the holy life" (Tapena brahmacariyena). Then, many monks, wishing to make him roar a lion's roar (sīhanāda), asked, "Friend Sunīta, from what family did you ordain? How did you ordain? And how did you penetrate the Four Noble Truths?" To reveal all of that, the Elder Sunīta said:

"I was born in a low family, poor and with little food.
My work was humble; I was a flower-scavenger.

I was loathed by people, despised, and reviled.
Humbling my mind, I paid homage to many people.

Then I saw the Fully Enlightened One, preceded by the community of monks,
The Great Hero entering the supreme city of the Magadhans (Rājagaha).

Having laid down my shoulder-pole, I approached to pay homage.
Out of compassion for me alone, the Supreme Man stood still.

Having worshipped the Teacher's feet, I stood to one side.
Then I requested ordination from the One supreme among all beings.

Then the Compassionate Teacher, who has compassion for the whole world,
Said to me, 'Come, monk'; that was my full ordination.

Being such, I dwelt alone in the forest, diligent.
I followed the Teacher's words, just as the Conqueror (Jina) exhorted me.

In the first watch of the night, I recollected my past lives.
In the middle watch of the night, I purified the divine eye.
In the last watch of the night, I tore asunder the mass of darkness."
226:
Then, at the end of the night, at sunrise, Indra and Brahmā came and paid homage to me with joined palms.

"Homage to you, O noble man! Homage to you, O supreme man! You whose taints are destroyed, O venerable one, you are worthy of offerings."

Then the Teacher, seeing me surrounded by the assembly of gods, manifested a smile and spoke this meaning:

"By austerity, by the holy life, by restraint, and by self-control—by this one becomes a Brahmin; this is the supreme Brahmin."

With these verses, he uttered a lion's roar.

In those verses, "nīce" means low, most inferior. The state of being high or low is relative among beings.
