Wishing to show that this [Elder Sunīta] was born in the most inferior family of flower-scavengers, he said "nīce kule jāto" (born in a low family). Therefore, it is said: "nīce" means low, most inferior.

"Daliddo" means poor. Some poor people occasionally obtain food and clothing and live without great hardship. But I, wishing to show that I lived with hardship at all times, never even seeing a drop of oil in the pot placed on the hearth, said "appabhojano" (having little food).

Even those born in low families and who are poor may have a livelihood that is not low. Wishing to show that it was not so for me, he said "hīnakammaṃ mamaṃ āsi" (my work was low).

What kind of work? I was a flower-scavenger (pupphachaddaka). Just as a person without hands might be called "hand-possessing" by way of metaphor, this designation "flower-scavenger" was mine. Or, because of the appearance of withered flowers spread on the refuse ground, it is so called.

"Jigucchito" means loathed or despised by both birth and occupation. "Manussānaṃ" means by people. "Paribhūto" means looked down upon or treated with contempt. "Vambhito" means reviled.

"Nīcaṃ manaṃ karitvāna" means making the mind humble or lowly, by exalting other people like Mount Sineru and making oneself lower than even the dust of their feet.
227:
"Vandissaṃ bahukaṃ janaṃ" means paying homage to the great multitude of people whenever they were seen, by placing the joined palms to the head.

The word "atha" is a particle used to indicate a transition to a new subject. "Addasāsi" means saw. "Magadhānaṃ" refers to the princes living in the region called Magadha. Even a single district where those princes reside is traditionally called "Magadhānaṃ" by usage (ruḷhī); it means "of the Magadhan country." "Puruttamaṃ" means the supreme city.

"Byābhaṅgiṃ" means a carrying pole. "Pabbajjaṃ ahamāyāciṃ" means when the Teacher gave the opportunity, saying "Sunīta, you will be able to go forth," I requested the going forth (ordination). "Āsūpasampadā" refers to the attainment of higher ordination (upasampadā) merely by the Teacher's words, "Come, bhikkhu." "Yathā maṃ ovadi" means I followed and practiced the Teacher's words exactly as he exhorted me, saying "Develop insight preceded by tranquility (samatha)."

The words beginning with "rattiyā" show the essence (rasa) or function of that practice. Therein, the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of the future (divine eye) involve much activity, so they are expressed in the accusative case (upayogavacana) by way of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga), as in "during the first watch, during the middle watch." The knowledge of the destruction of taints is not like that, as it occurs by way of a single penetration (ekābhisamaya); therefore, it should be understood as being expressed in the locative case (bhummavasena), as in "in the last watch."

"Indo" is Sakka, the king of gods. "Brahmā" is Mahābrahmā. By mentioning Indra and Brahmā, it should be understood that the coming of other sensual-sphere deities and Brahmas is also stated. This is an "eminent mention" (ukkaṭṭhaniddesa), just as when one says "the King has arrived" [implying his retinue]. "Namassiṃsu" means they performed homage by body and speech.

Therein, to show the homage performed by body, he said "pañjalī" (with joined palms), and then to show the homage performed by speech, he said "namo te" (homage to you), etc. In the phrase "devasaṅghapurakkhatā," by the word "deva," the Brahmas are also included because they are "gods by rebirth" (upapattideva).

"Sitaṃ pātukaritvāna" means the Teacher manifested a smile based on the great fruitfulness of his own exhortation and the excellence of the virtues of the devas and Brahmas. When manifesting a smile, he does not show his teeth like others, but opens his mouth only slightly. By that much alone, thick rays originating from his very white tusks (teeth)—which surpass the divine crystal and pearl-like radiance and mock the rays of the stars and the moon—emerge and circle the Teacher's face three times clockwise. Seeing those rays, even those following from behind recognize that the Teacher has manifested a smile.
228:
"Tapena" refers to the virtue of restraint of the senses (indriya-saṃvara-sīla); however, some teachers say it means "the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)." "Saṃyamena" means restraint through virtue (sīla). "Damena" means taming through wisdom (paññā). "Brahmacariyena" means practicing the remaining noble conduct. Because of these aforementioned practices such as austerity and so forth, one is called a "Brahmin" (brāhmaṇa) due to having warded off evil. "Etam" refers to the aforementioned practices like austerity and so forth. "Brāhmaṇamuttamaṃ" means a noble Brahmin, or the most excellent among all Brahmins; the word "ahu" (was) is an elliptical term. Alternatively, "Brāhmaṇa" refers to the state of being a Brahmin (brahmañña); the meaning is that such excellent Brahminhood does not arise from birth and so forth. Indeed, accomplishments in birth, lineage, family, and clan are not the causes for being a Noble One (ariya); rather, the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā) and so forth are the primary causes. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"As in a heap of rubbish, cast away on the highway, a lotus might grow there, pure-scented and delightful.

Even so, among the rubbish-like blind worldlings, the disciple of the Fully Enlightened One outshines them with wisdom." (Dhammapada 58-59)

Thus, the Elder, answering the meaning questioned by those monks with these verses, uttered a lion's roar.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sunīta Thera is finished.
## The Commentary on the Group of Twelve (Dvādasa Nipāta) is finished.
229:
## 13. Terasa Nipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Soṇa Koḷivisa Thera

In the Group of Thirteen (Terasa Nipāta), the verses beginning with "Yāhu raṭṭhe" are those of the Venerable Soṇa Koḷivisa. What is the background story of their origin? This Venerable Soṇa also had made an aspiration (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merits in various existences.

It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī, he was a wealthy merchant. Having gone to the monastery with lay devotees and heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, he was inspired. He had the Teacher's walking path (caṅkama) decorated with plaster, spread with flowers of various colors, and had a canopy of various colored cloths hung above. Furthermore, he built a long hall for the Teacher and the Saṅgha of monks and offered it.

Through that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in a merchant family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, and was named Sirivaḍḍha. When he reached maturity, he went to the monastery and, while listening to the Dhamma from the Teacher, saw the Teacher appoint a monk to the foremost position among those who have aroused energy (āraddhavīriya). Desiring that same position for himself, he performed a great almsgiving for seven days and made a resolution. The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, gave him the prophecy and departed.

He, too, performed meritorious deeds throughout his life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In the interval after the Parinibbāna of the Buddha Kassapa and before the appearance of our Buddha, he was reborn in a family home in Bārāṇasī. Having reached maturity and being wise, he built a leaf-roofed hut on the bank of the Ganges and respectfully served a Paccekabuddha with the four requisites for the three months of the rainy season. After the rainy season retreat, the Paccekabuddha, fully provided with requisites, went to Mount Gandhamādana.

That clansman also performed merits throughout his life in that existence, and after passing away from there, wandered through the realms of gods and humans. During the time of our Buddha, he took rebirth in the house of the merchant Usabha in the city of Campā. From the time of his conception, the merchant's great mass of wealth increased. On the day of his birth, the entire city was filled with great honor and offerings. Because he had previously offered a red blanket worth a hundred thousand to the Paccekabuddha, his body was golden in color and extremely delicate. Therefore, they named the child "Soṇa." With a great retinue...
230:
(That youth) grew up. The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet were the color of the Bandhujīvaka flower. They had a touch as soft as cotton-wool that has been beaten a hundred times. On the soles of his feet, hairs grew in a whorled shape like ruby earrings. When he reached the proper age, three palaces suitable for the three seasons were built for him, and he was attended by dancers. There, Soṇa lived like a young deva, enjoying great prosperity.

At that time, our Teacher, having attained omniscience and set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, was residing near the city of Rājagaha. Summoned by King Bimbisāra, Soṇa came to Rājagaha along with eighty thousand village headmen. Having gone to the presence of the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, he gained faith. With the permission of his parents, he went forth into the Dispensation and received higher ordination. Having taken a subject of meditation from the Teacher, he resided in the Sītavana forest to avoid association with people. He thought, "My body is very delicate; it is not possible to attain happiness through ease. It is proper for me to practice the Dhamma of a recluse by exerting my body." Thus, he undertook only the standing and walking postures and applied himself to the exertion. Although blisters broke out on the soles of his feet, he disregarded the pain and put forth firm effort. However, due to over-exertion, he was unable to attain any distinction. He then thought, "Even though I strive like this, I am unable to attain either the Path or the Fruit. What is the use of this monkhood to me? I shall return to the lower life, enjoy my wealth, and perform meritorious deeds."

The Teacher, knowing the thought in his mind, went there and exhorted him with the Simile of the Lute. Showing him the method of tuning his energy to an even pitch, the Teacher refined his meditation subject and then departed for Gijjhakūṭa Mountain. The Elder Soṇa, having received the exhortation in the presence of the Teacher, balanced his energy, applied himself to insight meditation, and was established in Arahantship. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"For the Sage Anomadassī, the Chief of the World, the Steadfast One, I plastered the walkway with lime and made an offering of it.

I strewed the walkway with flowers of various colors; having made a canopy in the sky, I offered a meal to the Buddha, the Supreme One.

Raising my hands in salutation and paying homage to the One of Good Vows, I then offered a long hall to the Blessed One.

Knowing my intention, the Teacher, the Unsurpassed One in the world, the Blessed One, the Visionary One, accepted it out of compassion."
231:
"Having accepted it, the Fully Enlightened One, worthy of offerings in the world with its devas, sat in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks and spoke these verses:

'He who with a joyful heart gave this long hall to me, I shall praise him; listen to my words as I speak.

At the time of death for this person who is endowed with meritorious deeds, a chariot harnessed with a thousand horses will appear at that very moment.

By that vehicle, this man will go to the deva world; the devas will rejoice for him, who is born of a noble family, upon his arrival.

He will rule and reside in a celestial mansion of great value and excellence, plastered with jewel-paste and endowed with excellent gabled chambers.

For thirty thousand aeons, he will delight in the deva world; for twenty-five aeons, he will be the king of the devas.

Seventy-seven times he will be a Wheel-turning Monarch; all of them will have the same name, Yasodhara.

Having enjoyed the two types of prosperity and increased his store of merit, in the twenty-eighth aeon, he will be a Wheel-turning Monarch.

In that state of a Wheel-turning Monarch, he will rule and reside in that city which has a celestial mansion created by Vissakamma and is not silent of the ten sounds.'

In an incalculable aeon from now, a king named Okkāka, of great psychic power, will arise in the country as a protector of the land.

Among sixteen thousand women, the most excellent of all, a Khattiyānī queen of noble birth, will give birth to nine sons.

After giving birth to the nine sons, that Khattiyānī queen will pass away; a young and beloved maiden will be made the chief queen.

Having pleased King Okkāka, that maiden will receive a boon; having received the boon, that maiden will cause the (king's elder) princes to be exiled."
232:
"All those exiled princes will go to an excellent city. Fearing the corruption of their lineage, all the princes will live together with their sisters.

One princess will be afflicted by diseases. Saying, 'Let not our lineage be corrupted,' the princes will bury (that princess) in the ground.

A king will take her out and live with her. At that time, there will be a split of the clan (the Koḷiyas) descending from the lineage of King Okkāka.

Their progeny will be of the clan named Koḷiya. In that clan, he will enjoy much human prosperity.

Passing away from that body, he will go to the deva world. In that deva world also, he will obtain a delightful and excellent celestial mansion.

Passing away from the deva world, urged by his root of merit, he will come to the human state and become one named Soṇa.

Being of stirred-up energy and resolute mind, while striving in the Teacher's Dispensation, he will fully understand all taints and, being taintless, will attain Nibbāna.

The Blessed One of infinite vision, Gotama, the Bull of the Sakyans, the Knower of Distinctions, the Great Hero, will place (me) in a pre-eminent position.

Standing on a courtyard where the grass is four finger-breadths high after the rain and is unmoved by the wind, for those devoted to the practice of meditation, there is no perfection higher than that.

Tamed by the highest taming, my mind is well-composed. I have laid down all burdens; I am cooled and free from taints.

The Great Naga named Aṅgīrasa, noble like a young maned lion, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, placed me in this foremost position.

The four analytical insights (have been realized) ... the Dispensation of the Buddha has been carried out."

Having attained Arahantship and reviewing his own practice, he spoke by way of an inspired utterance and by way of declaring his attainment of Arahantship:
233:
He who was once pre-eminent in the Anga kingdom (surrounded by eighty thousand householders), a wealthy attendant of King Bimbisāra of Anga, that Soṇa is now pre-eminent in the Dhamma, one who has reached the far shore of suffering (Nibbāna).

One should cut off the five (lower fetters), abandon the five (higher fetters), and further develop the five (faculties). A monk who has transcended the five attachments—lust, hatred, delusion, pride, and wrong view—is called one who has crossed the four floods.

For a monk who is conceited, heedless, and desires only external objects, virtue, concentration, and wisdom do not reach fulfillment.

Because they abandon what should be done and do what should not be done, the taints (āsavas) increase for those who are conceited and heedless.

For those who constantly and well practice mindfulness directed to the body, who do not engage in what should not be done but always perform what should be done, for those mindful and clearly comprehending ones, the taints come to an end.

When the straight path (the Path) has been taught, practice according to that teaching; do not fall back in between. One should urge oneself on and bring oneself to Nibbāna.

The Peerless One in the world, the Buddha endowed with the five eyes, taught me the Dhamma using the simile of the lute while I was over-exerting my energy. Having heard the words of the Blessed One, I dwelt delighting in the Dispensation.

To attain the noble fruit of Arahantship, I developed tranquility (samatha) and cultivated insight (vipassanā). I have attained the three knowledges in succession; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

With a mind inclined toward renunciation, seclusion of the mind, non-harming, the destruction of clinging, the destruction of craving, and non-delusion of the mind, and seeing the arising of the sense bases, the mind is rightly liberated through its causes.

For such a monk whose mind is rightly liberated and peaceful, there is no further accumulation (of kamma); there is nothing more to be done.
234:
‘Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, so too, all forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, as well as desirable and undesirable objects, cannot stir the stable mind of such a one (a Tādī) who is free from defilements; he contemplates the passing away of those objects.’ Thus he spoke these verses.

In those verses, ‘He who was pre-eminent in the kingdom’ means he who was exceedingly noble in the Anga kingdom due to his abundance of wealth and power, surpassing eighty thousand village headmen. ‘An attendant of the King of Anga’ means he was a distinguished householder who was a follower of King Bimbisāra, the ruler of Anga, who delighted his subjects with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu); it should be understood that he was a householder in that king's realm. ‘He is now pre-eminent in the Dhamma’ means that Soṇa is now noble in the supramundane states; he shows himself as if he were another, saying that just as he was noble compared to some during his time as a layman, he is also noble now during his time as a monk. ‘One who has reached the far shore of suffering’ means he is one who has reached the end of the entire suffering of the round of rebirths. By this, he specifies the general state of being ‘noble in the Dhamma’ by showing the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.

Now, wishing to show by another method the practice by which he reached the end of suffering, he spoke the verse beginning with ‘Cut off the five’. The meaning of that verse is: One should cut off the five lower fetters, which lead to the planes of misery and the sensual happy planes, with the three lower paths, just as a man cuts a rope tied to his feet with a weapon. One should abandon or cut off the five higher fetters, which lead to the fine-material and immaterial realms, with the highest path (the path of Arahantship), just as one cuts a rope tied to the neck. To abandon those higher fetters, one should greatly develop the five faculties, such as faith (saddhā).

A monk who has thus transcended the five attachments—namely the attachments of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, and wrong view—becomes a ‘transcender of the five attachments’ (pañcasaṅgātiga). Because he has crossed the four floods—the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance—he is called ‘one who has crossed the flood’ (oghatiṇṇa).

This practice of crossing the flood occurs only through the fulfillment of virtue and so on. Virtue and the rest reach fulfillment through the abandoning of pride and so forth, and cannot be reached in any other way; wishing to show this, he spoke the verse beginning with ‘For the conceited’. In that context, ‘unnalassa’ means of one who has uplifting and vain pride.
235:
Conceit is called 'naḷa' (a reed) because it has the nature of rising up and because of its emptiness. 'Pamattassa' refers to one who has fallen into negligence by abandoning mindfulness. 'Bāhirāsayassa' means one who has desire for external sense bases (āyatana), meaning one whose lust for sensual pleasures is not removed. 'Virtue, concentration, and wisdom do not reach fulfillment' means that for one who indulges in the opposites of virtue and so on, even mundane qualities like virtue do not first reach fulfillment, let alone supramundane qualities.

Regarding this, the reason is stated starting with 'Yañhi kiccaṃ'. For monks, from the time of ordination, tasks such as guarding the immeasurable aggregate of virtue, living in the forest, undertaking the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and delighting in meditation are called 'kicca' (duty). Those people abandon their own aforementioned duties by not performing them. 'Akicca' (non-duty) refers to things such as decorating the alms-bowl, decorating requisites like robes, waistbands, shoulder straps, umbrellas, sandals, fans, and water filters, and the abundance of requisites; these are called the non-duties of monks, yet they perform them. For those who wander about carrying the reed of conceit, who possess arrogant conceit, and who are negligent by abandoning mindfulness, the four taints (āsava) increase.

To show those for whom qualities such as wisdom increase, the passage starting with 'Yesaṃ' is stated. In that context, 'susammāraddhā' means well-exerted or well-upheld. 'Kāyagatāsati' refers to the development of mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā bhāvanā). 'Akiccaṃ te' means they do not indulge in or perform non-duties such as decorating the alms-bowl. 'Kicce' means they are constantly devoted to duties such as guarding the immeasurable aggregate of virtue which should be performed from the time of ordination. For those who are not devoid of mindfulness and who possess clear comprehension through the four types of clear comprehension—clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña), clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña), clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña)—the four taints reach destruction and non-existence.

Now, wishing to give an exhortation to the monks staying near him, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Ujumaggamhi'. In that verse, 'ujumaggamhi akkhāte' means when the Teacher has taught the Noble Path, which is the Middle Way, made straight by avoiding the two extremes and by abandoning crookedness of body and so on. 'Gacchatha' means 'you all should practice'. 'Mā nivattatha' means 'do not stop before reaching the end'. 'Attanā codayattānaṃ' means a young man of good family who desires his own welfare in this Dispensation...
236:
...exhorting oneself by reflecting on the fear of the states of misery (apāya-bhaya) and so on. 'One should lead oneself to Nibbāna' means one should practice in such a way as to realize Nibbāna. To show his own practice, saying 'Now I too have practiced thus,' he said 'Accāraddhamhi' and so on. 'I, while developing insight, became one with excessive energy because I did not balance energy with concentration but over-exerted it.' The fact of his having such excessive energy was already mentioned below. Regarding 'making the lute an analogy for me,' when the thought arose in the mind of the Venerable Soṇa: 'Whatever disciples of the Blessed One live with energy aroused, I am one of them; yet my mind is not yet liberated from the taints through non-clinging, therefore I shall return to the lay life,' the Teacher, manifesting himself before him through psychic power, asked: 'Soṇa, why did the thought "I shall return to the lay life" arise in you? Were you not formerly, as a layman, skilled in the strings and music of the lute?' When he replied, 'Yes, Bhante,' the Buddha asked: 'What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute were too tight, was your lute then tuneful or playable?' 'No, Bhante.' 'What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute were too loose, was your lute then tuneful or playable?' 'No, Bhante.' 'What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute were neither too tight nor too loose, but established in a balanced pitch, was your lute then tuneful or playable?' 'Yes, Bhante.' 'Even so, Soṇa, excessive energy leads to restlessness (uddhacca), and overly lax energy leads to laziness (kosajja). Therefore, Soṇa, resolve on the balance of energy and penetrate the balance of the faculties.' Thus, by the 'Exhortation on the Simile of the Lute' delivered by making the lute an analogy, he taught me the Dhamma. Hearing the word of the Blessed One—that is, hearing the exhortation on the simile of the lute—I abandoned the desire to return to lay life that had arisen in the meantime and remained greatly delighted in the Teacher's Dispensation.

While living so, I accomplished serenity (samatha) by joining the balance of energy, producing a harmony of concentration and energy just like that of faith and wisdom, based on meditative absorption (jhāna)...
238:
Because the task is done, there are no further duties such as full understanding (pariññā). For such a person, just as a solid rock mountain is not shaken or moved by the natural wind, so too, sense objects like sights, whether pleasant or unpleasant, do not shake or move the mind of one who has reached the state of tādi, whose mind is steady, unshakable, and unassociated with defilements because all sorrows have been abandoned. When entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) and practicing Vipassanā at all times, he repeatedly sees the nature of breaking and ceasing in every moment. Thus, he declared his attainment of Arahantship.

## The commentary on the verses of Venerable Soṇakoḷivisa is finished.

## The commentary on the Thirteenth Group (Terasa Nipāta) is finished.
239:
## 14. Cuddasaka Nipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata

In the Cuddasaka Nipāta, the verses beginning with "Yadā ahaṃ" are those of the Venerable Khadiravaniya Revata. What is the special occasion? Indeed, the verse of this Elder has appeared below in the Ekaka Nipāta. In that Ekaka Nipāta, the verse was included in the rehearsal (Sangāyanā) because it was shown only to arouse mindfulness in his nephews. These verses, however, are those that reveal his practice from the time of his ordination until his Parinibbāna, and thus they are included in this Cuddasaka Nipāta. The background story (atthuppatti) has been mentioned below.

This is the special detail: Having reached the fruit of Arahantship, the Elder would occasionally go to pay respects to the Teacher (the Buddha) and the Great Elders such as the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta). After staying there for a few days, he would return to the Khadiravana forest and spend his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) and the divine abidings (brahmavihāras). As time passed, he became old and advanced in years. One day, while traveling to pay respects to the Buddha, he stayed in a forest not far from Sāvatthī. At that time, thieves who had committed a robbery in the city were fleeing, pursued by guards. They dropped their stolen goods near the Elder and fled. The people pursuing them saw the goods near the Elder, bound him, and thinking he was a thief, arrested him and presented him to the King, saying, "Your Majesty, this man is the thief."

The King had the Elder released and asked, "Venerable Sir, did you commit this theft or not?" Although the Elder had never committed such a theft since birth, he wished to preach to the monks nearby and to the King to show that he had not done so since his ordination and that, having entirely eradicated defilements, he was incapable of such an act. Thus, he spoke:

"Since the time I went forth from the home life into homelessness,
I do not recall any ignoble thought associated with hatred.

'Let these beings be killed, let them be bound,
let them come to suffering'—
such a thought I do not recall during this long interval."
240:
I know loving-kindness (mettā), immeasurable and well-developed, practiced in due order just as it was taught by the Buddha.

Being a friend to all, a companion to all, compassionate towards all beings, I develop a mind of loving-kindness, always greatly delighting in promoting the welfare of beings.

I gladden the mind that is unconquerable by enemies and unshakeable by them; I develop the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) not frequented by ignoble persons (but frequented only by the noble ones).

Having entered the attainment (samāpatti) free from thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), I, a disciple of the Fully Enlightened One, am then endowed with noble silence (ariya-tuṇhībhāva).

Just as a solid rock mountain is unshakable and well-established, so a monk, through the destruction of delusion (moha), like a mountain, does not tremble.

To a virtuous person who is free from the blemish of defilements and always seeking purity, even a sin as small as the tip of a hair appears as large as a cloud.

Just as a border city is guarded both inside and out, so should you guard yourselves; let not the opportune moment (for practice) pass you by.

I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life; I await the time (of Parinibbāna) like a laborer awaiting his wages.

I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life; I await the time (of Parinibbāna) with clear comprehension and mindfulness.

I have served the Teacher (the Buddha); I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching. The heavy burden (of the five aggregates) has been laid down; the craving that leads to becoming has been uprooted.

The purpose for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—that purpose, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me.

Strive with diligence (to fulfill the path and fruit); this is my instruction. Now I shall attain Parinibbāna, being liberated from all defilements. — Thus he spoke these verses.
241:
In these verses, the word-by-word commentary is as follows: "For such a long time" means from the time I was ordained until this final moment; in this long interval of time, it should be connected as: "I do not know (have never conceived) any ignoble thought associated with anger, whether by the power of covetousness (abhijjhā) thinking 'May this wealth be mine,' or by the power of ill-will (byāpāda) such as 'May these beings be killed.'"

"I also know loving-kindness" means: it is called loving-kindness (mettā) because it loves or is affectionate; it is indeed non-ill-will (abyāpāda). Because there is loving-kindness, it refers to the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā), the divine abode of loving-kindness (mettā-brahmavihāra). By the word "ca" (and), the other divine abodes—compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā)—are also included. "I know" means knowing by direct realization. For one who reviews the attained jhāna, it becomes manifest before the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). What kind of loving-kindness? He says "immeasurable" and so on. That loving-kindness is called "immeasurable" (appamāṇa) because it takes immeasurable beings as its object through pervasive radiation without specification, just as taught by the Blessed Buddha. It is called "well-developed" (subhāvita) because it has been thoroughly developed to reach a state of proficiency and strength. It should be connected as: "I know that which has been practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed in due order: first loving-kindness, then compassion, then appreciative joy, and finally equanimity."

He is called "friend to all" (sabbamitta) because he is a friend to all beings, or because all those beings are his friends. One who develops loving-kindness tends to be beloved by beings. In the word "companion to all" (sabbasakha), the method is the same. "Compassionate towards all beings" (sabbabhūtānukampaka) means one who favors or helps all beings. "I develop a mind of loving-kindness" means I especially develop, increase, or—even if not spoken—make manifest the mind associated and conjoined with loving-kindness due to the excellence of its development. There is also a reading "mettāṃ cittañca bhāvemi"; its meaning is the same as stated above. "Delighting in harmlessness" (abyāpajjarato) means one who greatly delights in promoting the welfare of beings. "Always" (sadā) means at all times, thereby showing constant practice in that welfare.

"Unconquerable" (asaṃhīraṃ) means not to be led away; it cannot be pulled away by lust (rāga), which is the near enemy. "Unshakeable" (asaṃkuppaṃ) means not to be disturbed; it cannot be provoked by ill-will (byāpāda), which is the distant enemy. Having brought it to such a state, "I gladden, I greatly gladden my mind of loving-kindness; I develop the divine abode." "Not frequented by ignoble persons" (akāpurisasevitaṃ) means not frequented by low persons (kāpurisa), or it means the noble (akāpurisa), such as the Buddhas and others, frequent this noble, faultless dwelling (brahmavihāra) of loving-kindness and so on; "I develop, I increase it" is the meaning.
242:
Having thus shown his own practice through five verses by way of referring to himself, now, wishing to show that same practice by way of another designation [referring to the fruit of Arahantship], he spoke the four verses beginning with "Avitakkaṃ." Among those verses, "avitakkaṃ samāpanno" means attaining the second jhāna and so forth, which are devoid of initial thought. By this statement, the Elder, by way of another designation for the development of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra-bhāvanā), spoke of his own attainment of the jhānas such as the second jhāna. Because this Elder, making that very jhāna the basis, developed insight (vipassanā) and attained the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) in a single sitting, he spoke the words "avitakkaṃ samāpanno," followed by "sammāsambuddhasāvako; ariayena tuṇhībhāvena, upeto hoti tāvade," wishing to show that matter only by way of another designation for the fruit of Arahantship.

In that Pali text, the attainment devoid of initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) is called "Noble Silence" (ariya tuṇhībhāva) because of the absence of verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra). However, according to the teaching, "Monks, when you have gathered together, two things should be done: either Dhamma talk or Noble Silence" (M. i. 273), any meditative attainment whatsoever is called Noble Silence. But in this context, the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samāpatti) based on the fourth jhāna is intended.

Now, wishing to illustrate with a simile his unshakability by worldly conditions (lokadhamma) due to having attained that fruit of Arahantship, he spoke the verse beginning with "Yathāpi pabbato." In that verse, "yathāpi pabbato selo" means just as a great mountain made of solid rock, not an earthen mountain nor a mixed mountain, is a single solid mass. "Acalo suppatiṭṭhito" means its base is well-established, so it is immovable and unshakable by natural winds. Therefore, the fruit of Arahantship and Nibbāna are likewise [unshakable]. "Thus, through the destruction of delusion, the monk does not tremble like a mountain" means that because of the total abandonment of delusion, and because all unwholesome states have delusion as their root, the monk who has abandoned all unwholesome states does not tremble or shake due to worldly conditions, just as that great mountain is not shaken by natural winds. Alternatively, the fruit of Arahantship and Nibbāna are called by the name "mohakkhaya" (destruction of delusion). Therefore, because of the attainment of Nibbāna and the fruit of Arahantship, which are the causes for the destruction of delusion, one who is well-established in the Four Noble Truths does not tremble like a mountain even when not in meditative attainment, let alone when he is in attainment—this is the meaning.

Now, wishing to show that what is called evil is practiced only by one of impure virtue, and not by one of pure virtue, and that for one of pure virtue, even a matter as small as an atom appears as a heavy burden...
243:
He spoke the verse beginning with "Anaṅgaṇassa." The meaning of that verse is: For a virtuous person who is without blemish (anaṅgaṇa) due to the absence of defilements like lust (rāga), and who always seeks only pure and blameless states, even a mere trace of evil as small as the tip of a tail-hair or the tip of a head-hair appears as prominent as a great cloud-mass that stands pervading the entire world-element. Therefore, the meaning is that people should not suspect such actions in someone like me.

Since even towards those who are free from defilements, the extremely foolish raise such accusations, he spoke the verse beginning with "Nagaraṃ yathā," wishing to give the advice: "Therefore, those who desire their own welfare should carefully guard themselves." The meaning of that verse is: Just as people living in a border city guard it by making the gates and walls firm to protect the interior, and by making the high watchtowers and moats firm to protect the exterior, so too, you should establish mindfulness and close the six internal doors. Without letting go of mindfulness, which is like a gatekeeper, you should guard yourselves, moving about without abandoning the gatekeeper-mindfulness, so that the six external sense bases (āyatana), when being perceived, do not lead to the destruction of the internal sense bases. By not grasping them, make them firm so they cannot enter. Why? "Let not the moment pass you by." For if one does not guard oneself in this way, all these moments will pass him by: the moment of a Buddha's arising, the moment of obtaining human birth, the moment of being born in the middle country, the moment of acquiring right view, and the moment of having the six sense bases intact. Let not that moment pass you by.

Thus, the Elder, having exhorted the assembly including the King and the monks with this verse, spoke the verse beginning with "Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ," wishing to manifest once more his even-mindedness (samacittatā) towards death and life, and the completion of his task. Its meaning is the same as what was stated below [in the commentary].

Having spoken thus, seeing that the time for his Parinibbāna had arrived, he spoke the final verse, giving them a brief exhortation and making known his impending Parinibbāna. In that verse, "sampādetha appamādena" means: fulfill with diligence (appamāda) the things to be fulfilled, such as generosity (dāna) and virtue (sīla); be diligent in the duties of householders with their various benefits for the present and the future, in the preservation of virtue, in the devotion to tranquility (samatha), and in the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā). "Esā me anusāsanī" means: "Do not be negligent in generosity, virtue, and so forth"—this is my instruction and advice. Having thus shown the practice for the welfare of others which had reached its pinnacle, and wishing to bring the practice for his own welfare to its conclusion, he said, "Parinibbāyissaṃ vippamutto sabbadhi." In those words, "vippamutto sabbadhi" means: "I am one who is released from defilements and from [future] existences in every way; therefore, I shall surely attain Parinibbāna." Having spoken thus, while sitting in the cross-legged posture in the sky, he entered the meditative attainment of the fire element (tejodhātu-samāpatti)...
244:
Having thus demonstrated the practice for the welfare of others which had reached its pinnacle, and wishing to reach the consummation of the practice for his own welfare, he said: "Now I shall attain Parinibbāna; I am fully released in all things." In that statement, "I am fully released in all things" means being completely liberated from all defilements and from all rounds of existence; therefore, he meant that he would certainly attain Parinibbāna.

Having spoken thus, sitting cross-legged in the air, he entered the meditative attainment of the fire element and, while aflame, attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Khadiravaniya Revata is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Godatta

The verse beginning with "Yathāpi bhaddo" belongs to the Venerable Elder Godatta. What is its origin? This elder had also performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit that serves as a powerful support for liberation from the round of rebirths in various existences, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a family of caravan merchants. When he reached maturity under the name Godatta, and after his father had passed away, he maintained the family wealth and made a living by trading, traveling to and fro with five hundred carts. He also performed meritorious deeds according to his wealth.

One day, while on a journey, an ox harnessed to the yoke fell down, unable to carry the load. When the people were unable to make the ox stand up, he went there himself and pierced the ox's tail severely. The ox, becoming angry and thinking, "This base man, not knowing my strength or weakness, pierces me severely," spoke in human language and cursed him according to its wish: "O Godatta, for so long I have carried your burden without hiding my strength. Now, when I have fallen because I am unable, you oppress me excessively. So be it; after passing away from this life, may I become a powerful enemy capable of oppressing you in whatever place you are born."

Hearing those words, Godatta was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "What is the use of this livelihood by oppressing beings in such a way?" He renounced all his wealth and was ordained in the presence of a certain Great Elder. While practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahatship before long. Spending his time in the bliss of meditative attainment, one day, wishing to preach the Dhamma concerning the worldly conditions to the assembly of noble ones, both laypeople and monks, who had approached him—
245:
"Just as a noble thoroughbred bull, harnessed to the yoke and oppressed by a heavy burden, does not rebel against its yoke.

"Even so, the wise who are satisfied with wisdom, like the ocean with water, are not oppressed by others; only the Dhamma of the Noble Ones is accustomed to making beings complete in wisdom.

"People who, following the power of time, have come under the sway of existence and non-existence (gain and loss), encounter suffering; those young men grieve in this world.

"Elated by pleasant conditions and dejected by painful conditions, fools who do not see things as they truly are, are destroyed by these two.

"Those who have transcended craving, the seamstress, in the midst of suffering, happiness, and neutral feeling, stand firm like an Indra-pillar; they are neither elated nor dejected.

"Neither in gain nor loss, neither in fame nor disrepute, neither in blame nor praise, and neither in suffering nor happiness (are they shaken).

"They are not stained by any of these, just as a drop of water does not cling to a lotus leaf. The wise are happy in all circumstances and are undefeated by any worldly conditions.

"Between loss that is righteous and gain that is unrighteous, loss that is righteous is indeed better.

"Between the fame of those with little wisdom and the disrepute of the wise, the disrepute of the wise is indeed better.

"Between praise by fools and blame by the wise, blame by the wise is indeed better.

"Between happiness born of sensual pleasures and suffering born of seclusion, suffering born of seclusion is indeed better.

"Between life that is unrighteous and death that is righteous, death that is righteous is indeed better."
246:
“Those who have abandoned sensual desire and anger, who possess peaceful minds in various existences, and who live in the world unattached by craving and views—for them, there is no one dear or undear. Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the five faculties (indriya), and the five powers (bala), and having reached the supreme peace of Nibbāna, they, being free from taints (āsava), attain Parinibbāna.” Thus He spoke these verses.

In those verses, ‘ājañño’ refers to a noble bull (usabhājānīya). ‘Dhure yutto’ means well-yoked to the front of a cart. ‘Dhurassaho’ means one who is capable of carrying the burden. In the composition of the verse, it is referred to as ‘dhurassaho’ with a double ‘s’ for ease of meter; it means one capable of carrying the cart’s load. ‘Mathito atibhārena’ means oppressed by an excessively heavy burden. There is also a reading ‘maddito’, which has the same meaning. ‘Saṃyugaṃ’ means not exceeding the yoke placed on one’s shoulders, or not standing still by abandoning the burden without properly mounting the front of the cart. Just as that draft animal, due to its noble nature and firm effort, does not exceed or abandon the burden it must carry, likewise, those Noble Ones (Ariyas) are endowed with mundane and supramundane wisdom, like the great ocean is full of water. These wise ones do not oppress or despise others who have little wisdom.

The reason for this is stated as ‘ariyadhammova pāṇinaṃ’. Among beings, this is the nature of the Noble Ones; because their wisdom has reached fulfillment, there is no self-exaltation due to gain and the like, nor disparagement of others due to loss and the like.

After showing the happy living of the Noble Ones due to the fulfillment of wisdom, the words beginning with ‘kāle’ are spoken to show the miserable living of worldlings due to the absence of that wisdom. In those words, ‘kāle’ means the time when one encounters gain, loss, and so on. ‘Kālavasampattā’ means those who follow the will of the time, such as gain and loss; it means being joyful when there is gain and being dejected when there is loss. ‘Bhavābhavavasaṃ gatā’ means those who follow the will of circumstances such as having wealth or not, and who follow after prosperity and decline. Those people reach suffering. ‘Te dha socanti māṇavā’ means those beings called ‘māṇava’ fall into delight and anger through the power of gain, loss, prosperity, and decline, and thus they grieve in this present world and reach the suffering of hell and so on in the afterlife.
247:
With the verse beginning with ‘unnatā’, He also shows only the misfortune of beings through the power of worldly conditions (lokadhamma). In that verse, ‘sukhadhammena unnatā’ refers to those who have reached arrogance and intoxication due to the causes and conditions of happiness, such as the fulfillment of wealth. ‘Dukkhadhammena conatā’ refers to those who have reached lowliness and misery, such as poverty, due to the causes and conditions of suffering, such as the ruin of wealth. By these two—the aforementioned elation and depression, or gain and loss—foolish worldlings are oppressed; they are distressed and afflicted through the power of attachment and aversion. Why? Because they do not see things as they truly are (yathābhūtaṃ adassino). It means they do not know the nature of things correctly, they do not fully understand the aggregates (khandha), and they have not yet abandoned the defilements (kilesa). There is also a reading ‘yathābhūtaṃ adassanā’, meaning because of not seeing.

Those Noble Ones (Ariyas) who, through the attainment of the highest path (Arahatship), have transcended craving (sibbini), which is the desire and lust associated with painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neutral feeling. Those Noble Ones stand unshaken by the winds of worldly conditions, like a stone pillar (indakhīla). They are never elated or depressed because they completely lack attraction and repulsion.

Having thus shown the state of an Arahat who is unsmeared by craving in the foundation of feeling, He now speaks the words beginning with ‘na hevā’ to analyze the worldly conditions and show the state of being unsmeared in all things. There, ‘lābha’ means the acquisition of the four requisites such as robes, and ‘alābha’ means the non-acquisition or loss of those same requisites. ‘Na yasa’ means the loss of followers and the absence of fame. ‘Kitti’ means fame and the spreading of one’s reputation. ‘Nindā’ means blame in one’s presence, and ‘pasaṃsā’ means praising one’s virtues in one’s presence. In the cases of ‘dukkha’ (suffering) and ‘sukha’ (happiness), the method is the same.

In all the aforementioned eight worldly conditions, and in all the five sense objects such as forms, those who have destroyed the taints (Khīṇāsavas) are not smeared because they have completely abandoned the defilements. For example, just as a drop of water on a lotus leaf does not smear the leaf even though it stays on it, and the lotus leaf is not mixed with the water but remains separate, likewise, these Noble Ones remain separate and free, without being mixed, even when encountering gain and the like, or when sense objects such as forms come into range. For that very reason, those wise ones (dhīra), being led by knowledge in matters of gain and the like, reach happiness because they no longer have sorrow and the like caused by dear objects. Because gain, loss, and the like cannot oppress them, they are not defeated by any worldly conditions.
248:
They reach happiness through gain and so forth, and because they are not overcome by them (gain, loss, etc.), they are unvanquished in all circumstances.

Now, wishing to extract and show what is superior among gain, loss, and so forth, he said the verse beginning with "dhamma". In that context, "non-gain through Dhamma" (dhammaena ca alābho yo) refers to the non-attainment of gain, the absence of gain, or the loss of gain that occurs to one who protects the Dhamma, because of that protection. Unrighteous gain is that which arises through unrighteousness, through wrong means, or through methods rebuked by the Buddha. Between these two, righteous non-gain that brings Dhamma is superior. For one who avoids such [unrighteous] gain, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase. Such non-gain is more praiseworthy and brings benefit. "And if gain is unrighteous" (yañce lābho adhammiko) means that gain which arises through unrighteousness is not superior.

"Fame of the foolish, and infamy among the wise" (yaso ca appabuddhīnaṃ, viññūnaṃ ayaso ca yo) refers to the fame or retinue a person obtains through those of little wisdom, and the infamy or loss of fame through the wise or learned. Between these two, infamy among the wise is superior. For they [the wise] would desire such loss of fame for him so that his unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase. Only then can a person of fit nature abandon that lack of virtue and establish himself in virtue. Fame through those of little wisdom is not superior. For they might produce that fame even by speaking of non-existent qualities. That [false praise] brings harm to him, through the rebuke of the wise in this life, and through suffering and defilement in the miserable realms in the future life. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Gain, renown, honor, and the fame that is wrongly obtained," and "Honor kills the bad man."

"By the foolish" (dummedhehi) means by those without wisdom. "And if there is praise by fools" (yañce bālappasaṃsanā) means the kind of praise by fools and the ignorant.

"Consisting of sensuality" (kāmamayikaṃ) means consisting of objective sensuality, arising based on the strands of sensual pleasure. "And pain born of seclusion" (dukkhañca pavivekiyaṃ) means physical pain arising from seclusion, occurring by way of physical exhaustion, caused by uneven sitting, heat, and so forth. However, because it is a strong support for the end of the round of rebirth without worldly attachment, it is praised by the wise. Therefore, it is said: "Pain born of seclusion is superior."
249:
Making a living unrighteously or practicing unrighteously for the sake of life is called "living unrighteously". Righteous death means: even if someone says, "I will kill you if you do not do this evil," and kills him, the death of that person who does not do evil and does not violate the Dhamma is superior because it is for the sake of Dhamma. Such a death is righteous because it is not departed from Dhamma; it is highly praiseworthy by the wise because it leads to heaven and is a strong support for Nibbāna. For this reason, it is said:

"One should sacrifice wealth for the sake of a noble limb,
One should sacrifice a limb while protecting life,
A man, recollecting the Dhamma, should sacrifice limbs, wealth, and even all of life."

"And if one should live unrighteously" (yañce jīve adhammikaṃ) means that a man should not resort to a livelihood that is departed from Dhamma, because it is rebuked by the wise and leads to the states of deprivation.

Now, wishing to show the reason for the non-clinging of the Arahants mentioned, he spoke the verse beginning with "Those who have abandoned desire and anger" (kāmakopapahīnā).

In that verse, "those who have abandoned desire and anger" (kāmakopapahīnā) means those for whom compliance (attachment) and resistance (aversion) have been entirely abandoned by the Noble Path. "Peaceful-minded in various states of existence" (santacitta bhavābhave) means those with peaceful minds because the fever of defilements has been entirely abandoned in both small and great existences. "In the world" (loke) means in the world of the aggregates and so forth. "Unsupported" (asitā) means those who are not supported by way of the supports of craving and views. "There is for them no dear or undear" (natthi tesaṃ piyāpiyaṃ) means for those Arahants, there is nothing dear or undear in any gain and so forth, or in objects such as visible forms, because the defilements that are the cause of that [dearness or undearness] have been entirely cut off and eradicated.

Now, showing the meditation by which they became such, and taking the climax of the teaching with the Nibbāna element without remainder, he spoke the concluding verse beginning with "Having developed" (bhāvayitvāna). In that verse, "having reached" (pappuyya) means having attained. The rest is as explained in the manner mentioned below. These verses were also the declarations of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa) of the Elder.

## The Explanation of the Verses of the Elder Godatta is finished.
## The Explanation of the Numerical Collection of the Fourteen is finished.
250:
## 15. Soḷasakanipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña

In the Soḷasakanipāta (Book of the Sixteens), this verse beginning with "Esa bhiyyo" is the verse of the Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña. What is its origin? This Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña was also born into a wealthy householder family (gahapati-mahāsāla) in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Buddha Padumuttara. When he reached the age of discretion, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain monk to the chief position among those of long standing (rattaññū) who first realized the Four Noble Truths in His Dispensation. Aspiring for that same position, he performed a great alms-giving (mahādāna) for seven days to the Teacher, who was accompanied by one hundred thousand monks, and made his resolution. The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles for him, prophesied his future attainment. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, and when the Teacher attained Parinibbāna and a cetiya was being built, he had a jewel house constructed inside the cetiya. He also had one thousand jewel baskets made to surround the cetiya.

Having performed such meritorious deeds, he passed away from that life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. During the time of Buddha Vipassī, he became a householder named Mahākāla. In a field of about eight karīsas, he split open the rice embryos and prepared pure milk-rice from the grains obtained. Adding honey, butter, sugar, and other ingredients to that milk-rice, he offered it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Every time he split the rice embryos and took the grains, the place would be filled again. At the time of the first-cake offering, he gave the first-cakes. At the time of harvesting, he gave the first-harvest; at the time of binding, the first-binding; at the time of bundling, the first-bundle; the first-threshing, the first-gathering, the first-measuring, and the first-storing. Thus, he gave the offering of first-fruits nine times during a single crop season. That crop also became exceptionally abundant.

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he passed away and was reborn in the celestial realm. After wandering between the realms of gods and humans, even before the appearance of our Buddha, he was born into a wealthy brahmin family (brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla) in the brahmin village named Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu. He was given the name "Koṇḍañña" based on his clan. When he reached maturity, he studied the three Vedas and reached the completion of the science of marks. At that time, our...
251:
The Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita heaven and was born in the palace of King Suddhodana in the city of Kapilavatthu. On the naming day of the Bodhisatta prince, one hundred and eight brahmins were invited. Among the eight brahmins who were brought to the upper chamber for the purpose of examining the marks, Koṇḍañña was the youngest of all. Seeing the perfection of the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa), he reached the conclusion that "This prince will certainly become a Buddha," and he lived in anticipation of the Great Renunciation of the Great Being. As the Bodhisatta grew up with a great retinue, he eventually reached maturity and the ripening of his knowledge. In his twenty-ninth year, he departed in the Great Renunciation, became a monk on the banks of the Anomā River, and gradually proceeded to the Uruvelā forest to exert himself in striving.

At that time, the young Koṇḍañña heard of the Bodhisatta's renunciation. Together with the young Vappa and others, who were the sons of the brahmins who had read the marks, he became a monk as the fifth member of the group. Gradually approaching the Bodhisatta, he attended to him for six years. Becoming disillusioned when the Bodhisatta partook of solid food, he departed and went to the Isipatana Deer Park. Then, the Bodhisatta, having regained his physical strength by partaking of solid food, sat upon the Unconquered Throne (Aparājitapallaṅka) at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha). Overcoming the three Maras, he attained Buddhahood by realizing the Four Noble Truths and spent seven weeks at the site of the Bodhi tree. Knowing the ripening of the knowledge of the group of five monks (pañcavaggiya), he went to the Isipatana Deer Park on the full moon day of Waso (Āsāḷha) and preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta to them. At the end of the discourse, Venerable Koṇḍañña, along with eighteen crores of Brahmas, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Then, on the fifth day of the waning moon, he realized the fruit of Arahantship through the discourse of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"I first saw the Buddha Padumuttara, the Foremost of the World, the Guide, who had reached the stage of Buddhahood. As many as all the deities who had gathered at the foot of the Bodhi tree, they surrounded the Buddha and worshipped Him with joined palms. All those deities, with joyful minds, wandered through the sky, saying with delighted hearts, 'This Buddha, the dispeller of the darkness of ignorance, has arrived.'"
252:
A great, thunderous roar arose from those joyful deities: "We shall burn away the defilements in the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One!"

Knowing the noble speech of the deities, with a gladdened heart, I offered the very first alms-food.

Knowing my intention, the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world, sitting in the midst of the assembly of deities, spoke these verses:

"Having gone forth and having practiced for seven days, I attained Enlightenment. This first alms-food of mine is the sustenance for one living the sublime life.

The one who came here from the Tusita heaven and offered me alms-food; I shall praise him. Listen to what I say.

For thirty thousand aeons, he will exercise the sovereignty of a king of gods. Surpassing all other deities, he will dwell in the celestial realm.

Passing away from the deva world, he will reach the state of a human. There, he will be a Universal Monarch a thousand times.

One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka dynasty, will arise in the world.

Passing away from the celestial realm, he will reach the state of a human. Having gone forth from home and become a monk, he will practice for six years.

Then, in the seventh year, the Buddha will preach the Four Noble Truths. This person, named Koṇḍañña, will be the first to realize the Truth."

I followed the Buddha who had gone forth and I too went forth. I have practiced the meditation subjects well. To burn away the defilements, I entered the homeless life and became a monk.

The Buddha, the Knower of All in the world including the devas, went to the Migadāya forest named Isipatana and beat the drum of the Deathless.

I have now reached the unsurpassed state of peace, Nibbāna. Having fully understood all taints, I dwell free from taints.

The four analytical insights... (and so on) I have fulfilled the Buddha's Dispensation.
253:
Afterwards, while the Teacher was seated on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks at the Jetavana Monastery, wishing to show who first penetrated the Dhamma, He declared: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are of long standing (rattaññū), Aññāsi Koṇḍañña is the foremost," and thus placed him in the position of Etadagga. That Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, wishing to avoid the excessive respect shown to him by the two Chief Disciples and the crowded living in the monastery near the village, and desiring to dwell in the delight of solitude, considered even the act of receiving and greeting (paṭisanthāra) the laypeople and monks who approached him as an impediment (papañca). Thus, after asking permission from the Teacher, he entered the Himālaya forest and lived for twelve years on the banks of Lake Chaddanta, being attended to by the Chaddanta elephants. 

One day, while the Elder was living there, Sakka, the King of Devas, approached him, paid homage, and said: "Venerable Sir, please preach the Dhamma to me." The Elder preached the Dhamma to Sakka with the grace of a Buddha—a teaching that has the Four Noble Truths as its core, is connected with the Three Characteristics, is associated with Emptiness (suññatā), is adorned with various methods, and plunges into the Deathless. Having heard that teaching, Sakka, wishing to express his devotion, spoke the first verse:

"I am exceedingly gladdened by hearing this Dhamma of great flavor. The Dhamma of passionlessness (virāga) has been preached, without any clinging whatsoever."

In that verse, "I am exceedingly gladdened by hearing this Dhamma of great flavor" means: although he had heard the Dhamma many times in the presence of the Teacher and was already devoted, now, having heard this Dhamma of great flavor, which is adorned with various methods and is ever-fresh, he was even more gladdened. "The Dhamma of passionlessness has been preached, without any clinging whatsoever" means: it is called "passionlessness" (virāga) because it is the fading away of and the cause for the fading away of all defilements and all conditioned things. Because it proceeds by way of achieving liberation without clinging to or grasping any phenomenon such as form, it is called the Dhamma preached without any clinging whatsoever.

Thus, Sakka, the King of Devas, praised the Elder's teaching, paid homage to the Elder, and returned to his own place. Then one day, the Elder, seeing the mental behavior of some worldlings who were being oppressed by wrong thoughts, and recollecting the gradual path that is the opposite of those wrong thoughts, reflected on how his own mind had completely turned away from those wrong thoughts. Wishing to illustrate that meaning, he spoke these two verses:

In the world, sensual thoughts associated with passion remain entangled in many wondrous objects. My mind's thought is like the rain accompanied by wind that calms the rising dust; when one sees with wisdom that things are impermanent, then all sensual thoughts are calmed.
254:
One day, the Elder, seeing the mental thoughts of some worldlings who were being oppressed by wrong thoughts (micchāvitakka), and recollecting in order the qualities that are the opposite of those wrong thoughts, and having a mind that had completely withdrawn from those wrong thoughts himself, spoke these two verses to show that meaning:

'In the world, on this earth-circle, there are many wonders. I think that beautiful thoughts associated with lust stir the mind (of beings). Just as dust raised by the wind is calmed by a rain shower, so too, when one sees with wisdom, thoughts are calmed.'

In those verses, 'bahūni loke citrāni' means many diverse objects in the world, such as forms, and among them, blue, yellow, etc., and women, men, etc. 'Asmiṃ paṭhavimaṇḍale' refers to the manifest human world. 'Mathenti maññe saṅkappaṃ' means that wrong thoughts (micchāsaṅkappa), known as improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), exist as if stirring the mind, like fire produced by human effort and friction. What kind of thoughts? 'Subhaṃ rāgūpasaṃhitaṃ' means sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) associated with lust for the beautiful. They are called 'beautiful' because they are taken as having a beautiful aspect. In the phrase 'rajamuhatāñca vātena,' the word 'ca' is just a particle. Just as a great rain cloud raining down calms the dust raised by the wind in the last month of the summer season, 'evaṃ sammanti saṅkappā, yadā paññāya passati' means when a noble disciple sees those worldly wonders as they really are through wisdom—in terms of their origin, gratification, danger, and escape. Then, just as that dust is calmed by the rain, all wrong thoughts are calmed by wisdom. When right view (sammādiṭṭhi) has arisen, wrong thoughts find no footing. To show the manner of seeing with wisdom, he spoke these three verses:

'When one sees with wisdom that all formations are impermanent, then one becomes weary of suffering. This is the path to purity.'
'When one sees with wisdom that all formations are suffering... (as above) ... This is the path to purity.'
'When one sees with wisdom that all phenomena are non-self, then one becomes weary of suffering. This is the path to purity.'

In those verses, 'sabbe saṅkhārā' means all five aggregates occurring in the three realms, which are counted by way of the six objects, are impermanent. They are so because they have a beginning, middle, and end, by way of their impermanent nature.
255:
In those verses, 'sabbe saṅkhārā' refers to all five aggregates of the three realms included within the collection of the six objects. 'Aniccā' means they are not permanent because they have a beginning, middle, and end; because they end in impermanence; because they are temporary; and because they break up here and there. When one sees this with insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), 'atha nibbindati dukkhe'—then one becomes weary of this suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha). Being weary, one penetrates the Truths through the method of fully understanding suffering and so on. 'Esa maggo visuddhiyā' means this aforementioned method of insight is the path, the means of attainment, to the purity of knowledge and vision and to ultimate purity (Nibbāna).

'Dukkhā' means they are suffering because they are accompanied by danger, because they are constantly oppressed by rise and fall, because they are painful, and because they exclude happiness. The rest is as previously stated.

'Sabbe dhammā anattā' means all phenomena of the four planes are non-self. However, here only the phenomena of the three planes should be taken. They should be contemplated as non-self because they lack essence, are not subject to control, are empty, and exclude a self. The rest is similar to what was said before.

Having thus shown the method of insight, to show himself as one who has completed the task through that method, as if speaking of another, he spoke these two verses:

'The Elder Koṇḍañña, who awakened after the Buddhas, who is of strenuous effort, who has abandoned birth and death, and is consummate in the holy life.
Having cut the snare of the flood and the firm stake, and having broken the mountain so difficult to shatter; having cut the stake and the snare, and having shattered the rock of delusion so difficult to break,
The meditator who has crossed over and reached the far shore is liberated from Mara's bond.'

In those verses, 'buddhānubuddho' means one who awakens following the Buddhas; the meaning is that he awakens to the Truths realized by the Fully Enlightened Ones in accordance with their teaching. He is an 'Elder' (thero) because he is endowed with the firm essence of virtue of an adept (asekha) and so on. 'Koṇḍañña' is the mention of his clan name. 'Tibbanikkamo' means one of firm energy and steady persistence. He is one who has 'abandoned birth and death' because he has abandoned the causes of birth and death. 'Brahmacariyassa kevalī' means he has fulfilled the holy life of the path without remainder, or he has fulfilled the holy life of the path completely. Alternatively, 'kevalī' refers to Path-knowledge and Fruit-knowledge because they are unmixed with defilements; thus, it means one endowed with that Path and Fruit.
256:
Because there is no mixing with defilements in this Path and Fruition, he is called 'Kevalī'. Since both that Path and Fruition occur only by the power of the holy life of the Path and not otherwise, he is called 'Brahmacariyassa kevalī' (one who has completed the entirety of the holy life).

'Oghapāsa' refers to the four floods—the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance—and the snare of lust, which is 'like a snare moving in the sky that binds beings.' 'Daḷhakhila' refers to the five kinds of firm mental barrenness, described as 'doubting the Teacher, doubting the Dhamma, doubting the Saṅgha, doubting the three trainings, and being angry, displeased, and having a mind of ill-will towards fellow practitioners.' Because it cannot be broken by many people, it is called 'duppadālaya' (hard to shatter). For that very reason, because of its similarity to a mountain, it is also called 'pabbata' (mountain). It also refers to the various types of ignorance (aññāṇa) described by such methods as 'ignorance regarding suffering.' Thus, having cut all these four types of defilements—the barrenness and the snare—with the sword of the knowledge of the Noble Path; having shattered the mountain of delusion, which cannot be shattered by any other knowledge, with the diamond-like knowledge of the Path of Arahantship; and having crossed the four floods, he is called 'tiṇṇo pāraṅgato' (one who has crossed over and reached the further shore) because he stands in Nibbāna, the further shore of those floods. He meditates through both types of absorption: absorption on the object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and absorption on the characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). The phrase 'mutto so mārabandhanā' (he is released from the bond of Māra) means that such an Arahant is freed, fully released, and disconnected from all the bonds of the Māra of defilements. The Elder spoke this referring to himself.

Then one day, the Elder saw one of his resident pupils (saddhivihārika) living lazily, with diminished energy, restless, and frivolous due to association with bad friends. He went there by psychic power and advised him: 'Friend, do not do this. Abandon bad friends, associate with good friends, and practice the Dhamma of a recluse.' That monk did not heed the Elder's words. Because of that monk's disregard, the Elder was moved by religious urgency (saṃvega). Censuring wrong practice and praising right practice and living in seclusion through a discourse based on a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), he said:

'A restless and frivolous monk, depending on evil friends,
Sinks in the great flood, overwhelmed by the waves.
(Overwhelmed by the wave of anger, he sinks in the flood of saṃsāra.) ...'
257:
The Elder spoke. Then one day, the Elder saw one of his resident pupils living lazily, with diminished energy, restless and uncomposed due to association with bad friends. He went there by psychic power and advised him: 'Friend, do not do this. Abandon bad friends, associate with good friends, and practice the Dhamma of a recluse.' That monk did not heed the Elder's words. Because of that monk's disregard, the Elder felt religious urgency (saṃvega). Censuring wrong practice and praising right practice and living in seclusion through a discourse based on a person, he said—

A monk who is not restless, not frivolous, wise in his welfare, with restrained senses, having good friends and being sagacious, would make an end of the suffering of the round.

Resembling a black bamboo joint, lean, with veins showing, knowing moderation in food and drink, with a mind that is not dejected,

Though bitten by gadflies and mosquitoes in the great forest, like an elephant in the heat of battle, he should endure there mindfully.

685-6.
I do not delight in death ... mindful and clearly comprehending, I only wait for the time.
I have served the Teacher ... the craving for existence is uprooted.
The goal for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness, that goal I have attained; what use have I for a difficult-to-admonish resident pupil? Thus he recited these verses.

In those verses, 'uddhato' means one possessed of restlessness, uncomposed, with a distracted mind. 'Capalo' means one endowed with frivolity regarding the decoration of the bowl and robes, etc., being of a fickle nature. 'Mitte āgamma pāpake' means not practicing the Dhamma of a recluse by depending on bad friends. 'Saṃsīdati mahoghasmiṃ ūmiyā paṭikujjito' means that just as a person who has fallen into the great ocean sinks because he is overwhelmed by the waves and cannot raise his head, so too, while wandering in the great flood of saṃsāra, being overwhelmed and covered by the wave of anger and displeasure, he cannot raise the head of insight-wisdom and thus sinks in that very flood.

'Nipako' means clever, skillful in his own welfare and the welfare of others. 'Saṃvutindriyo' means one whose senses are closed through the restraint of the six sense bases, starting with the mind. 'Kalyāṇamitto' means one endowed with good friends. 'Medhāvī' means one possessed of wisdom, which is the essence of the Dhamma. 'Dukkhassantakaro siyā' means such a person would be one who makes an end of the entire suffering of the round.

The words beginning with 'kālapabbaṅgasaṅkāso' are a praise of delighting in seclusion. The words beginning with 'nābhinandāmi' show the state of one who has completed the task. All of that has the same meaning as previously stated. At the end...
258:
The phrase "What is the use of a co-resident to me?" was spoken with reference to his own co-resident. Therefore, the meaning is: "What benefit is there for me with such a difficult-to-admonish and disrespectful co-resident? I prefer living alone."

Having spoken thus, he went to Lake Chaddanta. Having lived there for twelve years, when the time for his final passing away (Parinibbāna) drew near, he approached the Blessed One, requested permission for his final passing away, and then returned to that very place and attained Parinibbāna.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña is Finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Udāyī

The verse beginning with "Manussabhūtaṃ" is that of the Venerable Udāyī. How did it originate? This elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating merit that serves as a powerful support for liberation (vivaṭṭa) in various existences. Wandering through the realms of devas and humans, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Kapilavatthu during the time of this Buddha's appearance and was named Udāyī. Upon reaching maturity, he saw the Buddha's majesty at the assembly of the Buddha's kinsmen. Having gained faith, he went forth (ordained). While practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship before long.

In fact, there are three elders named Udāyī: Kāḷudāyī, the son of a minister who arrived first; Lāludāyī, the son of Kovariya; and this Mahā Udāyī, the son of a brahmin. One day, the Blessed One, taking as an occasion the people's praise of a white elephant adorned with all ornaments, taught the Nāgopama Sutta. At the end of the teaching, reflecting on the Buddha's virtues according to the strength of his own wisdom, and with a mind uplifted by joy centered on the Buddha, he thought: "These people praise this animal elephant, but not the Great Elephant (Nāga) who is the Buddha. Now, I shall make known the virtues of the Great Fragrant Elephant who is the Buddha." Desiring to praise the Blessed One, he addressed him thus:

"The Fully Enlightened One, who has become human, with a self-tamed and concentrated mind,
Walking on the path of the sublime (Brahmapatha), delighting in the tranquility of the mind.

Whom humans worship, who has reached the far shore of all phenomena (dhamma),
Even the devas worship him—thus have I heard from the Worthy One (Arahant)."
259:
(The devas worship) that Blessed One who has transcended all fetters, who has reached Nibbāna, the place of safety, who delights in renunciation (the state of a monk) from sensual pleasures, who is liberated from defilements, and who is pure like refined gold from a mountain rock.

That Elephant King (the Blessed One) is exceedingly beautiful, like Mount Himavant among other mountains. Among all those named 'Nāga', he is the peerless and true Nāga.

I shall praise the virtues of the Nāga (Elephant King) to you; he does no evil or misconduct at all. Virtue (sīla) and compassion (karuṇā) are the two feet of that Nāga.

Mindfulness (sati) and wisdom (paññā) are the other two walking feet of that Nāga. Having faith (saddhā) as his hand (trunk) and equanimity (upekkhā) as his pure white tusks, he is called the Great Nāga.

Mindfulness is his neck, wisdom is his head, investigating and reflecting on wholesome states is his belly, and seclusion (viveka) is the tail of that noble elephant.

That noble elephant, entering meditative absorption (jhāna), delights in Nibbāna and has a well-concentrated mind within himself. While walking, he is concentrated; while standing, he is concentrated.

Even while sleeping, he is concentrated; while sitting, he is concentrated. Restrained in all sense faculties, that noble elephant is perfect in every way.

He partakes only of blameless alms-food and does not consume anything blameworthy. Having obtained food and robes, he avoids storing them up.

Having cut all fetters and bonds, both small and large, wherever he goes, he goes without any lingering attachment.

Just as a white lotus born in the water grows in the water but is not smeared by the water, being pure in scent and delightful,

Even so, the Buddha, though born in the world and dwelling in the world, is not smeared by the things of the world, just as the lotus is not smeared by water.

Just as a great blazing fire goes out when the fuel is exhausted, and when the embers are extinguished, it is said to be "quenched" (nibbūta).
