This simile, which makes the meaning known, has been shown by the wise. The Great Nāgas (Arahants) will understand the virtues of the Nāga (the Buddha) taught by the Nāga (the Buddha), [established in their own special qualities].
260:
“Free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, free from taints, that Nāga (the Buddha), abandoning the body, being free from taints, will attain Parinibbāna.” — He spoke these verses.

In those verses, ‘mānussabhūtaṃ’ means born among humans, or having attained the state of a human. For the Teacher, although he is liberated from all destinations (gati) through the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), he is still called a ‘human’ by virtue of the rebirth taken in his final existence. However, by virtue of his qualities, he is the ‘Atideva’ (God above gods) and ‘Atibrahma’ (Brahma above Brahmas). ‘Sambuddhaṃ’ means one who has realized the truths that should be known by himself. ‘Attadantaṃ’ means self-tamed. The Blessed One is tamed by the noble path produced by himself, with the supreme restraint from the eye... (etc.) ...to the mind. ‘Samāhitaṃ’ means concentrated by the eightfold concentration (samādhi) and the concentration of the Path and Fruition.

‘Iriyamānaṃ brahmapathe’ means one who exists by virtue of entering into the fourfold Brahma-vihāras or the noble Fruition Attainment (phala-samāpatti). Although the Blessed One does not always dwell in the aforementioned Brahma-path, it is said ‘iriyamānaṃ’ (dwelling/moving) because of his ability to dwell there and his inclination towards it. ‘Cittassūpasame rataṃ’ means delighting in Nibbāna, the cessation of all formations (saṅkhāra), which is the cause for the tranquility of the mind.

‘Yaṃ manussā namassanti sabbadhammāna pāragūṃ’ means that wise kings and other humans pay homage to that Fully Enlightened One who has reached the far shore (pāragū) of all dhammas such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense bases (āyatana) in six ways: reaching the far shore of higher knowledge (abhiññā), full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), development (bhāvanā), realization (sacchikiriyā), and attainment (samāpatti), thereby reaching supreme perfection. Honoring him with practice according to the Dhamma, they are inclined, leaned, and bent towards the Blessed One in body, speech, and mind. ‘Devāpi taṃ namassanti’ means not only humans, but indeed, gods in immeasurable world systems also pay homage to that Blessed One.

‘Iti me arahato sutaṃ’ shows that “thus I have heard” in the presence of the Blessed One, who is worthy of offerings (Arahat) due to reasons such as being far from defilements, and in the presence of persons such as the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) who say, “The Teacher of gods and humans,” etc.

‘Sabbasaṃyojanātītaṃ’ means one who has transcended all ten fetters (saṃyojana) along with their latent tendencies (vāsanā) through the four paths as appropriate. ‘Vanā nibbanaṃ āgataṃ’ means one who has come from the forest of defilements to Nibbāna, which is free from that forest. ‘Kါmehi nekkhamma-rataṃ’ means one who has emerged from all sense pleasures and delights in renunciation (nekkhamma) consisting of monkhood, jhāna, vipassanā, etc. ‘Muttaṃ selāva kañcanaṃ’ means like gold that has come out of the rock, having the nature of essence extracted from the non-essential; the connection is that “gods also pay homage to that Blessed One.”
261:
That Nāga (the Buddha) is indeed exceedingly radiant; he certainly does not commit evil (āguṃ) and does not go to a new existence; he is endowed with strength like a Nāga (noble elephant). The Fully Enlightened One, who has received the name ‘Nāga’, is ‘accaruci’ (exceedingly radiant), meaning he shines and is beautiful, surpassing the world with its gods through his physical radiance and the radiance of his wisdom. How? Just as the Himalaya, the king of mountains, surpasses other mountains with its qualities such as being firm, heavy, and having great essence, so he surpasses them—this is the meaning. He surpasses all those named ‘Nāga’, such as serpent-nāgas, elephant-nāgas, and man-nāgas, or the Nāgas who are learners (sekha), non-learners (asekha), and Paccekabuddhas. ‘Saccanāmo’ means he is named Nāga in truth. He himself will explain that truth of being named Nāga with the words “He does no evil,” etc.

Now, wishing to show the Buddha-Nāga by way of his limbs, he first shows him by name, saying, “That Nāga does no evil.” Because he does not commit any evil (āguṃ) or sin at all, he is called ‘Nāga’. ‘Soracca’ means virtue (sīla). ‘Avihiṃsā’ means compassion (karuṇā). Since these two are the precursors of the entire mass of qualities, they are appropriate as the two front feet of the Buddha-Nāga; thus he said, “Those two are the feet of the Nāga.”

Wishing to speak of the back feet, he said, “Mindfulness and clear comprehension are the other (back) feet of that Nāga.” There is also a variant reading ‘tyāpare’. The word division is ‘te apare’. Because faith (saddhā) is the trunk (hand) of this Nāga in taking up blameless dhammas, he is called ‘one with the trunk of faith’. Because the very pure feeling and equanimity (upekkhā) consisting of various types of knowledge are the white tusks of this Nāga, he is called ‘one with the white tusks of equanimity’.

Wisdom (paññā) is the head; the basis of that wisdom is mindfulness; thus he said, “Mindfulness is the neck, wisdom is the head.” ‘Vīmaṃsā’ means the investigation of dhammas. Just as the investigation of an elephant-nāga consists of touching and smelling with its trunk what should or should not be eaten, so the investigation of the Buddha-Nāga is the contemplation of dhammas such as wholesome states. Because they dwell here in harmony, it is called ‘samāvāsa’ (dwelling in harmony); the belly, being the container, is the ‘samāvāsa’. Because it is the basis for higher knowledge and tranquility, the Dhamma known as tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) dwells in harmony in the belly of this Nāga; thus he is called ‘one with the Dhamma-belly-dwelling’ (dhammakucchisamāvāsa). ‘Viveka’ means the seclusion from the substrata of existence (upadhi-viveka). Because it is the final part of that Buddha-Nāga, seclusion is called the tail.

‘Jhāyī’ means one who habitually meditates by way of object-scrutinizing meditation (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna). ‘Assāsarato’ means delighting in Nibbāna, which is the supreme relief. “Well-concentrated within himself” means...
262:
To show that such composure, being well-concentrated in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) which is the object, is well-concentrated at all times, it is said: "The elephant, while walking, is composed," and so forth. Indeed, because the Blessed One has abandoned restlessness (uddhacca) along with its latent tendencies (vāsana) and is free from distraction, he is always composed. Therefore, whatever posture he adopts, it should be understood that he adopts that posture only with composure.

"Sabbattha" (everywhere) means having a closed conduct in every sense-object and in every sense-door in every way. Therefore, it is said: "All bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge," and so forth. "Esā nāgassa sampadā" (This is the elephant's accomplishment) means the accomplishment of the Buddha-elephant, which is full of virtues, as already mentioned or to be mentioned in such phrases as "He does no wrong" and "The Fully Enlightened One."

"Bhuñjati anavajjāni" (He eats blameless things) means that because he has reached the supreme perfection of Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva), he partakes of alms-food and meals that are not to be censured. Having completely abandoned wrong livelihood along with its latent tendencies, he does not partake of blameworthy or censurable food, but partakes only of blameless food. In partaking thus, the connection is that he eats while avoiding hoarding (sannidhi).

"Saṃyojanaṃ" (Fetter) refers to the ten kinds of fetters capable of causing one to sink in the round of rebirths, because they bind the continuity of beings to the suffering of the round. "Aṇuṃ thūlaṃ" (Small and large) means small and great. "Sabbaṃ chetvāna bandhanaṃ" (Having cut all bonds) means having cut the bond of defilements (kilesa) without remainder through the Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). "Yena yena" (By whichever) means by whichever direction or region.

For example, just as a white lotus born in the water grows in the water but is not smeared by the water due to its nature of being unsmeared, even so, the Buddha, though born in the world and dwelling in the world, is not smeared by the world because of the absence of the smears of craving (taṇhā), wrong view (diṭṭhi), and conceit (māna).

"Gini" means fire. "Anāhāro" means fire without fuel.

"Atthassāyaṃ viññāpanī" (This is an explanation of the meaning) refers to this simile of the elephant which makes clear and reveals the meaning of the object of comparison, which is the virtue of the Teacher. "Viññūhi" (By the wise) refers to those who discern the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths realized by the Teacher, spoken with reference to himself. The phrase "Viññissanti" (They will understand) and so forth is the statement of reason. The meaning is: "Because the Great Elephants, the taintless ones (khīṇāsava), established in their own domain of knowledge, will understand the Great Elephant, the Tathāgata, as taught by me, the Elephant; therefore, I have spoken this simile for the purpose of making it known to other worldlings (puthujjana)."
263:
"Sarīraṃ vijahaṃ nāgo, parinibbissatyanāsavo" means that the Great Elephant, the Fully Enlightened One, who became taintless through the Nibbāna with fuel remaining (saupādisesa-parinibbāna) at the foot of the Bodhi tree, will now, while relinquishing the body and the individual existence, attain parinibbāna through the Nibbāna without fuel remaining (khandha-parinibbāna).

Thus, adorning with fourteen similes, praising the virtues of the Teacher with sixteen verses and sixty-four lines (pādas), he concluded the teaching with the Nibbāna element without fuel remaining (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Udāyī is finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of Sixteens is finished.
